title: ‘She never forgot where she came from’: Bonnie Tyler mourners turn out for Swansea service | Bonnie Tyler | The Guardian
description: Many in the crowd watching on screen outside minster have stories of meeting or knowing singer, who died in July
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Many in the crowd watching on screen outside minster have stories of meeting or knowing singer, who died in July
Content: A floral arrangement spells out the singer’s name outside Swansea Minster.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA floral arrangement spells out the singer’s name outside Swansea Minster.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianBonnie Tyler‘She never forgot where she came from’: Bonnie Tyler mourners turn out for Swansea serviceMany in the crowd watching on screen outside minster have stories of meeting or knowing singer, who died in JulyBethan McKernanWales correspondentMon 17 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBonnie Tyler’s songs have echoed through her home town of Swansea in recent days in memory of the late singer, but on Monday the church bells stopped and wellwishers lining the streets fell silent as her coffin arrived for a service celebrating her life.As the white coffin, covered in bouquets of white roses, was carried into the minster, shouts of “God bless you Bonnie” and “bye Bonnie” punctured the quiet. Those gathered to pay their respects burst into applause. Tyler’s If I Sing You a Love Song and It’s a Heartache played before the private service began, which mourners outside watched on a screen in nearby St David’s Square.View image in fullscreenThe service was broadcast in St David’s Square.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianTheTotal Eclipse of the Heartsinger, whose real name was Gaynor Hopkins, split her time between Mumbles, in a house overlooking Swansea Bay, and the Algarve. She died aged 75 in July in hospital in Portugal after a period of ill health and is survived by her husband of 53 years, Robert Sullivan.The couple were well known in the area, and many people the Guardian spoke to on Monday had met Tyler or knew her personally. Mourners began arriving from 7.30am for the noon service, bringing camping chairs and supplies, with some having travelled from as far away as Germany and Austria.“We went to a few parties at the Mumbles house, they were wonderful. There was karaoke, performances,” said Allyson Thomas, 58, whose partner played in a band with Tyler’s brother. “As we got in the taxi home, Bonnie handed us some champagne for the journey home. She was really special, she was so down to earth and a star at the same time.”View image in fullscreenAllyson Thomas (left) with friends.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianTyler grew up as one of six children in a musical family in a council house in Skewen, a village north-east ofSwansea. A “painfully shy” teenager, she started gaining confidence at 17 after singing and coming second in a local rugby club talent competition. “After that, she never looked back,” Roger Bell, the talent scout who discovered the singer, said in his tribute during Monday’s service.Sandra Bartlett, 63, from nearby Port Talbot, said she knew Sullivan during his days as a Swansea nightclub manager, and her ex-husband had been friendly with the couple. “We went out to the first house she had in Portugal and they were great hosts,” she said.“Gaynor was lovely, always ready for a chat or a gossip. She went from strength to strength as she got older, she was still performing a lot. I think it says a lot about her that she came home to Skewen. It’s not like she was from a big place like London or something. Now Bobby’s brought her home for the last time.”View image in fullscreenThe Cash family: Bill, Billy and Jane.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianThe Cash family said they had met Tyler a few times in Swansea’s shopping centre and Debenhams, when the singer was out with her mother. “She never forgot where she came from and she was proud of where she’s from,” said Bill, 50, who had come to pay his respects with his wife, Jane, 49, and son Billy, 11.Among several events in and around Swansea to mark Tyler’s passing, fans were invited to watch the procession as the singer’s coffin, wrapped in a Welsh flag, travelled to her home in Mumbles on Saturday, and again after the service at Swansea Minster as the hearse made its final journey to Tyler’s home village of Skewen.One onlooker in Skewen said: “I wouldn’t come out for the king. Half the people here wouldn’t.”View image in fullscreenThe coffin at Swansea Minster.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianThe singer achieved international fame in 1983 when Total Eclipse of the Heart shot to the top of the charts in the UK and the US. Recognisable for her husky voice, Tyler’s other hits include Holding Out for a Hero, It’s a Heartache and If You Were a Woman (and I Was a Man).She represented the UK in the 2013 Eurovision song contest and was still touring internationally, releasing records and active in charity work before she died.View image in fullscreenBonnie Tyler in 2013.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian“I class myself as a working-class girl, and I’ve never stopped working,” Tylertold the Guardian in 2013. “I do an awful lot [of performances] because I feel other people would love to be offered what I’m offered.”Ki Wodehouse, 26, from Clydach, said: “Bonnie was an amazing ambassador forWales. Wales gets forgotten about even in the rest of the UK, so for someone from here to get that level of recognition is a rare thing.”Explore more on these topicsBonnie TylerSwanseaWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Would you tell strangers how much debt you have? The people sharing how much money they owe online | Well actually | The Guardian
description: In an era of transparency, people are detailing their financial struggles on the internet, breaking one of the last social taboos
Author: Clover Hope
Headline: In an era of transparency, people are detailing their financial struggles on the internet, breaking one of the last social taboos
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesWell actuallyWould you tell strangers how much debt you have? The people sharing how much money they owe onlineIn an era of transparency, people are detailing their financial struggles on the internet, breaking one of the last social taboosClover HopeMon 17 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiscussions regarding personal finances have traditionally been taboo. But gen Z and millennials in the US are finallynormalizing conversationsabout money, openly sharing about salaries, rent and investment strategies, but also their (sometimes substantial) debt.In recent years, financial influencers (finfluencers) – some licensed professionals, others not – have gained visibility, sharing advice on once-covert, perhaps unsexy topics such as Roth IRA contributions, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and maxing out 401(k)s. The most popular have a big audience: for instance,Humphrey Yang, a former financial adviser, has more than 2 million YouTube subscribers, andErika Kullberg, an attorney and financial expert, has more than 20 million followers across social media.Americans seem eager for guidance on money. In a small 2025Gallup survey, 20% of respondents said they sought financial advice on social media, and half of those individuals followed finfluencers. Debt content, in particular, resonates, especially with the US wealth gap reachingits widestin more than 30 years. A Federal Reservereportin May found that credit card debt among US households reached an all-time high in 2025. Credit card balances in the first quarter of 2026 rose by 5.9% compared with a year earlier, along with higher mortgage, auto loans and home equity lines of credit.Debt is uniquely steeped in emotion; those carrying excessive amounts are presumed to be careless, financially irresponsible or undisciplined. “People don’t talk about it, so that sets up a kind of container for shame,” says Thomas Faupl, a San Francisco-based psychotherapist who specializes infinancial therapy. “If somebody’s … getting into debt, there’s this part of people that starts beating themselves up.”Master your money: 11 experts share hard-earned tips to budget, invest and retire earlyRead moreFinancial analysts have long recognized that debt is not just an individual issue but the result of multiple factors, including economic policies, systemic gaps and financial illiteracy. In the US, individuals bear the consequences of unpaid debt, including the risk of bankruptcy and imprisonment. In their 2024 book The Political Development of American Debt Relief, Emily Zackin and Chloe N Thurston frame debt as an inevitable byproduct of US sociopolitical structures and economic policies that disproportionately favor creditors, emphasizing that “when people are expected to meet their basic needs by borrowing, access to debt relief and the terms of that access are especially important”.So why does debt still feel like such a personal failing?“As Americans, we associate our net worth with our self-worth,” says Tori Dunlap, a New York Timesbestselling author and host of the podcast Financial Feminist, which aims to destigmatize debt. “The average American, in order to uplevel their life, has to take on debt, whether it’s to get a college degree, buy a home or start a business. Then, of course, we feel bad about it, but that’s the only way forward for a lot of us.”Earlier this year, I noticed a childhood friend, Erica Grace Martin, posting about her goal to pay off $164,000 in debt in 18 months. I was immediately intrigued when I saw that she was sharing daily updates with her 7,000-plus followers across Instagram and TikTok. For many, publicly documenting debt in real time helps ease feelings of guilt. Sharing about the experience, they say, keeps them on track financially. Some also monetize this content, using the income to pay down their debt.I spoke to Martin and several others who have shared their debt journeys online.Erica Grace Martin, 43View image in fullscreenErica Grace Martin.Photograph: Anthony Mitchell / @MortimerVisuals/Courtesy of Erica Grace MartinIn February, Martin, a VP of legal at an entertainment company, started posting about her debt. She had been divorced for two years and was managing a formerly two-income household alone: the three-bedroom, two-bath apartment in Manhattan’s Hell’s Kitchen that she and her husband once shared with their two children, now nine and six. Even with a six-figure salary, she struggled to cover monthly bills, including $4,000 for a nanny, $3,000 for Uber trips and $7,500 in rent.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Martin didn’t feel she was overspending, but expenses kept mounting. “I’m like, what did I buy? What am I spending? What’s happening?” she says. “I have the income.” She ended up putting her credit card on a payment plan, taking out a personal loan and opening a home equity line of credit on the property she owns in Queens, which she rents to tenants.When her Hell’s Kitchen rent went up by $1,000, she consulted two financial advisers and ChatGPT, which she can now laugh about. “I looked at the numbers, and I’m like, ‘You can’t do this,’” she says. To save money, she and her kids moved back into her childhood home, where her mother still lived. “It was like packing up my apartment and packing up my ego too with it.”That same month, Martin made her Instagram account public and posted a video titled “DAY 1: WELCOME TO ERICA’S DEBT TAKEDOWN JOURNEY.” Her posts included screenshots from a budgeting app: $33,575.63 in credit card debt, more than $78,000 in personal loans and $17,193.73 on her Bilt credit card, which, unlike other credit cards, offers rewards points on mortgage and rent payments.‘It’s not just for old rich people’: the case for making your estate plan nowRead more“I was so afraid. I did not intend to be posting every day,” she says. But she wanted to hold herself accountable.Then came an outpouring of support. One commenter wrote: “This level of transparency and relatability deserves all the respect … You doing this for you is pushing people to reevaluate it for themselves too.” One popular post – in which she tears up while celebrating paying off her credit card on day 66 – has more than 11,000 views on TikTok.There was criticism, too: why put her bills on autopay if her bank balance was low? Why didn’t she know the amortization schedule for her mortgage? One commenter accused her of discouraging Black people from buying homes.“I’m looking at these comments like, why do you feel so strongly about this?” she says.Yet she also gets it. “Seeing other people’s decisions makes you question yours. People don’t want to say, ‘I have a spending problem,’ because they don’t want to be judged,” she says. “Whether it’s good or bad, there’s judgment. So I was like, I’m gonna expose myself and get transparent and naked with it, and just deal with what comes.”Martin paid off $60,000 of her debt within 70 days. People she knew called her crying, thanking her for saving them from bleeding cash or filing for bankruptcy. “I think people like seeing a real person talk through something in real time,” she says. “There’s a difference between that and some white guy in a suit who’s like, ‘Do this and do that.’”Christian Juhl, 26View image in fullscreenChristian Juhl.Photograph: Courtesy of Christian JuhlAfter graduating four years ago, Christian Juhl accumulated $80,000 in debt, split between car payments, student loans and credit cards. During a trip to Iceland in 2023, he charged $6,000 to his credit card. When his car’s transmission blew, he put $5,000 in repairs on credit.“I honestly was just never taught how to use credit cards properly,” he says. “I started traveling and was like, Oh, you’re supposed to put [travel expenses] on your credit card for points.”Last May, Juhl moved from Phoenix to Los Angeles to pursue acting full-time while working as a server. Seeing content creators post about their debt online inspired him. In January, he started posting and set a goal to pay off $80,000 by the end of 2026. “Or I was gonna embarrass myself severely trying,” he jokes. In a debt breakdown video posted in June, he revealed that one of his credit cards carried $13,084.54 in debt; he’s since shared updates with more than 28,000 Instagram followers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe admits to living beyond his means. The monthly rent for his centrally located Hollywood apartment is $2,800, and he puts down $1,300 a month in minimum credit card payments. “Our entire lives, we’re told we need to go to college because we need to get the job we want. And on top of that, every single thing around us is constantly selling us things,” he says. “We’re such a consumeristic society that I think it’s interesting that we’re ashamed of going into debt.”There’s an obvious liability issue when posting about financial topics: viewers possibly confusing content creators with licensed financial advisers. (City and state government siteshave sharedwarningsabout trusting finfluencers.) There’s also potential for bad actors to give poor advice or promote dubious financial products online for the sake of brand deals.The people I spoke to say they include regular disclaimers on their posts, stating that they’re just sharing what works for them and aren’t licensed experts. “I’m not a coach, but I think it’s important to share what you’re learning because people come to learn or laugh or both,” says Juhl. “I can’t be hard on myself because I am doing the right things. I’m watching what I’m spending. I cut back on so much.”Even if he misses his goal, Juhl says he enjoys the community and accountability. “I really want to see it through, so that I can actually pursue what I want to do full-time without having to be weighed down,” he says. “The payoff has been difficult. But the pressure, the nerves and the fear have been helpful in the grand scheme of things.”What about those who can’t hit their payoff goal and end up feeling worse than when they started?Faupl believes the people who choose to share their debt online are risking privacy – ie, their personal finances becoming searchable – and future employment, or even relapse. “A certain percentage of people who are carrying a large amount of debt repeat that experience,” he says. “It’s fine to share information. But when people get into repetitive cycles of debt, they’re not addressing the trauma or the compulsive behavior.”Becca Droz and Nikki Nichols, 36 and 32View image in fullscreenBecca Droz and Nikki Nichols.Photograph: Courtesy of Becca Droz and Nikki NicholsOn Ramit Sethi’s podcast, Money For Couples, the New York Times bestselling author digs into guests’ family histories and trauma around money, performing a meticulous autopsy of their income, expenses, debt, investments and spending habits. Some couples report hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt.Predictably, comments on these episodes skew judgmental. Depending on each couple’s unique circumstances, YouTube reactions vary: from fair (“They don’t lack intelligence, they lack discipline”) to astonished (“My jaw is on the floor at him staying quiet about the debt while she shopped for a fifty-thousand-dollar car”) or scathing (“I never understand going into debt for a wedding, it’s the fucking dumbest thing in the world”). Generally, the higher the debt, the more disparaging the remarks.‘A lot of our parents were paid by the hour’: a first-gen money coach’s blueprint for wealthRead moreBecca Droz, a rock-climbing guide based in Boulder, Colorado, applied to be on the show to get an honest financial evaluation before marrying her partner, Nikki Nichols, a dental assistant turned postpartum doula.“I like being able to hear these things nobody ever talks about – how much they make a month, what they spend it on, their net worth,” says Droz. “That these people who are making as much as we make in a year in a single month still feel that they’re not making enough money or that they’re still spending beyond their means was encouraging to me, in a way. Like, ‘Oh, we’re actually OK.’”When couples talk about money on the podcast, relationship dynamics come to the fore. “Some of the tougher stories seem like so much of a reflection of the relationship,” says Nichols. “There are moments when I’m listening that I feel frustrated, like, Oh my God, how could you?”On their August 2025episode, Nichols discussed her $18,000 in student loan debt and feeling financially incompetent. YouTube commenters praised the couple’s maturity, noting that they seemed more “equally engaged” in the process than previous guests. The responses were overwhelmingly positive.Droz found the experience affirming. “Money is the thing we think about every day, and impacts our lives in the biggest ways,” she says. “Even if it doesn’t change anything about your reality to say ‘This is how much debt I have,’ [for that] to be witnessed is very powerful and liberating.”Ice Chattroranongsak, 30View image in fullscreenIce Chattroranongsak.Photograph: Courtesy  of Ice ChattroranongsakWatsamon Chattroranongsak, a CPA based in central Los Angeles who goes by the nickname Ice, also embarked on her journey after seeing other content creators post about their debt online. “I was carrying a lot of shame,” she says. “With friends, we don’t sit and talk about how much debt you’re in or what you put in your 401(k). There’s a lot of pressure to be the best version of yourself to people around you.”Like many others, she treated debt payoff as a personal challenge, posting an Instagram video in which she pledged to pay off $35,000 in credit card and student loan debt. She has since paid off $30,000 of her debt. “Even though you get negative comments, you’re still going to be working toward that goal,” she says. “There’s so much more positive that comes out of that.”Whether in private or in front of faceless people online, Faupl says individuals should, at some point, address unresolved trauma related to money. “If people don’t address the trauma, they’re going to be stuck in that cycle and talking about their debt a lot,” he says, pointing out that resources like Debtors Anonymous have been available for decades. “That’s why programs have steps. Part of it is sharing. Part of it is digging deep, and the other part is the action phase. We need to internally interrogate, have some resolution, and then go back and build that literacy muscle.”Sharing financial struggles with strangers online felt somehow less intimidating to Chattroranongsak than facing judgment from family members. “I used to fear people close to me finding out,” she says. “I told them, ‘If you see my account, don’t comment on anything. Just leave it.’ I wanted to work towards this goal without having voices that would stop me. I’m just doing an experiment for myself.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyUS personal financeDebt reliefUS work & careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My generation had no voice on Brexit – but Burnham gives the young fresh hope | Ceira Sergeant | The Guardian
description: Brexit didn’t create all the problems young people now face, but renewing close ties with Europe will give us so many opportunities, says student and activist Ceira Sergeant
Author: Ceira Sergeant
Headline: Brexit didn’t create all the problems young people now face, but renewing close ties with Europe will give us so many opportunities, says student and activist Ceira Sergeant
Content: The National Rejoin March in London, 20 June 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe National Rejoin March in London, 20 June 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesOpinionBrexitMy generation had no voice on Brexit – but Burnham gives the young fresh hopeCeira SergeantBrexit didn’t create all the problems young people now face, but renewing close ties with Europe will give us so many opportunitiesMon 17 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTShareI was 14 when the UK voted to leave the EU. Too young to vote, but not too young to understand that a decision was being made that would affect the rest of my life.In many ways,Brexitwas my political awakening. It taught me that politics matters, because decisions made by people in power can change your future before you’ve even been given a say.Ten years later, my generation is living with that decision. We lost the automatic right to live, work and study freely across 27 other countries. Opportunities previous generations took for granted are now more complicated, more expensive or completely out of reach. But with a new prime minister who has a recorded history of stating thatwe should rejoin the EU, perhaps we can start to hope.If you have money, many of these barriers can be overcome. You are better able to cope with the extra costs, paperwork and bureaucracy involved in moving abroad. Someone from a wealthy family can afford more expensive routes to studying or living overseas. But what about everyone else?Freedom of movement wasn’t just a nice perk for people who could already afford to travel. For working-class young people like me, it meant opportunity. It was the possibility of studying in Paris, working in Berlin, or falling in love in Barcelona and building a life there. It was about experiencing different cultures, learning languages and feeling part of something bigger.Young people are already facing a difficult economic future. Housing is increasingly unaffordable, wages haven’t kept pace with costs and many of us wonder whether we’ll ever have the security our parents got to enjoy. The median income for those aged 25 and under hasnot increased for two decades. We are becoming the first generation in modern times to seriously contemplate having less than our parents.Brexit didn’t create all of these problems. But putting up economic barriers against our largest neighbouring market certainly hasn’t helped. We were told Brexit would create opportunities. For many working-class young people, it did the opposite. I think often of my friend: a British citizen who married a German, only to face endless challenges just so they could live together. And countless young people in creative industries have had theircareers stifledthrough lack of access to the continent.This is why Andy Burnham’s approach toEuropeis so important.The prime minister must start removing some of the walls Brexit put up. Make it easier for young people to study and work in Europe, restore opportunities for musicians, artists and young creatives, and make sure those opportunities aren’t reserved for people wealthy enough to pay their way around the obstacles.But closer ties aren’t enough. My generation wants theUK to rejoin the EU. So my message to Burnham is simple: be brave.Don’t become another prime minister whose time in office is cut short trying to find another way to make Brexit work. My generation didn’t get a vote last time. Give us one now and I believe we’ll vote for our future in Europe. And this time, give 16- and 17-year-olds a vote too. If they’re old enough to live with the consequences of a decision for the rest of their lives, they’re old enough to have a say in it.We young people have grown up connected to the rest of Europe and the world. We don’t see someone in France, Germany, Poland or Spain as being on the other side of some great divide. They’re our friends, colleagues and partners.Politicians worry about young people becoming disengaged from politics. Perhaps they should ask why.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionImagine being told at 14 you’re too young to have a say in one of the biggest political decisions in generations, then spending your 20s living with the consequences, while politicians tell you reversing it is impossible or can’t even be discussed. Is it any wonder many people have stopped believing politics can change anything?That is the test for Burnham’s government. Don’t just tell young people you understand and pat us on the head. Give us a voice and hear us.In June 2027, the National Rejoin March will return to London. Every host and rally speaker will belong to the generation that was too young to vote in 2016. We were the silenced generation. For 10 years, we’ve heard what those who voted in 2016 wanted. It’s time to hear from those who couldn’t vote then.We can’t change the fact that we didn’t have a voice in 2016. But we’re adults now. We can vote. We can march. And we can demand something better. We don’t intend to stay silent.Ceira Sergeant is a student and the founder of National Rejoin March YouthExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionYoung peopleEuropean UnionForeign policyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Hayden Panettiere: an actor so magnetic that entire shows were rewritten for her | Television | The Guardian
description: She starred in her first soap opera at 4 – then the hit show Heroes was totally reworked to allow her character, Claire the regenerating cheerleader, to live on. We celebrate the star, who has died age 36
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: She starred in her first soap opera at 4 – then the hit show Heroes was totally reworked to allow her character, Claire the regenerating cheerleader, to live on. We celebrate the star, who has died age 36
Content: ‘She was more than an actress – she was a muse’ … Hayden Panettiere in Heroes.Photograph: Nbc/Universal Tv/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘She was more than an actress – she was a muse’ … Hayden Panettiere in Heroes.Photograph: Nbc/Universal Tv/Kobal/ShutterstockTelevisionHayden Panettiere: an actor so magnetic that entire shows were rewritten for herShe starred in her first soap opera at 4 – then the hit show Heroes was totally reworked to allow her character, Claire the regenerating cheerleader, to live on. We celebrate the star, whohas died age 36Hayden Panettiere – a life in picturesHayden Panettiere obituaryZoe WilliamsMon 17 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Hayden Panettiere arrived as Claire Bennet in Heroes, in 2006, she was 17 but not a newcomer. She’d starred in Tiger Cruise, a Disney Channel movie, two years before and was the pin-perfect image of that teen-star world – blond, cute, perky, resourceful and all-American. Bennet the superhero was all those things, amped up to the point of fascinating distortion. She was a cheerleader who could endlessly regenerate. It was a topic of hot debate on fan sites whether or not she could feel pain, a question that was resolved piecemeal through the series. She could, but could instantly overcome it with her superpower – that fact partly informed the view of one academic, professor Olvido Andújar Molina, that Bennet was standing in for the American dream, its core components being strength, resilience and a sweet-natured homeliness.In Tiger Cruise, Panettiere had filled a similar role, the cute-as-a-button daughter of a naval commander, producing this elemental, almost mournful Oz-like message: “Everything you long for is right here at home.” She was from a showbiz family, her mother, Lesley Vogel, was a soap actor, and her brother, Jansen, who also possessed those perfectly symmetrical features, co-starred in Tiger Cruise, and later, in 2011, in The Forger (better known as the last film Lauren Bacall ever made). Jansen also died horribly young, of complications from an engorged heart, in 2023 aged 28. Panettiere got her first soap opera gig, in One Life to Live, at the age of four, and went on to a recurring role into Guiding Light before she was 10. She was the voice of Dot in A Bug’s Life, and was nominated for a Grammy for her work on the film.View image in fullscreenPin-perfect image of the teen star … Hayden Panettiere with Bill Pullman in Tiger Cruise.Photograph: Disney/AllstarPerhaps because of how the cheerleader role landed on the collective imagination, and certainly because of Panettiere’s performance, which had a magnetic complexity that always seemed at odds with how appealing she was, Bennet came to define Heroes. The showrunners originally intended to refresh the superheroes each series, to create a giant stable of ridiculously capable archetypes. In the end, bowing to audience preference, they wrote Panettiere into all six seasons. At one fan convention, Panettiere addressed how she was funnelled towards certain roles by her inescapably wholesome good looks: “People look at me as either the popular cheerleader type or just the blond.”When Heroes ended in 2010, perhaps trying to branch out, she took the lead role in Amanda Knox: Murder on Trial in Italy, an ill-conceived and poorly received project. But in 2012, a role came along in Nashville, which was perfect for her. As Juliette Barnes, a young country singer in a hurry, Panettiere embodied that bubble gum country music trope, the Dolly-Parton-beautiful singer on to whom a nation projects all its fantasies – of sweetness and innocence, of pluck. That ran for six seasons, and viewers lapped it up, with its excesses of plot and heartache and intrigue, especially in the first two seasons.View image in fullscreen‘Dolly-Parton-beautiful’ … Hayden Panettiere as Juliette Barnes in Nashville.Photograph: ABC/AllstarDespite her on-screen success, Panettiere’s personal life was turbulent; after the birth of her daughter in 2014, she suffered postnatal depression. She separated from her fiance, the boxer Wladimir Klitschko, in 2018, relinquishing custody of their child to him the same year. Her relationship with her next boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was marred by domestic abuse allegations and Hickerson was arrested multiple times. In 2021, he was reportedly jailed after pleading no contest to domestic abuse charges. Unsurprisingly, she did very little work during this period. Bryan Fuller, a writer on Heroes, said in tribute that “she was more than an actress, she was a muse”. Such a patriarchally freighted remark, though clearly well meant, gestures at the challenges Panettiere faced, trying to create work while embodying so many people’s fantasies of girlhood; but they were challenges she met, and exceeded.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Next year’s Eurovision host is Burgas, not Sofia. Some Bulgarians are baffled | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Next year’s competition won’t take place in the country’s capital, an announcement that even surprised Bulgarian winner, Dara
Author: Eden Maclachlan
Headline: Next year’s competition won’t take place in the country’s capital, an announcement that even surprised Bulgarian winner, Dara
Content: All systems go … Burgas flies the flag for Bulgaria’s Eurovision Song Contest.Photograph: Valentina Petrova/APView image in fullscreenAll systems go … Burgas flies the flag for Bulgaria’s Eurovision Song Contest.Photograph: Valentina Petrova/APEurovisionNext year’s Eurovision host is Burgas, not Sofia. Some Bulgarians are baffledNext year’s competition won’t take place in the country’s capital, an announcement that even surprised Bulgarian winner, DaraEden Maclachlanin SofiaMon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver since Bulgarian singer Dara was crownedwinner of the Eurovision song contest this May, it has been clear that the Balkan nation would for the first time in its history have the opportunity to host Europe’s biggest party.So when Bulgarian officialsannounced last weekthat the world’s largest live music event in 2027 will be held not in the capital Sofia but in Burgas, a Black Sea port city home to 200,000 people, it came as a surprise – even to last year’s winner.“I am really surprised,” singer Dara told the Guardian. “I think that BNT [Bulgarian National Television] will do a great job at producing the whole show. I trust them completely. If they decided Burgas, then probably Burgas is better.”This spring in Vienna, Dara became the first Bulgarian to win Eurovision with her high energy party anthemBangaranga, in an edition boycotted byIreland, Spain, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Icelandover Israel’s participation.Following her victory, Bulgaria’s four largest cities, Sofia, Plovdiv, Dara’s home town of Varna and Burgas sent an application with only Sofia and Burgas left as possible candidates in recent weeks. As the country’s capital and international hub, Sofia always seemed the obvious choice.View image in fullscreen‘If they decided Burgas, then Burgas is probably better’ … Eurovision winner Dara.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe preference for Burgas, Bulgaria’s fourth largest city, has been heavily discussed across the Balkan country of 6.5 million people, with many taken aback.“We were surprised, because Sofia has the biggest arena,” said Pavel Stefanov, 29, an air traffic controller at Sofia airport.Milena Ouzounova, 54, a designer from Sofia said she was surprised and disappointed that the capital wasn’t chosen as host city and was sceptical over Burgas’ capacity to pull off such an event.“I’m disappointed,” she said. “I think Sofia is a better place, it is bigger, we have a big arena. Burgas is a nice place but I am not sure it could be prepared enough after one year. I think the space is much smaller in Burgas.”View image in fullscreenDiffering views … Katrin Ninova, left, is relieved Sofia will avoid Eurovision mayhem, while Milena Ouzounova, right, thinks it would be better in Sofia, as the city is bigger.Composite: Eden MaclachlanLocated on the southern Black Sea coast, approximately 400km east of Sofia, Burgas is closer in distance to Istanbul than the Bulgarian capital.Nestled among three lakes and the Black Sea, it has an established tourism industry and is a popular seaside destination among Bulgarian and international tourists. Meanwhile, it is home to Bulgaria’s second largest port and the largest oil refinery in southernEurope, accounting for a considerable chunk of the city’s industrial production.Earlier this year, it hosted the arrival of the first stage of the 2026 Giro d’Italia, the Italian equivalent to the Tour de France, and hosting Eurovision will most likely boost Burgas candidacy forEuropean Capital of Culture in 2032.Preparations to host the Eurovision grand final have already started aroundArena Burgas, the 15,000 concert capacity hall completed in 2023 which will have the herculean task of throwing Europe’s favourite party, while the city’s airport said it is ready to welcome the increased passenger flow for Eurovision 2027.The accompanyingEurovisionevents will be in the centre of Burgas and the Sea Garden, the city’s biggest public park directly facing the Black Sea, where locals usually gather to hang out or have a drink.View image in fullscreenReady to welcome big audiences … port view, Burgas.Photograph: Valentina Petrova/APHowever, it isn’t the smallest city to ever arrange Eurovision, still considerably bigger than Harrogate, which hosted it in 1982 following Bucks Fizz’s victory.The Eurovision final will take place on 15 May, with the semi-finals on 11 and 13 May and will have Canada participating for the first time. Meanwhile new rules will be implemented such as increasing the minimum participation age from 16 to 18 and potentially barring countries involved in armed conflicts from hosting.Many in Bulgaria believe this to be the perfect opportunity to showcase the beauty of the Bulgarian coast and boost tourism, while others are thankful it won’t be organised in Sofia.Dimitar Nikolov, mayor of Burgas, said he was honoured that Burgas was chosen and thanked BNT and the EBU [European Broadcasting Union] “for the unique chance to present the beauties of Bulgaria and, through Burgas, to all the guests and fans who will follow the live broadcast to feel Bulgaria.”Prime ministerRumen Radevtold local reporters that he believed Burgas will succeed in representing Bulgaria with dignity.“I think that every Bulgarian city has something to offer both in terms of culture and history, especially in terms of people and modern services. So let’s present ourselves with dignity. I think that Burgas is a really good choice,” he said.Katrin Ninova, 20, a data science student at the Sofia University said she was relieved that Sofia will avoid Eurovision mayhem. “It’s crowded enough here. We don’t need to organise Eurovision,” she said.Evtim Vodenicharov, 32, a data manager from Burgas said he was thrilled that his home town would be organising the event and believed that it will boost the region’s economy and tourism. Meanwhile, he hopes to attend next year’s Eurovision in the arena.“Of course I’m excited,” said Vodenicharov. “I hope I will be able to get a ticket and go watch it live instead of being at home and watching it on TV. It’s in my home town.”Meanwhile Dara urged visitors who will attend Eurovision to take the opportunity to visit Bulgaria, the Black Sea coast and discover the unique culture of the Balkan country.“We should look at all of the positive sides. I think people should go to the seaside and all around Burgas, there are really good places,” she said.Explore more on these topicsEurovisionEurovision 2026BulgariaEuropeAwards and prizesPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had to learn how to be a feminist’: Greg Dulli on surviving grunge, shunning misogyny, and Afghan Whigs’ glorious return | Music | The Guardian
description: With a soulful sound and soul-baring lyrics, the Afghan Whigs rode the post-Nirvana boom to the big leagues. Their frontman explains his exploration of the male ego – and how Usher got the band back together
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: With a soulful sound and soul-baring lyrics, the Afghan Whigs rode the post-Nirvana boom to the big leagues. Their frontman explains his exploration of the male ego – and how Usher got the band back together
Content: ‘Life is about adapting, continuing on’ … Afghan Whigs.Photograph: Orlando PerkinsView image in fullscreen‘Life is about adapting, continuing on’ … Afghan Whigs.Photograph: Orlando PerkinsMusicInterview‘I had to learn how to be a feminist’: Greg Dulli on surviving grunge, shunning misogyny, and Afghan Whigs’ glorious returnStevie ChickWith a soulful sound and soul-baring lyrics, the Afghan Whigs rode the post-Nirvana boom to the big leagues. Their frontman explains his exploration of the male ego – and how Usher got the band back togetherMon 17 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Afghan Whigs were always heavier than their grunge-era brethren. Not musically – their turbulent, sophisticated rock was rooted in soul and funk, and frontman Greg Dulli says the group only embraced distortion in order to be heard over the volume of metalhead drummer Steve Earle’s playing. “Any kind of jangle wasn’t gonna work.” But Dulli’s lyrics, inspired by the likes of Motown bards Holland/Dozier/Holland, were pitch-black, depicting lovers in co-dependent cycles of betrayal and recrimination. Afghan Whigs songs take place in a world where sin is irresistible, punishment inevitable and some kind of judgment inescapable.“My songs acknowledgeconsequence, more than they deal in judgment,” Dulli says, between sips of water in the bar of a London hotel. Forty years on from their formation, the Whigs are resurgent. Their new album, Soft Control, ably holds its own with earlier dark masterpieces such as their 1993 breakthrough Gentlemen, and its bleakly funky conceptual follow-up, 1996’s Black Love – records that affirmed their frontman as alt-rock’s poet of arch romantic dysfunction. “I understood sorrow and loss and loneliness from an early age,” he says. His dad was the youngest of 14; several of Dulli’s uncles died when he was young. “I had been there, so why wouldn’t I explore it?”View image in fullscreen‘Jangle wasn’t gonna work’ … the Afghan Whigs circa 1994: (from left) Rick McCollum, John Curley, Greg Dulli and Steve Earle.Photograph: Dave Tonge/Getty ImagesPossessed of devilish charm, Dulli was raised Catholic during a “very Huckleberry Finn childhood” in Hamilton, Ohio. “I was an altar boy,” he grins. “My attitude was, if I’m going to church, I might as well be on stage. I had a great seat, could scope out the talent. Clearly, I was into the attention.” By age 12, however, he was “asking hard questions. Like, what’s with all the kid killing? ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten son’? Not necessary. I told Mom: I’m not going to church any more, I don’t believe in it.” Dulli leers “We both know God ain’t real, baby” on one of the new album’s songs.Dulli’s dad “wasn’t around a lot”, so he was raised by his mother, grandmother and aunts. “When you’re surrounded by ladies you gotta work hard to get away with stuff, because they’re vigilant. But they were also nurturing, supportive and encouraging.” And his mum had a killer record collection: “Motown 45s and Jesus Christ Superstar,” Dulli remembers, smiling. Their influence would prove indelible, as would that of his first gig: psychedelic soulstersthe 5th Dimensionat Ohio state fair in 1973. “I developed a crush on Marilyn McCoo immediately. They did Let the Sunshine In, and her husband – Billy Davis Jr – went off on his full-on gospel lift. I was eight years old, but I washigh. Some kids want to be an astronaut or a cowboy; I always wanted to be a rock star.”He played his first gig at 14, wrote his first song at 15, and spent college in the pit for shows by Ramones, Hüsker Dü and Black Flag. Inspired, he formed the Black Republicans, whose shows were frequented by a bearded guy who regularly told him, “I’m better than your bassist.”“And hewas,” Dulli adds. The bearded guy, John Curley, asked if he and guitarist friend Rick McCollum could sit in. Soon, the Black Republicans were done, drummer Earle enlisted and the Afghan Whigs were ascendant. Their first rehearsal was Halloween 1986. “We played One Day by the Church, Psychedelic Shack by the Temptations and Powderfinger by Neil Young, and fucked around with 39 Lashes; Rick loved Jesus Christ Superstar as much as I did.”View image in fullscreenDevilish charm … Greg Dulli in 1994.Photograph: Dave Tonge/Getty ImagesWith their second album, 1990’s Up in It, the group became one of the first non-Seattle signings to the Sub Pop label – who had released Nirvana’s debut – building a buzz with their eclectic live cover versions. “We could learn them fast,” Dulli says. “Had no desire to be a covers band. But eight songs into our show and we wanna play Mandinka by Sinéad O’Connor?We would. We were onstage one night, a couple of us tripping on acid, and I told John, play the bass line to Hall & Oates’ Maneater. I started riffing on the Supremes’ My World Is Empty Without You. People freaked. We were subverting it, but still honouring it.”The Whigs wore their influences on their sleeves, particularly soul music. Further covers followed, on stage and as B-sides: Freda Payne’s Band of Gold; TLC’s Creep; the Supremes’ Come See About Me. “That song is sodesperate,” Dulli says, admiringly. “Motown songs are dark, but the music is peppy and happy. I thought, what if the music was more sympathetic to the lyrics? It darkens the song, it changes the meaning. And it’s exciting. You listen to the words, and it’s soawfulwhat’s happening to that person.”As the Whigs completed Congregation, their second album for Sub Pop, Nirvana became unlikely superstars. “Watching those dudes knock Michael Jackson off the No 1 spot … that escalated quickly,” Dulli says. When the post-Nevermind gold rush started, “our lives changed”. The group signed with Elektra, a major label. “But we weren’t worrying over if we’d be as big as Pearl Jam. We’d created our own sound.”Gentlmen was the product of Dulli’s “very stormy relationship” with a woman credited on the sleeve as Miss Ruby Belle, and whose voice had graced Congregation (her true identity has been the subject of fevered conjecture among Whigs devotees). “We were gone all the time, and nature abhors a vacuum,” he remembers. “I came back from a seven-week tour and my girlfriend had a new boyfriend, and he’d been in our bed. I asked her, ‘How dare you do this to me?’ Even though I’d done it to her all the time on tour. I was confronted with my own hypocrisy. Gentlemen became my exploration of my culpability.”The Afghan Whigs: My Lover – videoGentlemen also served as an examination of male ego, sexuality and chauvinism. “I’d grown up surrounded by women, but I come from a very patriarchal society,” he says. “Homemakers stayed home, made babies and dinner and shut the fuck up. I had to learn how to be, for lack of a better word, a feminist – to realise, there is another side to this.” The song What Jail Is Like posited fear of commitment as existential panic; Be Sweet had Dulli playing a suave lothario with “a dick for a brain”, using said brain to “sell my ass to you”. On My Curse, meanwhile, Dulli put forth “the counterpoint – I put myself in her head as best I could”, and drafted his friend, Marcy Mays of Ohio indie-rockers Scrawl, to sing its lyric of helpless, self-destructive infatuation. “I micromanaged Marcy’s performance,” Dulli remembers, “until she said: ‘I really wish you’d get the fuck out of here and let me do this by myself.’”When Dulli played his mother the record, he told me in 2004, “she couldn’t believe I still got laid”. Today, he says that midway through touring Gentlemen in 1993, he struck Be Sweet from the setlist, never to return. “It was a great lyric,” he says, but its central “dick for a brain” bon mot “became the pull-quote for every magazine story about us. I was like, ‘I’m not singing this fucking song – I don’t want to be that guy any more.’ I felt like an animal in a zoo.”The Whigs’ next album, the excellent Black Love, spun a film-noirish yarn, fulfilling “concept album ambitions” Dulli had developed since obsessing over Quadrophenia as a kid. “It is wildly misunderstood, and still one of my favourite things I’ve ever done,” he says. But the hits Elektra had been banking on never materialised. They moved to Columbia, releasing their next LP in 1998: 1965 was an open bid for mainstream success. “That was the only time I tried to write a hit song,” Dulli says. “That was our ‘the self-loathing is gone – it’sparty-time’ album. And I loved the freedom: thank God, I don’t have to be in fucking Hamlet again.”View image in fullscreen‘Mark’s for ever my brother’ … Greg Dulli and Mark Lanegan  in 2006.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThey toured with Aerosmith, “the nicest band” Dulli has ever toured with. Still, commercial success didn’t arrive. “By the end, we were three guys going in three different directions.”The Whigs parted, amicably, in 1999, Dulli pursuing his Twilight Singers project – an outlet for songs too soft for his Whigs bandmates – along with a side-gig as bar-owner (he co-owns five, with three in Los Angeles and two in New Orleans), and his Gutter Twins collaboration with best friend Mark Lanegan, which he compared in 2004 to “Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings getting together – we’re outlaws!”Then, in 2012, after Curley guested at some Twilight Singers shows, to rapturous response, they reformed. The tour was supposed to be a one-off, but Dulli found R&B superstar Usher’s invitation for the Whigs to serve as his backing band at SXSW in 2013 too hard to resist. (He told US magazine the Fader that the Whigs were one of his “favourite rock groups” and that he wanted to impress the rock-leaning crowd.) The show left Dulli and Curley energised in a way the reunion tour hadn’t. “After that show, John and I had dinner and wondered if we could make an album,” he says. Do to the Beast, the first post-reunion Whigs record, arrived the following spring and the Whigs’ proprietary blend of alt-rock and soul gravitas was as powerful as ever. They have continued ever since.View image in fullscreen‘I just love playing with a hot band’ … the Afghan Whigs performing in Los Angeles in May.Photograph: @marilynbellphoto‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againRead moreTheir fourth album since reuniting, Soft Control is darkly magnificent, the work of a 61-year-old more acquainted with mortality than he once was. The loss of Lanegan, who died in 2022 before they could record a long-mooted second Gutter Twins record, still haunts him. “Mark’s for ever my brother. It’s heartbreaking; every day, something will happen and I’ll want to text him about it. But he just isn’t there.”Religion, he said earlier in our conversation, was invented “to comfort people because they’re afraid of dying”. As our interview draws to a close, he cycles back to the subject. “People who fear death fail to realise that death is also the death of fear. But death is inevitable, and I’m accepting of it. Life is about adapting, continuing on. And ever since I was expelled from the birth canal, I’ve kept on walking, and I’m gonna just keep on going. And music has been my companion throughout, for my triumphant moments, my sad moments … my ‘I’m horny’ moments. Music is my co-pilot.”He says he might record further solo albums, but that the Whigs remain his constant. Curley is the only remaining member from the original lineup. “I love playing with John,” says Dulli. “He’s the Spock to my Kirk. I just love playing with a hot band. And the Afghan Whigs are a hot fuckin’ band.”Soft Control is released via Royal Cream/BMG on 21 August.The Afghan Whigs tour the UK, 19-26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reform’s Tice accused of misinformation after urging people to enjoy heatwaves  | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Backlash from nurses, medical experts and green campaigners in response to deputy leader dismissing efforts to reach net zero
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Backlash from nurses, medical experts and green campaigners in response to deputy leader dismissing efforts to reach net zero
Content: 1:29Not all 'doom and gloom': Reform's deputy leader downplays climate crisis – videoReform UKReform’s Tice accused of misinformation after urging people to enjoy heatwavesNurses, medical experts and green campaigners reject party deputy leader’s dismissal of efforts to reach net zeroKiran StaceyPolicy editorMon 17 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform’s deputy leader has been accused of spreading misinformation after he dismissed efforts to tackle the climate crisis and urged British people to enjoy the warmth of the recent heatwaves.Richard Tice prompted a backlash from nurses, medical experts and green campaigners on Monday after he told a press conference he believed it was “arrogant” to try to stop the climate emergency, while encouraging people to focus on upsides such as better English wine.Asked about the recent extreme heat, Tice told a press conference: “Of course, the climate changes, but where is the evidence that net zero is going to stop it? Where is the evidence? There is no evidence.“Climate change has always happened. It always will. Maybe the smarter thing to do is to adapt to it than think arrogantly that you can stop it.”He added: “When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.”Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Richard Tice’s comments are tone-deaf. With wildfires raging across the UK and drought threatening water supplies and food security, comments like these don’t just raise serious questions about his judgment – they also expose where his interests really lie.”Tice’s comments came amid a record-breaking summer during which temperatures have risen above 35C several times, causing thousands of deaths, millions of hospital visits and costing the UK an estimated £4bn in economic output.‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smokeRead moreThe governmenthas estimatedthat 2,877 people died as a result of high temperatures during the May and June heatwaves – double the figure for the whole of last summer.The climate breakdown has been linked to theincreasing frequency of wildfires, which are burning larger areas across many parts of the world. The so-calledfirewavethe UK witnessed weeks ago was the most widespread the country has seen, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.New figurespublished in the Lancet on Tuesdayreveal older people are affected by the heat at lower temperatures than previously thought, while medical professionals say they are struggling to deal with the surge in patients.A spokesperson for the Royal College of Nursing said: “Those calling for people to enjoy the impacts of climate change should say it to the nurses collapsing in hospitals where temperatures are hitting 36 degrees.“Or to the thousands of patients lining corridors every day as extreme heat causes severe illness among the vulnerable, older people and even those without pre-existing conditions.“Climate change is a public health emergency that’s getting worse in front of our eyes. The nursing profession doesn’t want out-of-touch interventions, but action to reduce emissions and make NHS and care facilities safe to work and be cared for in.”Simon Williams, a public health researcher at Swansea University, said: “It’s concerning to see someone so high profile spreading misinformation around climate change and its impacts.“Particularly for the elderly, heatwaves over time make them less capable of regulating their body temperature. Even a few degrees either way can have a major impact.”Caroline Abrahams, the charity director of Age UK, called the new findings into the impact of heat on older people “alarming”, adding: “This study means there’s now no denying that extreme heat poses a very real health threat to our older population.”The National Farmers’ Union, meanwhile,has saidfarmers are facing “one of the worst ever” harvests, while firefighters have battled wildfires in Derbyshire, the Midlands, Wales and Northern Ireland.Reform has long campaigned to scrap the government’s commitment to reaching net zero by 2050 and has promised to end green subsidies if elected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe partyhas takentens of millions of pounds in donations from people with connections to the fossil fuel industry since it was set up in 2019, most notably from the billionaire Christopher Harborne, who owns a jet fuel brokerage and whose£5m giftto Nigel Farage is now at the centre of a parliamentary inquiry.While Farage has questioned the role that human activity has played in changing the climate, his deputy leader has been more outspoken in denying that the planet is experiencing a climate crisis at all.Heposted in 2024: “We are not in climate emergency; nor is there a climate crisis. But yes, climate change is real because it has happened for millions of years past & will do in future.”On Monday he called on the government to invest in desalination plants, which he said worked well in the Middle East, wherehe spends much of his time. “Where’s been the discussion about desalination plants that are used in other parts of the world very, very successfully?” he said.“Yeah, there’s not much water on land in the Middle East. They use desalination plants. We’re surrounded by water. It is too difficult to build a reservoir – let’s look at desalination plants.”Last weekthe Guardian reportedthat Thames Water was preparing to restart the UK’s only mainland desalination plant to restart operations later this year – but it will not be ready until the winter.Alasdair Johnstone, the head of parliamentary engagement at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said: “Far from being an enjoyable experience, for many this summer will have brought hardship, with 2,877 deaths during the May and June heatwaves, over 1,100 of which are directly attributable to the extra heat added by climate change.“Firefighters have been called to over 1,000 wildfires, which have devastated the landscape, displaced people, and destroyed homes.“The only way these climate change impacts can be prevented from becoming more common and severe is to tackle the cause, which means reaching net zero emissions by 2050.”Amy Cameron, a programme director for Greenpeace UK, said: “Tice’s words show that a party bankrolled by fossil fuel interests will keep denying the climate crisis for its funders’ benefit even when its impacts are undeniable.“Reform should try telling nurses fainting on shifts, farmers losing their crops and people running from burning homes to enjoy the hot weather and see what reaction they’ll get.”Additional reporting byDenis CampbellandAjit NiranjanExplore more on these topicsReform UKRichard TiceClimate crisisWildfiresUK weatherExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s move to gut South Korea alliance is ‘inane, haphazard decision’, lawmakers say | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: US president’s abrupt order to scale back joint exercises with Seoul is meant to ‘flatter’ North Korea’s dictator, top Democrat says
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: US president’s abrupt order to scale back joint exercises with Seoul is meant to ‘flatter’ North Korea’s dictator, top Democrat says
Content: US soldiers are seen near military vehicles at Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek on 17 August 2026.Photograph: Yonhap/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS soldiers are seen near military vehicles at Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek on 17 August 2026.Photograph: Yonhap/AFP/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyTrump’s move to gut South Korea alliance is ‘inane, haphazard decision’, lawmakers sayUS president’s abrupt order to scale back joint exercises with Seoul is meant to ‘flatter’ North Korea’s dictator, top Democrat saysUS politics live – latest updatesJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonMon 17 Aug 2026 15.11 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s move to gut Washington’s 73-year-old military alliance with Seoul has been called “inane” and “shortsighted” as lawmakers warned it risked strengthening Russia’s hand in Ukraine.The US president abruptly ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint exercises withSouth Koreajust days after North Korea test-fired ballistic missiles, justifying the decision by citing his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong-un, the nuclear-armed dictator such exercises exist to deter.Trump announced the order on social media, directing the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to scale back Ulchi Freedom Shield, an 11-day exercise due to run from 17 to 27 August involving about 18,000 South Korean troops rehearsing scenarios including missile strikes, drone incursions and cyber-attacks.Trump framed the decision as a courtesy to Kim, writing that the drills “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful”, despite North Korea’s continued missile testing and its expanding nuclear arsenal.Democrats in Congress said the move handed Kim a propaganda win for nothing, while an ally was left paying the price for a war in the Middle East it never agreed to fight.Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, called it “another inane, haphazard decision by President Trump and his chaotic administration”.“When President Trump cuts military exercises to flatter a dictator or punishes South Korea for declining to join a war he started, all of our allies – and adversaries – think that America’s commitments are negotiable,” Reed said in a statement, describing the move as punishing Korea “for no reason beyond Trump’s ego”.Reed’s warning was echoed by Mark Kelly of Arizona, who sits on the same committee, and argued that the drills were not symbolic but the basis of the alliance’s ability to function in a crisis. “North and South Korea are still technically at war,” Kelly said. “Our ability to help defend our ally against the North Koreans is because our forces are well trained and able to coordinate with the South Koreans. Hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake.”In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details. “I understand him,” the president said. “He understands me.”The alliance Trump is now unwinding dates to the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty signed after the Korean war armistice. Roughly 28,500 American troopsremain stationedin South Korea, backed by a combined US-South Korean command structure and Washington’s pledge to extend its nuclear umbrella over Seoul.Despite Trump calling North Korea “unthreatening”, his own administration’s 2026 Annual Threat Assessment describes an “increasingly confident North Korean regime”, warning that its weapons of mass destruction, conventional forces and cyber operations threaten the US, South Korea and Japan. His former director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard,testified in Marchthat “North Korea’s ICBMs [intercontinental ballistic missiles] can already reach US soil”.Trump also tied his decision to the Iran war, saying he was unhappy that Seoul had declined to join the US military campaign against Iran, a campaign that has drained US missile stockpiles and, after Tehran shut the strait of Hormuz,helped push up prices at home. He acknowledged the two issues had little to do with one another, even as he punished Seoul over both.“While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks’!” Trump wrote.Andy Kim, the New Jersey senator who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, said linking the exercises to that refusal exposed a troubling attitude toward a key partner.“Our alliance with the Republic of Korea is critical for US security and prosperity – and I am concerned that President Trump’s post today suggests a disregard for this relationship,” Kim said. “South Korea is an essential partner in peace and security in a part of the world filled with risk; we should treat them that way instead of venting frustration on social media.”It is not the first time Trump has treated the drills as a bargaining chip. After his 2018 summit with Kim in Singapore, he suspended major exercises outright, calling them costly and provocative, before they were quietly restored once nuclear diplomacy with Pyongyang broke down.The dispute comes as Seoul has spent much of the past year charting its own path on the Middle East. In February, South Korea’s governmentsaid it had“grave concern” over Israeli measures expanding control in the occupied West Bank and urged Israel to “reverse its decisions immediately”.In April, Seoul’s ambassador to the United Nations told the security council that any unilateral annexation of Palestinian territory “should be revoked”. Lee Jae Myung, the president of South Korea, has twice clashed publicly with Israel: in April overremarks he madecomparing footage of an Israeli soldier’s treatment of a Palestinian man’s body to the Holocaust, and in May after two South Korean activistswere detainedon a Gaza-bound aid mission.Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, chimed in making the point that the butterfly effect of Trump’s decision would inadvertently benefit Russia.“South Korea has been a solid military ally for over 70 years that possesses exquisite military capabilities,” Tillis wrote on social media. “Reducing joint exercises with South Korea does nothing more than free up thousands of North Korea’s troops to support Putin’s systematic kidnapping, torture, rape and murder of innocent Ukrainian citizens.”Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyDonald TrumpSouth KoreaUS politicsTrump administrationAsia PacificUS national securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tens of thousands pay tribute to Jason Arday at Trafalgar Square vigil | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: MPs, friends and campaigners gathered to remember former Cambridge professor after his death on Friday
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: MPs, friends and campaigners gathered to remember former Cambridge professor after his death on Friday
Content: People gathered for a memorial event at Trafalgar Square for academic Jason Arday on Monday.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople gathered for a memorial event at Trafalgar Square for academic Jason Arday on Monday.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesJason ArdayTens of thousands pay tribute to Jason Arday at Trafalgar Square vigilMPs, friends and campaigners gathered to remember former Cambridge professor after his death on FridayRachel HallMon 17 Aug 2026 16.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTens of thousands of people gathered in Trafalgar Square in London to remember and pay tribute toJason Arday, the former Cambridge professor who died on Friday.Stand Up to Racism, which organised the vigil, estimated that 30,000 mourners had gathered in the square to listen to emotional speeches from MPs, friends and campaigners on Arday’s life and legacy and join in a minute’s silence. Many were dressed in black and held flowers, which they were asked to leave beneath Nelson’s column. People also carried placards reading “rest in power”.Arday, 41, waspronounced deadafter emergency services were called to his home in south London on Friday. He had just resigned from his role as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, after widespread scrutiny overaccusations of plagiarism, which he rejected, andinconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.Opening the event, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the local MP for Arday’s family in Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “I’m going to look around you and look at how many people have come tonight.“That tells you what Jason meant. He held doors open behind him. He kept them open and thousands of us walked through. That is why this place is full tonight. And I know that all of you are grieving. I know there are many people that aren’t even here.”View image in fullscreenTributes left after a vigil, organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism.Photograph: Yui Mok/PARibeiro-Addy asked that people respect the privacy of Arday’s family, who “lost their son, their brother. Not a professor, not a headline, not a symbol.” She asked that they be given “time, space and quiet” to grieve.She concluded the vigil by reading out a statement from Arday’s family. They said: “The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear. The outpouring of love, support, and grief since his death means so much to us. Although it is bittersweet now, kindness is needed in life, not just in death.”Many speeches focused on the role of the media in Arday’s death. Diane Abbott, MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, said there had been 249 articles about him within three weeks. “He must have felt that if he resigned, the attacks on him would stop. But in fact, they got even worse,” she said. “This is a vicious campaign.”View image in fullscreenThe crowd listened to speeches from friends, MPs and mentors of Arday, who was remembered as a ‘wonderful man’.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThe British singer Beverley Knight performed her song Keep This Fire Burning and Jermain Jackman, who won The Voice in 2014, performed a cover of Coldplay’s Fix You, requested by Arday’s family. The MPs Zack Polanski and Jeremy Corbyn were also in attendance.Simon Woolley, who was a mentor to Arday at Cambridge, said that when he had seen Arday shortly before his death, “we knew Jason was suffering” and feeling “hounded”, and he had hugged him. “We told him he was loved,” Woolley said.Remembering Arday as a “wonderful man [who] never stole a bag of crisps”, he urged that there “be some reckoning” after Arday’s death.Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon said the evening was the time to “pay our respects and to stand in solidarity with his grieving family”. “Let’s remember his life, his scholarship, his achievements, his determination and his humanity and the people that he inspired,” he said.View image in fullscreenMP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, Diane Abbott, speaking at the event.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockBut he added that it would be important to reflect on the role of “racism, institutional responsibility, accountability and the treatment of black families and black men” in Arday’s death, as well as why the “duty of care” to an autistic man known to be vulnerable had failed, potentially through a public inquiry.Samira Ali, an organiser at Stand Up to Racism, read out a statement from a close friend and colleague of Arday, which said: “Prof Jason, the words kind, beautiful and gentle seem to orbit so many dedications to him and they are not wrong. But in truth, words will never quite capture the type of person Prof Jason was or what he meant to people.”The statement referenced Arday’s work setting up mentoring schemes and mental health support for students and academics of colour. It said: “He worked tirelessly to inspire all students from marginalised backgrounds to believe that academia could also belong to them. He did not inspire one or two people to do a PhD; there are dozens of us over generations who have dreamed and are now doctors and soon-to-be professors because of him.”Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heat more dangerous for people 60 and over than previously thought | Older people | The Guardian
description: Study finds older adults could face harmful heat stress at just 1.5C of warming above preindustrial levels
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Study finds older adults could face harmful heat stress at just 1.5C of warming above preindustrial levels
Content: Extreme heat exposure is a growing threat to human health and older people are particularly vulnerable, the study showed.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExtreme heat exposure is a growing threat to human health and older people are particularly vulnerable, the study showed.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesOlder peopleExtreme heat more dangerous for people 60 and over than previously thoughtStudy finds older adults could face harmful heat stress at just 1.5C of warming above preindustrial levelsDenis CampbellHealth policy editorMon 17 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople aged 60 and overface dangers to their healthfrom exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought, research has found.Older adults will bear the brunt of increasingly frequent sustained spells of extreme heat globally as the world continues to warm up, according to a study in The Lancet PublicHealth.Heatwaves will leave huge and growing numbers of people worldwide of all ages suffering from uncompensable heat stress (UHS) – where the body loses the ability to cool itself – and thus at risk of serious damage to their health, including death.Heat exposure of older people across world to double by 2050, finds studyRead more“Our results suggest accounting for age stratified vulnerability, intolerable heat will be experienced at much larger scales and for longer durations, affecting far more people than previously thought,” according to the study, which was led by health academics from Stanford University in California.Older adults are known to be more in danger because of the effects of very high temperatures. They sweat less, their hearts work harder in the heat and their blood vessels are less able to widen, limiting their capacity to stay cool.However, previous studies did not properly set out the different risks faced by younger people aged 15-39, middle-aged adults (40-59) and older adults (aged 60 or over). That is because they applied thresholds at which people cannot maintain their heat balance – which were accurate for younger people – to all age groups, and so overlooking older people’s greater risk of, for example, heart attacks.A combination of rising global temperatures and the projected doubling in the world’s population of those aged 60 and over to 2.1bn by 2050 means more people in that age bracketwill suffer heat-related health problems, especially in low- and middle-income countries such as India and Pakistan.“UHS will become increasingly prevalent with global warming across all age groups. Older adults are projected to face far more frequent and widespread UHS than young adults,” the study says.The UK Health Security Agencysaid recentlythat it fears that 2026’s high temperatures in Britain – parts of which have experienced five heatwaves – are likely to mean that the country records its highest ever number of heat-related deaths in a year. The four-day heatwave in May and eight-day heatwave in June together caused 2,877 excess deaths, almost doublethe 1,504 seen during the summer of 2025.Dr Simon Williams, an expert in the impact of heat on human health and the resulting inequalities at Swansea University, said: “This is a very significant study, with findings suggesting that heatwaves and extreme heat exposure is going to be a growing threat to human health in the coming years. In particular, it shows that heatwaves have unequal health impacts, with older adults particularly vulnerable.”He added that the study suggested older adults were “at risk of harmful and potentially fatal heat stress” at just 1.5C of warming above preindustrial levels, compared with 4C for younger adults.Each additional degree of global heating “exposes roughly one million more people to at least 180 hours of UHS annually”, the study says. This burden falls disproportionately on older adults.If heating continues to escalate, parts of the tropics and subtropics could become uninhabitable, especially for older people, the authors said.Caroline Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said: “These findings are alarming. This study means there’s now no denying that extreme heat poses a very real health threat to our older population.“High temperatures can exacerbate certain medical problems that are common among older people and, more generally, ageing bodies find it harder to adapt to more extremes of heat and cold as we age.”Dr Hilary Williams, the clinical vice-president of the UK’s Royal College of Physicians, said: “Extreme weather, including severe heat, is a patient safety issue.“We know that heatwaves bring a surge in patients.Older peopleoften arrive with dehydration, having collapsed, or with existing conditions like heart and kidney disease made worse by the heat. Managing multiple health conditions at once is hard enough but doing it when the body’s ability to regulate its own temperature is less efficient makes it harder still.”One hospital doctor reported the temperature on thegeriatric ward where they work reaching 36Cduring this summer’s extreme heat. “That is not a safe environment for patients or staff,” said Williams.Explore more on these topicsOlder peopleExtreme heatClimate crisisHealthHealth policyPublic services policyHospitalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham scraps restrictions on disabled people’s bus passes in England | Transport policy | The Guardian
description: Move means holders will be able to travel free on local services at any time of day or night from April next year
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Move means holders will be able to travel free on local services at any time of day or night from April next year
Content: Andy Burnham said he was proud to roll out a measure he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester across the country as a wholePhotograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he was proud to roll out a measure he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester across the country as a wholePhotograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesTransport policyBurnham scraps restrictions on disabled people’s bus passes in EnglandMove means holders will be able to travel free on local services at any time of day or night from April next yearAletha AduPolitical correspondentMon 17 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDisabled people across England will be able to use their free bus passes at any time of day from next April, as Andy Burnham expands a policy he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester.The prime minister has said the current weekday restrictions on when disabled people can use their bus passes will be removed from 1 April 2027.
