title: My son is leaving home for university – and my severe denial has surprised me | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: My cherished first-born will soon be off to start a big new phase of his life, shiny saucepans in tow. ‘Empty nesting’ implies this is as nature intended, but it’s knocked me for six, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: My cherished first-born will soon be off to start a big new phase of his life, shiny saucepans in tow. ‘Empty nesting’ implies this is as nature intended, but it’s knocked me for six, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘He truly intends to take all his stuff to another city …’Photograph: Posed by model; Eleganza/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He truly intends to take all his stuff to another city …’Photograph: Posed by model; Eleganza/Getty ImagesOpinionHigher educationMy son is leaving home for university – and my severe denial has surprised meZoe WilliamsMy cherished first-born will soon be off to start a big new phase of his life, shiny saucepans in tow. ‘Empty nesting’ implies this is as nature intended, but it’s knocked me for sixMon 17 Aug 2026 11.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTShareMy son sent me a picture of his university accommodation, which looked perfectly nice, but there was something off about it. It was a little bit too tidy, of course, and had the slightly dystopian atmosphere of a neutral colour palette, but the main problem was that places look weird without people in them. That’s why architects, when they’re trying to sell a development, always add the magic ingredients: a child with a balloon, a couple pushing a buggy and a gentleman with a bicycle.So I squinted a bit and tried to imagine my son in that room, which is when it hit me: he’s actually serious about this. He truly intends, in one month’s time, to get all his stuff, put it in bags, take it to another city and live there. I can neither convey nor explain my surprise, which is bottomless. It’s not that I thought he wouldn’t get the grades; I’m not one of those harridan sceptic-parents. I just had “I’m going to university” filed as one of those cute, dumb things kids say, along with “I’m going to space”, “I’m changing my name to Unnamed Being” and “I’m an otter now”.I was right there for the entire process: the selection of the university, the offer, the maths A-level paper that was so hard there wasa petition against it on change.organd someone called it a war crime, and results day – when it became apparent that it wasn’t that hard and The Hague wouldn’t be necessary after all.If you’d asked me yesterday, I’d have said my cherished first-born and I were fully in lockstep, but somewhere along the line our expectations must have diverged. He expected all these things that proceeded naturally from one to the other simply to happen, whereas I expected him to remain seven. When I bought him a nest of saucepans and started wanging on about new thinking on the matter of poached eggs, I was basically role-playing a parent proudly anticipating their child’s next chapter. I never in a million years thought he would move those saucepans to some other dwelling altogether, let alone go with them.I had an early warning of this catastrophic denial the other night, when it got to 1.30am and he wasn’t home. On the one hand, I should have leapt on the opportunity to get used to the fact that he, a grown adult, was in an unknown place doing an unknown thing, as soon he will be every night of his unbearably precious life. On the other, I thought it best to check, so I woke up his sister, his dad, his girlfriend and his girlfriend’s mum. When someone finally furnished me with the information that he must be somewhere nearby because they could see his shoes, I went to sleep thinking: no harm done.Yet there must have been some tiny amount of harm, because the next day he took steps to ensure that this harmless behaviour never occurred again – he set us all up on a tracking app. It’s a little bit like Snap Maps, except a thousand times more invasive. I can now see not only where he is, but also how fast he is moving. He went Interrailing the day after, which is when it transpired that the app was unable to get its head around the concept of a train. His dad and I keep getting alerts saying: “TJ is moving at 109mph. Tell TJ to slow down.”I can see the battery life on his phone and how long it’s been since he went for a walk. I can see that it’s raining in Apfelberg and wonder whether he has a cagoule. This would be a great time to get used to the fact that he, a man, can make his own choices about which clothes to wear in what weather, yet the course of action I prefer is to send an umbrella emoji with a question mark, then a bunch more question marks, then call him. I am not incognisant of how annoying this must be, but irritation seems such a small price to pay to maintain the fiction that he, a seven-year-old, is not in another country at all, but probably downstairs, where it is not raining.They call it an empty nest to underline the fact that this is all unfolding as nature intended. You’re not supposed to keep your offspring as flightless pets; you’re merely granted the blessing of stewarding them towards flight. But what’s missing from this analogy is that birds, by the time their baby hatchlings unaccountably transform into adult birds, are probably glad of the space. I also have another egg still in the nest, but the family ecosystem we’re using as a role model here has nothing in common with ours. I suggest we change tack and operate more like silverbacks, where the young signal their maturation not by leaving, but by vanquishing the old in combat and taking our status and all our … I don’t know, fruit? I would be fine with that.A friend whose son went to university last year described dropping him off. She was trying to cheer me up, I think, when she launched into the saddest story I’ve ever heard. Once she’d said goodbye, she found herself unable to leave the vicinity, so instead she decided to make friends with the security guard. Every time he showed her something, she had an urgent follow-up question (“Yes, this common room is great. Now, where’s the nearest chemist?”), and he ended up effectively taking her on a tour of the city.Now that I write this story down, I see that it is not that sad, because that is one seriously nice guy (and the city is also nice, apparently). Really, the only sad bit is when she was crying so much on the way home that she drove into a bus lane.The night before A-level results come out, parents text each other on the quiet, wishing good luck, and we absolutely mean it in the moment. Everybody ardently wants everybody else’s kid to get to the place they have their heart set on. But none of us, surely, can have thought this all the way through.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHigher educationOpinionParents and parentingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: As Ebola kills thousands in DRC, a perfect storm is making the virus hard to stop | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: New species and regional instability are factors – but decisions made in the US and Britain are also costing lives, says Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: New species and regional instability are factors – but decisions made in the US and Britain are also costing lives, says Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
Content: Members of the Congolese Red Cross carry the coffin of a woman suspected of having died of Ebola, at a cemetery in Bunia in June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Congolese Red Cross carry the coffin of a woman suspected of having died of Ebola, at a cemetery in Bunia in June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionEbolaAs Ebola kills thousands in DRC, a perfect storm is making the virus hard to stopDevi SridharNew species and regional instability are factors – but decisions made in the US and Britain are also costing livesMon 17 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTShareDid you know that there is a major Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and it’s on trackto be the deadliest ever? It isalreadythe second-worst Ebola outbreak in history, with the fastest community transmission we have ever seen. It’s estimated that there have beenat least 4,900 cases and more than 2,300 deaths, giving a mortality rate close to 50%. The situation is bad. That’s the consensus among global health experts.Yet this Ebola outbreak isn’t attracting much media or public attention. If I compare it with working on the 2014 Ebola outbreak, the current silence is astounding. That year, Ebola wasone of the most Googled termsin the world, covered regularly on broadcast news in many countries outside the region, attracting newspaper headlines and magazine covers. Perhaps everyone is just tired of disease after the pandemic – Covid-19 fatigue, as it’s called. Trust me, no one wants to hear about infectious diseases.Unfortunately things are only getting worse in the region. A perfect storm of factors is making the spread hard to contain, even more difficult to slow down – and the health impact is devastating. One concerning factor is that most of the cases, and deaths, are happening in the community before patients even get to hospital: it’s estimated that local health workers are reaching only 30% of cases. Adding to the impact, children make up a quarter of confirmed cases, andalmost a third of all deaths. And those are just the direct deaths from the Ebola virus: routine health services such as childhood vaccination campaigns against measles and basic child survival interventions have been disrupted, meaning a higher number of indirect deaths from lack of healthcare.It’s not just children. Maternal deaths in Ituri (the worst-hit province) have doubled, from childbirth complications and a lack of trained health personnel but also because Ebola infection during pregnancy is linked tofoetal loss.Why is it proving so difficult to stop? First, there’s the virus itself. The outbreak was of a new species – Bundibugyo – and we don’t have an effective vaccine or antiviral against it. Previous outbreaks were the Zaire species. In addition,viral mutationhas been suggested as a factor behind why this outbreak is growing faster than efforts to stop it. Mutation could have made this species more transmissible, as community spread is large and faster than before.The location of the outbreak is also difficult: Ituri province is unstable, with roaming militias and ongoing conflict. Before it was confirmed asEbola, it looks as if the virus had been spreading for three months, being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. Effective government and safe living conditions are a prerequisite for health security, and both are missing right now.There are also larger global changes that make a coordinated response challenging. In the 2014 west Africa outbreak, the US, UK and French governments worked with the World Health Organization (WHO) to escalate a response, bringing military-like coordination, necessary resources, logistics and trained personnel. An Ebola commissionI co-chairedsoon after looked at some of the scientific lessons for the WHO health emergencies response, but we couldn’t predict what the next decade would bring politically.We’ve had two “America-First” Trump presidencies. The US isno longer partof the WHO or working multilaterally, favouring a “go-it-alone” response. This is in the context of the defunding of foreign aid, the censorship of scientists, the closure of USAID, the implosion of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and a“make America healthy again”movement focused on press-ups and visits to the sauna over core public health.Britain has also stepped back from its responsibilities, cutting foreign aid. It makes sense that the current prime minister, Andy Burnham, is focused on domestic issues: when health inequalities and rising poverty mean British children are some of theunhealthiest in western Europe, it’s tricky politically to divert resources overseas. But those political choices have consequences for countries left with fewer resources to fight the spread of disease.In a dire situation, a ray of hope is the vaccine and antiviral work under way. Using the same technology as the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine, Oxford Universityhas started human trialsof the Bundibugyo vaccine, while the WHO is sponsoringa clinical trial in the DRCon two existing antiviral therapies. It’s not just lab science. Social science and the humanities have been engaged to understand how to reach people in remote communities and how to build trust in public health campaigns: given the history of colonial health interventions and residents being used as“guinea pigs”, any health response must understand why people are fearful of external “help”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBudget cuts to higher education have also been consequential. Outbreaks such as this one demonstrate yet again why knowledge, education and research matter, and why political decisions taken in one part of the world have major ramifications for the lives of those in another.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsEbolaOpinionDemocratic Republic of the CongoInfectious diseasesAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Disabled creatives like me are behind many of your favourite shows – so why has our work support been withdrawn? | Annalisa Dinnella | The Guardian
description: Cuts to the Access to Work scheme will mean no more contributions to shows like Sex Education, Call the Midwife or The Hack. It will be devastating to lose such talent, says TV writer Annalisa Dinnella
Author: Annalisa Dinnella
Headline: Cuts to the Access to Work scheme will mean no more contributions to shows like Sex Education, Call the Midwife or The Hack. It will be devastating to lose such talent, says TV writer Annalisa Dinnella
Content: Chris McCausland and his dance partner, Dianne Buswell, lift the glitterball trophy after winning Strictly Come Dancing, 14 December 2024.Photograph: Guy Levy/PAView image in fullscreenChris McCausland and his dance partner, Dianne Buswell, lift the glitterball trophy after winning Strictly Come Dancing, 14 December 2024.Photograph: Guy Levy/PAOpinionDisabilityDisabled creatives like me are behind many of your favourite shows – so why has our work support been withdrawn?Annalisa DinnellaCuts to the Access to Work scheme will mean no more contributions to shows like Sex Education, Call the Midwife or The Hack. It will be devastating to lose such talentMon 17 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTShareWhen Chris McCausland won Strictly Come Dancing in 2024, he held his trophy aloft and said: “It’s for everyone out there that thought and got told they couldn’t do something. It just shows with opportunity and support and determination, anything can happen.” Later that month, he delivered Channel 4’sAlternative Christmas Message. In it, McCausland warned thatAccess to Work(AtW), a scheme run by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), was under threat due to a lack of funding.AtW provides grants to employers and self-employed workers to cover the cost of reasonable adjustments a disabled person may need in the workplace. Behind McCausland’s jovial reflection on the value of different mince pies was a heartfelt plea to protect this little-known yet vital cog in our national machine.Like Chris, I cannot do what I do without support. I am visually impaired (I have 5% vision) and I am a television writer. I’ve worked on shows such as Sex Education, Call the Midwife and The Hack. I am currently working on a drama for BBC One about the newspaper editor Harry Evans. My job is my passion, my obsession, my livelihood and a huge part of my identity. But thanks to recent cuts to my AtW support, it has become increasingly difficult, if not impossible, for me to perform.My grant from AtW is split into two pots: one for taxis (I cannot access public transport independently) and one for a support worker (sighted guide) when needed. In 2025, my grant was cut by 70%, and this year my travel pot was removed entirely. I need to travel. I can’t do my job without attending meetings, rehearsals, writers rooms, sets and post-production facilities. On top of that, I need to network in order to gain future contracts.AtW didn’t contest these needs – or, indeed, my sight loss – but argued that, as I’m self-employed, I can offset travel expenses against tax. This would reimburse only a fraction of my expenditure. Even more baffling, they also claimed I had failed to submit a contract for “work with ITV”. I had clearly stated that my current job is with the BBC, and had provided a contract and letter from my producer to back this up.I submitted a reconsideration request and my MP, Ellie Reeves, also contacted the DWP on my behalf. A few weeks later we both received a letter (by post and in small print, which they know I can’t read) informing us that my appeal had been rejected. They restated their earlier claims, including my failure to provide my mythical contract with ITV. So where do I go from here? Nowhere. There is no recourse to appeal against an appeal. I find myself at a legal dead end.Sadly I am not alone. In the past two years there have been many thousands of stories like mine. When challenged, AtW insists there has been no change in policy and points to a twofold increase in demand over the past five years. It’s true, the system is under strain. Increased demand without a corresponding increase in funding is going to cause a problem; I can’t argue with that. But I can ask: are these cuts by stealth really the best way to solve it?In 2011, theSayce reportfound that for every £1 the DWP put into AtW, it received £1.48 back; it’s obvious this scheme pays for itself. I can certainly prove that I am earning, and paying in tax, a sum far greater than the value of my grant. But must we reduce this argument to numbers on a spreadsheet? I could not make this claim at the beginning of my career. Was I less deserving then? Some claimants have more complex needs than others. Is anyone seriously arguing that their talents should go to waste?I’m also told this study didn’t take into account the money saved in health and social care. Being employed keeps us fit and well. It keeps the wolves of social isolation from the door. Sadly, it seems no further studies have been conducted. Somewhere along the line, AtW decided to stop collecting data.When sense-making grants were available, disabled newcomers had the freedom to take the same financial risks as their non-disabled counterparts. Comedians such as McCausland could dart around comedy festivals with their support workers, and many a star was born. Organisations such asGraeae Theatre(our national theatre for disabled people) became lighthouses for talented youngsters – Jack Thorne, the Emmy-winning writer of Adolescence, landed one of his first jobs writing for Graeae’s artistic director, Jenny Sealey (Jenny’s AtW grant was cut this year. After a fierce social media backlash and the support of her MP, it was restored). But in the past year, AtW has become so unworkable that it is already deterring potential talent. Call the switchboard and the recorded voice will tell you that the current waiting time for a new application is nine months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose of us campaigning to bring this scandal into public consciousness have spent much time wondering: is this cock-up or conspiracy? Is anyone at the DWP considering the impact on the McCauslands of the future? And what is the new prime minister going to do about it?If you back us, we will deliver. It’s what Chris was saying when he brandished his glitter ball trophy. A piece of public policy that made money and was a source of national pride has been twisted into something nonsensical, cruel and, quite frankly, shameful. It’s enough to make anyone stop dancing.Annalisa Dinnella is a television writerExplore more on these topicsDisabilityOpinionBlindness and visual impairmentChris McCauslandBenefitsWork & careersTV comedyComedycommentShareReuse this content

title: Nothing less than radical whole-system change is required to fix the NHS’s maternity services | Julia Sanders | The Guardian
description: It’s vital that Yvette Cooper’s taskforce acts on the Amos and Ockenden reports – and puts the needs of women and families at the heart of maternity services, says professor of midwifery Julia Sanders
Author: Julia Sanders
Headline: It’s vital that Yvette Cooper’s taskforce acts on the Amos and Ockenden reports – and puts the needs of women and families at the heart of maternity services, says professor of midwifery Julia Sanders
Content: ‘For women and families, cumulative systemic problems have resulted in failures of compassionate care.’Photograph: By Ian Miles-Flashpoint Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘For women and families, cumulative systemic problems have resulted in failures of compassionate care.’Photograph: By Ian Miles-Flashpoint Pictures/AlamyOpinionChildbirthNothing less than radical whole-system change is required to fix the NHS’s maternity servicesJulia SandersIt’s vital that Yvette Cooper’s taskforce acts on the Amos and Ockenden reports – and puts the needs of women and families at the heart of maternity servicesMon 17 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTShareIt is hard to find the words to describe the agony for those who have experienced preventable baby loss, injury or maternal death. Understandably, families who have been through this have campaigned relentlessly for local and national investigations. Every family deserves to know what caused their loss or trauma, but current and past reviews have failed to deliver on resolution and accountability.The vital debate about how to ensure safe maternity care has intensified since thepublication of two reports, led by Valerie Amos and Donna Ockenden, and the appointment of Yvette Cooper as secretary of state for health and social care, offering a golden opportunity for system-wide change. “I want to make it a personal crusade to put the cradle back at the heart of the NHS,” Coopertold the Guardian last week, adding that she was committed to introducing a new national maternity commissioner.For women and families, cumulative systemic problems have resulted in failures of compassionate care, with distressing examples described in both reports. Where behaviour is unkind or unprofessional, this is inexcusable, and the life-changing physical and psychological trauma caused by poor care must continue to be acknowledged.We also owe it to all staff groups, particularly midwives, who are often blamed in the media, to recognise that they provide high-quality care to many women every day, despite intense workplace pressures. TheAmos inquiryfound that just 22% of midwives reported having sufficient time to do their job well, while aGuardian reportlast month highlighted increasing numbers leaving the profession because of burnout.Undermining and villainising midwives helps no one. They are the only professional group working with women, babies and families throughout the entire maternity journey across hospital and community settings, providing the platform on which other services depend. For women and babies to be safe, all staff must work in supportive, well-managed and adequately resourced environments.By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive | Natalie MorrisRead moreThe public criticisms of maternity services over the past decade suggest poor care is common, but regular nationalsurveys by Oxford Universityreport high and relatively stable rates of overall satisfaction with care between 2006 and 2024.Poor outcomes do not necessarily equate to poor care. TheOckenden reviewincluded over 700 maternity cases with poor outcomes, including stillbirth, severe perineal trauma or major haemorrhage among more than 41,000 births between 2020 and May 2025. In over 80% of cases, care was judged to be in line with best practice, or it was considered that different management would not have altered the outcome.Work from theNeonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College Londonfound that the number of babies born at term with brain injury caused by oxygen deprivation declined between 2015 and 2021, and stillbirth rates have fallen. These are important gains,but reportsfrom the National Perinatal Epidemiology Unit at Oxford University show that in 2022-2024 the overall rate of maternal death in the UKwas20% higher than it was in 2009-2011and the Amos inquiry also found persistent inequalities, overt racism and continuingreports of physical and psychological trauma.Piecemeal initiatives have produced unintended consequences. Attempts to improve safety and maternal choice have been accompanied by rapidly rising obstetric intervention rates. NHS data shows thatlabour induction increasedfrom about 20% before 2010 to more than 34% by 2020, before slightly reducing.Caesarean section rates rosefrom 27% of births in 2016 to 45% in 2025, equating to about 100,000 additional caesarean births annuallycompared with a decade ago.Focusing on interventions as the solution to maternity safety risks displacing resources and overlooking a fundamental component of maternity care: women need more than technical interventions. Some need to be held safely through loss. All need skilled care, information and trusting relationships with their maternity team. Relationship-based midwifery continuity of care is proven to provide positive outcomes – but few women currently receive this.There is a risk that political, professional and media debate will deflect attention from the central priority: delivering safe and equitable care based on robust evidence and genuine partnership with women and families. The Amos inquiry concluded that nothing less than radical whole-system change is required.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis must be grounded in two key shifts. First, a fundamental reset of the relationship between services and women and families, to ensure that women, families and frontline staff have real influence over how services are designed, delivered and monitored. Second, decisions must be guided by evidence on effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, women’s experiences and sustainable implementation.Thenational maternity and neonatal taskforce, to be chaired by Cooper, has been challenged to deliver the recommendations of the Ockenden review and the Amos inquiry. It must be bold enough to redefine what NHS maternity services can and should provide and negotiate for the resources required. Strong commitment and accountability from politicians, NHS boards, regulators, professional leaders, educators and every member of the multidisciplinary team will be essential. The future health and wellbeing of our population requires nothing less.Julia Sanders is professor of clinical midwifery at Cardiff University and was an expert adviser to the national maternity and neonatal investigation led by Valerie AmosExplore more on these topicsChildbirthOpinionNHSPregnancyHealthWomenYvette CooperMaternal mortalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: Italy’s mythic ‘month off’ in August was hard won. It would be good for us all | Jamie Mackay | The Guardian
description: The villeggiatura, a month-long break, was popularised in the 1960s when trade unions were strong – and so was economic productivity, says writer and translator Jamie Mackay
Author: Jamie Mackay
Headline: The villeggiatura, a month-long break, was popularised in the 1960s when trade unions were strong – and so was economic productivity, says writer and translator Jamie Mackay
Content: The Old Bridge in Dolceacqua, Riviera di Ponente.Photograph: StevanZZ/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Old Bridge in Dolceacqua, Riviera di Ponente.Photograph: StevanZZ/AlamyOpinionItalyItaly’s mythic ‘month off’ in August was hard won. It would be good for us allJamie MackayThe villeggiatura, a month-long break, was popularised in the 1960s when trade unions were strong – and so was economic productivityMon 17 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTShareOn the Riviera di Ponente, sandwiched between the glitzy resort towns of the Ligurian coast, sits the Albenga plain. Dotted with campsites and bungalows, the area developed during Italy’s postwar boom as an affordable refuge for workers to escape the smog of nearby industrial cities like Turin and Milan. While much of the surrounding coast is now given over to boutique lidos, this corner of the riviera is still a place where families gather in the shade of eucalyptus trees to play cards, share picnics and nap through the afternoon heat to the chorus of cicadas. These are the stubborn devotees ofvilleggiatura: Italy’s mythic, month-long summer break.The origins ofvilleggiaturago back to the Renaissance, when nobles would leave their urban palazzos for gilded countryside villas in the hills, for weeks at a time. During the 20th century, however, middle- and working-class Italians made their own claim on it, transforming an aristocratic privilege into a mass ritual. By the 1960s, millions of Italians had come to consider a long summer break a fundamental right, spending holidays in ancestral villages, seaside campsites, or even company-sponsored holiday resorts. It was the era immortalised in Gino Paoli’s 1963 jukebox hit Sapore di Sale (The Taste of Salt), which celebrates “lazy days passing by” at the beach, dreaming “of a different world” beyond the factory and office.There is something undeniably nostalgic about this picture-postcard image, but the politics that made it possible are worth reflecting on, not least in contrast with our own overworked age. Italy’s enviable leisure culture did not emerge from nowhere. It was the once-powerful trade unions that fought for this right, securing Italian workerssome of the longest protected holidays in Europe. The forces of capital were forced to adapt. Firms like Fiat and Olivetti didn’t just shut down for most of August; they actively encouraged their employees to decamp for the summer, funding mountain retreats and seasidecoloniefor workers and their children. Even the state helped bankroll the long pause, offering low-cost train tickets and supporting budget holiday programmes to enable families of all classes to participate.There are analogues elsewhere in Europe, from the EnglishWakes Weeksto the Frenchvillages vacances. What was unique in Italy’s postwar period was the systemic collaboration between organised labour, business and the state, and it has provided Italy with a cherished ritual that remains rooted in the national culture to this day.Inevitably, some have bemoaned Italy’s August shutdown as the apotheosis of southern European laziness, asking how an entire country can simply pause for weeks on end. Yetvilleggiaturahas always possessed its own internal economic logic. During the 1960s, at the height of the phenomenon, Italian productivity grew at an average annual rate of 4-6%, higher than that of the US. Industrial output was robust, labour turnover was stable, and despite nascent protests against increased automation,urban unemployment reached historic lows. Decades on, international OECD data continues to show thatlonger working hours yield diminishing returns, thereby reinforcing a truth that many Italians once considered self-evident: that the right to rest sustains an economy, rather than depleting it.The true philosophy behindvilleggiatura, however, is less about economic metrics than human flourishing. In today’s Italy, where precarious employment has bred chronic insecurity, workers spend the year enduring long, erratic hours only to rush off on brief, overpriced breaks. The resulting cycle of burnout and manic consumption is, surely, unsustainable.Villeggiaturaoffers an alternative model. Instead of Airbnbs, it relies on long-term lets and family homes. Instead of sightseeing, it privileges sunbathing and sleep. Instead of tasting menus and overpriced cocktails, it prioritises simple rituals, like sharing focaccia and watermelon on the beach with family and friends.View image in fullscreenA beach at Torre dell’Orso, Italy, in August.Photograph: Diego Fiore/AlamyOn paper, this sounds like an ideal way to spend a summer. Unfortunately, though, fewer and fewer Italians are able to achieve it. Where workers were once able to decamp for weeks on end, the average holiday had dropped to 13 days by the 1990s as deregulation transformed the labour market, and the figure now stands at barely six. Last year, 35.7% of Italians reported beingunable to afford even a short break away. To make matters worse, the very concept ofvilleggiaturais being co-opted by luxury brands. The Belmond hotel group recently published a $120coffee table book titled Villeggiatura, explicitly appropriating the language of the long break to market hotels like Portofino’s Splendido, where a room can set you back several thousand euros a night.Despite these pressures, Italians have not yet surrendered their ritual. Places like Albenga remain popular destinations for long August breaks, as do the traditional lidos of the Riviera Romagnola on the Adriatic coast, where, despite the spread of exclusive beach clubs, pockets of affordability still endure. Heritage groups are working to revive the physical monuments of corporate vacation spots, from theEni village in Borca di Cadoreto Olivetti’s seaside retreat inMarina di Massa. Even remnants of state support persist, like government-funded grants that allow the children of lower-income public-sector workers to attend summer camps.For the most part, though,villeggiaturatoday requires far more compromise and financial strain than it once did. Many Italian workers opt for inland destinations away from the coast, where prices remain lower. Others juggle diminished workplace benefits, piecing together the limited time off their employers allow. Digital workers are perhaps the phenomenon’s most inventive contemporary adherents, with many choosing to forego pay to take time off, or surrendering some precious rest hours to answer emails from beneath a beach umbrella.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe fact that so many are fighting to keep this ritual alive against all odds tells us what is at stake here.Villeggiaturawas never just about taking a holiday, but reclaiming life from the totalising logic of the market. In an era when workers acrossEuropeare exhausted, isolated and struggling with the high cost of living, that simple idea remains quietly inspiring. Far from a relic of 60s nostalgia, or a gimmick for luxury brands, its true legacy is a defiant belief in the necessity of rest.Villeggiaturareminds us that a slower, healthier way of life should not just be an elite privilege, but a fundamental right – one that, with a dose of political will, could once again be accessible to the many.Jamie Mackay is a writer and translator based in FlorenceExplore more on these topicsItalyOpinionEuropeUnionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Is dating draining your bank account? Here’s a cheap solution | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: I understand gen Z’s concerns about the cost of romance. But anything can be a date if you want it to be
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: I understand gen Z’s concerns about the cost of romance. But anything can be a date if you want it to be
Content: ‘You’re better off enjoying the meal than worrying about the outcome.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘You’re better off enjoying the meal than worrying about the outcome.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionDatingIs dating draining your bank account? Here’s a cheap solutionDave SchillingI understand gen Z’s concerns about the cost of romance. But anything can be a date if you want it to beMon 17 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTShareAcouple of months ago, I wrote a columnimploring young peopleto keep trying to find love, to not become cynical about romance and avoid the temptation of the accursed “loneliness influencers” peddling antisocial behavior as some sort of newfangled experiment that no one had thought of before. I stand here today saying,hey, I can’t be right all the time. Maybe it is better to be alone, since it costs a hell of a lot less.Apparently, young people across the country are forgoing dating because it’s too damn expensive. Or at least, I think they are, based on themultiplenewspaperarticlessaying so that came out in the last two weeks. As the New York Times put it, the “prospect of a tab of $150 or more for two entrées, two drinks, an appetizer and tip” is too pricey for many gen Z singles. I say, only $150? Where are you going, Chili’s? I went on a date with (shameful brag incoming) a very famous political figure from the late 90s and spent twice that amount, sending my bank account into cardiac arrest. I practically begged her to get dessert, even though it was clear our decade of age difference and general lack of chemistry meant I was better off going home and journaling about it. I paid for the whole thing, and in return, I got an amazing story to tell at parties.People once cited romcoms to describe the love they hoped for. Now the doomscroll has replaced the meet-cute | Lisa PortolanRead moreDating is akin to gambling, in that it costs a lot and there’s no guarantee you’ll get anything out of it. I’m not suggesting that the money one spends on a date should entitle that person to love. That’s absurd and antithetical to the entire modern conception of romance as a mutual experience shared by two people with equal agency. Rather, I’m saying that you’re better off enjoying the meal than worrying about the outcome. At least you’ll feel like you got your money’s worth.And anyway, in a huge city like mine, there’s no need to go for the $150 dinner. Numerous affordable date options exist: free museums, art galleries, parks, the beach. You can make anything a date, as long as it affords you the opportunity to assess compatibility. Sitting in traffic on the 10 freeway at rush hour could be a date if you wanted it to be. You could stand outside a restaurant for 30 minutes and never go in. You could ride an elevator in a large building up and down, then see if sparks fly. If so, just hit the emergency button and spend the time waiting for the fire department, doing as you please.The real problem isn’t if you’re both broke, though. In that scenario, both participants in the relationship can agree to be thrifty. The trouble comes when one person is doing significantly better financially. In my last relationship, I was the broke writer and she was, well … not. Self-employed creative types sometimes have down months (or in my case, years). What started as a pairing of equals quickly turned into me wincing every time the check came.Some think you absolutelyshouldn’t date if you’re unemployed, that you should lock yourself in a cage and wear a chastity belt if you have to leave the house. I suppose that would at least save people the embarrassment I went through, as my savings dwindled and my girlfriend tried to reassure me that it was actually fine that she was paying for everything. Better, then, to wait until your life is more settled and you can go back to blowing your money on extravagant evenings again.To the new couples ‘turbulence testing’ their relationships: just relax and enjoy good times instead | Emma BeddingtonRead moreI see the wisdom in that. Dating can be a huge distraction. A whole other human being requires not just your money, but your time and emotional support. With the economy as troubled as it is, more and more people are having to decide if they can actually afford to be in love, or if they’ll end up like me, a freeloader happy to take what he can get. Maybe I’m being a bit hard on myself here, but guilt is kind of my thing.But there’s never a good time to date. There’s no more convenient time to love and be loved. At no point do people become perfect and wonderful and without actual problems. If you wait for a signal that you’ve got it all figured out, life will pass you by. Love just happens, if you open yourself up to it. It might seem like gambling when you add up how much it costs to try, but it’s healthier to think about it as a part of the personal growth process. It’s possible to meet someone who likes you, despite your having more fingers on your hands than dollars in your bank account. Isn’t that the ideal we’re all searching for anyway? You aren’t a social pariah. This current moment is perilous for millions of people. It’d be a lot easier with someone else to go through it with.So, try not to despair. Ignore the trend pieces and influencers. Go on the cheap date, be honest about your situation, and leave the chastity belt at home.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsDatingOpinionRelationshipscommentShareReuse this content

title: Every year, humans speak less and less. That’s bad news, even if you hate mindless chit-chat | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Silent retreats are all the rage; hotel guests are embracing ‘hushpitatility’. But won’t this leave us more isolated?
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Silent retreats are all the rage; hotel guests are embracing ‘hushpitatility’. But won’t this leave us more isolated?
Content: Time to take off the headphones?Photograph: Posed by models; Caia Image/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFView image in fullscreenTime to take off the headphones?Photograph: Posed by models; Caia Image/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFOpinionHealth & wellbeingEvery year, humans speak less and less. That’s bad news, even if you hate mindless chit-chatEmma BeddingtonSilent retreats are all the rage; hotel guests are embracing ‘hushpitatility’. But won’t this leave us more isolated?Mon 17 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.48 EDTShareAre we becoming too quiet? As a joyless, intolerant shrew, my kneejerk answer is a predictable “if only” (writing this on a train full of happy holidaymakers isn’t helping). But am I wrong? I find myself confronted with evidence that people are taking the expression “say less” literally. A study recently reported in theAtlanticfound that daily spoken word counts declined by around 300 every year between 2005 and 2019. A sample group of 2,197 participants, aged between 10 and 94, wore devices that randomly recorded them as they went about their lives; each year, they spoke on average 338 fewer words than the year before. For under-25s, the decline was even steeper: 451 fewer words.Even I can see that’s worrying.Spending time with other people is good for our brains, health and mood, while, as theUS surgeon general put it so starkly in 2023, “lacking social connection can increase the risk for premature death as much as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day”.But silence is seen as adesirable self-improvement tool; healthy even.“Silent walking” is a wellness hack, we’renoise cancellinglike never before andHilton’s trend report this yearhas introduced me to the horrid concept of “hushpitality”. Claiming “sometimes the best travel companion is silence”, Hilton reported on the (depressing) rise of digital and AI-enabled tools – virtual check-ins, text communication, bots – that allow travellers to “protect their peace”, and quoted a survey in which 57% of US travellers said they’d be interested in a silent or quiet retreat. We seem convinced we need quieter lives, but maybe we actually need more chat?It’s further evidence that knowing what’s good or bad for us has become baffling, labyrinthine, probably impossible.Lettuce is potentially deadly nowandNew Scientist informs me lightbulbs are “wrecking your metabolism”(doubtless soon darkmaxxing influencers will be promoting cave living). So, should people wear their headphones more or less, and is silence something to gorge on, or enjoy in moderation? Maybe we need a version ofMichael Pollan’s brilliantly simple dictum on food– “Eat food, not too much, mostly plants” – but for talking. How about: “Speak words, mostly in person, not too loud (and never on speakerphone)”? I’m open to other – quietly voiced – suggestions.Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingOpinionMental healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Jason Arday: a tragedy that demands reflection | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Legitimate scrutiny became entangled with a racial argument about merit and diversity. His death raises questions about how society treats black success and failure
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Legitimate scrutiny became entangled with a racial argument about merit and diversity. His death raises questions about how society treats black success and failure
Content: ‘Jason Arday’s story – an autistic child from a council estate who became a Cambridge professor aged just 37 – was remarkable.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Jason Arday’s story – an autistic child from a council estate who became a Cambridge professor aged just 37 – was remarkable.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianOpinionJason ArdayThe Guardian view on Jason Arday: a tragedy that demands reflectionEditorialLegitimate scrutiny became entangled with a racial argument about merit and diversity. His death raises questions about how society treats black success and failureMon 17 Aug 2026 14.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.42 EDTShareThe tragic death of Jason Arday raises serious questions about race, institutional authority and what happens to people in a society increasingly organised around public reputation. Arday, who resigned earlier this month as a professor at the University of Cambridge, wasfound deadat his home last week. He was 41. His family and friends have lost somebody they loved and cared for. Arday had publiclysaidthat the scrutiny of allegations concerning his academic work and claims he had made about his life was taking a profound toll. That he then died amid an intense and continuing media examination of his life is deeply troubling.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, was right to callthis“a moment for reflection”. This does not mean suppressing difficult questions, ignoring why there remain a pitifully small number ofblack professorsin British universities, or attacking legitimate journalism. But in a polarised world it should see the media ask how proper scrutiny can widen into something more encompassing; how race affects the meaning attached to an individual’s alleged failings; and whether separate valid stories can, via social media, have an overwhelming effect. In Arday’s case, alleged shortcomings in his record rapidly became weaponised by the right in an argument about diversity and black academic advancement.Arday’s story – an autistic child from a council estate who became a Cambridge professor aged just 37 – was remarkable. The university publicised the symbolic dimensions of his appointment as ayoung, black, neurodivergent man. He had been accused of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis – allegations an earlier Liverpool John Moores University investigation had not upheld. His latest accuser,Nathan Cofnas, had advanced ideas widely condemned as racist, making it impossible to regard his intervention as neutral. However, there was a clear public interest case for investigating such allegations.The Guardian sought to establish what was true. That is the proper function of journalism. Reporters were contacted by Arday over a year ago and worked extensively to verify what he had told them. In many instances they could not. It was right for the Guardian to publish its investigation, and it is wrong that the journalists who did their job responsibly are now being subjected to an onslaught of abuse. Cambridge, which has many of its own questions to answer, announced that it would hold an internal inquiry. In its journalism, the Guardian sought to meet tests of importance and proportionality, covering the issue with nuance. This could not be said of much of the rightwing media and its social media outriders.Arday became an exhibit in an ideological, almost Trumpian campaign against diversity and inclusion. The allegations were no longer simply about one academic’s behaviour or his past record. They were used to suggest that Arday had never deserved to be there – and that he had only been advanced because of his race. The attacks wererelentless, often partisan, and amplified without respite online.This is racism at work. White academics are generally allowed to fail as individuals. Black ones are not. Arday may have had questions to answer; that did not make black academics collectively answerable for him. A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to beflawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on a vibrant summer for British athletics: inspiring a generation | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Amy Hunt’s record haul of four golds in Birmingham showcased the sport’s appeal. More can be done to ensure it gets its fair share of the limelight
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Amy Hunt’s record haul of four golds in Birmingham showcased the sport’s appeal. More can be done to ensure it gets its fair share of the limelight
Content: Amy Hunt crosses the line to win the mixed relay in Birmingham.Photograph: Sean Walsh/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt crosses the line to win the mixed relay in Birmingham.Photograph: Sean Walsh/ShutterstockOpinionAthleticsThe Guardian view on a vibrant summer for British athletics: inspiring a generationEditorialAmy Hunt’s record haul of four golds in Birmingham showcased the sport’s appeal. More can be done to ensure it gets its fair share of the limelightMon 17 Aug 2026 14.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTShareTo win one gold medal is impressive. To win two indicates a certain relentlessness. To winfourin the space of one remarkable week of athletics may ensure further recognition for Amy Hunt as the BBC’s sports personality of the year. Ms Hunt’s record‑breaking achievement in winning the 100m, 200m, women’s relay and mixed relay at the first European championships to be held in Britain was an exhibition of world-class sprinting for the ages.Her triumph capped a week which reminded us that there is more to sporting life than football. By winning an 11th medal, Dina Asher-Smith became the most successful athlete in the history of the competition. And on Friday, at a packed Alexander athletics stadium in Birmingham, the crowd savoured a contest and burgeoning rivalry that recalled the halcyondaysof Sebastian Coe and Steve Ovett. Audrey Werro, the young Swiss star, and Keely Hodgkinson, Team GB’s Olympic champion, produced a thrillingly intense women’s 800mfinal, which Werro won with a time that broke a European record set in 1982.Athletics fans should relish the moment. The walls are closing in as another Premier League season begins, sucking the oxygen of publicity away from rival sports. An expanded World Cup, and thefalloutfrom plans to sell a stake in the competition to private equity, made it seem as if football never went away. But it has been a stellar couple of months for British athletes.Josh Kerr’sshatteringof the one-mile world record, in front of 60,000 spectators at July’s London Diamond League meet, was the sporting event of the summer until Hunt arguably trumped it. There was also a successful salvage operation in Scotland. Glasgow’sstagingof the Commonwealth Games at short notice, after the original Australian hosts pulled out, rescued the event from limbo.The only downside was that the rich talent on display did not, at times, get the fanfare it deserved. Glasgow’s efforts went somewhat under the national radar after cost-conscious organisers rejected a low offer from the BBC and sold rights to the Discovery channel. The boost that terrestrial coverage can give was shown by an audienceestimatedto be in the region of 4 million for the epic runoff between Werro and Hodgkinson.Birmingham, however, has had its own problems as cameras panned across acres of empty seats in the early part of last week. The former athlete and BBC commentator Steve Cram has been among those toquestionhigh ticket prices, and there was a notable lack of cut-price deals to attract the next generation of athletics fans. The promotion and marketing of the event in Birmingham itself, in stark contrast with the 2022 Commonwealth Games, was somewhat underwhelming.For a sport which can produce such scintillating moments of concentrated drama, and in which male and female athletes enjoy a genuine equality of esteem, that is a shame. British athletics is enjoying a golden era, and sassy personalities such as Hunt – a Cambridge graduate whoonce describedherself as “an ­academic badass and a track ­goddess” – have a charismatic appeal.The chosen motto of the London 2012 Olympics was “Inspire a generation”. As the likes of Hunt, Hodgkinson and Kerr do just that, more can be done to support and promote their efforts. Football may now be back. But Britain’s stars of track and field jumped through their annual summer window of opportunity to stunning effect.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsOpinionWorld CupOlympic GameseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Supporting young people so they don’t become Neets | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Daisy Christodoulou on predicting which children are at risk of future unemployment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Daisy Christodoulou on predicting which children are at risk of future unemployment
Content: ‘Suggesting we must separate children struggling at school from efforts to build our economy makes no sense.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Suggesting we must separate children struggling at school from efforts to build our economy makes no sense.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyYouth unemploymentLettersSupporting young people so they don’t become NeetsReaders respond to an article by Daisy Christodoulou on predicting which children are at risk of future unemploymentMon 17 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTShareDaisy Christodoulou suggests that teachers identifying children at risk of ending up not in education, employment or training (Neets) is like dentists helping children to learn to read (Could you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachers, 11 August). But dentists often help children learn to read by stopping the toothache that can derail education. Alan Milburn is not asking teachers to fix teeth. He wants the whole system to act when teachers identify barriers to learning.We conducted the research at the centre of this debate. Our study showed that children identified with developmental difficulties through the statutory early years foundation stage profile (EYFSP) school assessment are much more likely to become Neets in late adolescence. The EYFSP reveals the holistic educational needs of children – but teachers cannot diagnose autism, treat anxiety or fix housing. Milburn is not making teachers responsible for everything.Christodoulou is right that schools cannot eliminate poverty, repair the housing market or create jobs. But suggesting that we must separate children struggling at school from efforts to build our economy makes no sense. The tragedy of the rise in the number of Neets is that government acts by attaching an administrative label at the end of the journey through childhood. The research shows that there are warning signs years earlier when intervention is effective.Our Child of the North and Centre for Young Livescampaignhas consistently argued that children’s lives do not respect Whitehall boundaries. Health, education, social care and economic policy converge. Building a country that works for all children and young people is not the job of teachers alone. It’s everyone’s – including dentists.Mark Mon-WilliamsProfessor of cognitive psychology, University of LeedsI beg to differ with Daisy Christodoulou. It seems to me that good primary school teachers are more than adept at doing exactly what she is asking. My wife, starting her career in the slums of Newcastle and then in Wythenshawe, seemed to me to have an acute sense of the future that faced some children.It might have been encouraged when, years ago, on a supply posting in a secondary school in the mining valleys of Wales, she asked an exasperating teenager what he expected to do when he grew up: “A policeman, ’cos I’ve got big feet.”One thing she does know from bitter experience is the extent of Ofsted’s baleful influence on the role of teachers, especially in primary, in nurturing children. This was reinforced recently when a secondary school-trained Ofsted inspector effectively terminated the career of a much-loved and respected primary headteacher of our acquaintance after years of steady progress in a very difficult community. Let teachers get on with the job and give them the resources to do it.Neil BlackshawAlnwick, NorthumberlandDaisy Christodoulou’s response is fair. Primary teachers have enough to do without speculating on children’s futures. Providing measured evidence on current strengths and weaknesses should be enough for secondary schools and services like careers guidance to support planning strategies for career development. Secondary schools are best placed to assess short and long-term potential, but they also need better training and structures to make this happen.Simon SurteesLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Join a running community – you won’t regret it | Running | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which Ioan Marc Jones describes overcoming his hatred of running
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which Ioan Marc Jones describes overcoming his hatred of running
Content: A parkrun in Porthcawl. ‘I always thought that running was about being elite and competitive, but this showed me another way.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenA parkrun in Porthcawl. ‘I always thought that running was about being elite and competitive, but this showed me another way.’Photograph: GettyRunningLettersJoin a running community – you won’t regret itReaders respond to an article in which Ioan Marc Jones describes overcoming his hatred of runningMon 17 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTShareI loved Ioan Marc Jones’s article because it’s an honest reflection of the struggle of getting into running when you need exercise but don’t necessarily want it (Nipple tape, pickle juice and dinosaurs: how I learned to love running, the unorthodox way, 12 August). For me, the gamechanger was joining a running club. I’m not a naturally social person and I felt so nervous on my first session, but it’s such a warm, nonjudgmental community. I run with people of all ages and it’s really improved my pace and enjoyment of running.I think that’s true of a lot of the running community. I do parkrun here in Yorkshire, but recently ran it in Aviemore and Thurso in Scotland and received such a warm welcome. I always thought that running was about being elite and competitive, but this showed me another way.Sarah TolsonBaildon, West YorkshireI also hate running, but I’ve been doing the local parkrun for 12 years now and have clocked up 341, with the aim of reaching 500 by 2031. It’s always hard work, and it’s become harder as I’ve got older, especially after losing all the fitness I built up before Covid. I stopped running altogether during that period. Now it’s very much a lot of effort for little gain, but it’s worth it. Taking up parkrun is one of the best bits of advice given to me.Aziz Rajab-AliLondonAs a confirmed nonrunner, I enjoyed Ioan Marc Jones’s article about breaking through the boredom and pain of running. But if I could offer him some advice, it would be to try cycling instead. It provides a perfect speed to take in your surroundings, and the need to be in the moment is an antidote to boredom.Nicola RalstonLondonThanks, Ioan Marc Jones, for your funny, frank, inspiring article on finding your own way into the world of running. You’ve shown me how to find my own path and given me a perfect excuse to drink pickle juice. Also, I would have liked your nan, and since I once was in the automotive industry, will henceforth use her term “undercarriage”.Marcia SilvestriPlainville, Massachusetts, USHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Councils won’t be able to block betting shops | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Letters: Roger Cornwell says under government plans, councils will lose some planning powers, and Alan Knight says reducing high-street betting fuels illegal online gambling. Plus a letter from Katrina Kerr
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Roger Cornwell says under government plans, councils will lose some planning powers, and Alan Knight says reducing high-street betting fuels illegal online gambling. Plus a letter from Katrina Kerr
Content: ‘The notion that betting shops are proliferating like weeds is a myth.’Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The notion that betting shops are proliferating like weeds is a myth.’Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersGamblingLettersCouncils won’t be able to block betting shopsRoger Cornwellsays under government plans, councils will lose some planning powers, andAlan Knightsays reducing high-street betting fuels illegal online gambling. Plus a letter fromKatrina KerrMon 17 Aug 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTShareIn your report (Burnham to give councils more powers to block vape and betting shops, 10 August) Angela Rayner is quoted as saying: “We’re giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn’t belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves”. If only.Thenational scheme of delegation, due to come into force on 31 October, will take away the ability from council leaders and planning committees to determine most planning applications, including the change of use proposed here. Instead, they will be delegated to officers. Elected members and parish councils will lose the power to call controversial planning applications to committee. It’s not too late to reverse this decision, which is contrary to the government’s newfound enthusiasm for delegating decisions to local communities.Roger CornwellDurhamThe notion that betting shops are proliferating like weeds is a myth – their number has fallen bymore than a thirdsince 2019. Betting shops are well-regulated enterprises that contribute to the exchequer and serve as centres of local sociability (something I thought our new prime minister was in favour of).Of course, there is problem gambling, but there is also problem drinking, which you don’t solve by closing down pubs. And the more you clobber legal high-street betting, the more you fuel online illegal gambling. This ill-informed nanny-state posturing makes no sense.Alan KnightOxfordRegarding the article by Dawn Butler (To all the betting shops littering our high streets: people power is coming and the odds are against you, 11 August), as a borough councillor for the city centre in Chester, I was horrified to see an application for a slots outlet on one of the main shopping streets in the city. The location was opposite a shop called Smiggle, which sells backpacks and other paraphernalia for children and is on a main walking route to at least three schools. It is right next to the main nightclub in the city and overlapping opening hours were proposed. It is also an area frequented by students, many of whom are known to gamble in an attempt to stretch their meagre resources.The only available grounds for refusal was protection of children and vulnerable people. I had a strong case, backed up by help from Butler’s campaign, plus many protests submitted by nearby landlords, resident groups, schools, the university and other concerned individuals.Despite heartfelt pleas and what I thought was a basic common-sense argument, the panel of three councillors advised by licensing officers approved it. I went home and cried.Thank you, Andy Burnham. It’s too late for this, but in future this would never make it through planning, let alone get a licence.Katrina KerrChesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 13: Leeds | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: After keeping Leeds up last season and reaching an FA Cup semi-final, Daniel Farke has good reason to expect further improvement at Elland Road
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: After keeping Leeds up last season and reaching an FA Cup semi-final, Daniel Farke has good reason to expect further improvement at Elland Road
Content: Lukas Nmecha celebrates after his goal during the pre-season friendly match between Sunderland AFC and Leeds United  Photograph: Rebekah Wynkoop/SPP/ShutterstockAfter keeping Leeds up last season and reaching an FA Cup semi-final, Daniel Farke has good reason to expect further improvement at Elland RoadByLouise TaylorMon 17 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:12th (NB: this is not necessarily Louise Taylor’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:14thProspectsPretty bright. A team’s second season in thePremier Leaguefollowing promotion is traditionally regarded as hazardous but all the indications are that Daniel Farke’s side will not merely harbour a high degree of immunity to this syndrome but could debunk it as a lazy cliche. The spine of the side looks extremely robust and has been reinforced by the club record £40m signing of James Trafford from Manchester City and the £34m acquisition of the Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-half Tarik Muharemovic from Sassuolo.Much hinges on Dominic Calvert-Lewin remaining fit. At times last season, Farke’s centre-forward proved unplayable as Leeds finished a respectable 14th. This time round Calvert-Lewin and his fellow forwards should benefit from assists provided by the talented Harry Wilson, a free transfer recruit from Fulham.Significantly, survival was achieved last spring after an unconvincing start to the campaign that, by November, had placed Farke’s job in jeopardy. After a switch to a, broadly, 3-5-2 formation the team improved, radically. Indeed, were there a separate Premier League table for the second half of the season, Leeds’ form from the start of December would have left them seventh. Pre-season results can be notoriously misleading but it is worth noting that Leeds have impressed against some strong opposition. “Pre-season has given us confidence,” said Farke.While the manager aims to take Leeds to “a new level” such ambition is tempered by sensible caution. “Everyone is talking of Europe and trophies but it’s important we stay humble and grounded,” he said. “In the last 25 years our highest Premier League finish has been ninth so we need to go step by step. The second year after promotion can be difficult and dangerous but we are hopeful we can have a good season.”Past fiveOff-field pictureThe dated, if hugely atmospheric, Elland Road is undergoing a wholesale redevelopment in a project instigated by the club’s owners, 49ers Enterprises, the investment arm of the NFL’s San Francisco 49ers. One of the ideas behind this much-needed stadium modernisation – involving an increase in capacity from 37,792 to 53,000 – is to help increase commercial revenue streams and, in turn, be less restricted by football’s spending rules. Another priority is reducing the lengthy season ticket waiting list. Elland Road should remain fully operational on match days as work progresses on a design intended to be the centrepiece of a wider local regeneration. The only frustration is that city council plans for a new tram network have once again been heavily delayed. With public transport infrastructure poor in a part of Leeds notorious for serious traffic congestion that could prove a big problem on match days at an expanded arena.Owner-fan relationshipDecent. Leeds have had some unpredictable owners in recent years so the sense of stability, professionalism and vision introduced by the California-based 49ers Enterprises has been welcome. With Elland Road now in the process of being redeveloped, Trafford recently becoming the club’s record signing and commercial income being boosted appreciably, few doubt the ownership’s ambition. A senior executive team comprising chair, Paraag Marathe, managing director, Robbie Evans, and sporting director, Adam Underwood, is generally regarded as efficient, sensible and sufficiently realistic to remain on the right side of football’s spending rules.The managerFarke says his personality is “95% coffee and cake on the sofa and 5% fire beast”. An economics graduate who originally intended to become a sporting director, the 49-year-old one time lower division German striker and, later, Norwich manager is an interesting, multi-dimensional character with an engaging sense of humour and a love of literary fiction. In steering then newly promoted Leeds to the safety of 14thposition last season while also reaching an FA Cup semi-final, Farke lost the “trampoline man” tag that, rather unfairly, had suggested his career largely involved either winning promotion or facing relegation. A coach close to Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp and Thomas Tuchel has described himself as “a football romantic who has learned that romanticism shouldn’t blind you to reality”. As he explains: “My brand of football normally suits teams who dominate possession but I’m always switched on to what is necessary.”Star signingView image in fullscreenTarik Muharemovic comes in from Serie A to bolster the Leeds defence.Photograph: Richard Bierton/Every Second Media/ShutterstockThe 23-year-old left-sided central defender Muharemovic has looked outstanding in pre-season. The £34m signing from Serie A has imbued Farke’s defence with not merely robust physicality and controlled aggression but assurance on the ball and a refined passing range. The manner in which he bundled Sunderland’s formidable Netherlands centre-forward Brian Brobbey over in pre-season delighted Leeds fans who have already labelled him the Bosnian King. After helping Sassuolo win promotion from Serie B, Muharemovic played a big part in securing a mid-table Serie A finish last season. Comfortable in a back three or a back four, he appears an inspired reinforcement for a team that, further forward, also seem likely to benefit from Wilson’s arrival.Set for a breakthroughIn recruiting Trafford, Leeds pulled off quite a coup. The 23-year-old England goalkeeper, currently understudy to Jordan Pickford in Tuchel’s squad, shone at Burnley in the Championship and arguably deserved more than to be No 2 at City last term. Trafford’s excellence with his feet can only enhance Farke’s team and his all-round talent and impressive poise under pressure should guarantee Leeds some invaluable extra points. All the indications are that the son of a Cumbrian farmer who still tries to lend a hand at lambing time is about to show the world how good he really is.World Cup impactAlthough the versatile forward ended last season in fine form for Leeds, Noah Okafor played just 25 minutes as a substitute – against Algeria – as Switzerland reached the quarter-finals, eventually bowing out to Argentina. Given Okafor’s previous rift with Murat Yakin, Switzerland’s head coach, there was a degree of surprise when he was included in his World Cup squad and it appears he had not done quite enough to earn Yakin’s full trust. Despite making one appearance for the United States as they reached the last 16 it was still a good summer for Brenden Aaronson. Farke’s trusted attacking midfielder briefly left the US pre-tournament training camp in late May and returned a married man after his long-planned wedding to Milana D’Ambra.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Leeds UnitedPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter consider selling Chelsea shares to Clearlake Capital | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in Chelsea in a deal that would give the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, full control
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in Chelsea in a deal that would give the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, full control
Content: Todd Boehly’s group and Clearlake have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenTodd Boehly’s group and Clearlake have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersChelseaTodd Boehly and Mark Walter consider selling Chelsea shares to Clearlake CapitalChelsea chair Boehly and Walter each own about 13%Sale would give Clearlake effective control of club at 86%Matt HughesMon 17 Aug 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheChelseachair, Todd Boehly, and director Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in the club to the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, in a deal that would give the private equity company complete control at Stamford Bridge.Clearlake, whose investment is managed by Behdad Eghbali and José E Feliciano, already owns more than 60% of Chelsea, but in an unusual arrangement agreedwhen buying the clubfrom Roman Abramovich four years ago, they share operational control with a consortium led by Boehly, who along with Walter and Hansjörg Wyss each own about 13%.The two ownership groups have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years when reports first emerged thatthey were seeking to buy each other outfollowing a disagreement over strategy, particularly regarding theirplans for a new stadium.Premier League to allow audio of conversations between players and refereesRead moreDiscussions over a potential deal, which would value the club at more than £5bn, have resumed over the past few weeks however,as first reported by the Financial Times, as Walter is seeking to raise funds to pay off insurers following a US federal investigation over alleged tax fraud.Walter is being investigated by the US Department of Justice over $21bn in loans which it has been alleged were not disclosed to state insurance regulators, which has led to the sudden sale of assets to pay down some of the loans. Walter last week sold the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh ⁠Kushner and Bob Iger ⁠for $12.5bn just a year after buying the NBA franchise for $10bn, leading to speculation that the 66-year-old may also seek to exit Chelsea.Boehly and Walter are close friends as well as longstanding business partners, having previously invested together in the LA Dodgers Major League Baseball team and the LA Sparks WNBA franchise.Together with Wyss, the pair control 38% of Chelsea through Blueco 22 Holdings, although it is unclear whether the Swiss billionaire is also willing to sell. Under the terms of their £2.5bn purchase from Abramovich after the Russian was sanctioned by the UK government following the invasion of Ukraine however, none of Chelsea’s shareholders can sell to a third party without the consent of their partners.An external sale is therefore unlikely, putting Clearlake in a strong position to gain the complete control it has been seeking for some time, although Boehly and Walter will demand a significant premium on the £325m they paid for their shares four years ago.View image in fullscreenTodd Boehly leaving would give Behdad Eghbali’s Clearlake Capital effective control of Chelsea.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesA sale by Boehly and Walter would leave Clearlake with more than 86% of Chelsea’s shares and effective control of the club, including the bid to build a new stadium, which they want to locate at Stamford Bridge.Walter has been a silent and barely visible partner at Chelsea, but Boehly was the public face of the club following the 2022 takeover and acted as interim sporting director during that year’s summer transfer window, leading the purchase of players such as Raheem Sterling and Marc Cucurella.Boehly stepped back from that hands-on role after 12 months, with Eghbali taking more operational control on behalf of Clearlake, but has often been blamed by Chelsea fans for the side’s underperformance.Boehly was due to stand down as chair at the end of the season, with a Clearlake representative to replace him for the next five years under the terms of the ownership agreement.The timing of an exit at this stage would be ironic, as after spending years investing heavily in young players with resale value at Clearlake’s behest, Chelsea have returned to Boehly’s original strategy this summer by signing experienced players such as Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson.Representatives of Clearlake, Boehly and Chelsea were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsChelseanewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunter Bell sets sights on Hodgkinson, Werro and Broeders-Bol in 800m clash of titans | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Georgia Hunter Bell says she is ready to take on the ‘Big Three’ of Audrey Werro, Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol in a race for the ages in Zurich next week
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Georgia Hunter Bell says she is ready to take on the ‘Big Three’ of Audrey Werro, Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol in a race for the ages in Zurich next week
