Content: Georgia Hunter Bell celebrates with the gold after her win in the 1500m in Birmingham.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APView image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell celebrates with the gold after her win in the 1500m in Birmingham.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsHunter Bell sets sights on Hodgkinson, Werro and Broeders-Bol in 800m clash of titansBig Three and Hunter Bell to meet in Zurich next week‘I am really excited to throw my hat into the ring there’Sean IngleMon 17 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgia Hunter Bell says she is ready to take on the “Big Three” of Audrey Werro, Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol in a race for the ages over 800m in Zurich next week.Hunter Bell has had an extraordinary season, adding the1500m European Championship titleon Sunday to herCommonwealth 800m goldand 1500m world indoor crown. She is now ready to put herself to the test in a fast-paced 800m against the three Birmingham medallists.‘Champagne and a KFC’: how Hunt celebrated historic haul at European ChampionshipsRead more“There is still a lot left of the season,” said Hunter Bell. “I haven’t done a paced 800m yet, I have one coming up with the speedy girls. I am really excited to throw my hat into the ring there. Had a bit of fomo when I saw them on the podium. It’s such an exciting time. I am really happy.”There are some who believe that a fast-paced 800m in Zurich could get close to the world record of 1min 53.28sec, set in 1983 by the Czech Jarmila Kratochvilova, especially with the Swiss star Werro having run 1:53.80 this season – the third fastest in history.Hunter Bell could certainly be in the mix given she appears to be in the form of her life. “I haven’t run a personal best so far this year yet but weirdly you could say I’m having my best year because I keep on winning,” she said.Hunter Bell also revealed that she and the top trio had been talking to the world champion Lilian Odira about setting up a big five clash before the end of 2026.“I can’t wait for that, hopefully the big five will come together soon,” she added. “We’ve been talking after the races. ‘When are you racing? You should get into this one.’ There’s a good competitive spirit.”The most likely opportunity is the Ultimate Championships in Budapest next month, where there will be a $150,000 (£110,000) first prize on the line. “In a good way, people aren’t swerving opportunities, everyone is trying to do it together,” Hunter Bell said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHunter Bell agreed that the leading women 800m runners were like prizefighters, who believed they could beat anyone. “But there’s respect too,” she said. “Obviously you want to win. If you are in the same race, everyone runs really fast, whoever comes out on top, that’s fun. We’ll see how it goes.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s time for freakishly gifted Harry Brook to come of age in England’s post-Bazball era | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Test captaincy came too soon for 27-year-old but Pakistan series is latest chapter in year that could be the making of him
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Test captaincy came too soon for 27-year-old but Pakistan series is latest chapter in year that could be the making of him
Content: Coming out swinging? Harry Brook will play at his home ground of Headingley in England’s first Test against Pakistan.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenComing out swinging? Harry Brook will play at his home ground of Headingley in England’s first Test against Pakistan.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEngland cricket teamIt’s time for freakishly gifted Harry Brook to come of age in England’s post-Bazball eraAli MartinTest captaincy came too soon for 27-year-old but Pakistan series is latest chapter in year that could be the making of himMon 17 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTShareYou have to hand it to Bazball. Even when seemingly killed off, and the England team it left behind is thousands of miles away, preparing for a series against Pakistan, it has still managed to muscle its way into the fallout fromBangladesh’s seismic victory over Australiain Darwin. Talk about main character energy.By definition, thatnine-wicket victory for Bangladeshwas no fluke. Najmul Hossain Shanto’s men didn’t jag a tight one but rather dominated their hosts over four days. And in doing so, they also managed to unite Ashes rivals by demonstrating what a golden opportunity England blew against Australia’s greybeards last winter.Appointment of Root and Fleming has been a mess but they could be a good blend | Mark RamprakashRead moreTo say as much back then was to risk being called as deluded as the team itself; to be an enabler of the hubris that underpinned England’s gung-ho approach. Stuart Broad, for example, was widely lampooned for saying that Australia, though an excellent side, were ageing and as vulnerable as they had been for a long time.But plenty of Australian voices are now making the same point, either directly or by implication. A common refrain has been that, had England batted “sensibly” – ie with the same gimlet-eyed application of Bangladesh in a match-defining 400-plus total amassed over 138 overs –that sorry 4-1 defeatcould have been very different.While England’s bowling has been forgotten here – Bangladesh opted against feeding Travis Head’s cut shot like it was a goose being fattened for foie gras – thoughts certainly do go back to the defining collapses in Perth and Brisbane, when a string of batters hardwired to attack ignored the risk that seemed so obvious.Among them was Harry Brook, whose most recent act in the whites of England was to go down swingingagainst New Zealandand trigger another wave of chuntering about there being more brains in a pork pie. Brook was following team orders but all people saw was 21 off nine balls and yet another example of Harry-kiri.In a parallel universe Brook is about to captain England’s Test team for the first time at his home ground of Headingley this week. Instead, England have turned back to Joe Root as the successor to Ben Stokes, with Rob Key saying the vacancy had come “too soon” for Brook and hinting that greater maturity was needed.Perhaps it was too great an ask for Brook to lead across all three formats, or too messy to hive off the T20 captaincy to another player under split coaches. Of course the unsaid bit here isthat nightclub incidentin Wellington last November – the spark for the chain reaction that ultimately created the vacancy.Although beyond learning that knocking back hazy pale ales the night before captaining in a one-day international is probably a bad idea, how much does Brook actually need to change his approach?Clearly driving on the up in unfamiliar Perth was not smart from Brook, likewise trying to larrup Mitchell Starc under lights in his first pink-ball Test. Overall his Ashes was disappointing and a year has passed since his last Test century – a period in which wicketkeepers Alex Carey and Tom Blundell standing up to the quicks has caused him issues.But as much asthe removal of Brendon McCullumas England’s Test head coach after the 2-1 defeat by New Zealand signals a desire for the pendulum to swing back a touch overall, Brook feels the very least of their problems right now. The fact is, for all that his dismissals can be triggering in the moment, Brook has already put up the kind of numbers that mark him out as a truly remarkable talent. After 38 Tests he averages 53, has scored 10 centuries (includinga triple in Multan), and he sits second in the Test batting rankings behind Head.View image in fullscreenInconsistency struck again for Harry Brook, who was out for 21 in Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes’s final innings with England against New Zealand.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesAs per the good people at CricViz, Brook has achieved this by trying to smack 44% of deliveries to or over the boundary – a figure only Head can match. More broadly, the 27-year-old looks to score off 65% of balls he faces, and defend or leave 35%. The average split for top-seven batters since his debut in 2022 has been 52/48.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe lazy assumption is that this has been achieved on flat pitches. But while true Brook is lethal in these conditions – Pakistan know better than anyone, victims of four Brook centuries on home soil, including that career-best 317 – like Head, he can come into his own when the ball is doing plenty for the bowlers.His century in Wellingtonin late 2024 is a prime example, compiled from just 91 balls, and on an opening day when 15 wickets tumbled. A personal view is that he should have been player of the matchin Melbourne last winter, with his 41 on the opening day of that crapshoot absolutely central to the end result.Quick GuideCharlie Dean to captain England for Ireland ODI seriesShowCharlie Dean will captain England in next month’s three one-day internationals against Ireland in the absence of Nat Sciver-Brunt.Dean stood in for Sciver-Brunt during white-ball series against New Zealand and India this summer then again when the all-rounder was injured during the group stage of the T20 World Cup.Sciver-Brunt is continuing to manage her fitness and recovery, as is Danni Wyatt-Hodge, so they will miss the Ireland series, alongside fellow senior players Sophie Ecclestone, Lauren Bell and Amy Jones.England squad to face Ireland:C Dean (captain), M Bouchier, A Capsey, K Chathli, T Corteen-Coleman, S Dunkley, L Filer, D Gibson, J Grewcock, F Kemp, R MacDonald-Gay, C Pavely, G Potts, M Villiers, I Wong.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Naturally people still want more. Stokes even took Brook aside at the end of that Ashes series and told him he should be averaging “65, even 70” in Test cricket. The diagnosis here was that Brook, like a lot of modern players, has a 360-degree armoury of shots but is still learning when and where to deploy them.For AB de Villiers, whose remarkable hand-eye ability was comparable to Brook, it similarly comes down to risk assessment; being able to spot when the odds are against him and, whether it is five deliveries or an hour, holding firm until it flips in his favour. “Definitely don’t lose the aggressive nature of your batting or the creative side,”De Villiers told For The Love of Cricket. “Just earn the right.”As pera recent chat with BBC Sport, Brook acknowledges this and gets as frustrated as the next person at some of his dismissals. But his stated aim is still to be a matchwinner for England first and foremost. “I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games,” he said.Some supporters may recoil at this but really they should be encouraged. As much as the excesses of Bazball squandered a golden chance in Australia, overall it allowed the freakishly gifted Brook to discover the limits of what is possible. Avoid an over-correction and this tricky last year could yet be the making of him.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamHarry BrookPakistan cricket teamCricketcommentShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fery gives Alex de Minaur stern test before bowing out in Cincinnati | Arthur Fery | The Guardian
description: Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery was beaten 7-5, 7-6 by Alex de Minaur on the day he was called up to the GB Davis Cup squad to play Ecuador next month
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery was beaten 7-5, 7-6 by Alex de Minaur on the day he was called up to the GB Davis Cup squad to play Ecuador next month
Content: Arthur Fery hits a forehand shot in his defeat by Alex de Minaur.Photograph: Scott Stuart/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenArthur Fery hits a forehand shot in his defeat by Alex de Minaur.Photograph: Scott Stuart/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockArthur FeryArthur Fery gives Alex de Minaur stern test before bowing out in CincinnatiWimbledon semi-finalist loses 7-5, 7-6 in third roundDisappointment on day of GB Davis Cup squad call-upTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiMon 17 Aug 2026 18.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most pertinent question surrounding the rapidly blossoming career ofArthur Feryis exactly how far he could possibly take his game. Fery’s unexpected breakthrough run at Wimbledon last month was immense, but now he faces the intriguing challenge of seeing how he stacks up against the elite over the course of a gruelling 52 weeks on tour.Fery ended his first tournament since Wimbledon with countless reasons to be positive about his progress even as he was outperformed by Alex de Minaur in a rain-swept encounter, with Fery, the 32nd seed, making life incredibly difficult for the fifth seed for over two hours and fighting desperately until the end before falling 7-5, 7-6 (3) in the third round of the Cincinnati Open.Elena Rybakina leads call for changes to 2028 calendar after schedule chaosRead moreThis was a tight encounter even once De Minaur took control of the match. Fery began serving well, but after not facing a break point in his first five service games, one loose game on his serve allowed the Australian to break through.De Minaur, who was cheered on from his player box by his wife and Fery’s fellow British No 2 Katie Boulter, returned from the rain delay between the first and second sets on fire, his supreme defensive skills narrowing the court and exposing Fery’s relative lack of raw firepower. However, a rain delay at 5-7, 1-5 allowed Fery to regroup and he returned from the break completely relaxed and striking the ball beautifully as he dragged De Minaur into a tie-break before surrendering the match.Fery leaves Mason, Ohio, having put together another strong week filled with valuable experiences. Exactly a year ago, the 24-year-old won his first ATP Challenger title in Barranquilla, a monumental result in his career. Here, he reached the third round of a Masters 1000 with just one win, a bruising 6-4, 2-6, 7-6(4) victory over James Duckworth after receiving a first-round bye. He still earned nearly as many points – 50 to 75 – for one win in Cincinnati and his prize money of $36,110 here, his biggest paycheck outside his three grand slam main-draw appearances, is $22,000 greater than his earnings in Colombia.When players first reach the top level of the ATP or WTA tours, one significant adjustment is understanding that they will not win as many matches as they are used to, but they are still performing at a much higher level. Fery’s victory over the world No 86 Duckworth was, by ranking, the sixth-best win of his career. Competing regularly against players of De Minaur’s quality is what will allow him to continue to progress as a player.Such is the uncertainty of tennis scheduling, Fery and De Minaur already had to wait around for hours as Flavio Cobolli, the seventh seed, completed his two-hour, 29-minute comeback win against Alexander Blockx.Quick GuideFery gets first Davis Cup call-upShowArthur Fery has been named in the Great Britain Davis Cup team for the home qualifying tie against Ecuador next month.The 24-year-old, who  reached the semi-finals at Wimbledon this summer, is joined by Cameron Norrie and the doubles players Henry Patten and Lloyd Glasspool.There remains a fifth spot up for grabs, which could go to Jack Draper if the former world No 4 can get back to fitness after an injury-ravaged year.“We know Ecuador will be right up for the challenge, so to be able to call on our top two singles players and two of the world’s best doubles players – all of whom have had good results in recent weeks – gives us a great chance of securing the win,” said the GB captain Leon Smith.The tie takes place at London’s Copper Box on September 19-20, with the winners going through to the Final 8 in November.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Once they finally made it to the court, they played less than two games before rain forced them off. Fery and De Minaur returned to stiflingly humid conditions, with both players sweating profusely and trying to remain as fresh as possible in a physical match.Fery looked comfortable early on, taking care of his service games well as he constantly looked to take the ball early, dictate from the baseline and conjure opportunities to close down the net. The margins at this level, however, are so narrow. Fifty minutes into the match, with the score tied at 5-5, De Minaur took advantage of a couple of missed first serves from Fery, attacking from early in the first two points to lead 0-30.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA loose forehand error at 30-30 and then a forehand volley error off an excellent dipping passing shot from De Minaur were the difference between them. De Minaur, who had faced three break points earlier in the set, followed up the break with a quick love hold and Fery was suddenly down a set. By the time they sat down at the changeover, the skies opened again and rain forced them off the court.There would be no positive momentum shift for Fery after the second rain delay, with De Minaur’s excellent defensive skills separating them as he eked out a series of tight games to establish a double-break lead in the set. With De Minaur leading 7-5, 5-1, they were forced off once more.This time, the momentum could not have shifted more dramatically. Fery was suddenly commanding the baseline, controlling every point and dominating against an increasingly tense De Minaur. Fery incredibly reeled off five consecutive games from the rain delay to reach 6-5, but De Minaur regrouped with a timely hold before confidently closing out the match in a tie-break.Elsewhere, Iga Swiatek continued to build her confidence and form on the court as she recovered from a set down to continue her title defence by reaching the fourth round with a 4-6, 6-1, 6-1 win over Maria Sakkari, the 29th seed. Elena Rybakina, the second seed, advanced with a 6-4, 7-6 (2) win over Magdalena Frech. Earlier on Monday, Fery was announced as part of his second Davis Cup team, with Fery and Cameron Norrie leading the Great Britain team in their tie against Ecuador in the second round of the Davis Cup qualifiers next month at the Copper Box in London.Explore more on these topicsArthur FeryTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rubin Colwill’s last-gasp free-kick earns Cardiff dramatic point against Wrexham | Championship | The Guardian
description: Rubin Colwill’s stoppage-time equaliser earned Cardiff a 1-1 draw with Welsh rivals Wrexham after Kieffer Moore had given the visitors a third-minute lead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rubin Colwill’s stoppage-time equaliser earned Cardiff a 1-1 draw with Welsh rivals Wrexham after Kieffer Moore had given the visitors a third-minute lead
Content: Rubin Colwill’s free-kick heads for the back of the net as Cardiff snatch a point deep into added time.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRubin Colwill’s free-kick heads for the back of the net as Cardiff snatch a point deep into added time.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockChampionshipRubin Colwill’s last-gasp free-kick earns Cardiff dramatic point against WrexhamPA MediaMon 17 Aug 2026 17.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRubin Colwill scored a ferocious equaliser with almost the final kick of the match to earn Cardiff a 1-1Championshipdraw with Wrexham.Wrexham appeared to have the Welsh derby bragging rights sewn up as the contest ticked into the eighth minute of added time atCardiff CityStadium.Flemming’s dramatic Burnley double pegs back West Ham on Championship returnRead moreBut George Dobson brought down Joel Colwill on the edge of the box, and his brother Rubin stepped up to lash a brilliant free-kick over the wall and past Anthony Patterson in theWrexhamgoal.Colwill’s strike cancelled out Kieffer Moore’s third-minute effort, the former Cardiff forward continuing his habit of scoring against his former employers – his seventh goal against the Bluebirds.Wrexham had 18 goal attempts to 11 and, in truth, should have prevented any late anxiety by putting the game beyond the hosts back at this level after a season in League One.Cardiff’s defensive resources had been stretched by injuries to Calum Chambers, Dylan Lawlor and Will Fish, so much so that the usual left-back Joel Bagan was switched inside to partner Gabriel Osho in the heart of defence.The new-look partnership was exposed immediately after Cardiff only managed to clear a Lewis O’Brien free-kick as far as Danny Imray, and his ball forward caught the hosts napping.Osho played Moore onside and the striker broke beyond Bagan to rifle the ball above Nathan Trott’s head for his first goal since February, ending his run of 11 Wrexham games without scoring.Trott tipped over Callum Doyle’s header as Cardiff appeared to struggle to get to grips with the pace of Championship football. But the Bluebirds slowly improved and had a good spell midway through the first half after Zak Vyner left a back pass short and Patterson reacted smartly to beat Yousef Salech to the loose ball.View image in fullscreenWrexham’s Kieffer Moore roars in delight after giving his side an early lead at Cardiff.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAJack Moylan then scooped over and Patterson made a comfortable save from Cian Ashford after some slick Cardiff passing.Wrexham went close to a second when Moore rose well from an O’Brien cross and skimmed the crossbar with a header. Imray’s scuffed shot then forced a save from Trott, although the ball appeared to be heading wide anyway.Just as they had at the start of the game, Cardiff switched off after the restart. Ollie Rathbone’s ball inside found Doyle, but Trott was alive at the near post to save with his foot. Trott made a more comfortable stop from Nathan Broadhead before Doyle lashed a rasping drive past him and on to a post.Cardiff sent on the Colwill brothers just after the hour mark to try to shift momentum in their favour, and Moylan saw his deflected effort drift just wide.Dominic Hyam headed against his own crossbar, but Cardiff kept pushing and ultimately denied Wrexham their first win in the Welsh capital since 1992.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipCardiff CityWrexhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City opener was startlingly bad | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Community Shield isn’t always a sign of things to come, but City’s form in their defeat to Arsenal is concerning in the wake of Pep Guardiola’s departure
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The Community Shield isn’t always a sign of things to come, but City’s form in their defeat to Arsenal is concerning in the wake of Pep Guardiola’s departure
Content: Elliot Anderson, Enzo Maresca and Mateo Kovacic endured a tough afternoon on Sunday.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElliot Anderson, Enzo Maresca and Mateo Kovacic endured a tough afternoon on Sunday.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonSoccerEnzo Maresca’s Manchester City opener was startlingly badThe Community Shield isn’t always a sign of things to come, but City’s form in their defeat to Arsenal is concerning in the wake of Pep Guardiola’s departureSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 17 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are caveats. It was only the Community Shield – and no side has gone on to win the league after lifting the Community Shield since 2018. It was against the league champions, whose pre-season has involved far less strenuous travel than their own. By the time the season really gets going, there will be greater clarity in central midfield, with Rodriset to complete his move to Barcelonaimminently. But this was a startlingly bad opening for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City.Succeeding a manager of Pep Guardiola’s stature is never easy, as numerous clubs have found. But it’s not just Guardiola’s stature, the sense that whoever follows him stands in his shadow. It’s that his style of play is so idiosyncratic that the transition process inevitably becomes more difficult. Even though Maresca was Guardiola’s assistant at City in 2022-23, and his football is Guardiola-inspired, it is not identical, not least because Guardiola was always evolving. Even allowing for all that, though, it was remarkable how poorly City defended intheir 3-0 defeat by Arsenal on Sunday.Arsenal played well. There was a sharpness to them and a slickness to their passing that wasn’t always present last season. Fears that they may have lost their appetite having ended their 22-year wait for the title may have been overstated (although much, much tougher tests await). But City were a rabble, limited going forward and a shambles at the back.Are Manchester United returning to relevance under Michael Carrick? | Jonathan WilsonRead moreIt was the second goal that will really have worried them, because Arsenal had to do so little to score. Martin Ødegaard was given time to measure his cross. Christos Tzolis wandered off the back of Abdukodir Khusanov. Then Kai Havertz, slightly more explicably, pulled away from Rúben Dias. In Khusanov’s defence, it probably should be acknowledged that he does not usually play at right-back, but he has occupied the role before. A wide player drifting off your back should not come as a shock; perhaps it’s just pre-season and he was not as alert as he will be, but it was a baffling error. But it was of a piece with the wider whole; throughout, City seemed off the pace, not as focused as Arsenal. Even if that improves as the season goes on, it’s a problem if City have title aspirations; how far clear will Arsenal be by the time City finally click – if they do click?But there were structural issues on that flank as well. Antoine Semenyo was barely involved. Elliot Anderson, on the right of the midfield two, was unable to check the forward surges of Riccardo Calafiori, who scored the first and whose run played a key role in the third. An attacking left-back, even one with as much freedom to drift infield as the Italian enjoys, shouldn’t cause that much trouble.The midfield issue desperately needs resolving. Rodri was an unused substitute as talks about his possible likely move to Barcelona go on (City accepted a bidfor him on Sunday night). It’s not just his quality that will be missed; his organisational abilities will be too. Enzo Fernández, who worked with Maresca at Chelsea, did seem to have been lined up as a replacement for Rodri but City did not submit a bid before the Friday 5pm deadline Chelsea had placed for selling the midfielder. Mateo Kovacic spent much of last season deputising for Rodri but he is 32 now; he is not the future. Factor in the loss of Bernardo Silva as well, and there is a serious shortfall in midfield.Generally, in fact, City’s squad looks a little short. Dias and Marc Guéhi are the only defenders over 25. There are plenty of attacking midfielders but Omar Marmoush has never really convinced as a back-up to Erling Haaland. The £200m spree in January 2025 may have helped stop the rot, but the players who came in then – not just Marmoush and Khusanov but also Vitor Reis and Nico González – would not be badly missed now. City, once so focused in their spending, have started to make mistakes. Tijjani Reijnders, brought in last summer for £50m, is about to be shipped on. Rayan Aït-Nouri was a baffling signing when he arrived and nothing in the past year has changed that view.Maresca must have looked at Arsenal’s squad, the extraordinary options available to Mikel Arteta in midfield, and despaired. Put generously, his is a squad in transition, although it’s starting to look as though it may be a squad in decline. The sense over the past couple of years was of Guardiola, slowly, passing his peak, but in retrospect perhaps it was only his genius that kept an ailing City competitive.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe evidence of Sunday, with all due caveats about the stage of the season, is that this may be a very bad time for Maresca to have replaced Guardiola. Taking over from a legend would be extremely challenging in the best of circumstances, and these are starting to look like they may be very bad circumstances.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsFootballSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester CityEnzo MarescaPremier LeaguenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Finland halts deportation of Russian family who ‘risked everything’ to oppose Ukraine invasion | Finland | The Guardian
description: Mother and son Olga and Nikita Belov say they were facing jail and potential torture after asylum case was rejected
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Mother and son Olga and Nikita Belov say they were facing jail and potential torture after asylum case was rejected
Content: Since their arrival in Finland, Nikita Belov and his mother, Olga, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine including by sending aid.Photograph: Nikita BelovView image in fullscreenSince their arrival in Finland, Nikita Belov and his mother, Olga, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine including by sending aid.Photograph: Nikita BelovFinlandFinland halts deportation of Russian family who ‘risked everything’ to oppose Ukraine invasionMother and son Olga and Nikita Belov say they were facing jail and potential torture after asylum case was rejectedMiranda BryantNordic correspondentMon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian familywho were on the brink of being deported from Finlandafter repeatedly being denied asylum – despite the threat of arrest, imprisonment and torture for their pro-Ukrainian activism – have won a court appeal and will have their case reconsidered.Nikita Belov and his mother, Olga Belov, fled their homeland for Finland in 2022 after attracting the attention of Russian authorities – including a military summons, threatening messages and attempts to locate them – for expressing opposition to the full-scale invasion ofUkraine.They were due to be deported fromFinlandwithin weeks after the Finnish immigration service said they faced “no real risk” if they returned to Russia. In April they were temporarily detained by authorities pending deportation.The administrative court has quashed the decision, citing new evidence, including media coverage in Finnish, Russian and internationally, and referred the case back to the immigration service for fresh consideration.The Belovs’ case has gained political traction in neighbouring Norway. Last week politicians from Norway’s Green party tried to stage an intervention, proposing to the government that if the Belovs’ deportation went through, Norway should offer them asylum instead.The political activist and Putin criticBill Browder, who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, has said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”.Nikita, 25, left his engineering job at a research institute in Moscow specialising in metallurgical technologies after finding out the work he was doing was connected to the Russian war effort.Since their arrival in Finland, Nikita and Olga, 55, a nurse anaesthetist, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine, sending humanitarian aid, including to the Ukrainian armed forces.Olga said the court’s decision marked the first positive news they had received in four years but that it was overshadowed by “constant uncertainty and fear of deportation”.She added: “My health has deteriorated over these four years, and we still have to wait for a final decision. This is very stressful, and nobody knows how long it will take. This experience has already left a lasting mark on our lives, and we will have to cope with the consequences. No matter what, I’d like to thank everybody who helps us, supports us, and literally saves us from death.”Nikita said: “Previously, when I imagined my reaction to a positive decision, I was sure it would be a very emotional moment. But actually, I felt nothing. It’s weird, but now it seems to me that I’m already mentally exhausted. We still have to wait for a final decision.”Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, hopes they will be granted asylum soon. “The court has overturned the negative asylum decision as the clients have provided so much new evidence on them being profiled as being at risk of persecution,” they said. “The international attention and vast media coverage on the case and whether it puts them at risk has to be assessed accurately by the Finnish immigration service.”Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitskydied at the hands of Putin’s regime, said the latest decision was an “important victory for Nikita and Olga, but it should never have got this far”.He added: “Finland is on the frontline of defendingEuropeagainst Putin’s aggression. It would be completely perverse for it to send two people who have stood publicly against that aggression straight back into Putin’s hands. I hope the Finnish authorities will now grant Nikita and Olga the protection they deserve.”Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection at the Finnish immigration service, said he was unable to comment on individual cases, but added: “Only approximately 5% of all decisions are returned for reconsideration each year. The vast majority of these cases are due to the applicant presenting new information about their situation during the judicial proceedings.“The asylum decisions of the Finnish immigration service therefore correspond well with national legal practice and are also in line with the average decision-making practices of EU member states.”Explore more on these topicsFinlandRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it ‘gets in the way’ of ending Iran war | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: President issues threat to ‘bomb the shit out of them’ after previously threatening Gulf ally in May
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: President issues threat to ‘bomb the shit out of them’ after previously threatening Gulf ally in May
Content: Donald Trump yells to reporters after disembarking Air Force One on Sunday at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump yells to reporters after disembarking Air Force One on Sunday at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APUS-Israel war on IranDonald Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it ‘gets in the way’ of ending Iran warPresident issues threat to ‘bomb the shit out of them’ after previously threatening Gulf ally in MayJoseph GedeonandAndrew Rothin WashingtonMon 17 Aug 2026 09.43 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has again threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of his effort to end theUS-Israel war on Iran, as the two-month window to negotiate peace with Iran expired on Monday with no end to the conflict in sight.The latest threats againstOman, which is not a party to the war, have illustrated how Trump’s unpredictable and often outrageous approach to diplomacy has upset US partners and failed to achieve the breakthrough that he has promised to end the war.“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trumptold Fox Newson Monday, the second time he has directed such a threat at Muscat, a longtime US strategic partner that has traditionally served as a key backchannel between Washington and Tehran.The various conflicts in the Middle East continued on Monday, with Yemen’s Houthis claiming to have targeted military ships from Saudi Arabia – a US ally – in a missile and drone strike in the Red Sea. Saudi officials did not confirm the strike, which the Houthis said had struck a Saudi military ship and four escort vessels. The attack is said to have taken place at a port close to the Bab-al Mandeb strait, an important global shipping route that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.In Israel, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met Benjamin Netanyahu for more than four hours after the Israeli prime minister rejected a US-backed peace plan for the Gaza war that included a withdrawal of Israeli troops from the devastated territory. Netanyahu has said he rejected any withdrawal that would take place before Hamas fully disarms. Kushner was said to have told Netanyahu not to create obstacles to a peace deal, US officials told media outlets.Trump has staked the political legacy of his second presidential term as being the “peacemaker-in-chief”, but his efforts to disengage the US from conflicts across the Middle East are stalling.The US president delivered the threat against Oman as hestruggles to draw the conflict to a conclusion, almost six months after it was launched, and as a diplomatic window agreed with Tehran ran out with no final agreement in sight. But Trump also claimed during Monday’s interview that he was “not in a hurry” to reach a deal.That two-month window for a negotiated settlement closed on Monday without a breakthrough. Trump has repeatedly claimed the war would end “soon”, and talked up the prospect of a lasting peace deal in recent months, without such a breakthrough materialising.In the same interview, Trump saidIranshould “put up the white flag of surrender”, but signalled he was not about to impose a fresh deadline on Tehran. “I have no time schedule. I’m not in a hurry,” he said.Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Iran at the Palace of Versailles on 17 June, on the sidelines of the G7 summit, which had paused hostilities and set a maximum 60-day window – extendable only by mutual consent – for the two sides to reach a comprehensive deal covering sanctions relief, Iran’s nuclear programme and other disputes.Trump also dismissed concerns that Washington’s own arsenal was being depleted by nearly six months of fighting, telling Fox News that what the US had expended against Iran so far was “peanuts”.He suggested many of the US’s more advanced munitions, including air defence systems, had already been “given away” to Ukraine under his predecessor, Joe Biden – a claim that echoes warnings from defence analysts earlier in the war that US and allied stockpiles were being drawn down faster than they could be replenished.The remarks came after Trump used his Truth Social platform to restate his negotiating red line. “The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon,” he wrote.The strait of Hormuz – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIran is to the north of the strait. Oman is to the south. The two countries have been in talks over control of the strait.In a casual aside at a cabinet meeting in May, the presidentalso threatened to “blow up”Oman if it failed to “behave”.It comes after Trump alsothreatened to declare the strait of Hormuzas “a territory of the United States” during a speech on Friday.In addition to Oman’s decades-long military and economic ties with the US, the Gulf nation of 5.3 million people has played a mediation role in the war and has itself come under attack from Tehran.Iran’s foreign ministry said on Monday that talks with Oman were “continuing in earnest”, despite Trump’s latest outburst.Trump also confirmed for the first time that Washington had opened a direct backchannel to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which the US and Israel have targeted throughout the conflict.“They’re good poker players, but they’re dying,” he said of the IRGC leadership.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpOmanIranUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: People with severe intellectual disabilities live 24 years less on average | Learning disability | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Research also finds stark ethnic disparities, and 40% of deaths among group classed as avoidable
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Exclusive: Research also finds stark ethnic disparities, and 40% of deaths among group classed as avoidable
Content: A meeting of a book club aimed at people with intellectual or developmental disabilities.Photograph: Chris Stephens/APView image in fullscreenA meeting of a book club aimed at people with intellectual or developmental disabilities.Photograph: Chris Stephens/APLearning disabilityPeople with severe intellectual disabilities live 24 years less on averageExclusive: Research also finds stark ethnic disparities, and 40% of deaths among group classed as avoidableTobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentMon 17 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople living with severe intellectual disabilities are dying 24 years younger on average than the wider population, a study has found, with 40% of such deaths being avoidable.The study also found that within this group, people from minority ethnic backgrounds were dying 14 years younger than their white counterparts.Researchers from King’s College London analysed data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and theLeDeR programmeof 1,301 adults with severe or profound intellectual disability who died in England between 2021 and 2023.They then compared this with 2,626 adults with a mild or moderate intellectual disability and 536,311 adults from the general population who died in 2022.People with severe or profound intellectual disability died at an average age of 58, compared with 65 for those with a mild or moderate intellectual disability and 82 for the general population.Two in five of the first group’s deaths were judged to be avoidable. Avoidable deaths were defined as deaths occurring before the age of 75 due to preventable or treatable causes.Pneumonia and epilepsy were the leading avoidable causes, notably higher than in the other two groups, followed by cerebrovascular disease (concerning blood flow and blood vessels in the brain).Jon Sparkes, the chief executive of learning disability charity Mencap, called the findings shocking but “sadly unsurprising”. “Much more must be done to ensure people with the most complex needs can access care,” he said.View image in fullscreenJon Sparkes, the chief executive of Mencap.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“Organisational failings were identified in more than 40% of deaths reviewed last year, showing the way the NHS just isn’t designed to work for people with a learning disability.“This research shows why it is so vital that that the government and NHS consider and meet the needs of people with a learning disability, whether in the new neighbourhood health schemes, through work on moving the NHS to be more digital, or preventing poor health. Only by doing this will we address and end the deep-rooted healthcare inequalities that are cutting lives short.”The analysis also found stark ethnic disparities. Within the group of people living with severe or profound intellectual disabilities, those from Black, Asian and other minority ethnic backgrounds were likely to die significantly sooner than their white peers, with a 14-year disparity.According to the researchers, this variance may highlight additional challenges in accessing healthcare encountered by people from ethnic minorities, and also reflects how compounding inequalities exacerbate the already poorer health outcomes people with disabilities face.Dr Michael Kwan Leung Yu, the first author of the study and a postdoctoral research associate at King’s College, said: “LeDeR provides a unique national lens that no single trust or region can offer. Its scale allows us, for the first time, to examine avoidable deaths among adults with severe or profound intellectual disabilities through a population-based analysis and explore this in greater detail.“The findings point to a need for targeted interventions, including annual health checks, vaccination programmes and timely management of conditions such as pneumonia and epilepsy, reaching adults with severe or profound intellectual disability consistently, with particular attention to those from ethnic minority backgrounds.”Dr Rory Sheehan, a co-first author of the study and senior clinical lecturer at King’s institute of psychiatry, psychology and neuroscience, said: “Pneumonia and epilepsy are largely treatable, so seeing them as leading causes of avoidable death in this group points to a gap between the care people could receive and the care they are getting.“Closing that gap means making sure basic interventions, health checks, vaccination [and] timely treatment reliably reach adults with severe or profound intellectual disability.”Explore more on these topicsLearning disabilityDisabilityRacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: gang leader plotted killing to avenge beating of nephew, court hears | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors accuse Duane Davis of orchestrating 1996 shooting in retaliation for attack by rapper’s entourage
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Prosecutors accuse Duane Davis of orchestrating 1996 shooting in retaliation for attack by rapper’s entourage
Content: Rapper Tupac Shakur after his performance at the Regal Theater in Chicago, Illinois, in March 1994.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRapper Tupac Shakur after his performance at the Regal Theater in Chicago, Illinois, in March 1994.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesTupac ShakurTupac Shakur murder trial: gang leader plotted killing to avenge beating of nephew, court hearsProsecutors accuse Duane Davis of orchestrating 1996 shooting in retaliation for attack by rapper’s entourageDani AnguianoandSam LevinMon 17 Aug 2026 18.50 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trial of a former gang leader accused of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap starTupac Shakurbegan in aLas Vegascourtroom on Monday, featuring testimony from a witness to the shooting and a former police officer.Duane “Keffe D” Davis is on trial for murder for his alleged role in the shooting of Shakur, who died after a drive-by shooting. Prosecutors allege Davis was the “on-the-ground, on-site commander of the effort to kill Tupac” and that he planned the shooting in retaliation for Shakur’s entourage attacking Davis’s nephew.Davis has pleaded not guilty, though he acknowledged a role in the shooting in a 2019 memoir that authorities have said is key to the case against the 63-year-old. Davis is the only living witness from the car that fired shots at Shakur.Last week, a jury of six men and 10 women was selected in the trial, which is expected to last about a month.What we know about Tupac Shakur’s death and what to expect from murder trialRead moreDavis entered the courtroom in a blue suit and tie and scanned the audience to see who was there before sitting next to his lawyer, Michael Sanft, once the jury was sworn in and seated on Monday morning.Members of Shakur’s family, including his stepbrother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur, sat quietly in the front row of the courtroom behind prosecutors.Binu Palal, the chief deputy district attorney, showed jurors a picture of the Mike Tyson-Bruce Seldon fight with the date “September 7, 1996” and showed video of Shakur’s entourage beating Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’s nephew.“Let’s be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew,” Palal said. “Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself.”Palal showed multiple video clips and played audio of Davis describing his alleged role in the incident and anger toward Shakur for the attack on his nephew.Sanft, the defense lawyer, meanwhile, said that after 30 years, investigators still have very little evidence to prove their case.“At the end ​of the day you have to ask yourself: is what they are saying truth ‌or fiction?” Sanft told the jury.Sanft argued that while Davis spoke about the killing to different law enforcement agencies over the years, including the FBI, they did not follow up because, Sanft said, they did not believe what Davis said was credible.3:35Tupac Shakur murder trial: opening statements begin – videoThe trial is a major development in thecasethat for decades was unsolved.On 7 September 1996, the rap icon was attacked just off theLas Vegasstrip as he headed to an afterparty with the Death Row Records founder, Marion “Suge” Knight. While traveling in the vehicle, a Cadillac pulled up next to Shakur’s vehicle and fired eight shots. Shakur was hospitalized for his injuries and died days later.Shakur’s killing spawned countless conspiracy theories, and books and documentaries seeking to determine who was responsible for his death. But a fuller picture of what may have occurred that night has emerged in recent years as Davis, who was the last surviving passenger in the Cadillac, began speaking publicly.Earlier that evening Shakur had attended the Tyson fight at the MGM Grand hotel and afterward was involved in a physical confrontation with Davis’s nephew and several others.Davis sought retribution for Anderson and allegedly obtained a gun with the intent to “hunt down” Shakur and confront Knight. Theincidentunfolded quickly, Davis wrote.“No words were exchanged, the time for talking had passed, the shit was on! Tupac made an erratic move and began to reach down beneath his seat. It was the first and only time in my life that I could relate to the police command to, ‘Keep your hands where I can see them.’ Instead, Pac pulled out a strap, and that’s when the fireworks started. One of my guys from the back seat grabbed the Glock and started bustin’ back,” he wrote.Tupac Shakur: jury selected in trial of ex-gang boss accused of ordering killingRead moreProsecutors have said that Davis’s tell-all book and public statements ultimately revived the Las Vegas investigation.“Had he decided to never write the book, he would not, probably, have ever been prosecuted for the crime,” prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo recently said.His attorneys sought to exclude the book from trial by arguing that he and his co-author exaggerated in an effort to “falsely place himself at the center of it all for personal gain”. A judge denied the request.The first witness called by prosecutors was Garry Dale, a former Las Vegas officer who pulled over Shakur and Knight on the night of the shooting. Hesaidhe stopped the car because it lacked a license plate on the back, and that the interaction was “congenial”. The officer recounted later riding in the ambulance with Shakur after the shooting, saying he tried to convince the rapper to name his assailants, but that Shakurresponded: “No, we’ll take care of it.”Prosecutors’ second witness was Ingrid Stokes, a woman who was in a car with friends near Shakur’s car at the time of the shooting. Stokes’s car and Shakur’s car were both going to the same club, she said. “We heard the gunshots … all hell broke loose,” she said. Stokes added that she didn’t see who was in the car that fired on Skakur, and that she later spoke to police who were “rude” and “treated us like suspects”.Stokes said she didn’t think she had any valuable information to share with officers, and that she and her friends had fear at the time about talking to officers and being labeled as “snitches”.Brent Becker, a former homicide detective from Las Vegas, also took the stand and recounted interviewing Knight after the shooting, saying the record label boss was “very timid” and had three attorneys with him: “He just basically said he didn’t know anything. He didn’t recognize anybody.”Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s killing, can a murder trial offer justice?Read moreKnight, who is currently in prison over a different case, recently suggested he did not want to cooperate with police,telling ABC Newsin an interview last week: “This trial has nothing to do with me and if somebody brings me there, it’s gonna hurt whoever brings me there. I promise you that.”On the stand, Becker further recounted his collaboration with Los Angeles police who helped identify people connected to the beating of Anderson. While the southern California officers shared “interesting” information with Becker about how Shakur’s killing might be connected to other conflicts, Becker said they didn’t have reliable sources who would speak in court: “The problem was it was all from informants. We didn’t have any actual people that would come forward and testify.”The day ended with testimony from Fred Miller, a former Los Angeles police detective who had investigated Davis in connection with the 1997 murder of Christopher Wallace, the rapper known as Biggie Smalls or the Notorious BIG. Attorneys played a lengthy audio recording of Miller questioning Davis at the time.Davis was present at a party that Wallace had attended before he was shot, but Davis’s attorney emphasized he was not charged in Wallace’s murder, and the judge told jurors that law enforcement did not believe Davis was involved.The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurLas VegasRapUS crimeHip-hopnewsShareReuse this content

title: Luigi Mangione New York murder trial postponed after guilty plea in federal case | Brian Thompson shooting | The Guardian
description: Lawyers seek dismissal of state charges after Mangione pleaded guilty in federal case over Brian Thompson killing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lawyers seek dismissal of state charges after Mangione pleaded guilty in federal case over Brian Thompson killing
Content: Luigi Mangione in Manhattan supreme court in May.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuigi Mangione in Manhattan supreme court in May.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersBrian Thompson shootingLuigi Mangione New York murder trial postponed after guilty plea in federal caseLawyers seek dismissal of state charges after Mangione pleaded guilty in federal case over Brian Thompson killingGuardian staff and agencyMon 17 Aug 2026 17.26 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA New York state ⁠judge on Monday ⁠effectively ​postponed Luigi Mangione’s trial on murder and weapons charges over ⁠the2024 killingof a health insurance company CEO, after Mangionepleaded ⁠guiltylast week to separate federal charges.The ​trial had ‌previously been ‌scheduled to begin on September 8. Mangione ‌has pleaded not guilty to the state charges. Mangione’s lawyers on Friday asked New York state justice Gregory Carro, who is overseeing the state case, ‌to dismiss the charges.They argued that Mangione should not have to ​be punished for the same conduct twice, under New York’s law prohibitingdouble jeopardy.In a brief written order on ⁠Monday, Carro gave prosecutors until 9 October ​to ​respond to Mangione’s ​motion. The judge set Mangione’s next ​appearance in ‌state court ​for ​10 December, meaning the trial will not go forward next month.Mangione, 28,confessedthat he shot and killed Brian Thompson outside a New York City hotel on 4 December 2024.He had a dispute with UnitedHealthcare, the US insurance giant Thompson ran, about his treatment for severe back pain and, hetold the courtlast week, had problems with “navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others”.In his federal case, Mangione faced stalking charges, after other charges, including murder, were dropped.A spokesperson for Manhattan district attorney, Alvin Bragg, who brought the state charges against Mangione, referred to a Friday statement indicating that the office was prepared ‌to litigate the defense motions. Mangione’s defense lawyers declined to comment.Mangione entered his guilty plea in the federal case without reaching an agreement with prosecutors, and there was ​no guarantee that his acceptance of responsibility would result in leniency at sentencing.Sentencing is due in the federal case on 18 December. Federal prosecutors said on Friday that they intend to seek a life sentence, the maximum allowable.In the state case, Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.If Carro decides to dismiss the state ⁠case, it would eliminate the possibility of Mangione having to serve consecutive prison sentences in the ​two cases.Bennett Gershman, a law professor ​at Pace University in New York, said it ​was unlikely Carro would dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds.New York state’s double jeopardy law ​carves out exceptions for crimes ‌that have different elements ​or are aimed at preventing “very ​different kinds of harm or evil”.The federal stalking charges to which Mangione pleaded guilty to still require intent to kill but do not require that the death occurs.“The elements in stalking and the elements of murder are very, very distinguishable,” Gershman said.Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsBrian Thompson shootingnewsShareReuse this content

title: European farmers face ‘unprecedented crisis’ after successive heatwaves | Farming | The Guardian
description: Vegetable and grain growers call for urgent action, warning of ‘catastrophic’ harvests due to continent-wide drought
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Vegetable and grain growers call for urgent action, warning of ‘catastrophic’ harvests due to continent-wide drought
Content: The French agriculture ministry estimates its maize harvest will be down 35% on 2025 levels.Photograph: Mourad Allili/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe French agriculture ministry estimates its maize harvest will be down 35% on 2025 levels.Photograph: Mourad Allili/SIPA/ShutterstockFarmingEuropean farmers face ‘unprecedented crisis’ after successive heatwavesVegetable and grain growers call for urgent action, warning of ‘catastrophic’ harvests due to continent-wide droughtJon Henleyin Paris,Angela Giuffridain Rome andStephen Burgenin BarcelonaMon 17 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuccessive intense heatwaves and an increasingly severe, continent-wide drought have left many of Europe’s farmers in an “unprecedented” crisis, with vegetable and grain growers in particular warning of “catastrophic” harvests.French vegetable production is down by “a very significant extent” compared with previous years, French growers have said, with shortfalls put at 25% for courgettes, 35% for lettuces, 40% for peas, 60% for broccoli and 50% to 100% for artichokes.“The vegetable sector is facing a historic crisis,”saidPrince de Bretagne, which groups together more than 1,300 vegetable producers in Brittany, calling for “urgent action” to address a “dramatic” fall in yields and in the quality of many crops.Accelerated, human-caused global heating and a supersized El Niño have scorched fields across Europe this summer, with plant development prevented by temperatures routinely exceeding 30C and often 35C, almost no rainfall, and hot winds.“Usually one region fares better, which helps compensate,” Eric Legras, of the 4,400-member French canned and frozen vegetable producers’ association,told Le Monde. “This year, all our main production areas have been hit, and at the same time.”Cereal production has been equally hard hit, with the agriculture ministry estimating the maize harvest in France – Europe’s largest grains producer – will be down by 35% on 2025 levels at about 9m tonnes, a quantity last seen in 1980.Part of the fall is due to farmers’ switching to other crops, such as sunflowers, the ministry said, but it also reflects the impact of this summer’s vicious heatwaves, which have battered the crucial crop during critical stages of its growth cycle.That is likely to cause big problems for livestock farmers. With dairy cows typically starting to suffer from heat stress above 25C, many producers have already reported milk yields down by 10%-15%. Most are now also concerned about winter feed.Burnham announces £65m for drought-hit farmers after Labour pressureRead moreAgreste, the agriculture ministry’s statistics service, said last week that production of hay for winter cattle forage was running about 30% lower than the 1989-2018 average, a shortfall that “is worsening and is now affecting a growing numbers of regions”.Egg production, too, has been hit by a catastrophic mortality rate in poultry houses, particularly during the June heatwave. According to France’s national egg promotion board, output has is about 1m eggs a day lower than the norm.In Italy, about 60% of farmland across the country is now affected by drought ranging from mild to severe, according to data published earlier this month byColdiretti, the country’s largest farmers’ organisation.Crop yields, especially for corn, rice and soya beans as well as vegetables and fruit, have been badly hit, and milk production has fallen by 20%. The overall cost to the sector, including damage caused by wildfires and heavy storms, is put atmore than €3bn.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of a rice field in Italy earlier this month showing a sharp contrast between a yellowed and dried section affected by severe heat stress and the remaining area where rows of green rice plants are still visible in Novara, in the Po valley, where growers have been forced to irrigate crops only on alternate weeks.Photograph: Simone Padovani/Getty ImagesThe drought is particularly acute in the Po valley, a huge geographical area straddling four northern regions, the backbone of Italian agriculture and home to about 80% of the Italian rice production, due to severe depletion of the country’s longest river.Italy is Europe’s largest ⁠rice producer, with about 235,000 hectares (580,000 acres) planted in 2025. This year, however, the severe drought has forced growers to adopt an unprecedented response to save the season, irrigating crops only on alternate weeks.In Spain, cereal harvests are 35% below the previous year in Castilla y León, 49% in the Madrid region and 24% in Andalucía. Sheep and goat’s milk production is also down 6.5% and 10.8% respectively, authorities have said.After a disastrous harvest in drought-stricken 2024, olive oil production increased significantly last year and the wet winter and spring were good news for a crop not harvested until late autumn. Growers say it is too early to say how this year will look.However, Spain’s national wine federation has predicted a 20% fall in production for 2026, and its director, José Luis Benítez, warned that successive heatwaves will reduce crops as grapes are smaller for lack of moisture.Governments have pledged costly aid packages to help the sector. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has promised €145m (£124) in immediate aid, along with “structural support and investment measures” in the 2027 budget.Explore more on these topicsFarmingEuropeFood & drink industryClimate crisisExtreme weatherDroughtFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK government ‘irresponsible’ for not publishing emergency drought plans | Drought | The Guardian
description: Campaigners demand greater transparency into water companies’ plans not made public due to ‘security reasons’
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Campaigners demand greater transparency into water companies’ plans not made public due to ‘security reasons’
Content: Alongside statutory drought plans, water companies must produce emergency drought plans, details of which are kept secret to ‘avoid alarming the public’.Photograph: Jon Super/APView image in fullscreenAlongside statutory drought plans, water companies must produce emergency drought plans, details of which are kept secret to ‘avoid alarming the public’.Photograph: Jon Super/APDroughtUK government ‘irresponsible’ for not publishing emergency drought plansCampaigners demand greater transparency into water companies’ plans not made public due to ‘security reasons’Pippa NeillEnvironment reporterMon 17 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government has been accused of a lack of transparency and of acting irresponsibly for refusing to publish the emergency drought plans that are produced by water companies.Water firms are required to publish statutory drought plans every five years to detail the actions needed to ensure public water supply is maintained and the environment is protected during drought.Water levels at fivekey reservoirsin England and Wales are now “exceptionally low” andthree-quarters of Englandand the whole of Wales are in drought.The 2027-32 drought plans, which are under consultation, detail what will happen in different scenarios, with the most extreme actions ranging from standpipes in the street to rota cuts, where water is limited to a few hours each day.Alongside these publicly available plans, water companies are required to produce separate emergency drought plans.A water industry source said these plans were not published to avoid alarming the public. The government said the plans were not published for security reasons.Alastair Chisholm, the water, policy, regulation and governance lead at the consultancy firm Arup, said that in the “new normal” of the climate crisis causing droughts to become more frequent and more extreme, there would probably be situations where “some quite difficult decisions need to be taken with some quite significant imposition’s on people’s lifestyles”.He pointed toDay Zeroin Cape Town, South Africa, in 2018, when millions of households faced drastic water shortages after the worst drought to hit the city in almost a century.“People do genuinely start to be scared that they’re not going to be able to get water to drink, and that has got all manner of sort of social connotations which is going to need to be very carefully managed,” Chisholm said.Prof Liz Bentley, the chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said it made sense not to publish these plans because drought could lead to widespread impacts on certain critical industries. For example, recent drought and extreme heat in Europe forced several nuclear power plants toshut down.“If you start to see significant shortages of water that impact major industries then these are the kind of things you want to keep confidential because that could have widespread effects on the security of the country,” Bentley said.In some areas of England, the impact of water shortages is already being felt. Sussex, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Norfolk have all seen housing and business development delayed due to water supply availability and ageing or inadequate water infrastructure.Water shortages are also affecting food security, with global food prices at athree-year highas heatwaves, drought and war push up the cost of crops.With water increasingly becoming a scarce commodity and as demand for water increases due to the rapid growth of water-hungry industries such as datacentres, the trade body Water UK recentlytold the Guardianit had asked the government to publish a drought hierarchy to set out which sectors would be prioritised in times of water shortages, but that ministers had yet to do so.“Without this there will be a trade-off across society,” said Jon Chappell, Water UK’s deputy director.Ollie Hayes, the head of big tech and campaigns at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said that amid increasing concern that datacentres could be prioritised over other sectors for water, it was irresponsible for the government to keep its emergency drought plans from the public.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“People are deeply anxious about dwindling water supplies and want to know what the plan is. Will water-hungry AI datacentres be prioritised in a drought emergency? The secrecy only adds to a sense that controversial decisions like this may have already been made,” he said.The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was “deeply worrying that emergency drought plans are being hidden from the public”. “People deserve to know what plans – if any – are in place to protect our water supply,” he said.Polanski said full nationalisation of water companies must be at the top of the government’s agenda to “prevent catastrophic water shortages in the years ahead”.On Sunday it wasreportedthat the industry regulator, Ofwat, was considering allowing water companies to raise bills during periods of drought.Amy Fairman, the head of campaigns at campaign group River Action, criticised the government’s overall lack of transparency over how the country will deal with drought as the climate crisis intensifies.“My key concern is around the lack of a holistic plan to deal with water shortages going forward. There is no more precious resource than water, and yet there isn’t a national water security plan in place,” she said.The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said emergency drought plans were in addition to publicly available statutory drought plans and would not be published for security reasons.A Water UK spokesperson said: “Each water company publishes a drought plan, which is consulted on publicly and sets out the actions the company will take at each stage of a drought. Planning for a severe drought sits under a separate framework, and publication is a matter for government. We support calls from the House of Lords environment and climate change committee for the government to decide how water should be prioritised in a severe drought.”Explore more on these topicsDroughtWaterWater industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our new normal’: how marine heatwaves affect life in British seas | Marine life | The Guardian
description: As warming seas push native species to cooler waters farther north, once-rare visitors have become more common
Author: Melissa Hobson
Headline: As warming seas push native species to cooler waters farther north, once-rare visitors have become more common
Content: The small spotted catshark (or lesser-spotted dogfish), a widely found species in British seas, may be moving into deeper waters as temperatures rise.  Photograph: Matthew Oxley/AlamyAs warming seas push native species to cooler waters farther north, once-rare visitors have become more commonByMelissa HobsonSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentMon 17 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It sounds silly but I thought it was a person in the water waving,” says Kurt Lander, skipper of the Yellowfin charter boat, based out of Brighton. But when he grabbed his binoculars, he realised the fluttering movement he had noticed in the middle of the Channel shipping lane was a pair of sunfish.The huge fish were lying on their sides and flapping their fins. “Apparently, they do it as a visual attraction to birds,” he says. “They’re trying to get the birds to eat the parasites off them.”Lander has seen the huge fish with their unusual round bodies before. But the difference is that those that he spotted this year arepart of a surge in sightingsof the species off British shores this summer, probably as a result of a marine heatwave.Marine heatwaves usually follow long hot spells on land as seas also warm. Last year waslabelled “exceptional” by the Met Office, with some parts of British waters seeing heatwave conditions for three-quarters of the year, and 2026 is already showing more of the same.The extraordinary temperatures are causing shifts in marine life far beyond an increase in sunfish. Some species are moving away from warmer waters, other “invaders” are appearing for the first time around Britain’s coastline, while some marine life is dying off under the rays of the sun.View image in fullscreenSunfish are being sighted more often.Photograph: C Hood/AlamyLander notices the change in the species of fish he now lands. “I used to catch at least a couple of hundred cod a year,” he says. Now, bringing in cod is rare. If he catches any, he adds, “it’s probably about one or two a year in the summer.”Colder water species are just nowhere to be seen off the southern coastline, says Dr Zoe Jacobs, a senior researcher at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. Shifting their range to cooler seas farther north, they are now thriving inScotland. “Temporarily or permanently, we don’t know,” she says.Meanwhile, Lander is catching more warm-water fish, such as bass, comber and triggerfish. According to last year’sState of the South-West Seas report, other species found in warmer waters – such as sardines and anchovies – are also doing well.Gio Reale, a diver based in the Cornish port of Falmouth, says: “Small water temperature changes have such big effects on marine life.” It has been weeks since he last saw his favourite shark species: the small spotted catshark (also called the lesser-spotted dogfish). These small sharks – which grow no bigger than a metre and are spattered with delicate freckles – prefer water temperatures of about 16-17C (61-63F).View image in fullscreenCornish trawlermen working off the Manacles rocks. Their catch of lobster has been depleted by rising numbers of octopuses.Photograph: Hugh Hastings/Getty“This summer, like every day, the water has been about 20C,” he says, adding that he thinks the sharks may have moved into deeper, cooler waters, replicating the way they behave in the Mediterranean.These sharks may be missing butcommon octopuses have arrived in force since Januarylast year, when warmer waters in Devon and Cornwall created perfect conditions for them. This species is native to the UK but not usually seen.An octopus carrying off a lobster. Video: Olivia Langmead/Marine Biological AssociationThe bloom caused issues for some crab and lobster fishers. “Everyone’s complaining, ‘oh, they’re taking all our crabs’,” says Reale. “But obviously, for the octopus, that’s just a really easy meal. You can just get into a trap where the crabs can’t go anywhere and eat them.”Some boats have switched to targeting the now-abundant octopuses, with catches soaring in 2026. The octopuses also provide food for predators, which could explainan increase in sightingsof summer visitors such as Risso’s dolphins.As sea swimmers know, warmer waters also bring jellyfish – another food source. But these blooms “have high and low years”, says Jacobs, and interpreting sightings can be tricky: reports may increase simply because more people are at the beach.Seeing lots of nativemoon, compass and barrel jellyfishis normal for summer. However, the arrival of moremauve stingersfrom the Mediterranean would be “a different story”, she says. “That might well be due to the warming.”View image in fullscreenA mauve stinger jellyfish, more usually found in the Mediterranean Sea.Photograph: A Martin UW Photography/GettyWarmer waters can bring new species altogether. A few smalltooth sand tiger sharks – an “exceptionally rare visitor” in local waters – havewashed up on UK beaches in recent years, and hair curler sea slugs,usually found in the Caribbean and Mediterranean,werefirst recorded in 2025.Some outsiders can cause problems for native animals. For example, scientists arewatching a newly arrived sea squirt, calledDidemnum pseudovexillum,closely. It is almost identical to another invader called the carpet sea squirt (Didemnum vexillum) that can smother the seabed, but they do not yet know if this new sea squirt will cause similar damage.Elsewhere in the world, extreme marine heatwaveshave caused extensive loss of seagrassand kelp in countries including Australia and the US. “Huge areas have just been completely wiped out, and they’ve not returned,” says Jacobs.View image in fullscreenA hair curler sea slug, native to the Caribbean and Mediterranean, was found off Cornwall.Photograph: Britta Saffron Holmes/Devon Wildlife TrustChris Williams, founder of the volunteer-runHastings Kelp Project, is worried. The UK may havelost about 92% of its seagrass meadowssince the 1930s. Exactly how much kelp has vanished is unclear but, in Sussex,it could be more than 96%.And this is hidden under the sea. “You don’t see a degrading kelp forest from the land like you might see a woodland burning down or dying off because of the temperatures,” he says.Kelp prefers waters of about 8-12C and even Williams’s controlled laboratory is struggling. “Because of the heatwave, our chillers in the lab haven’t been able to keep the tanks below 12C,” he says.His kelp is growing but he thinks this is because he can control other variables, such as lighting.Seagrass and kelp provide vital habitats for many animals, protect shorelines from erosion and flooding, and store carbon, which is why Williams hopes to grow kelp that can withstand warmer seas. TheSeagrass Ocean Rescue projectsimilarly aims to restore 15% of UK seagrass meadows by 2030.Warmer waters can also trigger harmful algal blooms, which can harbour nasty pathogens that make animals and people extremely sick. In the Bay of Biscay, theauthorities closed beachesto protect swimmers. While the same thing could happen here, our infrastructure is not yet set up for such closures, says Jacobs. “We’re just not ready,” she says.The impact of repeated heatwaves on fisheries may take a couple of years to become apparent because, even if adults survived the elevated temperatures, eggs and juveniles may have been affected. And experts do not know if the cold-water fishes that moved north will return after the heatwaves end.View image in fullscreenA kelp forest in the Channel. Like seagrass, it is a vital habitat that also protects shorelines and stores carbon.Photograph: Dan Smale/Sussex Wildlife Trust/PA“It might be that our cod and mackerel fisheries are done,” says Jacobs.
