Secondly, I looked around and the room was so quiet because people were weeping silently.When his speech ended, the host of the evening said, my brother, we will not forget what you have done for us.”Early in the film, Teng is seen standing in the home of Perlmutter, questioning whether they should display the most graphic, shattering footage of children shredded by US-made bombs in Gaza. Perlmutter turns to her, his face taut with moral outrage, demands to know why she is there if she refuses to show the unvarnished truth.Teng reflects: “He’s told me this before: ‘If you weren’t gonna film it, I was ready to kick you out of my house.’ I said, yeah, I probably deserved it. As a film-maker, as a former journalist, where there’s discomfort it is very important for us to run towards it because that’s where the biggest realisation and growth is going to be and, if we learn something from it, maybe others can too.”While Perlmutter is the blunt, emotional firebrand and Ahmad is the measured, politically strategic voice who walked out of a meeting with President Joe Biden during Ramadan, Sidhwa is the cool, analytical anchor of the trio. When Teng first approached him about being filmed, his reaction was sceptical.Sidhwa, 44, says via Zoom: “I told Poh she’s welcome to follow me around with a camera if she wants to but I told her it would be a waste of her time. I told her, do you know how many documentaries there are about the Gaza Strip? Nobody cares. It was a very defeatist sensebutI’m very glad that she didn’t listen to me because it turns out this movie does resonate with people quite a bit.”View image in fullscreenFeroze Sidhwa in American Doctor.Photograph: Watermelon PicturesSidhwa has volunteered in Gaza twice: first in March and April 2024, and again in March and April 2025. When he tried to return for a third time in November 2025, the Israeli authorities blocked his entry. He is now part of a legal petition to the Israeli high court of justice challenging the systematic blocking of healthcare workers.American Doctor captures the unfathomable destruction in Gaza, the fear and grief of its people and the steely determination of medical professionals working at the front line of hospitals that are constantly overwhelmed. To understand the scale of what he and the other doctors witnessed, Sidhwa argues you must first dismantle the abstract language used by military spokespeople and politicians.The entire Gaza strip is smaller than theUkrainian capital Kyivand has a smaller population. “When you unleash the entire might of the American and Israeli military on a place that size, it’s going to be destroyed and that’s exactly what happened.”Almost every house, mosque and government building has been destroyed, Sidhwa continues, along with half of hospitals, and those that remain are starved of supplies and barely functioning. “Something like 10% of the healthcare workforce is dead or has fled Gaza. The largest killing of humanitarian aid workers that’s ever happened has happened in the Gaza Strip over the past three years. The same with thekilling of physicians, nurses and children.”There is also a catastrophic breakdown of infrastructure. “Everybody lives in a tent. The rodents are attacking children and literallygnawing on the faces of babiesat night. You can imagine their panicked mother wakes up in a completely dark tent with no ability to turn the light on to her baby screaming and she has no ability to even figure out what’s going on.“When it rains, everything is flooded. This is a laboratory for death and disease, and again in a place that’s 70% refugees and half children. There’s nothing like this that’s being done anywhere else in the world.”View image in fullscreenThaer Ahmad in American Doctor.Photograph: Watermelon PicturesBut the moral weight of American Doctor lies not just in its depiction of Gaza but its unflinching examination of the political and media machinery that enables it. Teng chimes in: “There are lots of films that are, ‘Oh, this is what’s happening,’ which is very important. There’s enough on social media too, depending on your feed, to see sheer horror.“But at the end of the day, it’s very important for those in the west, especially Americans, to take a good look at themselves. Are they OK with rats gnawing at children’s faces? Who’s responsible for that? We are responsible for that and so it was very important to bring the message of what was happening there back home to the American psyche.”This may be why American Doctor has had a profound impact on audienceson the festival circuit. Teng continues: “There are war movies and American Doctor is nowhere near that. I don’t think it’s actually the graphic nature of it; I think it’s the guilt.“I’ve watched documentaries across the board, just so that I am aware and know what kind of art that is being made on conflicts and wars and genocide. American Doctor doesn’t even come close. But I think the challenge here is people sometimes having to reckon with what they’re part of and that does something to you.”Sidhwa agrees. “This idea of ‘righteous’ or ‘clean’ violence. People don’t think of our bombs doing the same thing that Russian bombs do, which is very weird: they’re both bombs. They work exactly the same way but they just don’t think of it. I don’t know why. But I think when they see it then it’s the guilt of saying, ‘I knew we were responsible for what was going on but I didn’t realise this is what’s going on.’The film elicits different reactions in different countries, Teng adds.“Here’s a film that can maybe help tell people about what’s going on and help people to look at themselves in the mirror. Next year, five years from now, 20 years from now, can we see ourselves? Can we accept what we have done or have not done? If, as individuals, we live in a democracy then we really need to be part of it and fight for the living.”American Doctor is out in US cinemas now and in the UK on 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fated to become a cult classic’: why Barcelona is my feelgood movie | Romance films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most pleasurable comfort films is a trip to 1980s Spain courtesy of Whit Stillman
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most pleasurable comfort films is a trip to 1980s Spain courtesy of Whit Stillman
Content: A still from Whit Stillman’s Barcelona.Photograph: RONALD GRANTView image in fullscreenA still from Whit Stillman’s Barcelona.Photograph: RONALD GRANTMy feelgood movieRomance films‘Fated to become a cult classic’: why Barcelona is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers detailing their most pleasurable comfort films is a trip to 1980s Spain courtesy of Whit StillmanRyan ChapmanMon 17 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn hour into Whit Stillman’s 1994 film, Barcelona, the protagonist, Ted Boynton (Taylor Nichols), considers using “maneuver x” in his stalled romantic life. He’s an American working in the Spanish branch of an auto conglomerate, looking for love in the titular city’s post-Franco, sexually liberated nightlife. As Ted explains to his cousin Fred (Chris Eigeman) – visiting as an underqualified scout for a naval diplomatic mission – the sales tactic of “maneuver x” involves removing all pressure and allowing the customer to cross the threshold themselves. No tricks, no cloying, no badgering. Fred thinks the move is just another way of “playing it cool”, and it’s a handy metonym for the film. Barcelona plays it very, very cool.‘I am left grinning’: why The Dish is my feelgood movieRead moreWhich isn’t to say Stillman’s second film, after his Oscar-nominated Metropolitan, is itself cool. Ted likes Glen Miller. He opens conversations with “You know how at parties, everybody talks about marketing?” If you want cool, look to Stillman’s The Last Days of Disco, where Chloë Sevigny frequents an unnamed Studio 54.Barcelona, on the other hand, is my feelgood movie because it’s several movies in one. An Austenesque romantic comedy, with wit dry as an albariño. A slow-boil cold war intrigue, where characters discuss the consequences of American foreign policy. A nostalgic, autobiographical portrait of young Americans abroad. And, however improbably, a defense of business-section self-help books. Where Stillman’s contemporaries riffed on Death of a Salesman, he offers us Willy Loman’s Homage to Catalonia.The scope is both modest and international. It’s the early 80s. Two American cousins pursue love while endlessly debating and taxonomizing it. Stillman, who loves verbose characters like Scorsese loves needle-dropping the Rolling Stones,callshis films “moralistic identity comedies for young people”, and here he throws in US-Spanish relations and the locals’ hyperawareness of anything signifying fascism. The joke is that Fred’s Reagan-era patriotism strikes them as “facha”; in 2026, it’s no longer funny. The incompetent diplomat, always primed for offense, would rise quickly in Trump’s administration. In the penultimate scene Fred orders a Cuba libre, so perhaps there’s hope?As for the plot: characters fall in and out of love; they step on rakes. In a twist out of a Graham Greene novel, someone is violently attacked as a result of a misinformation campaign. The ugly Americans never understand how ugly they are, even if the film does. On a rewatch, note the extras’ silent reactions to Fred’s complaints. Though even he isn’t completely oblivious. After a disastrous picnic with an influential journalist, Fred tells his cousin: “I did not confirm their worst assumptions. I am their worst assumptions.”Barcelona was fated to become a cult classic. It hit theatres during American independent cinema’s annus mirabilis and was pushed down critics’ lists by Pulp Fiction, Hoop Dreams and debuts from Kevin Smith, James Gray and Kelly Reichardt. Other films set in the Catalan capital make Stillman’s look drab by comparison. Take Almodóvar’s technicolor melodrama All About My Mother, from 1999, or Cédric Klapisch’s EU-philic sex comedy L’Auberge espagnole, from 2002. It also doesn’t help that most of the Spanish roles are played by Americans, Australians and Brits – though Mira Sorvino and Tushka Bergen are wonderful.Perhaps feelgood movies, like cult classics, require the gift of time. If Barcelona is several films in one, it’s also several films over time. Pete Townshend once referred to Dylan’s Like a Rolling Stone as “quantum”: its lyrics mean something wholly different to you at each decade of life.When I was in college, Ted’s transcontinental lifestyle felt aspirational. To live abroad, besotted by locals while positing undercooked theories about love! I took its advice to heart, too. Sometimes it really is too early for dancing.By my early 30s, having traveled a fair bit, I better understood Stillman’s caustic take on global politics. I could appreciate, too, his prescience. Wherever Americans discover romance and an asymmetric exchange rate, set the countdown to over-tourism. (I can confirm the gilda pintxo in La Boqueria is better than a dozen cheeseburgers.) And the American adventurism and Spanish anti-Nato isolationism remains sadly topical. Reagan’s “shining city on a hill” became gold flake stapled to the wall of the Oval Office.Now, in my 40s, I empathize with the sentimental attachment to the film’s pre-globalized milieu. A time of all-night dancing, a rejection of the old order and dating without smartphones. The costume design has come back around, too. Ted’s preppy, oversize fits can be seen at Ralph Lauren, Noah and Jonathan Anderson’s Dior.Barcelona still feels good because it’s uniquely of its time and of our time. Stillman created a film that’s knotty, ambiguous – but never ambivalent – and unafraid of confronting politics alongside its characters’ quotidian concerns. Perhaps indie cinema will make more like it. (Although I know Fred would say, “God, your naiveté is astounding!”) The directorput it best: “[Y]ou can look at films with a critical eye, a skeptical eye, or just a sort of sit-back-and-enjoy-it eye.” The beauty of Barcelona is you can do all three at once, and over time. That’s quantum.Barcelona is available on YouTube in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsRomance filmsMy feelgood movieComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lanterns review – Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre’s alien-hunting superhero caper is a bust | Television | The Guardian
description: Sure, it’s got evil extraterrestrials trying to detonate whole towns … but not even the almighty Green Lantern and his mesmerising protege can save this show from feeling a whole lot of meh
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Sure, it’s got evil extraterrestrials trying to detonate whole towns … but not even the almighty Green Lantern and his mesmerising protege can save this show from feeling a whole lot of meh
Content: Ever-dependable … Kyle Chandler in Lanterns.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenEver-dependable … Kyle Chandler in Lanterns.Photograph: HBO MaxTV reviewTelevisionReviewLanterns review – Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre’s alien-hunting superhero caper is a bustSure, it’s got evil extraterrestrials trying to detonate whole towns … but not even the almighty Green Lantern and his mesmerising protege can save this show from feeling a whole lot of mehLucy ManganMon 17 Aug 2026 06.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is my personal belief that you are starting off on the back foot whenever you’re given a superhero who draws their powers from an extrinsic item. Captain America is nothing without his shield. Elon Musk could build a metal suit and proto-heart and become Iron Man, which tells you everything you need to know about the problem. And, most pertinently, as we’re about to discuss the latest iteration of the Green Lantern legend, there’s the Green Lantern and his big green ring. It grants the wearer mighty powers but periodically needs recharging from a big green power pack. Plus, Green Lanterns themselves are ultimately employees of Green Lantern Corps, a cosmic law enforcement agency run by the Guardians. They are a race of immortals who live on the planet Oa, but by that point there’s a lot of meh to cut your way through.View image in fullscreenA lot of meh to cut your way through … Lanterns.Photograph: HBOMaxLanterns, the new televisual venture into the DC Comics universe, keeps all of the above elements and adds a mentor-mentee buddy-cop spine that plays out across two timelines – 2016 and 2026. The ever-dependable Kyle Chandler plays Earth’s current Green Lantern, Hal Jordan. Rising star and mesmerising screen presenceAaron Pierreplays his trainee John Stewart (one of DC’s first African American superheroes, who made his debut in 1971). In 2016, Hal is weary and lazy when it comes to teaching John to be – as he sees it – his backup. He has no intention of retiring or being killed (which is an enormous amount of trust to place in a piece of jewellery that comes with a battery worse than your phone’s). The 2016 John, a well-disciplined son of a marine, and a former sniper and architect (and vegan), is a model of quiet endurance, retaining his poise and respecting the chain of command.View image in fullscreenRising star … Aaron Pierre in Lanterns.Photograph: HBO MaxBut by 2026, Hal isn’t looking quite so confident about his immortality prospects and it’s John’s time to shine. This is where the story begins, with Hal sending a hologram-Hal to himself with a mysterious message that sees him immediately flying off to Nebraska. John must follow via car and plane. He arrives to find four people dead in a shooting at Rushville’s football stadium. They were all visiting fans and – Hal claims – aliens. Rushville’s sheriff, Kerry Cane (a miscast Kelly Macdonald, who gives us a whiny rather than capable officer of the law, perpetually on the verge of tears), says not and would quite like him to leave. But Hal knows an alien crashed a spaceship in Nebraska years ago and he is going nowhere.The local big man, William Macon (Garret Dillahunt), who works for an even bigger but anonymous man, gets involved. He is Kerry’s father-in-law (she is married to his weaselly lawyer son Billy, played by Jason Ritter) and takes care of a large ranch patrolled by a band of militia-type men. He is very keen to help anyone repel aliens who may be seeking to take control of his land and/or the US. It’s possible he is a metaphor of some kind. We’ll have to wait and see.View image in fullscreenMiscast … Kelly Macdonald, with Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns.Photograph: HBO MaxLanterns is the kind of reboot that gives you roughly one set piece per episode. The opener’s comes when Hal interviews a suspected alien from the stadium, trying to expose his extraterrestriality with questions about Harry Potter’s school and probing his reactions to Barack Obama’s name (some very heavy-handed exposition has informed us that medical tests are no good because alien technology can emulate the human form too well). Eventually, the suspect cracks, revealing that he is not just an alien but that he has a biometric neutron device woven in to his skeleton! Hal’s ring throws a giant green bubble around him just as the alien detonates and Hal saves the town from annihilation. But now we have to hunt aliens and uncover their dastardly plans for seven more episodes that are never really in danger of catching fire.Lanterns is following the trend for setting fantastical IP in as gritty and realistic a world as possible. This can work brilliantly – look at The Penguin and Watchmen – but when it doesn’t, it can be a real bust. Lanterns works hard and has its moments, but it always feels slightly dull and flat. You long for more, either in terms of spectacle or in a Penguin-style reckoning with the human condition. It may be enough to please fans, but I’ll be surprised if it delights them. For the rest of us, there are better options out there.Lanterns is on HBO Max nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDramareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon review – a brave glimpse inside the mind of the Scottish artist | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Finlay Pretsell captures Gordon setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint and throwing shapes with a bullwhip
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Director Finlay Pretsell captures Gordon setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint and throwing shapes with a bullwhip
Content: Blowing bubbles … Douglas Gordon in Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon.Photograph: Courtesy Edinburgh Film FestivalView image in fullscreenBlowing bubbles … Douglas Gordon in Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon.Photograph: Courtesy Edinburgh Film FestivalMoviesReviewDouglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon review – a brave glimpse inside the mind of the Scottish artistDirector Finlay Pretsell captures Gordon setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint and throwing shapes with a bullwhipAndrew PulverMon 17 Aug 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a brave and not entirely orthodox artist documentary; not so much a dates-and-shows-and-talking-heads profile, but resembling something of an act of art in itself. The subject is Douglas Gordon, the Scottish film and video-maker, possibly best known for 24 Hour Psycho, his radically slowed-down presentation of Alfred Hitchcock’s masterwork, andZidane: A 21st Century Portrait, the feature-length film about the legendary French footballer he co-directed with Philippe Pareno – which apart from anything else popularised the single-player camera that is now a fixture of mainstream TV coverage.The film’s intention is essentially to put you inside Gordon’s day-to-day wrestling with the act of creativity, and therefore inside his mind; the vast majority of which is spent inside his Berlin warehouse studio, where Gordon cuts a basically solitary figure. Apart from the camera crew of course; Gordon spends a good deal of the film’s running time berating director Finlay Pretsell, in between setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint, throwing shapes with a bullwhip and blowing bubbles from a family-sizebubble tube.Gordon appears to be acutely aware that the way he conducts himself – like a kid, as he openly admits – may appear self-indulgent and even ridiculous; and he’s not wrong; someone with this apparently radioactive level of self-involvement is hardly the most engaging of characters. But, as Gordon labours to explain, his art is all about taking a risk, generating interesting moments, and attempting to preserve them even decades down the line. The struggle to articulate this is what keeps Gordon – leathery, grizzled, inked all over, just about to turn 60 – committed to the film: he even suggests a title, Portrait of a Perilous Character, that would actually work pretty well.Pretsell, you would think, has to have the patience of a saint to put up with this, but allows Gordon the time and space to get his point across. (The film’s actual title, with that “by Douglas Gordon”, suggests that the subject is pretty keen to assert his authorship of the final result.) Be that as it may, Pretsell drops in blip-sized clips of Gordon’s previous work, which is just about all the context we are allowed – other than a short bit of archive footage showing an amazingly fresh-faced Gordon collecting the Turner prize in 1996. The way that time makes fools of us all is a sub-theme here, especially when we see Gordon sobbing over his absent kids while encased in a pair of leopard-print leggings.For all his flamboyance, Gordon remains a somewhat elusive figure; by the end we’re not much closer to identifying what really spurs him on. You get the sense he doesn’t really know either, and perhaps that’s the point.Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon screened at the Edinburgh film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsDouglas GordonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Brandon Flowers: Thrasher review – Killers frontman’s country pivot is a rootin’ tootin’ cowboy-bootin’ hoot! | Brandon Flowers | The Guardian
description: Even a couple of bafflingly misguided social commentary songs can’t detract from the joys of Flowers’ classically full-throated commitment to the Nashville bit
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Even a couple of bafflingly misguided social commentary songs can’t detract from the joys of Flowers’ classically full-throated commitment to the Nashville bit
Content: Never does anything by halves … Brandon Flowers.View image in fullscreenNever does anything by halves … Brandon Flowers.Brandon FlowersReviewBrandon Flowers: Thrasher review – Killers frontman’s country pivot is a rootin’ tootin’ cowboy-bootin’ hoot!(Island)Even a couple of bafflingly misguided social commentary songs can’t detract from the joys of Flowers’ classically full-throated commitment to the Nashville bitShaad D'SouzaMon 17 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere are three immutable facts about Brandon Richard Flowers: he was born just outside Las Vegas, Nevada. He is 45 years old. And he never does anything by halves. When he and his band the Killers debuted in the early 2000s, as disaffected New York cool was on the rise, he was writing scream-along choruses sung in his upper register. When the Killers were searching for a sound even bigger and grander than the euphoric Springsteen pastiche of 2006’s Sam’s Town, they didn’t think twice before recruiting Stuart Price to produce the spangly 2008 disco-rock record Day & Age.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Thrasher.That’s how you get a record like Thrasher. Flowers’ third solo album finds Vegas’s chosen son decamping to Nashville for a full-throated exploration of country music – not subtle, trendy Americana, but rip-snorting, honky-tonking, Nudie suit-wearing country. In many ways, Thrasher is a stylistic follow-up to the Killers’ maudlin 2021 Pressure Machine, which saw Flowers explore windswept balladry and tasteful story-songs. But that record was as forgettable as Thrasher is a hoot; Flowers wilts when he doesn’t fully commit, as was the case on Pressure Machine, and he doesn’t make that mistake here. Thrasher features many of Nashville’s most revered country musicians, including pedal steel legend Bruce Bouton, 85-year-old harmonica player Charlie McCoy, Gillian Welch’s musical partner Dave Rawlings and lauded Americana musician Margo Price.This deep bench doesn’t obscure Flowers’ oddball tendencies. On rollicking opener Does It Ever Cross Your Mind?, he writes like a man who’s done his 10,000 hours absorbing pop music cliches and now feels equipped to write his own. “I could’ve been born in Bangladesh / But I wasn’t, I was born here / With just enough jellybeans in my basket / To ask you to go a’wishing on a star,” he sings, injecting his nonsense with such gravitas and moxie that it’s easy to believe that’s something people say.Brandon Flowers: Paradise (Live From Historic RCA Studio A) – videoThose weird turns of phrase invigorate Thrasher’s many character studies. Tiger’s Blood would be good-but-ordinary Springsteen pastiche, with its repeated refrain of “like a runaway train”, but Flowers makes this story of a “cheerleader working the till [who] wants to get outta this podunk place” his own with weird, specific images – of “peach-fuzz boys getting hard in the corner on Mortal Kombat” and a “swamp cooler leaking down the bricks outside”. Especially great is all the idiosyncratic detail on closer An American Dream, its universal-sounding title concealing seemingly the most surreal song on Thrasher. As it builds, Flowers stacks evocative image upon evocative image: “A Guinness World Record holder / For the longest fall living”; “Elvis in a Tesla Model X”; “lights that flicker on hubcap chrome.”As on Pressure Machine, Flowers takes a couple of big swings, both of them misses. On Miss America, he writes from the perspective of a young woman in an abusive relationship. Although this is something of a pet topic for Flowers, he is not a particularly elegant writer; amid all the salacious euphemisms for abuse, he sings things like: “Truth be told / Grown men have noticed me since I was 12 years old / It always made me feel like some kind of prize / I guess I saw my worth through their porno eyes.” But even that feels graceful in comparison to Angel. There’s no way to sugarcoat it: Angel is a song about a talented Black baseball player who starts dating a white girl. Angel and the girl have a daughter, and Angel is deployed to be in the navy, after which he abandons his wife and kid to become a drug smuggler. The song ends with Angel being pulled over by the cops and attempting to evade them on foot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia TaitRead moreIt’s impossible to comprehend how Flowers thought this song was a good idea. When Angel and his girlfriend have their baby, he sings the lines “Chocolate and vanilla swirls / There’s gonna be a little girl”. Flowers supposedly wrote more than 30 songs for the record, meaning there were at least 20 alternatives. The place Flowers lands – “It don’t matter how far you’ve come / Or how well you ran the race / You’re gonna have to come face to face / With that thing you’ve always known to be true / That you buried inside of you” – could be a critique of American racial hegemony, or it could be flat-out racist, implying that our fates are hardwired. I strongly suspect that it’s an attempt at the former, but that it could feasibly be taken either way is an indictment in itself.Flowers has always had occasional bouts of foot-in-mouth – this simply feels like a particularly bad one. A big part of Angel’s failure is that it is one of the few genuinely dull songs on the album – plodding and dirgey, with an attempt at a pathos-drenched chorus that has little of the spark or fleet-footedness of the rest of the album. Although it lacks the attention-grabbing singles of 2015’s The Desired Effect, Flowers’ last solo record, Thrasher is front-to-back a far stronger, more enjoyable album that could even win over fans who haven’t tapped in since Mr Brightside. The westernwear suits him.Explore more on these topicsBrandon FlowersThe KillersPop and rockCountryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Swedish Chamber Orchestra/Fröst review – dance, dynamism and a wild rumpus as maverick clarinettist-conductor takes charge | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: The ferociously dynamic Swedish Chamber Orchestra help Fröst drill down to the rhythmic essence of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony as well as works by contemporary composers
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The ferociously dynamic Swedish Chamber Orchestra help Fröst drill down to the rhythmic essence of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony as well as works by contemporary composers
Content: Charismatic … Martin Fröst and the Swedish Chamber Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenCharismatic … Martin Fröst and the Swedish Chamber Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewSwedish Chamber Orchestra/Fröst review – dance, dynamism and a wild rumpus as maverick clarinettist-conductor takes chargeRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe ferociously dynamic SCO help Fröst drill down to the rhythmic essence of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony as well as works by contemporary composersAlexandra CoghlanMon 17 Aug 2026 05.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a Sunday morning, and as the Royal Albert Hall darkens and the stage is suddenly back-lit, spotlighting a charismatic figure speaking sibilantly at its centre, you’d almost swear you’d wandered into an American megachurch. But the gospel preached by maverick clarinettist-conductor Martin Fröst is altogether more ancient and more primal: dance. What could be more fundamental, not just to music but life itself, he argues. And with the ferociously dynamic Swedish Chamber Orchestra helping him make his case, it’s hard to disagree.Wagner famously declared Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony “the apotheosis of the dance”, and the SCO’s DNA project (“Dance Now Always”) transforms his description into a concert that drills down to the rhythmic essence of the symphony, seizing those cells and pulses that are its heartbeat and amplifying them into an ear-bending, time-warping sequence that suspends the work at the centre of its own musical genealogy – past and future.So while the symphony stands alone after the interval, we approach it via a continuous first-half drawing together works by Bach and Rameau, contemporary composers Jacob Mühlrad, Shai Wosner and both Fröst and his brother Göran, into a constantly evolving commentary and dialogue.View image in fullscreenPrincipal cellist and dancer Anna Garde  with Martin Fröst and the Swedish Chamber OrchestraPhotograph: Chris ChristodoulouThe fluid arabesques of Fröst’s solo Cradle Song (nobody makes the instrument sing in so many different voices) stretched imperceptibly into Mühlrad’s Helix – a specially commissioned introduction that demands principal cello Anna Garde set aside her instrument and turn dancer, mirroring and melting into Fröst as jazz, klezmer and the concert-hall dissolve into a haunting miniature. Drift for even a second and you’ll have missed the arrival of a Gigue from Rameau’s Dardanus – arrangements by Hans Ek smudging the edges of the baroque works into the new until we lose stylistic landmarks and it’s all just pulse and energy and sensation.But the real test of the programme was the symphony itself. Suspense built irresistibly through the opening before the Vivace released a performance that was pure impulsion. The silvery spareness of the SCO sound sketched a swift, architectural account, the gorgeous woodwind solos the only embellishment. Fröst stripped performing conventions away to reveal the work’s sharp corners and discontinuities – the motoric finale not just a dance but the original wild rumpus.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 16 September. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: An Agatha Christie classic with an impressive cast: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Toni Collette heads a list of familiar voices playing out the village murder-mystery. Plus, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe go off on some rather wild tangents
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Toni Collette heads a list of familiar voices playing out the village murder-mystery. Plus, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe go off on some rather wild tangents
Content: Toni Collette stars as Miss Marple in The Murder at the Vicarage.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenToni Collette stars as Miss Marple in The Murder at the Vicarage.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioAn Agatha Christie classic with an impressive cast: best podcasts of the weekToni Collette heads a list of familiar voices playing out the village murder-mystery. Plus, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe go off on some rather wild tangentsHannah J DaviesMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe Murder at the VicarageToni Collette is an eagle-eyed amateur sleuth in this big adaptation of Agatha Christie’s first Miss Marple novel. When Colonel Protheroe is found dead in sleepy St Mary Mead, suspects include his spouse, Anne, and daughter, Lettice. But as false confessions and red herrings stack up, can Marple crack the case? Kit Harington, Lolly Adefope and Vicki Pepperdine – who wrote the adaptation – are among the cast.Widely available, episodes weeklyGuz and Kiell Will Not SurviveView image in fullscreenKiell Smith-Bynoe teams up with Guz Khan in Guz and Kiell Will Not Survive.Photograph: Fred Hayes/Getty Images for SAGindieIn something of a contrast to Off Menu-style podcasts where celebrities put themselves in nice, imaginary situations, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe (pictured right) find themselves imagining life in tick-laden swamps and icy peril for this new series. It’s silly stuff, but survival expert Megan Hine helps to keep it on the right side of self indulgent.Audible, all episodes out nowGangster: The Story of the MilkmanInfamous cocaine trafficker Brian Brendan Wright was nicknamed the Milkman because “he always delivers”. So says a law enforcement source in this new series. title: Conversations with an Executioner: a chilling classic reveals the mind of a Nazi mass murderer | Books | The Guardian
description: Polish war hero Kazimierz Moczarski spent 255 days sharing a cell with an SS general. Nearly 50 years after it was published, an uncensored version of his account is appearing in English for the first time
Author: Jo Glanville
Headline: Polish war hero Kazimierz Moczarski spent 255 days sharing a cell with an SS general. Nearly 50 years after it was published, an uncensored version of his account is appearing in English for the first time
Content: In a cell with the enemy … Kazimierz Moczarski in 1944, before his imprisonment and torture. He was finally released in 1956.Photograph: Lokajski/archiwum Elzbiety Moczarskiej/Elzbieta Moczarska/FotonovaView image in fullscreenIn a cell with the enemy … Kazimierz Moczarski in 1944, before his imprisonment and torture. He was finally released in 1956.Photograph: Lokajski/archiwum Elzbiety Moczarskiej/Elzbieta Moczarska/FotonovaBooksConversations with an Executioner: a chilling classic reveals the mind of a Nazi mass murdererPolish war hero Kazimierz Moczarski spent 255 days sharing a cell with an SS general. Nearly 50 years after it was published, an uncensored version of his account is appearing in English for the first timeJo GlanvilleMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1949, Kazimierz Moczarski, a leading member of the Polish resistance, was in his fourth year of incarceration when he was moved into a cell with two Nazis at Warsaw’s Mokotów prison. One of them was Jürgen Stroop – a war criminal and SS general who had led the infamous destruction of the Warsaw ghetto and was responsible for the murder or capture of more than 56,000 Jews. They shared the same four walls for 255 consecutive days.A celebrated figure in modern-dayPoland, Moczarski was regarded as a threat to the power of the postwar communist regime in the country. Like other resistance members, he was accused of collaboration and arrested. But Moczarski, who spoke German, used his imprisonment with Stroop as an opportunity to investigate a question: what turned some Germans into mass murderers, seeking to impose their “Ordnung”, order, across the world? His book about the experience, Conversations with an Executioner, was published in 1977. An instant bestseller, it was performed as a play the same year, directed by Andrzej Wajda. It is finally being published in the UK this month, in its first uncensored translation into English by Sean Gasper Bye.Publisher Clare Bullock heard about the book by chance nearly 10 years ago when she was studying Polish. “In one of my lessons, we were talking about books, Polish classics. And this wonderful teacher, he said, ‘Well, there’s this one book. I don’t understand why it’s never been published here. It’s absolutely extraordinary.’” It was not until she joined Duckworth Books as editorial director in 2024 that she had the opportunity to publish it. Next year is the 50th anniversary of the book’s publication and the 120th of Moczarski’s birth. There will be events to mark the occasion in Poland.Stroop was an unrepentant fascist. He had been sentenced to death by the US military tribunal at Dachau and was awaiting trial in Poland. His cellmate Moczarski had been a member of the Home Army, the main resistance group, and had even taken part in plans to assassinate him. Yet Stroop told him his life story with little inhibition, from his rapid rise in the SS to the shocking details of the obliteration of the Warsaw ghetto in 1943.View image in fullscreenKazimierz Moczarski in 1956.Photograph: archiwum Elzbiety Moczarskiej/FotonovaThe memoir offers a remarkable insight into the genesis and mindset of a Nazi war criminal. “Remember that Stroop lived in the shadow of the gallows,” Moczarski later said in an interview, “and this situation encourages people to talk.” The third man in the cell, Gustav Schielke, had been a low-ranking SS officer, who was not fully signed up to the Nazi cause, and he joined Moczarski in cross-questioning Stroop about his activities during the war. The highly charged relationship between the three men reads like a drama: they sparred with each other, but they also shared a solidarity as prisoners, becoming anxious when one of them was taken out of the cell for interrogation.Jürgen Stroop was executed in Poland in 1952, while Moczarski was released from prison in 1956. He wrote the book while working as a journalist and assiduously factchecked Stroop’s version of events. “My father tried to talk to publishers in the late 60s, but the book was banned, totally banned,” says Elżbieta Moczarska, who was born in 1958, the only child of Moczarski and his wife Zofia. Her mother was also in the resistance and was arrested after the war as well. “Everyone obviously wanted to hear about the Nazis, but nobody wanted to have information on why a hero, somebody who was very high in the resistance, was put into the same cell [as Nazis] and was imprisoned for such a long time.” It was finally serialised in a literary magazine in the early 70s and then published as a book after Moczarski’s death, with the permission of the Communist party, in a censored edition. Elżbieta spent nearly 40 years trying to get a complete translation published in English.Moczarski allowed Stroop to condemn himself in his own words. The Nazi unashamedly relived his genocidal glory days despite his hostile audience, holding forth about his life with such candour that he is sometimes as comic as he is chilling. In one memorable scene, Stroop demonstrated how to ride a horse in the prison cell, whinnying and snorting. His repeated lascivious references to women’s breasts are almost a running gag. “I think we all talk about Hannah Arendt and the banality of evil, but this is it in one man,” says Bullock.It was not possible for Moczarski to take any notes in prison and he had to write the book from memory, so can his reports of the conversations with Stroop and Schielke be trusted as a reliable account? “My father built a kind of castle in his head,” says his daughter Elżbieta. “He could write in his head. He said once that for long-term prisoners the ability to hear is different and you learn to remember.”Moczarski said that he could replay his conversations with Stroop as if they were a tape recording. Bullock points to Solzhenitsyn’s similarly exceptional memory when imprisoned – he was able to compose and remember a poem of 7,000 lines in his head. “I think a lot of it must just have been astonishing recall backed up by serious research,” she says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The chances of Moczarski remembering every single word exactly as they happened, I’m not sure that’s possible. But in terms of retaining the truth of the interactions and the dynamics and what’s happening in the cell, it feels so true.”Conversations with an Executioner by Kazimierz Moczarski (Duckworth Books, £25). title: Agrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient Rome  | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for power
Author: Sam Leith
Headline: This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for power
Content: A Roman statue of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa.Photograph: Andrea Izzotti/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Roman statue of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa.Photograph: Andrea Izzotti/AlamyBook of the dayFictionReviewAgrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient RomeThis fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for powerSam LeithMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week,Robert Harrishas you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assassination of Julius Caesar, with all the bickering and bloodshed that follows, on to the decisive battle of Actium and Octavius’s apotheosis as Caesar Augustus. We meet Cicero, Fulvia, Lepidus, two Caesars and a burly Antony (“Imagine, if you will, a statue of Hercules with a club in one hand, a wineskin in the other”).Here’s the clever bit: he narrates it all from the point of view of Octavius’s right-hand man, Agrippa, a much less well-remembered figure. Harris tells us he “left behind no speeches, few letters and only a couple of sentences of direct quotation”. Yet Agrippa was “effective co-ruler of the Roman world for many years” and “the greatest general of the period”. Octavius couldn’t have risen without him, but he seems to have done his best to write him out of the story afterwards, according him only two passing mentions in the Res Gestae Divi Augusti.Harris’s Octavius is vain, clever, sickly, ambitious, manipulative and prickly. His childhood friend Agrippa, the only person he sort-of trusts, is established early on as a bit of a meathead. Their first encounter is when Agrippa duffs up a couple of bullies he catches picking on a weaker boy; mostly for the pleasure of duffing a couple of people up. He doesn’t know at the time that the beneficiary of this duffing is Caesar’s nephew. They become friends: “He helped me with my classwork. I showed him how to fight.” They share a teacher: “He instilled in Octavius especially a lifelong love of poetry, although my literary tastes, to his despair, have always tended towards works on engineering and military history.” Even as they rise to power, our man’s eye is on the duffing. Octavius returns to Rome amid great danger to give a rousing speech, and Agrippa reports only: “His voice carried well. I did not pay much attention to what he said. I was too preoccupied scanning his audience for potential assassins.”double quotation markIt is a sign of Harris’s discipline as a novelist that he has Agrippa tell his tale in almost comically unambitious proseHarris’s framing conceit is that the text we are reading is Agrippa’s memoir, written in some haste and high feeling. Agrippa, now an old man of 50, has come home early from an expedition to duff up the barbarians in Illyricum. He has a gammy leg, which is about to kill him. He limps in to find his wife in bed with his son-in-law. Since the son-in-law is also the emperor’s adopted son, he hesitates to get busy with his sword and instead retreats to his chamber. He’s feeling a bit sorry for himself and, uncharacteristically, he turns to words.It is a sign of Harris’s discipline as a novelist that he has Agrippa tell his tale in almost comically unambitious prose. There’s a lot of pipe-laying in the military history department, of the “then the legions would wheel around the far side of the Black Sea by way of Hyrcania, the Captain Sea and the Caucasus, and march west” type. And he’s a bastard for an aqueduct, is Agrippa. Loves them; maybe even more than having a scrap. He’s never happier than when building infrastructure and explaining the engineering principles and logistics to the reader.When Agrippa is stirred to reflection, he tends to reach for a well-worn phrase. “The sickly, pungent stink of death lurked round every corner.” “Mercy was now the order of the day.” “War, which I had once so relished, was gouged into the countryside like an open wound.” “Power makes monsters of us all.” “In the words of the old saying – if you strike at the king, you must be sure not to miss.” (That particular old saying, I think, comes from The Wire, but never mind.)But from all this elegantly drab stuff emerges a more subtle portrait of the man and the age than you might expect. You get a persuasive portrait of a Rome exhausted by civil strife, and of the serpentine manoeuvrings of its rulers. Everyone is betraying everyone else, raising armies, marrying each other’s children, forming and breaking alliances. It’s hectic. And, gosh, all these people redrawing the map of the world and changing the course of history areyoung. The plot twist – a feature of scholarly speculation since 1937, Harris’s afterword tells us – concerns the real parentage of the apparently low-born Agrippa.But that, like much else, it suited him to keep quiet about. His most enduring real-world monument is seven terse words in stone above the entrance to the Pantheon: M F AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIUM FECIT. “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, in his third consulship, did it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatments | Books | The Guardian
description: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted him
Author: Oliver Bullough
Headline: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted him
Content: A Sonoran desert toad.Photograph: Tierfotoagentur/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Sonoran desert toad.Photograph: Tierfotoagentur/AlamyBooksReviewThe Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatmentsA journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted himOliver BulloughMon 17 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhich, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you don’t have to choose between them. He’s all five wrapped into one objectionable package, and so much more besides.The tale begins with the Sonoran desert toad, an improbable amphibian that spends most of its life hiding underground in the baking badlands along the Mexico-Arizona border, and has done so blamelessly for millions of years. Whenever it rains, the toads emerge from their hiding places to mate, laying strings of eggs wherever water has pooled.There have long been fanciful tales of hippies getting high by licking toads, but these ones are the real deal: the world’s only known psychoactive animal. In the early 1980s, humans discovered that the toad’s poison glands secrete a venom that contains, among other chemicals, 5-MeO-DMT, a potent hallucinogen also known as the “God molecule”. The first known user squirted the glands of a toad that his dog caught on to the windscreen of his Chevy Sport, where the substance dried and he smoked it.He wrote a manual describing “an overload of thoughts and perception, brief collapse of the ego, and loss of the space-time continuum”. It was, in short, a lot. The prospect enticed other users, and those included, two decades later, Rettig.A troubled young man from Mexico, Rettig started smoking dried toad venom in the first decade of this century, and claims it helped him kick his crack cocaine habit. That was a time when popular interest in psychedelics was re-emerging after the long post-1960s winter, and many medical practitioners were wondering if these mind-altering chemicals couldn’t help patients who weren’t responding to their traditional treatments. Much of the focus had been on LSD, psilocybin and ketamine, but 5-MeO-DMT provided a whole new level of experience. The shatteringly powerful effect of the chemical was said to replicate the effect of years of therapy in just half an hour, which is clearly an attractive prospect for a psychedelic entrepreneur keen to maximise patient throughput.double quotation markHe engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakesRettig was no pioneer in his enthusiasm for smoking toad. Instead, his contribution was to create a tradition for this new hallucinogen, thus giving it the kind of mystical authenticity that peyote, morning glory and ayahuasca gain among devotees thanks to their association with ancient Native American rituals.The Seri people, who live between the Sonoran Desert and the Gulf of California, have suffered terribly both under the Spanish colony of Mexico, and the independent republic. By the time Rettig visited in 2011, there were just a few hundred of them left, living in squalid and trash-strewn villages, predated upon by drug cartels and plagued by addiction. Rettig adopted their chants, claimed their ancient toad-based tradition had been suppressed and was only now being rediscovered, and started presenting himself globally as a practitioner of indigenous medicine.There may well be a medical case for treatment with 5-MeO-DMT, but it’s hard to see any argument for treating people with it the way that Rettig did. He offered huge doses with minimal screening, sometimes inflicting treatment forcibly. (In response to footage of him being aggressive to clients, he told De Greef: “I am open to acknowledge that some of my actions might be disturbing for most audiences, but this is a very deep therapeutic work.”) He engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakes. Rettig claims: “My work has been misunderstood, misinterpreted, and misused.” But it is an incredibly dark tale.A different writer might have been tempted to go gonzo, to smoke toad himself, and to come back with stories of ego death, the space-time continuum and the rest of it, but Kimon de Greef mercifully avoids that temptation. A South African, he came to the story of Rettig not from the world of psychedelics but from researching wildlife smuggling, which gives him an unusually clear-eyed view of how grim these kinds of practices are.A lot of the reporting for this book began life in the New Yorker, and it is as methodical, exacting, well-written and exceptionally reported as you’d expect. Fortunately, De Greef avoids the fate that can befall books based on American magazine articles that fail to break free of them, and really enjoys the extra space. He launches into entertaining digressions into how exactly the toads’ psychedelic powers were first discovered, into how pharmaceutical companies are harnessing 5-MeO-DMT for their own ends, introducing fascinating cameos, before he returns to the main story.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe is not a man for grand conclusions, but I challenge any reader not to see this highly enjoyable book as a parable for so much that’s wrong with the current economy. Everything from the undeserved authority of charlatans, to the rampant exploitation of the natural world, to the hiding of hyper-capitalism behind a shield of cod-mystical woo-woo: it’s all in there.Rettig’s ultimate fate has been to be largely forgotten by the movement he helped to popularise, which has mutated and expanded at the speed of social media, with new influencers appearing and new markets opening. The toads, meanwhile, have become just another commodity to be exploited.The Ego Trip: Psychedelic Toads, a Trail of Deaths, and the Guru Who Peddled Transcendence by Kimon de Greef is published by White Rabbit (£23).
