title: The Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high water | Games | The Guardian
description: Frogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edges
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Frogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edges
Content: ‘Distant howls of rabid fish men’ … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresView image in fullscreen‘Distant howls of rabid fish men’ … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresGamesReviewThe Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high waterPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; FrogwaresFrogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edgesNic RuebenMon 17 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m standing in the prosthetics lab of a campy horror hospital, hunting for a preacher’s flayed face to wear so I can trick the world’s grisliest smart doorbell. Pinned to a board in the corner of the room are a dozen X-rays: shattered bones and metal splints in sepia negative, each with a note attached. It’s a stark, clinical intrusion on the theatrical gore elsewhere. It takes a beat to realise that I’m reading the stories of injuries sustained by soldiers fighting for Frogwares’ native Ukraine. Fingers amputated after severe burns. Limbs lost in mine explosions. Toes torn off by shell fire.Like so many of my favourite PS3-era seven-out-of-tens, The Sinking City 2 is a pulpy action horror. It’s fuelled by scrappy ambition, Lovecraft fan fiction and wonderfully unhinged scenario design. A puzzle that has you determine which talking jarred brain is telling porkies. A scavenger hunt to fix a crane to move a rotting whale carcass. A gunfight amid the grisly results of a siren pop star’s fan meet-up turned battle royale.Frogwares’ latest is also fuelled by the trauma and grit of developers who refused to let an invasion stop them making it. “As of writing, 85,183 air raid sirens registered across our cities,” reads an intro screen. “Work continued, and so did life.” As Weird Tales magazine-cover gumshoe Calvin Rafferty steps out from his apartment, sirens and the public address system blare out over the flooded town of Arkham, heralding the final calls for evacuees.View image in fullscreenTime to evacuate … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresThrough an open window, a couple resign themselves to abandoning their dead daughter’s toys. Rafferty’s decided to stick around, despite the floods and the strange infestation of worms that came with them. His girlfriend’s in a coma, and it’s “cursed pacts with interdimensional gods” serious. Hoping for a cure, he hops in the boat you’ll use to explore the first act’s semi-open city map, and makes for the Miskatonic library.Out is the first Sinking City’s clumsy but earnest exploration of Lovecraft’s provincial racism; in is shooting unknowable cosmic horrors in whatever passes for the face with a tommy gun. To be fair, it’s a great tommy gun. The influence of 2019’sResident Evil 2remake is immediately apparent from the identical UI of an achievements menu. Inventory space is tight, as are the corridors that diverge and fold back into themselves like puzzle boxes. Supplies are scarce but ambushes frequent. The distant howls of rabid fish men and worm-riddled zombies dare you to preserve bullets, while the score and every instinct scream at you to let loose like a startled skunk.Frogwares cut its teeth on Sherlock Holmes games, a lineage evident here in some clever puzzles that offer a reason to veer off the main path. Things get rougher when the studio ventures into new territory. Enemies are so relentless that most combat is unavoidable, undermining the intricate map design by offering no reason to take advantage of shortcuts. Elsewhere, the plot’s central romance flops like a soggy fish finger due to some stiff acting and overwrought dialogue.Generous doses of squishy gallows humour, elaborate secrets and expert tension pick up the slack. As does writing that skirts the grim glorification of overt war allegory to tell a story about refusing to leave what you love in the rubble, so long as the faintest signs of life remain. If you’re going to create, wrote Bukowski, you’ll do it “while the whole city trembles in earthquake, bombardment, flood and fire”. And there’s me thinking he was being dramatic.The Sinking City 2 is out 18 AugustExplore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5PCXbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ithaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent moment | Games | The Guardian
description: The latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with it
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with it
Content: Tantalising … Ithaca.Illustration: the Pixel HuntView image in fullscreenTantalising … Ithaca.Illustration: the Pixel HuntSummer games previewsGamesIthaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent momentThe latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with itLewis GordonMon 17 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIthaca has one hell of an opening: Penelope, a disillusioned environmental lawyer, stops her car at a petrol station. But upon returning, she discovers something shocking: the unconscious body of an oil company CEO in her boot, his hands hog-tied together, dangling limply towards the vehicle’s number plate.This tantalising eco-thriller setup is a long way off the typical knights-and-castles fantasy fare of most role-playing games, moreHow To Blow Up a PipelinethanDragon Quest. But road-trip RPG Ithaca arrives via refreshingly original developer the Pixel Hunt, a French outfit that specialises in what it calls “reality-inspired” games. The studio has made a number of arresting works in recent years.One was about a Syrian refugee couplemaking a perilous migrant journey across Europe;another tackledthe life-shattering effects of child sexual abuse. The climate crisis was always in the back of Pixel Hunt founder and Ithaca writer Florent Maurin’s mind. After all, he says, it is the uber problem of our day, the problem that touches all others. It was just a case of when, and, more importantly: “What do we say about it?”Then, one summer afternoon a few years ago, while out for lunch in the French medieval town of Cluny, Maurin was posed a question by his wife: “How, considering all we know scientifically about the climate crisis, do we explain to our daughters that we didn’t spend every weekend marching, protesting and demanding the powers that be to take meaningful action?” Maurin was silenced. “I had no fucking clue,” he says. “I had no answer to that question.”View image in fullscreenRaising prickly, ethical questions … Ithaca.Illustration: The Pixel HuntMaurin’s eventual response was to tackle the subject the way he knew best – by making a video game. In Ithaca, you drive along a procedurally generated road, soaking up vistas of huge windfarms, mountains passes and gorges filled with clean blue water. You talk to family and friends, with the decisions you make affecting the direction you take on the asphalt highway and the branching storyline. Slowly, you uncover what the radical climate group Penelope is now part of, the Earth Protection Association, is really planning to do with the oil exec in her car’s trunk, this nefarious avatar of petro-capitalism. Does he walk free or pay for his Earth-heating sins? Or does something else happen entirely?The prickly, ethical questions that Ithaca raises are influenced by the real world’s growing upheaval. Maurin has been struck by what he sees as a sea change in attitudes towards political violence. He cites the reactions to Luigi Mangione’s alleged killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and the assassination of rightwing activist Charlie Kirk. “You might have expected people to say this is not something that they, or anybody, should do, but actually, a sizable part of the population in the US cheered and was like: ‘This is right. It’s deserved.’”The road Penelope ventures down is something of a metaphor for “where we are all heading”, says Maurin. As the mythic home of Odysseus, Ithaca, Penelope’s ultimate destination, was chosen for its allegorical meaning: Maurin says it offers an opportunity to think through ideas of home in a broader, almost planetary sense. He sees the current moment as one in which “we’re trying to discover where we want to go collectively as a species”.Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanRead moreIt is an urgent question, dovetailing with Ithaca’s high-octane story and what Maurin sees around him on a daily basis in Burgundy, central France. When he arrived, 10 years ago, it was verdant, an almost staggeringly green place. “You felt as if water was everywhere in the landscape,” he says. Now, drought arrives every summer, killing any trees ill-suited to such high temperatures and a lack of water. Hillsides are littered with their grey and yellow arboreal remains. “Every time, I look out of the window and I think, ‘We have to talk about this very fast,’” says Maurin. “Because things are changing way too quickly for nature to be able to adapt.”Ithaca is in development now for PC and consoles for release in 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour review – fringe gem leaves you ecstatic | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Connor Dariol, AKA Australian clown Conk, does exactly what he claims – and with such skill and relentless pep we are helpless to resist
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Connor Dariol, AKA Australian clown Conk, does exactly what he claims – and with such skill and relentless pep we are helpless to resist
Content: We are all involved by the end … Australian clown Conk in Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour.Photograph: Madeline RoyceView image in fullscreenWe are all involved by the end … Australian clown Conk in Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour.Photograph: Madeline RoyceEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMan Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour review – fringe gem leaves you ecstaticSummerhall, EdinburghConnor Dariol, AKA Australian clown Conk, does exactly what he claims – and with such skill and relentless pep we are helpless to resistBrian LoganMon 17 Aug 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I saw the title to the Australian clown Conk’s show Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour, I thought I knew what the trick would be. Yes, the terms of the show’s billing would be fulfilled, but (I imagined) by twisting whatever that song was into a diverting variety of new shapes – rather as the comedy trio Sheeps did when performing the same sketch repeatedly for an hourway back in 2014.More fool me, for doubting that Conk – AKA Connor Dariol – would keep things as ruthlessly simple as his Ronseal title suggests. He really does sing the same song over and again, with the same backing track and surprisingly little embellishment, for 60 minutes – with a bloody great clock marking the limits of your endurance on an upstage screen. And wait until you hear what song it is! Its opening chords are greeted by an aghast laugh from the audience. Reader, this experience felt like an endurance test before that song had reached the end of its first cycle.Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughRead moreOne recalls with unease that the US military tortured people during the “war on terror” by playing bad songs at them over and again. So how does Conk fashion this experiment in patience-testing into one of the most joyful hours in town? It’s a subtle process. His near-relentless pep is part of it. Then, he starts throwing the odd anxious glance at the clock:how longis there still to go?! It’s not till the fourth or fifth performance that he modulates the delivery of the lyrics, putting a suddenly funny spin on the singer’s relationship to the story the song tells.We’re deep into the second half before he really cuts loose, and even then his wilder antics usually remain tethered to the truth of this deeply ridiculous song, now performed in a sinister whisper or while posed scantily-clad on a chair. Without the show ever having coerced us – call it Stockholm syndrome – we’re all involved by the end, Conk’s exercise in absurdist perseverance devolving into the most ecstatic communal experience I’ve shared at this year’s fringe.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreSummerhallComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lara Ricote: Inkling review – this fizzy standup’s smart new set is her best yet | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A show about maturing and learning to listen to life’s signals doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and has some great gags
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A show about maturing and learning to listen to life’s signals doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and has some great gags
Content: Great command … Lara Ricote performing at Monkey Barrel Comedy.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenGreat command … Lara Ricote performing at Monkey Barrel Comedy.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLara Ricote: Inkling review – this fizzy standup’s smart new set is her best yetMonkey Barrel Comedy, EdinburghA show about maturing and learning to listen to life’s signals doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and has some great gagsBrian LoganMon 17 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 11.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat a rich and enjoyable show this is fromLara Ricote, a leap forwards from her already-excellentfirst two shows. It finds the Mexican-American comic in as endearing fettle as ever, her urge to communicate bubbling over in a show about divining the messages life puts your way, however indecipherable they (like this show) can sometimes appear.It begins at the oracle at Delphi, with a hymn to belief over rationalism. “This is a show about mystery and messages,” says Ricote, and if we only understand 65% of it, that need be no bar to our appreciation. And there’s truth in that – I often felt I was chasing along in the show’s slipstream. It flits and fizzes between narrative strands, Ricote abstracting her voice into burbling, and blurting water over herself, for (at least at first) minimal apparent reason.View image in fullscreenFinding herself … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThere is reason, but it’s up to us make the connections, while Ricote recounts the end of a long-term relationship, and the beginning of a friendship with another comic who, like her, is hard of hearing. How does that condition relate to her sense of two-thirds understanding as the golden mean? And why is she so down on sign language? A further encounter, in which a man tries to discuss a painting with her in a museum, dramatises her interest in the signals life sends us, and her (and our) difficulty in always perceiving them.Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughRead moreRicote weaves these sections with great command (“blackout!”), but also a goofy amusement at her presumption in doing so. This show about maturing doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and great jokes – see Ricote deploying her whole body to imitate “split-tongue guy”, or the very funny establishing shot she performs to evoke New York City. But Inkling also lets us watch her grow up as if in real time, as her confidence grows in interpreting the world for herself, and as she inches towards a fuller embrace of her hard-of-hearing identity. The sense, and it’s an exciting one, is both of a person finding themselves, and an artist too.AtMonkey Barrel Comedy, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’ve got to see this girl!’ Tanita Tikaram on making Twist in My Sobriety | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘People tell me it helped them with their rehab. I have to explain: Sorry, it’s not about alcohol – I was just a kid singing about injustice’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: ‘People tell me it helped them with their rehab. I have to explain: Sorry, it’s not about alcohol – I was just a kid singing about injustice’
Content: ‘Once I had the groovy guitar riff, the song fell together’ … Tanita Tikaram on stage in 1989.Photograph: Gie Knaeps/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Once I had the groovy guitar riff, the song fell together’ … Tanita Tikaram on stage in 1989.Photograph: Gie Knaeps/Getty ImagesHow we madeMusic‘You’ve got to see this girl!’ Tanita Tikaram on making Twist in My Sobriety‘People tell me it helped them with their rehab. I have to explain: Sorry, it’s not about alcohol – I was just a kid singing about injustice’Interviews byDave SimpsonMon 17 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTanita Tikaram, singer-songwriterI wrote the lyrics on the floor of my bedroom in Basingstoke when I was 16 or 17, as a way of decompressing from studying for my A-levels. I had the idea for “Twist in my …” something, but didn’t know what else to put in there. I tried “Twist in my gravity” before ending up with “sobriety”, but it’s not a song about alcohol. It’s about feeling that things aren’t right in the world, and that adults can do terrible or immoral things – but none of it will change you. Fundamentally, it’s a song by an alienated teenager who feels there’s a lot of injustice. There’s something lovely about how intensely you feel things as a teenager.The opening line, “All God’s children need travelling shoes,” is the title of a book by Maya Angelou. Then “All good people read good books” is the language of a kid who reads a lot. It’s a little road song: you’re on a journey, kind of travelling, but really looking for something. Once I had the groovy little guitar riff, the song just fell together.double quotation markUnusually, I came up with a part for oboeI’d only previously sung in a school play, but some guys from a local band helped me record my songs in a nearby studio, so suddenly I had a tape. I sent it to the Mean Fiddler in Harlesden, London, and they gave me a spot at their open mic night. I played there to just three people, but one of them was the venue-owner,Vince Power, who told an agent: “You’ve got to see this girl!” Soon enough, I’d signed to a record label and they suggested Rod Argent and Peter Van Hooke as co-producers. Like me, Rod had been very young when he had his first hit inthe Zombies, so there was empathy there.Peter would pick me up at the train station and we’d drive to Rod’s home studio in St Albans, where we recorded Twist in My Sobriety. Rod wanted the right sound for the melody line and went through the whole woodwind section of samples. In those days, samples were all on floppy discs so you’d sit there for ages waiting for them to load, but then suddenly he tried a synthetic oboe and said: “My God, that works!”I never had an inkling that the song was going to be a hit, but it took off in continental Europe and everywhere else followed. I’m very proud of it. Recently, a young woman came up to me and said: “That song takes me to my happy place.” It’s a dark song to do that for someone. In the US, people tell me it helped them with their sobriety or rehab. I have to explain: “Sorry, it’s not about alcohol. I was just a kid.”Rod Argent, co-producerWhen Peter and I first met Tanita, she’d only ever played her own guitar. We thought she was really talented: we wanted to match the strength and direction of her composition with a really colourful, inventive backing. My studio was in a wonderful Georgian house called Red House, where we had two rooms: a control room and a recording room with a piano in it. Everything was done in there – and in those days we recorded on to tape.Pete came up with the brilliant idea of recording a master vocal with Tanita playing guitar to a guide rhythm track we’d then dispense with, because that was the way she was used to playing. That gave us a really confident vocal – Tanita sounded really in command. But it meant we could be really inventive around it, conjuring up a scenario with strings and such. We built up every track on her Ancient Heart album like that.View image in fullscreenThe 7in single sleeve for Twist in My Sobriety, 1988.Photograph: sjvinyl/AlamyFor Twist in My Sobriety, Pete created a definitive drum part and I had a ball coming up with the instrumental sections. The booming synth sounds at the beginning have a lot of attack, then I came up with a part for – unusually – oboe, which Pete was very unsure about at first as he wanted a more folky thing. But there was something classical about it that sounded really lovely. We did it using the oboe sound on the synth first, then a professional player called Malcolm Messiter came in and played an actual oboe.I thought the finished song had a fantastic feel: there was something very unusual about it. I played it this morning for the first time in a long time – and it sounded absolutely brilliant.Tanita Tikaram plays Beautiful Days,Escot Park, Devon, 20-23 August.Explore more on these topicsMusicHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beatles film recreates iconic Abbey Road album cover | Movies | The Guardian
description: Social media footage this weekend revealed the cast of Sam Mendes’ four-film band biopic on the zebra crossing near the studio, posing for the famous image
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Social media footage this weekend revealed the cast of Sam Mendes’ four-film band biopic on the zebra crossing near the studio, posing for the famous image
Content: All you need is hair … Harris Dickinson, Barry Keoghan, Paul Mescal and Joseph Quinn filming in Abbey Road, LondonPhotograph: MCPIX/JBURNSView image in fullscreenAll you need is hair … Harris Dickinson, Barry Keoghan, Paul Mescal and Joseph Quinn filming in Abbey Road, LondonPhotograph: MCPIX/JBURNSMoviesBeatles film recreates iconic Abbey Road album coverSocial media footage this weekend revealed the cast of Sam Mendes’ four-film band biopic on the zebra crossing near the studio, posing for the famous imageAndrew PulverMon 17 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 17.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe production team behind the forthcoming four-film Beatles biopic, directed bySam Mendes, has been spotted filming outside Abbey Road studios in London; this included a recreation of the celebrated Abbey Road album cover, for which the band was photographed on the nearby pedestrian crossing – now a popular tourist landmark.Footage posted on social mediaon Sunday shows the actors playing the Beatles lining up on the kerb and walking across the road. Harris Dickinson, as John Lennon, is leading the walk, with Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr, Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney and Joseph Quinn as George Harrison following in sequence.View image in fullscreenThe fab four … Harris Dickinson (John Lennon), Paul Mescal (Paul McCartney), Barry Keoghan (Ringo Starr), and Joseph Quinn (George Harrison).Photograph: John Russo/Rex/ShutterstockThe Beatles recorded Abbey Road mostly in the summer of 1969, and thecover photo was taken on 8 Augustafter an initial idea to travel to Nepal for a photograph was abandoned. (The album’s working title was Everest, after a cigarette brand smoked by engineer Geoff Emerick.) Freelance photographer Iain Macmillan was commissioned to take the image, and took six stills from a stepladder positioned in the middle of the road – of which one was chosen.Mendes announced the project in February 2024– four films that each focus on an individual Beatle – with backing from Hollywood studio Sony Pictures and the permission of both McCartney and Starr, as well as from the estates of Lennon and Harrison. In addition to the actors playing the central roles, a host of major names have joined the cast, including Saoirse Ronan as Linda McCartney, James Norton as Brian Epstein and Lucy Boynton as Jane Asher.The films are due for release in April 2028.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe Beatles filmsSam MendesThe BeatlesLondonPaul MescalBarry KeoghannewsShareReuse this content

title: Johnny Depp in talks to return to Pirates of the Caribbean franchise  | Johnny Depp | The Guardian
description: The actor, who previously said he would not play Captain Jack Sparrow again for ‘$300m and a million alpacas’, is being lined up for sixth film in the series according to producer Jerry Bruckheimer
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: The actor, who previously said he would not play Captain Jack Sparrow again for ‘$300m and a million alpacas’, is being lined up for sixth film in the series according to producer Jerry Bruckheimer
Content: Johnny Depp as Jack Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (2011).Photograph: Peter Mountain/APView image in fullscreenJohnny Depp as Jack Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (2011).Photograph: Peter Mountain/APJohnny DeppJohnny Depp in talks to return to Pirates of the Caribbean franchiseThe actor, who previously said he would not play Captain Jack Sparrow again for ‘$300m and a million alpacas’, is being lined up for sixth film in the series according to producer Jerry BruckheimerLaurence PhelanMon 17 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohnny Depp is in talks to return as Captain Jack Sparrow in a sixth Pirates of the Caribbean film, according to the producer of the series, Jerry Bruckheimer. Bruckheimertold Deadline: “We’re talking with Johnny, we’re working on a screenplay, and hopefully we can get this done.” This is despite the actor having said under oath in 2022, during the notorious televised trial of the defamation case he brought against his ex-wife, Amber Heard, that Disney had dropped him from the series and he would not play Sparrow again even if he were offered “$300m and a million alpacas”.Depp first appeared as the charismatic, roguish, rum-swilling Captain Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl in 2003, and it has become his most recognisable – and profitable – role. Taking its name and golden age of piracy setting from a ride at the Disney World theme park, the swashbuckling adventure also featured Keira Knightley, Orlando Bloom and Geoffrey Rush, and grossed more than $650m (£480m) at the worldwide box office.Four sequels followed between 2006 and 2017, and it was the first franchise to produce two films that each made more than $1bn. The series has made more than $4.5bn in total. The most recent entry, Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, was released in 2017. Although reviews were not especially positive, it grossed almost $800m.However, Depp has had well-publicised legal issues since then, which have affected his career. The defamation trial against Heard in the US was preceded in 2020 by a libel lawsuit he brought in the UK after the Sun newspaper characterised him as a “wife-beater”;the court foundthe characterisation was “substantially true”. After this verdict, Depp wasasked by Warner Bros to resignfrom the Fantastic Beasts franchise, when shooting on a third film had already begun.The jury in the 2022 trialruled in Depp’s favour, finding that Heard had defamed her ex-husband in a Washington Post editorial in which she said she “became a public figure representing domestic abuse”.Depp subsequently played Louis XV in the 2023 French-language historical dramaJeanne du Barry, and voiced a puffin in the feature-length animation Johnny Puff: Secret Mission in 2024. But whether audiences will welcome him making a comeback as a major film star may be determined when he plays Scrooge inEbenezer, directed by Ti West, due to be released in the UK and US in November.Explore more on these topicsJohnny DeppPirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales (aka Salazar's Revenge)Action and adventure filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Life behind bars in Britain’s surviving Victorian prisons – photo essay | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Photographer Andy Aitchison’s book Incarcerated explores how Victorian prison infrastructure has persisted and what these old buildings mean for the people who live and work inside
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Photographer Andy Aitchison’s book Incarcerated explores how Victorian prison infrastructure has persisted and what these old buildings mean for the people who live and work inside
Content: Men wait for a delivery in the rubbish and recycling centre at HMP Lincoln. The category B men’s jail and young offender institution, which has space for 650 prisoners, opened in 1872. Photograph: Andy AitchisonDozens of prisons were built in Britain between 1842 and 1877, many of which are still in use today. For more than 20 years, Andy Aitchison has photographed behind the walls. His bookIncarceratedexplores how Victorian prison infrastructure has persisted, and what these old buildings mean for the people who live and work insideByAndy AitchisonMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat is now HMP Lincoln opened at the end of the most prolific period of prison construction in British history, when 90 prisons were built or significantly expanded between 1842 and 1877. Here, observes the introductory essay to Incarcerated, “was the Victorian faith in ‘progress’, rendered in bricks and mortar and applied to the challenge of remaking those who had set themselves against law and society”.View image in fullscreenJohn, from E wing at HMP Lincoln, has dementia and spends his days shouting and screaming in his cell. When he gets out into the exercise yard he sits in silence and enjoys the space, fresh air and sunshineLess than 50 years later, in their 1922 study English Prisons Today: Being the Report of the Prison System Enquiry Committee, Stephen Hobhouse and Fenner Brockway argued: “The only reform to which [these Victorian] buildings can be usefully subjected is dynamite.”Despite the continued power of this critique, today prisons such as HMP Lincoln and HMP Liverpool seem as permanent as ever. More than 30 remain in use, collectively holding about a quarter of the UK’s prison population.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenHMP Wandsworth, clockwise from top left: prisoners return from their jobs to their wings for lunch; an area known as the central star, which leads to all original wings of the prison; cell windows in D wing; a prisoner stands outside his cell on C wingAndy Aitchison has been taking photographs inside Britain’s prisons for more than 20 years. His interest began in 2004 when he was asked by the Big Issue to photograph inside HMP Wandsworth, another Victorian prison.double quotation markAs soon as I got in, the environment fascinated me. The architecture was incredible and the prisoners were just normal peopleAndy AitchisonView image in fullscreenA view of wing A, HMP Wandsworth. This wing has suicide netting between each floor. The prison, in south-west London, was built in 1851 and is one of the largest jails in western Europe. It can accommodate 1,456 prisonersHe later told Time Out: “I went on to one of the wings and there was the usual shouting, but when I got to the radio room it was like a bit of a sanctuary. Once the guys stepped in there, it was a work environment and they became almost different people.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenHMP Lincoln, left to right: men from E wing return to their cells after time in the exercise yard; prisoners line up to get food in the canteen on A wing“I enjoyed it so much that after the shoot, I got in touch to ask if I could go back to make more pictures. I went 10 or 15 times over a six-month period. I started meeting guys the same age as me, who had a kid like me – they were in the same situation in life as me, but they were in prison and I wasn’t.”View image in fullscreenKev reads a book in his cell on E wing, HMP LincolnSince that assignment, Aitchison has photographed nearly 50 prisons, often making repeat visits as he works on long-term projects. His work has been used extensively by charities and published nationally and internationally. He regularly contributes to Inside Time, the UK’s leading prison newspaper.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenHMP Lincoln, left to right: suicide netting in the main central atrium of A wing; a prisoner walks down stairs next to the first night centreAitchison has to work under strict conditions. His equipment is searched on entry and exit, consent forms must be signed by any prisoner he photographs, and certain objects – keys, locks, fence numbers – must never be pictured.Faces of the prisoners are not shown: in order to publish a photograph of a serving prisoner, explicit permission from the Ministry of Justice is required.View image in fullscreenRobert, 77, sits in his wheelchair outside his cell at HMP Lincoln. His chair does not fit through his cell door on C wingThe images in Incarcerated are part of continuing research on the long afterlives of Britain’s Victorian prison estate by geographers, criminologists and historians. Together they explore how the fabric and function of prisons built in the 19th century have changed over time, the tensions between architectural obsolescence and persistence, and what it has felt like to live and work in Victorian prisons then and now.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: two men look through the window in their cell door on K wing, HMP Liverpool; the single-occupancy exercise yard for the Care and Support Unit wing inside HMP Lincoln; suicide netting on E wing of HMP Lincoln; two staff members vape during a lunch break against the brick wall of an outer perimeter fence at HMP LincolnPresented in conversation with essays written by members of the project team, Aitchison’s photographs form a unique portrait of Britain’s still-functioning Victorian prisons, and those who live and work in them.Incarceratedis available direct from the publisherBluecoat PressExplore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayPrisons and probationPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Paul McCartney asked for my autograph!’ Su Pollard on Hi-de-Hi! and her amazing celebrity encounters | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: Even after half a century in the limelight, the actor can still surprise. Who’d have guessed she went clubbing with Freddie Mercury? Or that she watched Blair and Brown strike their fateful deal at Granita?
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: Even after half a century in the limelight, the actor can still surprise. Who’d have guessed she went clubbing with Freddie Mercury? Or that she watched Blair and Brown strike their fateful deal at Granita?
Content: Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe big interviewTV comedy‘Paul McCartney asked for my autograph!’ Su Pollard on Hi-de-Hi! and her amazing celebrity encountersEven after half a century in the limelight, the actor can still surprise. Who’d have guessed she went clubbing with Freddie Mercury? Or that she watched Blair and Brown strike their fateful deal at Granita?Emine SanerMon 17 Aug 2026 02.18 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareA quick run-through of some of the 20th-century icons that Su Pollard has met. Paul McCartney? “Absolutely fabulous,” Pollard says. “He was sat leaning against a wall, next to Linda.” She does a great impression of McCartney’s accent. “‘Hey Su, how are you? Love the show. Can I have your autograph? For my mother.’” The show was, of course, the hugely successful BBC sitcom Hi-de-Hi!, set on an Essex holiday camp and for which Pollard, playing chalet maid Peggy, will for ever be best known.Queen Elizabeth, after a Royal Variety Performance? “She was absolutely marvellous. What struck me – I’ve always said this – was her skin. I was drawn to her skin. It was all peachified. And beautiful smile, her own teeth. Very regal, very straight-backed, not very tall, and quite a voluptuous bosom.”Diana, Princess of Wales, did a little tap-dance with Pollard at a function. “I found her very charming. Although she was classed as quite shy, I don’t think she was. She was very open to meeting people, but perhaps it was a slow burn with her.”double quotation markThe queen was marvellous. She had quite a voluptuous bosomAt a club in Earl’s Court in London, Pollard was “having it large”, she says, when a man approached her and asked if he could join in. “I went: ‘Stop! It’s never you, is it?’” It was – Queen singer Freddie Mercury. She does an impression of him too, overbite protruding. “He went: ‘I could be anybody, dear.’ His teeth were fantastic. Another wonderful smile. His friend took a picture of us.”At various Downing Street functions, Pollard met Margaret Thatcher – “marvellous, but it was very fleeting” – and Theresa May. “She went: ‘Hi de hi.’ I said: ‘Ho de ho.’ She was fabulous – I liked her. She was very warm. Getting on with the job the best she could.” Tony Blair? Gordon Brown? No, she says. “But I did see Tony and Gordon in … what’s that lovely restaurant?” Might it have been Granita? (Blair was a near-neighbour at the time in north London.) Pollard looks astonished. “That’s it! How do you know that?”View image in fullscreen‘I was the luckiest person in the world at that time’ ... Pollard, far left, with Simon Cadell, Michael Knowles and Ruth Madoc in Hi-de-Hi!Photograph: PA Images/AlamyGranita was, you may remember, the venue of the 1994 pact, where Brown agreed Blair would run for the Labour leadership. “That’s the first I’ve heard of that,” says Pollard. “God, I feel a shiver. That’s what they were talking about!” I mean, we don’t know that’s what they were discussing at that precise moment, but let’s go with it. “I gawked at them through the window and waved.”Much has been written about that fateful night, and to it we can perhaps now add the mental image of Pollard – wearing, I like to think, bright owlish glasses, maybe a feather boa, and manic grin – excitedly waving at the two serious men, history in their hands, through the window. “They just kind of went” – she gives a harassed smile – “and then hurried back to talking. I bet they thought: ‘It’s that Hi-de-Hi! person.’”We meet in London at the Club for Acts and Actors, the social and support organisation of which Pollard is president, in a room surrounded by old portraits of stars and posters for shows. Pollard, 76, has just written her memoir, Fully Charged, hoofing through her 52-year career, which has spanned theatre, musicals and TV. She is such funny company, and her book – which one can’t help reading in her throaty Nottingham accent – has some gems. On changing her name from Sue to Su: “I can’t prove it, but I maintain that losing that vowel gave me some kind of momentum.” And on spotting a pop superstar, not known for his sense of humour, at the infamous 1987 It’s a Royal Knockout TV event, which she co-hosted: “I saw a sight I never expected to witness – Cliff Richard dressed as a leek.”It was “lovely”, she says, to write the book (with her friend and collaborator Paul Boyd), “because it reminded me, and gave me time to reflect, going: ‘God, that was funny.’ Then it makes you think, ‘I’ve had far more ups than downs’, and that’s what you’ve got to be in life, I think – positive.”View image in fullscreenInfamous … Pollard and Les Dawson in It’s a Royal Knockout, 1987.Photograph: Kevin Holt/ANL/Rex/ShutterstockIt has been an extraordinary life. Pollard grew up in Nottingham, an only child until she was eight. Her parents both worked in a cigarette factory, but Pollard discovered an interest in the stage while taking part in her school nativity. She was playing an “assistant” angel and when she stood to deliver her lines, on a cardboard box that had been taped together, she fell through it. The audience laughed and Pollard was hooked. When she was about 14, writing a school essay about where she hoped to be in 10 years, “I wrote: ‘I see myself at the Palladium.’ And funnily enough, I was.”What did her parents make of her? She laughs and does an impression of her mother, Hilda (she started calling her by her name as a teenager, “because I was a hippy” and she thought her mother deserved more than to be identified only as “Mum”). “Su, if you don’t mind, do you think you could walk behind me?”She thinks she was wearing a full-length fur coat that day, but it could have been any number of outlandish outfits. Clothes had become her costume, and gave her a sense of permission to be bold, visible and fun (today she’s wearing a black sequined dress, sparkly red waistcoat, maroon specs, beads and a portrait of Frida Kahlo around her neck, with a pair of miniature Ferrero Rocher chocolate packets for earrings). “I was creating my own style, albeit I looked like a morris dancer at one point because I had scarves round my knees and ankles. No wonder my poor mother …” She laughs. “It was fabulous. What I’m saying is, just be yourself in life.”View image in fullscreen‘Just be yourself in life.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianSometimes people would stare at her so hard and so long they’d walk into a lamp-post. People would comment but it never bothered her. “You think: ‘Why are you so pathetically feeble-minded? Just because you’ve seen something different.’ And then you think: ‘Oh, it’s not their fault – forget it.’” Her headteacher reprimanded her for wearing her school coat “like an opera cape” but also, recognising her “theatrical leanings”, as Pollard puts it, introduced her to a friend who ran the local amateur dramatic group.Pollard was off – in am-dram roles, and performing in local working men’s clubs. In 1974, she appeared on the TV talent show Opportunity Knocks, but came second to a “singing” jack russell (she alleges the owner would insert a finger into its bottom to make it howl on cue). “I’ve never liked jack russells ever since,” she says with a laugh. “I cross the road to avoid them.”Her first big professional job was in a touring production of Godspell, produced by a young Cameron Mackintosh, who would go on to become a titan of theatre. Did she ever feel out of place as a working-class actor? “No, funnily enough, because I met several that were very similar to me.” Now, she says, “there’s more privately educated people, perhaps, than there are from comprehensives. But I didn’t feel out of place, whether I was with my peers or with people that had been to ‘radar’.” She hoots at herself. People would assume she was so uneducated that she didn’t know how to pronounce Rada, the acronym for the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. “It used to make me laugh. I used to do it, just for fun. To me, it never matters where you come from, as long as you’re a good team player, you’ve got the discipline and the passion for it. And reliability – I always believed in a work ethic.”Impostor syndrome never plagued her. She was lucky, she says, to have been supported by her parents and teachers. “You didn’t feel that you weren’t good enough. I tried never to get above myself, but I thought: ‘Su, you’ve got enough talent, just as much as anyone else.’”double quotation markA lot of producers think it’s time for you to go. No! I’m too youngPollard had been working in theatre for five years and approaching 30 when she got the role in Hi-de-Hi! (She had appeared in another sitcom just before that, Two Up, Two Down.) “I was just beside myself. I was the luckiest person – we all were – in the world at that time.” Did they know it would become so big? “No, but we had an inkling that it was on the right track when we did the pilot and the whole crew were killing themselves laughing.” The humour, she says, hasn’t really dated. “It’s adults looking ridiculous and silly situations. Mostly slapstick stuff – that’s what I loved about it because I like physical humour.” (It remains big in Hungary.)She still loves talking about the show, she says, and never feels resentful about being asked about it, especially by fans. “People have loved it and you have to respect that you were part of somebody’s life. I think it’s rotten to disrespect your audience.” The cast, or at least those that are still around, continue to get together. “We call ourselves “the Undead”, the ones that are still here. We go: ‘Weren’t we lucky to have brought people all that joy?’”View image in fullscreen‘I tried never to get above myself, but I thought: you’ve got enough talent’ … pictured in 2007.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianBoyd brings her a cup of tea and Pollard rummages through her handbag – it’s decorated with all the names of her shows on it – looking for something to fish the teabag out with. Has she got a tomato in there? (Appearing on the TV panel show Would I Lie to You?, Pollard revealed she never went anywhere without a tomato, to jazz up restaurant salads, and a party blower, to jazz up … life). No tomatoes today. “I don’t put them in there now because people started pinching them.” A party blower? Again she rummages in her bag, and brings one out and toots it. “Sometimes, suddenly on the train …” She blows it loudly and laughs. “Pathetic. Honestly! I’m in my 70s. It just makes me laugh.”In 1984, Pollard married Peter Keogh, whom she met when he was working as a stagehand on the Hi-de-Hi! musical. She knew that he’d had boyfriends, but when the tabloids found out, it unleashed years of homophobic coverage. “It’s not a very nice thing [to be hounded by reporters], especially when you’ve got to work,” she says. There were constant stories alleging he had continued to have affairs with men.It was also around the time of the HIV and Aids crisis, which made the tabloids even more rabid. Pollard, a longtime ally of the gay community, watched with horror as friends started becoming ill. She remembers doing an early fundraiser at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern, the iconic London LGBTQ+ venue. “I didn’t know enough about it at the time; I don’t think anyone did. People were great, giving money. But then, of course, people I knew started dying. One of the first was a friend from Godspell. That was a really tragic thing – he was amazing. Then a very close friend. It was devastating, really.” She would hear about friends of friends. “There was no real consolation.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m not going to be waiting for the phone to ring’ ... Pollard in the Benidorm Christmas Special in 2010.Photograph: Tiger Aspect/ITVPollard is still great friends with her ex-husband – they divorced in 1992 – and his husband. “You can’t regret things in your life. You might feel sad that things didn’t turn out the way you initially hoped, but no grudges, no regrets.” She had another long-term relationship. “But since then, I can’t be bothered. I’m more passionate about showbiz than a man.”This was the reason she never wanted to have children. “Why would I want to be a mother? How can I learn my lines if I’m going: ‘Stop that, Carol – eat your dinner.’ I don’t know how people do it, darling.” It’s hard enough for women who choose to remain child-free now; was she judged for it in the 80s? “No, because I think people knew better than to actually be … And you know the greatest thing? Hilda and me dad never once said: ‘When are we going to be grandparents?’” Jean, her sister, also didn’t have children. “It was not at all because of bad parenting – they were marvellous – we just never thought to go down that route. No thank you.”About 25 years ago, when Pollard had just turned 50, she had a bit of a career lull. “At the time, you think: ‘Oh, flippin’ ’eck, here I am, middle-aged.’ I thought: ‘I’ve got to make a concerted effort. I’m not going to be proud, waiting for the phone to ring.’” She wrote to writers and directors, reminding people she was around and wanting to work. “I wrote to Jonathan Harvey, who I liked.” The playwright had been writing the BBC comedy Gimme Gimme Gimme, and offered Pollard a guest spot. “That sort of kickstarted my career again, so I was really fortunate. Then I got offered more musicals.” She went into the touring production of Annie, and continued for many years. “I think a lot of producers, and even writers, probably think, ‘Well, they’ve had a good innings’, and it’s time for you to go. No! I’m too young. I never say the R-word.” Camply, she stage-whispers: “Retirement.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ve had far more ups than downs.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThis year, Pollard will do her 43rd panto, playing a fairy in Sleeping Beauty in Crewe, and she continues with her one-woman show. She has enviable energy – the work helps. “If you like the piece, you’re energised by it.” But she also does all the sensible things: walks a lot, sees friends, eats healthily, sleeps well. “My favourite sleep time is 2am till nine.” What does she do until 2am? Read mostly, she says. Gone are the days of dancing in clubs, but only because London nightlife is so “pathetic” (she almost spits the word). “Sadiq Khan [the London mayor], God love him, he’s doing his best trying to get the night-time economy back. Ever since Covid, it’s the saddest thing. I can’t believe, in a capital city of the world, there’s nowhere open at midnight. You must be having a laugh. I’ve been furious since then.”She is so irrepressible; does she ever have down days? “I wouldn’t say down. I would describe it as dissatisfied. I’m more likely to get irritable. But then I go: ‘Oh, forget it, Su.’” She used to dwell on things, she says. “I’ve learned over the years you’re better not to. I get sad for other people sometimes. I get very sad about losing mates. But then again, I still talk to them and say, ‘just thinking of you, babe’, and then that moment passes.”To use the theatre cliche, the show must go on, of course. And I think – as she reapplies lipstick, grins and adjusts her sequin minidress – that to be Su Pollard must be like being in one glorious, joyful show that runs and runs.Su Pollard: Fully Charged is published by Mirror Books (£22). title: The one change that worked: I sent myself a letter – and realised what’s missing in this world of WhatsApp | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I’ve started writing to my sister, my mum, my friends … Not everyone writes back, but when we connect it’s on a deeper level than any group chat
Author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi
Headline: I’ve started writing to my sister, my mum, my friends … Not everyone writes back, but when we connect it’s on a deeper level than any group chat
Content: ‘It was like opening a time capsule of my thoughts and feelings’ … Mabel Banfield-Nwachi in Madrid.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It was like opening a time capsule of my thoughts and feelings’ … Mabel Banfield-Nwachi in Madrid.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: I sent myself a letter – and realised what’s missing in this world of WhatsAppI’ve started writing to my sister, my mum, my friends … Not everyone writes back, but when we connect it’s on a deeper level than any group chatMabel Banfield-NwachiMon 17 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast January, I received a letter. Most of my post was predictably boring – a statement from the water company, my credit card bill, the occasional update about my pension contributions – but this letter was different. The envelope felt heavier than the run-of-the-mill ones I was used to. It was postmarked Paris, a place I had little connection to, and, most strikingly, it was addressed in messy handwriting – my own.I had completely forgotten I’d written it until it turned up on my doorstep. On a trip to Paris the year before, I had visited a letter-writing cafe. The idea was simple: you wrote a letter (usually to yourself), the cafe kept it safe and sent it a year later. So, alongside tryingescargotsfor the first time, I wrote a letter filled with questions about my not-so-distant future and addressed it to my home, in London. What will you be doing? Where will you be living? Do you have a boyfriend?The questions weren’t especially profound, but receiving the letter felt strangely comforting. It was from me, but I felt removed from the person who had written it. It was like opening a time capsule of my thoughts and feelings that photos from that time, or even journal entries, hadn’t quite captured.View image in fullscreen‘Writing letters became a ritual I grew to treasure.’Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianI started writing to other people. At first, it was a monthly letter to my mum in London, updating her on my new life abroad in Madrid. Sometimes I would include a ticket or receipt, explaining which museums or galleries I had been visiting, or proving that I really had found the ripest avocado for 40p. Although we spoke on the phone every week, I loved the space it gave me to say things I wouldn’t otherwise, such as how slowly people walk here, and to reflect.After a few months, I was writing even more letters. At least once a week, I’d be in the queue at the post office with a letter for my sister, a friend from home, or my little cousins. Not everyone wrote back, but just sending them felt cathartic. It became a ritual I grew to treasure, and one that quietly added up.View image in fullscreenMabel Banfield-Nwachi in Paris.Photograph: Courtesy of Mabel Banfield-NwachiThe feel of pen on paper, or even the taste of the gummed envelope flap, couldn’t be replicated by a FaceTime call or a message in the family WhatsApp group. More than that, the urge to constantly be in touch started to feel less pressing, because I found I was saying more in those letters than I could ever convey even in person. And while I got a lot out of writing and sending them, much of the joy came from anticipating one in return.I loved the weight of a letter, my name written out in someone else’s handwriting. I wouldn’t open it straight away. I would let my imagination dance around who it might be from, what it might say, all while making my way up the stairs to my flat. At my desk, I would read it slowly, deliberately, savouring it. Small details would start to stand out – a pen running out, a crossed-out word or phrase. The words people repeated again and again.We don’t often pay attention in that way any more. Even finishing a book can feel like a stretch. Messages are written quickly, sent in a hurry and forgotten just as rapidly: glanced at, replied to and moved on from. A letter doesn’t work like that. You have to slow down, think about what you’re reading, what you’re saying. That was what I liked about it. So, just as the new commute to work had become part of my life away from Britain, so, before long, had checking the letterbox in the entrance to the apartment building on the way out.​​I haven’t stopped messaging or suddenly sworn off my phone, but it does feel less urgent. I’ve muted some group chats, archived others, and no longer get that sinking feeling if I forget to reply straight away. I have found myself slowing down in other ways too – thinking a little more before replying, choosing my words more carefully, calling when a planned catch-up has drifted into text.This routine has given me something stable to return to, wherever I am living. This January, I sent another letter to myself, back to my childhood home in London, where it will be waiting for me. I wonder if I’ll still recognise the person who wrote it.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe one change that workedFamilyFriendshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I thought testing ice-cream makers would be fun – then came the milk-fuelled madness | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: After three dozen eggs, 30 lemons and a concerning amount of unplanned butter, our tester learned the hard way how to make the perfect ice-cream. Plus, how to buy a bike
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: After three dozen eggs, 30 lemons and a concerning amount of unplanned butter, our tester learned the hard way how to make the perfect ice-cream. Plus, how to buy a bike
Content: Inside scoop: testing 13 ice-cream makers wasn’t always as sweet as it looked.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianView image in fullscreenInside scoop: testing 13 ice-cream makers wasn’t always as sweet as it looked.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Filter UK newsletterIce-cream and sorbetI thought testing ice-cream makers would be fun – then came the milk-fuelled madnessAfter three dozen eggs, 30 lemons and a concerning amount of unplanned butter, our tester learned the hard way how to make the perfect ice-cream. Plus, how to buy a bikeDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereDanielle AmatoMon 17 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou probably knowthat song about ice-cream, and it’s been playing in my head non-stop for the past month. But since I tested 13 ice-cream machines at once during the hottest days of the year, it has taken on a slightly different meaning for me – particularly the screaming part.Testing thebest ice-cream makersfor the Filter has deepened my appreciation for frozen desserts. After cracking more than three dozen eggs, zesting 30 lemons and running to the shops for several emergency pints of milk after an unplanned butter disaster, I feel as though I’ve finally mastered the art of making ice-cream at home.Churn of eventsView image in fullscreenTesting situation: some of the contenders lined up for a summer of churning.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianThe first challenge was figuring out how many ingredients I needed to test all those machines – a lot, as it turns out. I witnessed great confusion in my food delivery driver’s eyes when he arrived at my door for the second time in a week, carrying bags filled with nothing but eggs, lemons, milk, cream and sugar.After I got over the embarrassment of my absurd ingredients order, I got to work making batches of Felicity Cloake’sperfect vanilla ice-creamandlemon sorbetrecipes in each machine. I also tested a standard recipe consisting of double cream, sugar and milk, a variant of which could often be found in each machine’s accompanying booklet.I then tasted each batch for flavour and consistency, before leaving them in my freezer for a few days to see how each held up.Caso Design’s compressor IceCreamercame out on top as my favourite overall, while the originalNinja Creamiwas an easy-to-use, freeze-first winner.Making delicious ice-cream, then consuming it – what a great life, I thought to myself. Little did I know this would be the start of my descent into several long weeks of milk-fuelled madness during record-breaking July heatwaves.I accidentally made butter – twice – when a recipe from one machine’s booklet took too long to churn, turning the high-fat mixture into butter before it was able to freeze. And while I love making my own butter, I wouldn’t recommend anyone do this in a soft-serve machine. You’ll spend the next 45 minutes scraping it from every nook, spout and corner, trying not to completely lose the plot.Then there was the smell. My longsuffering partner burst into my office on one occasion, despairing that the “whole house stinks of milk”. (Don’t feel too sorry for him, though: he got to eat a lot of ice-cream.)The cold hard truthMilk-related disasters aside, my time testing ice-cream machines taught me a few things. The first is that some of the best models require a lot of counter space. I did find a couple of excellent compact versions in the form of theNutribullet ChillandCuisinart Solo Scoops, but complex models such as theGreenPan Frostare magnificent beasts that command all of your space and attention.They’re also heavy. I can’t believe I’m not absolutely ripped by now (though my partner reminds me that he’s actually done a lot of the heavy lifting).But despite it all, I’m still not sick of ice-cream. In fact, I’ve gained a real appreciation for just how good homemade ice-cream can be. That said, I might stick to Ben & Jerry’s for the rest of the summer – or at least until the house stops smelling of milk.This week’s picksSuri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush review: this new budget model is still sustainable – and the one I’d buyThe best electric toothbrushes for every budget – testedHow I Shop with Fred Sirieix: ‘It’s nice to buy stuff from people you know’I spent 18 months testing the best video doorbells – here are my favouritesDo I really need air conditioning in the UK? Everything to know before you buy‘The bar here is low’: the best (and worst) supermarket brioche burger buns, tasted and ratedEditor’s pickView image in fullscreenOn your bike … after you’ve found the right ride for you.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianIt’s healthy, affordable and kind to the planet. Cycling is one of the best ways to get around, but choosing the right bike can be tricky: do you need a road bike, amountain bike, agravel bike– or ahybrid? Cycling expert Paddy Maddison explains it all in hisguide to how to buy a bike, including how much to spend, what to look for, and what accessories you might need.Hannah BoothEditor, the FilterIn case you missed it …View image in fullscreenCampfires might be banned because of the risk of wildfires, as human-caused climate breakdown brings hotter, drier conditions and the UK continues to bake, but we’re still in peak camping season. Make the most of it with something comfortable to sit on: outdoor expert Sian Lewis put 15 of thebest folding camping chairsto the test (her favourite: Montbell’sBase Camp chair).If you need advice on camping with kids, Matt Collins and a host of fellow parents offer theirhard-won tips(after a brush with a tick this summer, we’re packing thetick remover). And if that’s not enough, Sian recently answered all yourcamping questions, including her favourite camping spots in the UK.Get involvedView image in fullscreenGreen fingers: tell us about the garden buys you couldn’t live without.What’s the best thing you’ve bought for your garden? Was it a tool that made weeding easier, a bag of bulbs that brightened up a gloomy February, or a gorgeous planter for a balcony? Let us know by emailing us atthefilter@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe Filter UK newsletterCyclingHobbiesFitnessCamping holidaysnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: No oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Cucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to life
Content: Alexina Anatole’s cucumber and avocado gazpacho.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s cucumber and avocado gazpacho.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.Quick and easyFoodNo oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipesCucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to lifeAlexina AnatoleMon 17 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeat brings caramelisation, char, the slow collapse of ingredients into something rich and deep, but when it’s too hot to cook, flavour has to be built differently – through contrast, texture and a more deliberate hand with seasoning. Salt, in particular, becomes transformative: drawing out moisture, softening structure, shifting raw into something more yielding. That principle underpins this carrot salad, inspired by the Japaneseyamitsuki(‘addictive’) method most commonly used on cabbage, while a chilled cucumber gazpacho offers clean, cooling clarity.Cucumber and avocado gazpacho (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep20 minChill1 hr+Serves4For the gazpacho4 cucumbers(about 1.2kg),peeled and deseeded100ml extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to garnishZest and juice of 1 lime2garlic cloves,peeled and finely grated1 tsp flaky salt1 tsp white miso pasteFlesh of 1 avocadoTo garnishBlack olives,slicedWhite grapes,sliced,Soft herbs(mint, dill, basil, say)Black pepperPut all the gazpacho ingredients except the avocado in a food processor, add 100ml cold water and blend thoroughly. Add the avocado, blend again until well combined, then taste and adjust the seasoning to your liking.Pass the soup through a fine sieve, pressing it down with the back of a spoon. For a silky-smooth soup, blend again with a stick blender for one to two minutes, then cover and refrigerate for at least an hour, until well chilled.Serve the gazpacho in bowls, and garnish with sliced black olives and grapes, herbs, freshly cracked black pepper and a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Addictive carrotsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s addictive carrots.This is an extremely simple but delicious salad that can be bolstered with the likes of chickpeas, avocado and feta, should you want to make it more substantial.Prep15 minRest25 min+Serves4 as a side3 large carrots(about 500g), topped and tailed1 tsp flaky sea salt1 garlic clove, peeled and finely grated½ tsp dashi powder, or to taste (optional)1 tbsp toasted sesame oil, plus extra to garnish1 tbsp sesame seeds, lightly toastedPeel the carrots, then run them through the slicing attachment on a food processor (alternatively, slice very finely on a mandoline). Transfer to a large bowl, scatter over the salt and gently massage for a minute. Leave to soften for 10 minutes.Drain off any liquid from the carrots, taste and adjust the salt as preferred (if they’re too salty, rinse the carrots and pat dry, but this shouldn’t be necessary!).Whisk the garlic and dashi powder into the sesame oil, then pour over the carrots along and scatter over two-thirds of the sesame seeds. Toss thoroughly to combine, then transfer to the fridge for 15 minutes to an hour to give the flavours time to meld (the carrot mix will keep for three to five days in the fridge).Serve cold, garnished with the remaining sesame seeds.Alexina Anatole is the author of theSmall Wins Substackand Sweet: the Secret to the Best Desserts, published by Square Peg (£27). title: Sabrina Ghayour’s recipes for mango and chilli chicken, sticky spring onions and latke | Food | The Guardian
description: A sweet, tangy and spicy chicken dish that matches well with crisp fried potatoes and apricot-glazed spring onions
Author: Sabrina Ghayour
Headline: A sweet, tangy and spicy chicken dish that matches well with crisp fried potatoes and apricot-glazed spring onions
Content: Sabrina Ghayour’s mango, lime and chilli chicken.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenSabrina Ghayour’s mango, lime and chilli chicken.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodSabrina Ghayour’s recipes for mango and chilli chicken, sticky spring onions and latkeA sweet, tangy and spicy chicken dish that matches well with crisp fried potatoes and apricot-glazed spring onionsSabrina GhayourMon 17 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 04.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIuse this exact cooking method to make every kind of traybaked chicken, and this one is a blend of store-cupboard staples with the addition of fresh lime to push the flavour. Then, I love hash browns, röstis and latkes – give me crispy fried potatoes of any description, and I’m a happy girl – but I won’t lie and tell you that I love frying, because, if I can avoid it, I do: it’s messy, greasy, smelly and uses a fair bit of oil, which is pretty costly. But how to produce a perfectly crispy latke by baking? Well, I’ve managed to do it, and I’m really happy with the results.Mango, lime and chilli chicken (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIf you don’t have mango chutney, use any sweet chutney instead.Prep5 minCook45 minServes3-4600gboneless, skinless chicken thighsFor the marinade3 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed3tbsp sweet mango chutney2tbsp Greek-style yoghurt1 heapedtsp sriracha, or any chilli sauce1tsp ground turmeric1tsp paprika1tsp olive oilFinely grated zest and juice of 1 unwaxed limeFlaky sea saltandblack pepperHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7, and line an oven tray with baking paper. Arrange the chicken thighs in a single layer on the lined tray.Mix all the marinade ingredients in a small bowl, adding a generous amount of salt and pepper, until well combined. Pour this all over the chicken thighs and then, using your hands, toss to coat both sides really well.Bake the chicken thighs for 40 minutes, until they’re burnished, cooked through and juicy, then serve with the latkeand spring onions below.Ludicrously good traybaked latkeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenSabrina Ghayour’s ludicrously good traybaked latkes.Prep10 minCook1 hr 10 minServes3-41–1½kgfloury potatoes(maris piper or russets), peeled or unpeeled, scrubbed and coarsely grated1 very large onion, peeled and grated, or blitzed in a small bullet blender or mini food processorFlaky sea salt andblack pepper1 heapedtsp dried sage1 heapedtsp dried oregano1 heapedtsp garlic granules2tbsp cornflourOlive oil spray or olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6, and line a large oven tray with baking paper.Put the grated potatoes and onion in a large bowl, add a generous amount of salt and, using your hands, mix well. Leave to sit for 10 minutes.Put the potato mixture in a clean cotton tea towel, gather up the corners and spend a good five minutes squeezing out as much liquid as you can – the drier the mix, the crispier the latke. Transfer the mixture to a dry bowl, season, then add the dried herbs, garlic granules and cornflour, and mix really well until evenly combined.Spray or brush the baking paper with a generous amount of olive oil and loosely scatter the potato mixture evenly on top – I like to make one big rectangular latke, but you can form it into any shape you like, or even make individual ones. Pat the latke flat without pressing too hard, tidy the edges, if need be, then spray or brush the top generously all over with more olive oil.Bake for 40–45 minutes until deeply crisp and golden with burnished edges (if making smaller ones, you will need to check them after 35 or so minutes). Remove from the oven, cut into squares and serve.Sticky-glazed spring onions with sesameWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenSabrina Ghayour’s sticky glazed spring onions with sesame.If the Spaniards can obsess about eating calçots (a cross between a leek and a spring onion), then I can happily allow myself to eat spring onions as a vegetable in their own right. If you know my books, you’ll know I’ve shared a few spring onion recipes before, and here is another one of my favourites. They’re great with grilled meat or fish or in wraps with kebabs.Prep5 minCook20 minServes3-42 bunchesfat spring onions(14–16), thoroughly washed and patted dryOlive oil spray, or olive oil1tbsp sesame seeds(I use a mix of black and white)For the glaze2tbsp apricot jamFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemon½tspblack pepper1 pinchflakysea saltHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/ gas 9 and line a large oven tray with baking paper.Mix the glaze ingredients in a small bowl until evenly combined.Put the spring onions on the lined tray, spray or drizzle them with olive oil, rubbing in to ensure each one is well coated, then roast for seven minutes.Remove from the oven and pour the glaze over the spring onions until well coated. Sprinkle over the sesame seeds (do not stir), then roast for another six or so minutes, until the seeds are toasted – check after three minutes to ensure the spring onions are not drying out. Serve immediately.These recipes are edited extracts from Persiana One, by Sabrina Ghayour, published by Mitchell Beazley at £28.
