Content: China’s Sea Legend has launched a regular service through the Arctic’s northern sea route, suggesting it could be an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz and Suez canal.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenChina’s Sea Legend has launched a regular service through the Arctic’s northern sea route, suggesting it could be an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz and Suez canal.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyArcticAfter Hormuz, China looks to the promise – and peril – of the Arctic’s ‘ice silk road’China has established the first scheduled transit through the northern sea route, but questions remain over the environmental and political risksJonathan Yerushalmyand Alicia Chen in TaipeiSun 16 Aug 2026 20.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 20.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Marco Rubio suggested that the world should look to new shipping lanes to bypass the logjammed strait of Hormuz, it’s unlikely he had the Arctic’s northern sea route in mind.And yet in recent months the promise of this 5,500km channel – cleaved through frozen seas by nuclear-powered icebreakers and illuminated by a sun that never dips below the Arctic horizon – has grown.Japan, Korea and India have all expressed interest in sending cargoes through the northern sea route (NSR), but it’sChinathat has established the first scheduled transit, with shipping company Sea Legend launching a regular service in recent days.The NSR, which cuts through the Arctic Circle along Russia’s northern coast, is only navigable during warmer months, but that window has widened due to shrinking summer sea ice. For some vessels, the route can more than halve the time it takes to get from China to Europe, but the benefits come with serious environmental and political risks that have the potential to outweigh the gains.Map of northern sea route.After a single pilot voyage in 2025, Sea Legend has launched a regular container service via the Arctic route. That direct journey from Ningbo-Zhoushan to Felixstowe in the UK takes as little as 18 days compared with more than 40 days via the Suez canal.Experts say the route is ideal for cargo that is sensitive to temperature, including electric vehicles, lithium batteries and solar products – among which China has become a dominant global exporter.As the only regular commercial cargo service on the route, Sea Legend will test whether Beijing’s longstanding Arctic ambitions can translate into a viable regular China-Europe trade route.The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, first publicly called forChina and Russia to develop Arctic shipping routesand build a “polar Silk Road” in 2017. Russia, which controls much of the northern sea route, was initially wary of China’s growing presence in the Arctic. But after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has been left increasingly dependent on Beijing in the high north, giving China greater leverage and access.Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom issues navigation permits and oversees shipping along the route, while also providing the nuclear-power icebreakers that are needed to accompany most vessels.Rosatom advert showing icebreaker convoying LNG tanker along the Northern Sea RouteSea Legend says the Arctic route will roughly halve emissions because of the shorter sailing time between China and Europe, but according to experts, the environmental risks inherent in the journey could easily erase any emissions savings.Some shipping companies have faced criticism for operating vessels that use heavy fuel oil (HFO), which was banned from the Arctic in 2024.According to a 2025 report from the Bellona Environmental Foundation, fuel spills pose huge dangers in the Arctic because HFO is thicker than other types,making it difficult to clean up. Oil also decomposes more slowly in colder weather and is almost impossible to remove once trapped in ice.Their report argues Russia is completely unprepared to deal with such a disaster should it occur. The distances of the NSR – along with its isolation – mean that specialised recovery teams could take weeks to reach a spill site.“Due to the remoteness of the region and lack of logistical support, the probability of a prolonged machinery breakdown and consequential grounding is much higher. This poses the risk of an environmental oil spill in a fragile ecosystem,” says Capt Nitin Chopra, Allianz principal marine risk consultant for Asia.Bellona also flags the danger of black carbon – one of the emissions from HFO – calling it “one of the most potent absorbers of solar radiation”. Black carbon can reduce the reflectivity of the Arctic region, making it absorb more sunlight while trapping heat, exacerbating global warming.Frozen highway for the shadow fleetLi Xiaobin, chief operating officer of Sea Legend, said this month that thecrisis in the Middle Easthas exposed the vulnerability of the Suez canal and strait of Hormuz to regional turmoil, heightening the need to develop alternative trade routes between China and Europe.Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, has echoed those comments. Moscow would like to redraw the map of world trade, but its control of the NSR – which is largely in Russia’s exclusive economic zone – is seen as too great a risk for many operators.View image in fullscreenRussia’s Dudinka seaport of the northern sea route.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyInternational sanctions imposed on Russia after the invasion of Ukraine could complicate rescue efforts if a vessel gets into trouble and requires assistance, insurer Allianz Commercial said in its 2026 safety and shipping review.Experts say that for now, much of the traffic along the NSR is taken up by Moscow’s shadow fleet: tankers often operating without insurance or proper regulatory oversight, making ad hoc journeys to evade sanctions on Russia’s oil.“In 2025 there were a hundred such ships under international sanctions – or nearly a third of the cargo ships sailing the route,”Bellona’s Ksenia Vakhrusheva wrote in a report last year. In 2026, reports suggest shadow fleet shipments through the NSR are happening at an even faster rate, thanks to milder summer conditions that are aiding navigation.“With the current climate change, we may be able to see more time of the years that the northern sea route will be open for commercial shipping,” says Vinh Thai, professor of logistics and supply chain management at RMIT University, adding that there is some evidence it is already happening.A Russian transporter of LNG was able to start an early transit through the route in May, thanks to the shrinking summer sea ice. In the past week, ship-watchers spotted an unprecedented convoy of Russian tankers taking an unusually northern path through the NSR. The fleet of vessels, reportedly carrying about 8m barrels of oil, passed within 500 miles of the north pole.Despite Russia’s bold – perhaps reckless – efforts to push the NSR as a viable alternative for international shipping, experts say that for now the economics don’t add up. Safety concerns, high operating costs, a short sailing season and sanctions risks will probably continue to constrain Arctic shipping.Any oil spill could therefore be an “environmental as well as economic disaster”, says Thai. “Not only for Russia, but also the surrounding area as well.“So can the northern sea route be used as a substitute for the strait of Hormuz and the Suez canal? The short answer is no, not for the moment.”Explore more on these topicsArcticShipping industryInternational tradeGlobal economyChinaRussiaStrait of HormuzfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City opener was startlingly bad | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Community Shield isn’t always a sign of things to come, but City’s form in their defeat to Arsenal is concerning in the wake of Pep Guardiola’s departure
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The Community Shield isn’t always a sign of things to come, but City’s form in their defeat to Arsenal is concerning in the wake of Pep Guardiola’s departure
Content: Elliot Anderson, Enzo Maresca and Mateo Kovacic endured a tough afternoon on Sunday.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElliot Anderson, Enzo Maresca and Mateo Kovacic endured a tough afternoon on Sunday.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonSoccerEnzo Maresca’s Manchester City opener was startlingly badThe Community Shield isn’t always a sign of things to come, but City’s form in their defeat to Arsenal is concerning in the wake of Pep Guardiola’s departureSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 17 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are caveats. It was only the Community Shield – and no side has gone on to win the league after lifting the Community Shield since 2018. It was against the league champions, whose pre-season has involved far less strenuous travel than their own. By the time the season really gets going, there will be greater clarity in central midfield, with Rodriset to complete his move to Barcelonaimminently. But this was a startlingly bad opening for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City.Succeeding a manager of Pep Guardiola’s stature is never easy, as numerous clubs have found. But it’s not just Guardiola’s stature, the sense that whoever follows him stands in his shadow. It’s that his style of play is so idiosyncratic that the transition process inevitably becomes more difficult. Even though Maresca was Guardiola’s assistant at City in 2022-23, and his football is Guardiola-inspired, it is not identical, not least because Guardiola was always evolving. Even allowing for all that, though, it was remarkable how poorly City defended intheir 3-0 defeat by Arsenal on Sunday.Arsenal played well. There was a sharpness to them and a slickness to their passing that wasn’t always present last season. Fears that they may have lost their appetite having ended their 22-year wait for the title may have been overstated (although much, much tougher tests await). But City were a rabble, limited going forward and a shambles at the back.Are Manchester United returning to relevance under Michael Carrick? | Jonathan WilsonRead moreIt was the second goal that will really have worried them, because Arsenal had to do so little to score. Martin Ødegaard was given time to measure his cross. Christos Tzolis wandered off the back of Abdukodir Khusanov. Then Kai Havertz, slightly more explicably, pulled away from Rúben Dias. In Khusanov’s defence, it probably should be acknowledged that he does not usually play at right-back, but he has occupied the role before. A wide player drifting off your back should not come as a shock; perhaps it’s just pre-season and he was not as alert as he will be, but it was a baffling error. But it was of a piece with the wider whole; throughout, City seemed off the pace, not as focused as Arsenal. Even if that improves as the season goes on, it’s a problem if City have title aspirations; how far clear will Arsenal be by the time City finally click – if they do click?But there were structural issues on that flank as well. Antoine Semenyo was barely involved. Elliot Anderson, on the right of the midfield two, was unable to check the forward surges of Riccardo Calafiori, who scored the first and whose run played a key role in the third. An attacking left-back, even one with as much freedom to drift infield as the Italian enjoys, shouldn’t cause that much trouble.The midfield issue desperately needs resolving. Rodri was an unused substitute as talks about his possible likely move to Barcelona go on (City accepted a bidfor him on Sunday night). It’s not just his quality that will be missed; his organisational abilities will be too. Enzo Fernández, who worked with Maresca at Chelsea, did seem to have been lined up as a replacement for Rodri but City did not submit a bid before the Friday 5pm deadline Chelsea had placed for selling the midfielder. Mateo Kovacic spent much of last season deputising for Rodri but he is 32 now; he is not the future. Factor in the loss of Bernardo Silva as well, and there is a serious shortfall in midfield.Generally, in fact, City’s squad looks a little short. Dias and Marc Guéhi are the only defenders over 25. There are plenty of attacking midfielders but Omar Marmoush has never really convinced as a back-up to Erling Haaland. The £200m spree in January 2025 may have helped stop the rot, but the players who came in then – not just Marmoush and Khusanov but also Vitor Reis and Nico González – would not be badly missed now. City, once so focused in their spending, have started to make mistakes. Tijjani Reijnders, brought in last summer for £50m, is about to be shipped on. Rayan Aït-Nouri was a baffling signing when he arrived and nothing in the past year has changed that view.Maresca must have looked at Arsenal’s squad, the extraordinary options available to Mikel Arteta in midfield, and despaired. Put generously, his is a squad in transition, although it’s starting to look as though it may be a squad in decline. The sense over the past couple of years was of Guardiola, slowly, passing his peak, but in retrospect perhaps it was only his genius that kept an ailing City competitive.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe evidence of Sunday, with all due caveats about the stage of the season, is that this may be a very bad time for Maresca to have replaced Guardiola. Taking over from a legend would be extremely challenging in the best of circumstances, and these are starting to look like they may be very bad circumstances.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsFootballSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester CityEnzo MarescaPremier LeaguenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Fifa chief sacked after criticism of Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has been sacked after openly criticising Gianni Infantino’s ill-fated plan to sell parts of the World Cup to private investors
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has been sacked after openly criticising Gianni Infantino’s ill-fated plan to sell parts of the World Cup to private investors
Content: Kevin Lamour had come out against the World Cup plan, saying Gianni Infantino ‘believes he embodies Fifa when he is supposed to be at its service’.Photograph: Joosep Martinson/UEFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Lamour had come out against the World Cup plan, saying Gianni Infantino ‘believes he embodies Fifa when he is supposed to be at its service’.Photograph: Joosep Martinson/UEFA/Getty ImagesFifaFifa chief sacked after criticism of Infantino’s World Cup sell-off planKevin Lamour said Fifa administration was ‘deceived’Chief operating officer knew he could lose his jobNick AmesMon 17 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has been sacked after openly criticising Gianni Infantino’s ill-fated plan tosell parts of the World Cupto private investors.In a significant development at the pinnacle of world football’s deeply troubled governing body, Lamour has departed less than two years after joining from a previous role at Uefa. He had come out strongly against Infantino’s FFE scheme after it was revealed, saying Fifa’s administration had been “deceived” and that the president “believes he embodiesFifawhen he is supposed to be at its service”.Women’s U20 World Cup boycott may hurt in short term but can send Fifa a vital message | Tom GarryRead moreLamour had also made clear that he would countenance losing his job as a consequence of opposing the plan, which was shelved hours after he spoke out on 31 July. “If that means I lose my job, then so be it,” he said in a statement. “I will understand and respect that decision. At least I’ll sleep well tonight.”The precise circumstances of his sacking are unclear but the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, informed staff in an email that Lamour would be leaving the organisation.A Fifa spokesperson said: “Fifa can confirm that the working relationship between Fifa and Kevin Lamour as Fifa’s chief operating officer has ended on 17 August 2026. Fifa thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter.”In the statement that appears to have expedited his departure, Lamour also said his colleagues “deserve better than contempt and intimidation”. He added: “My feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.” On the same day one of Infantino’s senior advisers, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned in protest at Infantino’s proposals.Lamour had been Uefa’s deputy secretary general before joining Fifa, and had first joined the European body in 2007. His departure is all the more eye-catching for his longstanding working relationship with Infantino, with whom he also worked at Uefa. Infantino continues to be under huge pressure after the failure of his scheme, with efforts to force his removal continuing.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: NBA blasts ESPN for ‘inaccuracies’ in report on Kawhi Leonard-Clippers investigation | NBA | The Guardian
description: ESPN’s report claimed the NBA was not able to show proof that Steve Ballmer funneled money to Leonard via team sponsorships to bypass the salary cap
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: ESPN’s report claimed the NBA was not able to show proof that Steve Ballmer funneled money to Leonard via team sponsorships to bypass the salary cap
Content: Kawhi Leonard is a seven-time All-Star.Photograph: Matt Slocum/APView image in fullscreenKawhi Leonard is a seven-time All-Star.Photograph: Matt Slocum/APNBANBA blasts ESPN for ‘inaccuracies’ in report on Kawhi Leonard-Clippers investigationNBA is looking into claims of salary cap circumventionESPN says league has no proof owner funneled moneySteve Ballmer denies allegations; Leonard trade on holdGuardian sportand AgenciesMon 17 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NBA has disputedan ESPN reporton the league’s investigation into possible salary cap circumvention by the Los Angeles Clippers.On Monday, ESPN reported that, after an 11-month investigation, the NBA was not able to show proof that Clippers ownerSteve Ballmerfunneled money to Kawhi Leonard via team sponsorships to bypass the salary cap. The outlet also said the two sides have been “negotiating a resolution to the investigation”.“ESPN’s article regarding the LA Clippers investigation – for which theNBAdeclined to cooperate – contains numerous and significant inaccuracies,” league spokesperson Mike Bass said in a statement released Monday afternoon. “The results in this matter will be made clear once the investigation is concluded.”LA Clippers’ Steve Ballmer denies Kawhi Leonard salary-cap circumvention schemeRead moreThe league did not clarify which parts of ESPN’s reporting it was disputing.Per the ESPN report, the NBA is looking into ⁠whether introducing Leonard ⁠to team sponsors violates ​the league’s rules against salary cap circumvention, and if the Clippers committed a “failure to supervise” regarding their employees. What rule the organization may ⁠have violated or the potential punishment is not yet known.The allegations first came to light last September in a report by journalist Pablo Torre. The Clippers were accused of feeding $28m to Leonard in the form of a“no-show” endorsement dealwith Aspiration, a green-banking firm partly funded by Ballmer that went bankrupt last year.Aspiration and three other companies that also signed sponsorship deals with ⁠the Clippers have been involved in the investigation, per the ESPN report. Aspiration’s co-founder wound up in ‌prison after pleading guilty ‌to fraud charges involving $248m.According to ESPN, the league presented its initial findings late last month and ‌has recently been in the process of resolving the investigation, which began last September.In a statement to ESPN, the Clippers said the team “introduced players, including Kawhi Leonard, to companies with which we had business relationships. Making introductions between players and team partners is both an ordinary practice by NBA teams and a common request ‌of players and representatives.“According to the statement, the Clippers did not “negotiate or dictate” the terms of Leonard’s endorsement deals and added that a player-company business relationship does not ​prove any salary-cap circumvention.TheToronto Raptors, who lost Leonard in free agency after winning the 2019 NBA championship, agreed in principle at the end of June to bring him back. The deal hasn’t been completed, and the NBA made it clear Toronto “would assume the risk of any potential outcome ⁠of the investigation impacting Kawhi”.“In light of this,” the Raptors stated, “we will wait ​until the league’s investigation is complete.”The ​Clippers, who have repeatedly denied ​any wrongdoing related to Leonard’s contract, also confirmed the deal was on hold. ​Ballmerhas also denied‌the allegations.Leonard, 35, is ​a two-time NBA ​Finals MVP, having won the award in title runs with the San Antonio Spurs (2014) and Toronto. He averaged 27.9 points, 6.4 rebounds and 3.6 assists in 65 games for the Clippers last season. A seven-time All-Star and two-time Defensive Player of the Year, he has made the NBA’s All-Defensive Team seven times.NBA commissioner Adam Silver said last month that he hoped the investigation would be complete by the end of the summer. Training camps open on 29 September.Explore more on these topicsNBABasketballUS sportsSteve BallmerLos Angeles ClippersToronto RaptorsShareReuse this content

title: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter consider selling Chelsea shares to Clearlake Capital | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in Chelsea in a deal that would give the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, full control
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in Chelsea in a deal that would give the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, full control
Content: Todd Boehly’s group and Clearlake have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenTodd Boehly’s group and Clearlake have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersChelseaTodd Boehly and Mark Walter consider selling Chelsea shares to Clearlake CapitalChelsea chair Boehly and Walter each own about 13%Sale would give Clearlake effective control of club at 86%Matt HughesMon 17 Aug 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheChelseachair, Todd Boehly, and director Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in the club to the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, in a deal that would give the private equity company complete control at Stamford Bridge.Clearlake, whose investment is managed by Behdad Eghbali and José E Feliciano, already owns more than 60% of Chelsea, but in an unusual arrangement agreedwhen buying the clubfrom Roman Abramovich four years ago, they share operational control with a consortium led by Boehly, who along with Walter and Hansjörg Wyss each own about 13%.The two ownership groups have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years when reports first emerged thatthey were seeking to buy each other outfollowing a disagreement over strategy, particularly regarding theirplans for a new stadium.Premier League to allow audio of conversations between players and refereesRead moreDiscussions over a potential deal, which would value the club at more than £5bn, have resumed over the past few weeks however,as first reported by the Financial Times, as Walter is seeking to raise funds to pay off insurers following a US federal investigation over alleged tax fraud.Walter is being investigated by the US Department of Justice over $21bn in loans which it has been alleged were not disclosed to state insurance regulators, which has led to the sudden sale of assets to pay down some of the loans. Walter last week sold the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh ⁠Kushner and Bob Iger ⁠for $12.5bn just a year after buying the NBA franchise for $10bn, leading to speculation that the 66-year-old may also seek to exit Chelsea.Boehly and Walter are close friends as well as longstanding business partners, having previously invested together in the LA Dodgers Major League Baseball team and the LA Sparks WNBA franchise.Together with Wyss, the pair control 38% of Chelsea through Blueco 22 Holdings, although it is unclear whether the Swiss billionaire is also willing to sell. Under the terms of their £2.5bn purchase from Abramovich after the Russian was sanctioned by the UK government following the invasion of Ukraine however, none of Chelsea’s shareholders can sell to a third party without the consent of their partners.An external sale is therefore unlikely, putting Clearlake in a strong position to gain the complete control it has been seeking for some time, although Boehly and Walter will demand a significant premium on the £325m they paid for their shares four years ago.View image in fullscreenTodd Boehly leaving would give Behdad Eghbali’s Clearlake Capital effective control of Chelsea.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesA sale by Boehly and Walter would leave Clearlake with more than 86% of Chelsea’s shares and effective control of the club, including the bid to build a new stadium, which they want to locate at Stamford Bridge.Walter has been a silent and barely visible partner at Chelsea, but Boehly was the public face of the club following the 2022 takeover and acted as interim sporting director during that year’s summer transfer window, leading the purchase of players such as Raheem Sterling and Marc Cucurella.Boehly stepped back from that hands-on role after 12 months, with Eghbali taking more operational control on behalf of Clearlake, but has often been blamed by Chelsea fans for the side’s underperformance.Boehly was due to stand down as chair at the end of the season, with a Clearlake representative to replace him for the next five years under the terms of the ownership agreement.The timing of an exit at this stage would be ironic, as after spending years investing heavily in young players with resale value at Clearlake’s behest, Chelsea have returned to Boehly’s original strategy this summer by signing experienced players such as Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson.Representatives of Clearlake, Boehly and Chelsea were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsChelseanewsShareReuse this content

title: Geno Auriemma on UConn’s basketball dynasty: ‘We’ve tried for 40 years to empower women’ | College basketball | The Guardian
description: The 12-time national title-winning coach discusses UConn’s rise, his bond with Paige Bueckers, the Pat Summitt rivalry and why he isn’t retiring just yet
Author: Stephanie Kaloi
Headline: The 12-time national title-winning coach discusses UConn’s rise, his bond with Paige Bueckers, the Pat Summitt rivalry and why he isn’t retiring just yet
Content: Geno Auriemma has coached stars such as Paige Bueckers during his long career at UConn.Photograph: Steph Chambers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeno Auriemma has coached stars such as Paige Bueckers during his long career at UConn.Photograph: Steph Chambers/Getty ImagesCollege basketballInterviewGeno Auriemma on UConn’s basketball dynasty: ‘We’ve tried for 40 years to empower women’Stephanie KaloiThe 12-time national title-winning coach discusses Connecticut’s time on top, his bond with Paige Bueckers, the Pat Summitt rivalry and why he isn’t retiring just yetMon 17 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLet’s get one thing out of the way right from the jump: UConn Huskies coach Geno Auriemma says he isn’t retiring anytime in the “foreseeable future”.That may come as a relief to fans of the program who have never known anyone else to be at its helm. Though he declined to promise an exact timeline, Auriemma made one thing clear while speaking to the Guardian last week: he’s going to be sticking around.As he should.At this point, and for decades prior, Auriemma and UConn have been synonymous. The history is well known, but let’s indulge: he began his coaching career at Bishop McDevitt High School in Wyncote, Pennsylvania. By 1981, he was an assistant at the University of Virginia, and he took over the head coaching job at the University of Connecticut in 1985. Auriemma was competing against many highly qualified women for the UConn job. One of those was Chris Dailey, who has coached at his side for the past 40-plus years. In that time, the Huskies have become arguably the most successful sports teams in the US.The town of Storrs, Connecticut, and Huskies basketball, provide the backdrop for Apple TV’s three-part docuseries,The Dynasty: UConn Huskies, which premieres on Friday. The project was made with the full participation of Auriemma, who is shown in all his forms: emotional, frustrated, borderline angry, happy, thoughtful, but never reticent.Auriemma’s decision to take part in the documentary wasn’t due to a looming sense that the end of his time at the program is near, though that’s certainly a theme that’s woven throughout, and a question that’s asked. And it’s something Auriemma clearly wanted to shut down.“I don’t know [why we did it],” Auriemma tells the Guardian. “It came along. I think maybe the fact that it was Paige’s senior year, there were a lot of things that happened in the three or four years before that that we had to try to overcome. The timing was right. The interest was right. And no one knew at the beginning, ‘Hey, if you do it this year, you’re going to follow us and win the national championship’. Nobody knew that.”Not only did the Huskieswin the national championship– a feat the third episode of the series heavily focuses on – they did so with a 37-3 record. But the documentary is about much more than one season, and it was a challenge to attempt to condense 40 years of a truly singular story into something bite-sized and appealing to a broad swath of viewers, from UConn mega-fans to those who have never heard of the team.“I don’t know that we could give a full 100% picture of the whole 40 years, you know, taking in stretches,” Auriemma says. “But I think it gives a pretty clear picture of what we do, who we are, what we value, what we stand for, how hard we work, how committed we are. So in that respect, I think it was pretty on point.”Dailey is featured in the series but perhaps not as prominently as someone who has led the Huskies alongside Auriemma this entire time. That wasn’t on purpose, he says. “I think that if you’re here on a regular basis, or if you watch us, everything that we do, Chris is a huge part of everything that we do. Is it possible to do what we’ve done without her input? No, I don’t think so.”When it comes to what UConn does, the list is exhaustive. It includes 12 NCAA Division I national championships, more than 50 conference and regular-season title, and the longest winning streak in men’s or women’s college basketball history. More than 50 Huskies have gone on to play in the WNBA; as of May, 17 were on active rosters. But that’s just the tip of the iceberg.While the team’s coaches are crucial, the athletes who have made up UConn’s rosters over the years represent a who’s who of the women’s game, including Rebecca Lobo, Sue Bird, Diana Taurasi, Napheesa Collier, Maya Moore, Breanna Stewart, Swin Cash, Tina Charles, Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd. Many of them participated in the film, which underscored the idea that to speak of UConn is to speak of Auriemma, and to speak of Auriemma is to speak of all the women, from Dailey to Moore to Bueckers and more, who have been a foundational part of his legacy.Lobo will go down in history as the first big get of Auriemma’s career, and someone who took the program from the unknown and rocketed it firmly into the known. Taurasi, whose own eponymous documentary premiered on Amazon Prime last year, was open and relaxed while looking back on her time with the program.View image in fullscreenUConn celebrate at a pep rally in their honor after winning the 1995 NCAA title.Photograph: Robert W Stowell Jr/Getty ImagesTaurasi, Auriemma says, didn’t want her own documentary to be a puff piece “and make her look like Lady Di”. At UConn “we talk a lot about when you’re really, really good, you don’t have to say anything. Other people say it for you.”But it’s Bueckers who makes Auriemma’s eyes light up as soon as her name is mentioned. The pair’s up and down relationship is documented in the series, and it seems much more up than down – the pair still speak weekly, Auriemma says.Bueckers spoke to reporters about how she’s grown as a leader while at All-Star Weekend in Chicago last month. Auriemma, who stomped that path alongside her, says that leadership was “one of the big struggles we had”.“‘What kind of leader do you want to be?’” he says. “Paige was the best player in the country as a freshman, won every award. And she thought, ‘Well, people will just follow my example.’ Well, that’s one kind of leadership, but there’s [also] a leadership where you have to own it. You have to own what they do, too.”Leading a team like UConn means you have to be able to be the face of the program, no matter if your teammates are older or younger than you, he also said. Leaders “make you better. They take on responsibility for you. They feel responsible for you.”View image in fullscreenBreanna Stewart, Auriemma, Morgan Tuck and Kia Nurse (from left) celebrate winning the 2016 national championship.Photograph: Joe Robbins/Getty ImagesBueckers “thought she was doing that”, and a tension grew between the two – a tension that is tangible in the docuseries’ third episode. “Today’s kids, I think, are very non-confrontational in a lot of ways,” Auriemma says. “So I always kept telling her, ‘Paige, you either do this now and we get some results or in March, we’re going to lose again in the Final Four and you’re going to wish you did.’“So I don’t know what happened, but eventually in her senior year, she got there. And I told her, ‘You’re not going to be able to walk into a WNBA training camp. They’re going to hand you the ball and say, you’re our starting point guard and you’re going to look around and you’re going to go, OK, well, I’m not ready to lead this team. You’re not going to have a choice.’”Auriemma says that Bueckers has since “found her voice,” and “she knows when to use it, how to use it. She still has a ways to go and some things that we talk about it every week. There isn’t a week that goes by that we don’t talk about how she’s feeling physically, mentally, emotionally, how you’re handling all this. And I’m proud of her.”There’s another woman whose legacy looms over the series: Pat Summitt, the University of Tennessee’s legendary coach.What began as a fun back-and-forth between two of women’s basketball’s best programs, eventually turned into a kind of cold civil war. When asked if there’s anything he wishes he’d done differently during that rivalry, Auriemma says more attention should have been paid to the players on the court.“I think for the longest time that we [Sumitt and Auriemma] competed against each other, it was great. It was a great rivalry. It was great theater on the court, because there were so many great players playing against each other,” he says. “I think at some point, when we started playing each other twice every year, and then we played the NCAA Tournament, so that was three times, I think it got a little bit much.”View image in fullscreenAuriemma coached the US women to two Olympic gold medals as head coach, in 2012 and 2016.Photograph: Tom Pennington/Getty ImagesMuch like some of the discourse we see surrounding women’s basketball today, the focus of the game was lost.“And things being the way they are always, it unfortunately became Geno versus Pat. Pat and Geno, Geno and Pat, Pat and Geno, blah, blah, blah,” he says. “And the great players that were playing kind of were secondary, and I thought that was lousy. I thought that that’s not where we want this to be.”What’s most regrettable is that Summitt, who announced her diagnosis of early-onset Alzheimer’s in 2011 and died in 2016 at the age of 64, didn’t have more time.“I wish that we would have had another 10, 12, 15 years where it would have just been two great teams playing against each other every night, because every one of my players so looked forward to that game,” says Auriemma. “I know that they talk about how big the [women’s] game is today and these rivalries today. [But] there was nothing like that rivalry,ever.”Auriemma has a reputation of being a stalwart supporter not only of the women’s game, but of women themselves.“I’m a woman’s basketball coach, right? I coach basketball, and the players that play for me happen to be women, but I would coach a boys team the same way,” Auriemma says. “So the longer I’m with this, the longer I’ve been with this, I see the way the game has changed on the court, the way it’s changed off the court, and I see the difference in the way the game has been covered by the media.”When he first started taking questions at press conferences, “if you saw a girl, young girl or woman, they were probably from the student newspaper or something, or just somebody who’s doing an internship or something,” he says. “And now you look out at the Final Four and with all the new social media outlets, it was just incredible to see a sea of young women who can look around and say, ‘I can do this for a living. I can be what used to be almost exclusively for men only.’ So I’m proud of that. I think that’s something that we’ve done at Connecticut for 40 years: try to empower women, try to get them to believe that anything, anything’s possible.”Explore more on these topicsCollege basketballBasketballCollege sportsUS sportsUSA women's basketball teaminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League to allow audio of conversations between players and referees  | Premier League | The Guardian
description: On-field audio is to be used during live broadcasts for the first time this season, with the move a part of an expansion of the RefCam system
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: On-field audio is to be used during live broadcasts for the first time this season, with the move a part of an expansion of the RefCam system
Content: This season fans may be able to listen to conversations such as this between Sandro Tonali and the referee Robert Jones.Photograph: Ian Walton/ReutersView image in fullscreenThis season fans may be able to listen to conversations such as this between Sandro Tonali and the referee Robert Jones.Photograph: Ian Walton/ReutersPremier LeaguePremier League to allow audio of conversations between players and refereesAudio to be used during live broadcasts for first timeMove is part of an expansion of the RefCam systemExclusive byMatt HughesMon 17 Aug 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThePremier Leaguewill permit audio of on-field conversations between players and referees during live broadcasts for the first time this season.The use of audio by the Premier League’s domestic TV rights holders, Sky Sports and TNT Sports, is part of an expansion of the RefCam system, which became a permanent feature of top-flight coverage last season after a six-week trial at the start of the campaign. The head-mounted RefCams were used by broadcasters to ­provide near‑instant replays of match ­incidents from a new angle in an attempt to enhance the viewer experience, but under the terms of their agreement with clubs the audio captured by the cameras was not televised until several days later.The regulations will be relaxed this season, however, to permit a limited use of RefCam audio during live matches, with one or two incidents to be broadcast from each of the Premier League’s 38 match rounds.The audio will not be broadcast live or include any incidents that are referred to the video assistant referee, as that is not permitted under the laws of the game, which are set by the International Football Association Board (Ifab). The new audio offering will be made available as part of near-live instant replays, however, while the number of TV games featuring RefCam will increase from 20 to about 45. The audio experiment will be trialled first before being rolled out and will not feature on the Premier League’s opening weekend.Football has been slow to replicate the broadcasting innovations embraced by other sports, with in-match interviews and dressing room cameras long since accepted in cricket and both codes of rugby, as well as many American sports. Under increasing pressure from rights holders, football is belatedly looking to open up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Premier League and refereeing body Pro Ref – formerly PGMOL – are understood to be lobbying Ifab over relaxing the rules that prevent live audio from being broadcast.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueRefereesLaws of footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heat has changed elite sport this summer – it must adapt to survive | Sport | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: how climate crisis is affecting athletes and what steps are being taken to protect them from rising temperatures
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: In today’s newsletter: how climate crisis is affecting athletes and what steps are being taken to protect them from rising temperatures
Content: Ekaterina Alexandrova was forced to leave the court due to a heat-related emergency during the Memphis Classic in July.Photograph: Justin Ford/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEkaterina Alexandrova was forced to leave the court due to a heat-related emergency during the Memphis Classic in July.Photograph: Justin Ford/Getty ImagesThe HotspotSportExtreme heat has changed elite sport this summer – it must adapt to surviveIn today’s newsletter: how climate crisis is affecting athletes and what steps are being taken to protect them from rising temperaturesTanya AldredMon 17 Aug 2026 05.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe mercury-shattering European summer pants alongside us on the back straight, looming as we hug the shadows, sweaty sandals on the parched earth. AcrossAsia, Africa and North America, inhabitants have endured the warmest July of their lives.In Toronto, Alex Hutchinson, author of the bestsellerEndure: Mind, Body, and the Curiously Elastic Limits of Human Performance,has just come back from an early run. “Here I am in Canada, a famously frosty country, and my general take when I wrote ‘Endure’in the 2010s was that heat was not that big a deal. Occasionally, people died of heat, often in the deep south of the US, often returning to football practise in August, when they were not prepared, but that was rare.How can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars? | Andy BeckettRead more“Now I’m a lot more cautious. My general thesis is that the brain is pretty good at protecting you. Even if you try to deliberately run yourself to collapse, you won’t be able to. You’ll get tired before that happens. But heat is one of the very few things that can trick the brain’s protective circuitry.”This summer has felt like a sea change in elite sport. Somehow we have reached a stage where it is no longer shocking to see a tennis player collapse on court, likeEkaterina Alexandrova in MemphisorJakub Mensik in Paris.Cyclist Tom Pidcock called the Tour de France a “war zone” and much-mocked referee Ilgiz Tantashev, who officiated France’s chaotic last-16 win over Paraguay, was later found to besuffering from heat strain. On 7 August, the youngFijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi died of suspected heatstrokein the southern Japanese city of Fukuoka, where temperatures had hit 35C, after training with his club, Kyuden Voltex.Dr Lee Taylor, from Loughborough University, is one of the world leaders in preparing elite athletes for extreme environments, “The reality is that we live in a climate-change world,” he says.“It’s inevitable, whatever sport you play, at whatever level, that more of that training and playing is going to be in a hot environment. So either we stop playing sport altogether or we adapt.”Logistics, timings, player preparation, shading, cooling, all can be tweaked, and we saw some of those adaptations in the World Cup – scatter-gun style. There were mandated hydration breaks, but nothing extra for games with a wet bulb globe temperature [a measure of heat stress on the human body] of more than 32C. There was no flexibility to extend the length of half-time – except for the Ronaldo, Ronaldinho, Madonna show in the final – despite there being, in Taylor’s words, “a clear rationale to do so in some games as a very robust way to make the players safe by reducing their body temperature”. The dollar held the upper hand. One of the challenges in preparing players for the World Cup was the limited number of days for acclimatisation at the end of the season. In recent years, recreational runners have hit a similar problem at the spring time London Marathon, a suddenly warm day when many participants have not had a hot run for six months.But given adequate preparation time, experts like Taylor can see the heat as a performance opportunity for elite athletes. “If you look at the [2019] Doha World Athletics Championships, for example, up to 40% in the road races did not finish because they weren’t prepared properly, so just by being prepared appropriately you’ve beaten nearly half the field.“ What I worry about is athletes who have undeclared sickness, a prior viral load or diarrhoea, or are perhaps on some undeclared medications – that can be quite a dangerous combination to exercise in the heat. Or if an event isn’t well prepared with something we call a ‘heat deck’ – appropriate medical expertise and facilities to rapidly cool someone with a potentially fatal exertional heat stroke – where aggressive whole body cooling is the gold standard to protect health and potentially life.”Autumn is approaching in the northern hemisphere and with it the Premier League, which kicks off on Friday. Taylor thinks the unseasonable heat could have brought pre-season advantages. “If someone has engaged in about six weeks of heat training, they can expand their haemoglobin mass by approximately 3%-6%. That’s the same type of adaptation we get in those red blood cells at an altitude camp – super desirable for our eliteskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDenis Zakaria (left) and Remo Freuler of Switzerland take a drink during a hydration break at the World Cup.Photograph: Alex Livesey/FIFA/Getty Images“athletes. So clubs will be regarding the weather in some parts as a performance opportunity. Most were probably looking to expose their players to the heat to gain some of those adaptations. The challenge is getting the quality of the training sessions because doing anything in the heat is more tiring and it compromises your recovery.”But there is an existential problem, for elite athletes and the rest of us– the unpredictability of the future.Diligently doing your homework is no longer good enough. “We used to prepare for the worst possible outcome,” says Taylor. “What does the historical data tell us is going to be the most challenging humidity and heat? But that’s gone out the window over the last five years because we have these crazy outliers.” And when the data doctor says the data can’t help, you know you’re in trouble.This is an extract from our newsletter, The Hotspot.
