How many, and are all of them in its possession?Nadella appeared to gesture at this question on a podcast late last year called All Things AI, where he talked about Microsoft’s datacentre build-out. The biggest problem, he said, was electrical power and building datacentres close enough to where power was located.“If you can’t do that, you may actually have a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in. In fact, that is my problem today. It’s not a supply issue of chips. It’s actually the fact that I don’t have warm shells to plug into.”A Microsoft spokesperson said: “Over several decades, Microsoft has built a global infrastructure to meet rapidly growing customer demand for cloud and AI services. Our datacentres combine custom silicon, AMD, Intel and Nvidia chips across multiple generations with the networking, storage and systems infrastructure required to operate at scale.“Microsoft does not report on the volume of specific chips in its AI infrastructure. The estimates the Guardian has shared with us are inaccurate, drawing the wrong conclusions from incorrect assumptions.”Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.How to calculate numbers of chips from a company’s ‘AI capacity’The world’s biggest technology companies give figures for their AI capacity in terms of power: gigawatts. One gigawatt powers between 700,000 and 1m homes. Meta says its controversial Hyperion datacentre in Louisiana will have 5GW of capacity. The UK company DataVita is planning a 1GW datacentre in Lanarkshire.Converting these figures into chips means calculating how many chips can be run with that amount of power. The Guardian used the following methodology, reviewing these calculations with Abdeltawab Hendawi, a professor at the University of Rhode Island, and Ren.The first anti-AI protester to be jailed has a message for OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta: ‘Regain your humanity’Read moreTo get a very broad approximation of how many chips there are in a datacentre, you could divide the power usage of that datacentre by the power usage of an AI chip – for example, an H100. A single H100 uses 700W. If Microsoft has 10GW of capacity, dividing this by 700 watts suggests it should have 12m chips.H100s make up the bulk of the chips described in the internal document. It also indicates that Microsoft has A100s, which use less power, and Blackwells, which use more.But this approximation does not account for several factors. First, datacentres have cooling systems and other equipment, which also use electricity. Ren estimates that in a given AI datacentre, 80% of the electricity goes to computer chips. This is roughly inaccordancewith figures from the International Energy Agency, although the number depends on the efficiency of the datacentre. Eighty per cent of 10GW would suggest 8GW may actually be in use.This is slightly lower than Microsoft’s own figures for its datacentre efficiency, which appear in a 2024 sustainabilityreportand suggest that 89% of the electricity in its new datacentres powers the IT systems, with an 11% overhead.Second, not all the chips in a datacentre are AI chips. Instead, AI chips are fitted on to server racks with other computer chips, such as memory chips, that help them run calculations. A server with eight H100 GPUs uses a maximum of about 10kW of power.Dividing 8GW by 10kW gives 800,000 servers, or 6.4m chips.This is a conservative estimate, as in practice companies such as Microsoft oversubscribe their power capacity to some extent – putting more chips in a datacentre than can be supported by their IT capacity, said Ren.Explore more on these topicsMicrosoftAI (artificial intelligence)NvidiaDatacentresComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Temperatures to fall across Europe as substantial rain heading for parts of UK | Environment | The Guardian
description: Temperatures could drop by more than 15C compared with last Thursday as cold front moves in
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Temperatures could drop by more than 15C compared with last Thursday as cold front moves in
Content: The scorched grass of Primrose Hill in London last Thursday as the UK endured its fifth heatwave of the summer.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe scorched grass of Primrose Hill in London last Thursday as the UK endured its fifth heatwave of the summer.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockWeather trackerEnvironmentAnalysisTemperatures to fall across Europe as substantial rain heading for parts of UKJodie Woodcock for MetDeskTemperatures could drop by more than 15C compared with last Thursday as cold front moves inMon 17 Aug 2026 08.44 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 05.37 EDTShareRelief from the unrelenting heat is finally arriving this week across westernEurope, with more unsettled conditions bringing the chance of rain. Temperatures are expected to fall back towards the seasonal norm, with some parts of the UK even falling about 3C below normal by Thursday. After such a scorching summer, and with a temperature drop of more than 15C compared with last Thursday’s heat, it may feel surprisingly chilly.There are signs that some substantial rain could be on the cards for the south of the UK this week as a cold front moves in from the Atlantic on Monday night into Tuesday. As of Monday, parts of southern England had endured 62 consecutive days of no rainfall – this is observed at a Met Office weather station in Wisley, Surrey. Even the last recorded rainfall here on 16 June amounted to just 0.4mm.The more interesting weather arrives from Wednesday into the weekend, as low pressure moves across the UK, bringing frequent sharp showers and potentially thundery downpours.After such a prolonged dry spell, even a few substantial bursts of rain will make a noticeable difference to the environment. Continental Europe is also likely to turn wetter as the main cold front sinks southwards into France and Germany on Wednesday. Farther south, however, rainfall is likely to be more hit and miss, relying heavily on showers and thunderstorms, with this risk really rising from Thursday.While the heat is subsiding on this side of the Atlantic, the southern US states have extended extreme heat warnings this week. There is a significant lack of overnight cooling and relief from the heat, with overnight lows not falling much below 27-28C (low 80sF). For perspective, the UK’s highest overnight minimum during the late June heatwave reached about 22-23C.High humidity is also contributing to the uncomfortable conditions and is helping push the heat index to such high levels to warrant the extreme heat warnings. The combination of air temperature and humidity produces the heat index, or apparent temperature, which better reflects how hot conditions feel. Apparent temperatures of 31-33C are being modelled as the overnight lows, with the National Weather Service warning of “dangerously hot conditions” as the forecasted daytime heat index values could exceed 46C, especially across Louisiana and Mississippi.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentWeather trackerUK weatherEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Claude to start watermarking AI-generated text – but will it make quality worse? | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Anthropic says it will change way chatbot makes small, random choices, to comply with EU regulation
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Anthropic says it will change way chatbot makes small, random choices, to comply with EU regulation
Content: The changes to the Claude AI chatbot will leave a pattern in the text that is detectable to Anthropic itself and to those able to decode it.Photograph: David Talukdar/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe changes to the Claude AI chatbot will leave a pattern in the text that is detectable to Anthropic itself and to those able to decode it.Photograph: David Talukdar/ShutterstockAnthropicClaude to start watermarking AI-generated text – but will it make quality worse?Anthropic says it will change way chatbot makes small, random choices, to comply with EU regulationAisha DownMon 17 Aug 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world is familiar by now with the usual tropes of machine-generated text: overuse of the word “delve”, an excess of em dashes, and thechirpy, relentless construction of “it’s not X but Y”.But is it about to get even worse?Over the weekend,Anthropicreleased an update saying it would change how its Claude AI model generated prose. This is to comply with an EU regulation that requires all AI-generated text to be watermarked starting in December.Anthropic said the changes would be made at the granular, random level at which its models generated text and would be undetectable to the average reader.But at least one commentator thinks otherwise. “This entire endeavour is a perverse adulteration of what it means to write,”wrote John Gruber, a veteran tech blogger. He argued the watermark would constrain Claude, forcing it to make worse, less precise word choices overall. While it may not make the model’s writing less accurate, he suggested these limits would make it worse.Are Microsoft’s AI plans being held back by a shortage of chips?Read moreThere is a stochastic element in the small choices that an AI model makes in framing a sentence: whether it chooses to call a day“grey” or “overcast”, for example, or refers to a running water as a “stream” or a “brook”.Anthropic’s new watermark will alter these random choices, it said, leaving a pattern that will be detectable to Anthropic itself, and to those who have a key to decode it.Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London, said the change “probably wouldn’t have any noticeable impact”.Gruber’s complaint appears to centre on the fact that watermarking will make a large language model less free to decide which word comes next in a sentence, and may therefore not pick the best choice.However, LLMs already do not make the best choices. “There’s already randomness involved in any of these large language models,” said Murdoch. “It’s pretty essential to how they work. If it wasn’t for this randomness, then they’d get stuck in loops and start repeating the same thing over and over again.”In other words, a chatbot does not necessarily decide to call running water a “stream” as opposed to a “brook” because the latter might have a more old-fashioned register. The model does not contemplate these choices: it makes them by chance.Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk ordersRead moreThis was evidenced recently when a paper in a leading chemistry journalhad to be retractedbecause the authors appeared to have used an AI tool to draft part of the publication. The tool used the phrase “mass killing of an ethnic group” as an alternative for “final solution”, though the paragraph in question appeared to be about a zinc nanogel.On the update, Murdoch said: “There’s going to be no noticeable difference. There’s the same random number generators there – it just used to be completely random, and now it’s statistically predictable, but still random.”The regulation, whichapplies to all AI companies operating in the EU, means they will have to put in place these watermarks within months. This could make it harder for students, lawyers and university professors topass off chatbot-written content as their own.There is another reason to watermark AI content, though, Murdoch said: there’s so much of it already out there that it might damage the models themselves. Training AI on AI-written content creates “model collapse”, leading models to confuse concepts.In other words, watermarking is not just a quietly powerful way to combat disinformation – it’s a deeply transformative system to ensure the chatbots don’t go insane. If you delve into it.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingRegulatorsInternetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Report supporting Australia’s teen social media ban appears to contain AI hallucinations, Senate hears | Social media ban | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds one section of report includes links to academic articles that do not exist, but authors deny the references were made up by AI
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds one section of report includes links to academic articles that do not exist, but authors deny the references were made up by AI
Content: The communications minister, Anika Wells, had said the report showed ‘many effective options’ for online age verification in implementing Australia’s social media ban.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/APView image in fullscreenThe communications minister, Anika Wells, had said the report showed ‘many effective options’ for online age verification in implementing Australia’s social media ban.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/APSocial media banReport supporting Australia’s teen social media ban appears to contain AI hallucinations, Senate hearsExclusive:Guardian analysis finds one section of report includes links to academic articles that do not exist, but authors deny the references were made up by AIFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorandNick EvershedSun 16 Aug 2026 22.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 00.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe authors of a report testing the technology underpinning Australia’s social media ban have concededChatGPTwas used in editing, but denied a number of citation errors in the report were due to AI hallucinations.The $3.48mage assurance technology trial, run by the UK-based Age Check Certification Scheme (ACCS) last year, tested various types of technology that could be used by social media platforms as part of Australia’s under-16 social media ban.The communications minister, Anika Wells, heralded the report as showing “many effective options” for checking people’s ages, and it paved the way for the ban to come into effect in December last year.Most of the report is based on tests the authors did of the various age-verification technologies currently available, but one chapter covers “emerging technologies” and cites a number of journal papers about potential new ways to check ages.An ongoing Senate inquiry seeking to further strengthen the social media ban law received a submission highlighting at least two citation errors in the report. The “citations … appear to be AI hallucinated, rather than being based on real sources,” it said.Use of VPNs to bypass age checks on porn sites to be investigated by Australia’s eSafety watchdogRead moreWhen asked about the allegation by Guardian Australia this month, a spokesperson for ACCS initially denied the use of AI in the report, but later conceded that AI had been used to rewrite paragraphs more succinctly.“We did not use AI in the generation of the report or the cited materials … Each one of them were checked as genuine links and reports and that they were relevant to the specific issue being cited,” they said.However, Guardian Australia’s own analysis of the report identified six references in the same section that contained errors.The errors include: Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs – unique combinations of letters and numbers which are associated with specific academic articles) that link to papers that do not exist; DOIs that point to incorrect papers; author name, journal and publication year combinations that do not match any known references; and DOI links to papers that did not say what the report suggested they said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe spokesperson later provided clarifications and new references to the research ACCS had relied on, but this response too contained errors.A list of journal articles intended to correct those in the report included years, authors and journal titles not matching the original citations in the report.One article ACCS cited was apparently accessed in March 2025. However, one of the lead authors of this study confirmed to the Guardian that their article was not publicly accessible until it was published in June 2025. They also confirmed that the person originally cited by ACCS as the paper’s lead author, “Jamil”, had never been on the paper, and that the ACCS report had summarised their paper incorrectly.The ACCS spokesperson provided further clarification regarding another reference that could not be found in the journal cited – “Weber et al. 2011” – by saying it was cited in a study by Monash University, which they provided to the Guardian. However there was no reference attributed to Weber in the Monash paper ACCS sent.The spokesperson only conceded AI had been used after the Guardian identified four links in part E and part K of the report that contained metadata identifying that the source of the link was ChatGPT.They maintained that by including the metadata of ChatGPT in the links the organisation had disclosed its use, and given the links were correct, they did not see that as a problem.They said AI had been used to rewrite some paragraphs more succinctly, but was not used for originating research or for the generation of the report.“All of the links were checked and verified and, whilst I apologise if there is an inadvertent error, this was all done by human verification.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe federal government has previously taken a dim view of contractors using AI in reports to government.Deloitte last year refunded part of its $440,000 contractwith the government after errors were identified, and the consultant firm admitted to using AI.Questions to Wells’ office were redirected to her department.Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent researchRead more“The department is examining the concerns raised below and will engage with ACCS as appropriate,” a spokesperson for the department said last Friday.In a hearing for the Senate inquiry on Friday, department officials said they met with ACCS, who claimed that the errors were due to links breaking that had previously worked. The officials have not independently verified this, stating it would be “very difficult” to go back and check.They said it was a “handful of errors” in 26 pages of citations for a 1,000-page report.“[ACCS] assured us that the links were all checked at the time that the document was published, and they all worked then,” the department’s first assistant secretary, Sarah Vandenbroek, said. “So, something may have changed in the interim. [They] did also assure us that while some of the links may have been broken, though the source documents do still exist, they are still valid.”Prof Christian Downie, from the school of regulation and global governance at the Australian National University,who has previously examined submissions to government that contained AI hallucinations, said if reports or submissions to government are found to have false citations in them – AI or otherwise – it could lead to bad decisions, and “erode public confidence and trust” in institutions.“One would assume the government is already thinking about this, and that is going to have to require contractual arrangements and presumably penalties to discourage this type of behaviour,” he said.Fatima Payman, an independent senator, said: “The saga of last year’s Deloitte AI slop report should have marked the end of slack referencing in reports by government contractors.”“The government must demand an apology and refund from the contractor behind the report,” she said.Explore more on these topicsSocial media banAI (artificial intelligence)Labor partyChatGPTAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high water | Games | The Guardian
description: Frogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edges
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Frogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edges
Content: ‘Distant howls of rabid fish men’ … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresView image in fullscreen‘Distant howls of rabid fish men’ … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresGamesReviewThe Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high waterPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; FrogwaresFrogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edgesNic RuebenMon 17 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m standing in the prosthetics lab of a campy horror hospital, hunting for a preacher’s flayed face to wear so I can trick the world’s grisliest smart doorbell. Pinned to a board in the corner of the room are a dozen X-rays: shattered bones and metal splints in sepia negative, each with a note attached. It’s a stark, clinical intrusion on the theatrical gore elsewhere. It takes a beat to realise that I’m reading the stories of injuries sustained by soldiers fighting for Frogwares’ native Ukraine. Fingers amputated after severe burns. Limbs lost in mine explosions. Toes torn off by shell fire.Like so many of my favourite PS3-era seven-out-of-tens, The Sinking City 2 is a pulpy action horror. It’s fuelled by scrappy ambition, Lovecraft fan fiction and wonderfully unhinged scenario design. A puzzle that has you determine which talking jarred brain is telling porkies. A scavenger hunt to fix a crane to move a rotting whale carcass. A gunfight amid the grisly results of a siren pop star’s fan meet-up turned battle royale.Frogwares’ latest is also fuelled by the trauma and grit of developers who refused to let an invasion stop them making it. “As of writing, 85,183 air raid sirens registered across our cities,” reads an intro screen. “Work continued, and so did life.” As Weird Tales magazine-cover gumshoe Calvin Rafferty steps out from his apartment, sirens and the public address system blare out over the flooded town of Arkham, heralding the final calls for evacuees.View image in fullscreenTime to evacuate … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresThrough an open window, a couple resign themselves to abandoning their dead daughter’s toys. Rafferty’s decided to stick around, despite the floods and the strange infestation of worms that came with them. His girlfriend’s in a coma, and it’s “cursed pacts with interdimensional gods” serious. Hoping for a cure, he hops in the boat you’ll use to explore the first act’s semi-open city map, and makes for the Miskatonic library.Out is the first Sinking City’s clumsy but earnest exploration of Lovecraft’s provincial racism; in is shooting unknowable cosmic horrors in whatever passes for the face with a tommy gun. To be fair, it’s a great tommy gun. The influence of 2019’sResident Evil 2remake is immediately apparent from the identical UI of an achievements menu. Inventory space is tight, as are the corridors that diverge and fold back into themselves like puzzle boxes. Supplies are scarce but ambushes frequent. The distant howls of rabid fish men and worm-riddled zombies dare you to preserve bullets, while the score and every instinct scream at you to let loose like a startled skunk.Frogwares cut its teeth on Sherlock Holmes games, a lineage evident here in some clever puzzles that offer a reason to veer off the main path. Things get rougher when the studio ventures into new territory. Enemies are so relentless that most combat is unavoidable, undermining the intricate map design by offering no reason to take advantage of shortcuts. Elsewhere, the plot’s central romance flops like a soggy fish finger due to some stiff acting and overwrought dialogue.Generous doses of squishy gallows humour, elaborate secrets and expert tension pick up the slack. As does writing that skirts the grim glorification of overt war allegory to tell a story about refusing to leave what you love in the rubble, so long as the faintest signs of life remain. If you’re going to create, wrote Bukowski, you’ll do it “while the whole city trembles in earthquake, bombardment, flood and fire”. And there’s me thinking he was being dramatic.The Sinking City 2 is out 18 AugustExplore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5PCXbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ithaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent moment | Games | The Guardian
description: The latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with it
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with it
Content: Tantalising … Ithaca.Illustration: the Pixel HuntView image in fullscreenTantalising … Ithaca.Illustration: the Pixel HuntSummer games previewsGamesIthaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent momentThe latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with itLewis GordonMon 17 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIthaca has one hell of an opening: Penelope, a disillusioned environmental lawyer, stops her car at a petrol station. But upon returning, she discovers something shocking: the unconscious body of an oil company CEO in her boot, his hands hog-tied together, dangling limply towards the vehicle’s number plate.This tantalising eco-thriller setup is a long way off the typical knights-and-castles fantasy fare of most role-playing games, moreHow To Blow Up a PipelinethanDragon Quest. But road-trip RPG Ithaca arrives via refreshingly original developer the Pixel Hunt, a French outfit that specialises in what it calls “reality-inspired” games. The studio has made a number of arresting works in recent years.One was about a Syrian refugee couplemaking a perilous migrant journey across Europe;another tackledthe life-shattering effects of child sexual abuse. The climate crisis was always in the back of Pixel Hunt founder and Ithaca writer Florent Maurin’s mind. After all, he says, it is the uber problem of our day, the problem that touches all others. It was just a case of when, and, more importantly: “What do we say about it?”Then, one summer afternoon a few years ago, while out for lunch in the French medieval town of Cluny, Maurin was posed a question by his wife: “How, considering all we know scientifically about the climate crisis, do we explain to our daughters that we didn’t spend every weekend marching, protesting and demanding the powers that be to take meaningful action?” Maurin was silenced. “I had no fucking clue,” he says. “I had no answer to that question.”View image in fullscreenRaising prickly, ethical questions … Ithaca.Illustration: The Pixel HuntMaurin’s eventual response was to tackle the subject the way he knew best – by making a video game. In Ithaca, you drive along a procedurally generated road, soaking up vistas of huge windfarms, mountains passes and gorges filled with clean blue water. You talk to family and friends, with the decisions you make affecting the direction you take on the asphalt highway and the branching storyline. Slowly, you uncover what the radical climate group Penelope is now part of, the Earth Protection Association, is really planning to do with the oil exec in her car’s trunk, this nefarious avatar of petro-capitalism. Does he walk free or pay for his Earth-heating sins? Or does something else happen entirely?The prickly, ethical questions that Ithaca raises are influenced by the real world’s growing upheaval. Maurin has been struck by what he sees as a sea change in attitudes towards political violence. He cites the reactions to Luigi Mangione’s alleged killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and the assassination of rightwing activist Charlie Kirk. “You might have expected people to say this is not something that they, or anybody, should do, but actually, a sizable part of the population in the US cheered and was like: ‘This is right. It’s deserved.’”The road Penelope ventures down is something of a metaphor for “where we are all heading”, says Maurin. As the mythic home of Odysseus, Ithaca, Penelope’s ultimate destination, was chosen for its allegorical meaning: Maurin says it offers an opportunity to think through ideas of home in a broader, almost planetary sense. He sees the current moment as one in which “we’re trying to discover where we want to go collectively as a species”.Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanRead moreIt is an urgent question, dovetailing with Ithaca’s high-octane story and what Maurin sees around him on a daily basis in Burgundy, central France. When he arrived, 10 years ago, it was verdant, an almost staggeringly green place. “You felt as if water was everywhere in the landscape,” he says. Now, drought arrives every summer, killing any trees ill-suited to such high temperatures and a lack of water. Hillsides are littered with their grey and yellow arboreal remains. “Every time, I look out of the window and I think, ‘We have to talk about this very fast,’” says Maurin. “Because things are changing way too quickly for nature to be able to adapt.”Ithaca is in development now for PC and consoles for release in 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is dating draining your bank account? Here’s a cheap solution | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: I understand gen Z’s concerns about the cost of romance. But anything can be a date if you want it to be
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: I understand gen Z’s concerns about the cost of romance. But anything can be a date if you want it to be
Content: ‘You’re better off enjoying the meal than worrying about the outcome.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘You’re better off enjoying the meal than worrying about the outcome.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionDatingIs dating draining your bank account? Here’s a cheap solutionDave SchillingI understand gen Z’s concerns about the cost of romance. But anything can be a date if you want it to beMon 17 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTShareAcouple of months ago, I wrote a columnimploring young peopleto keep trying to find love, to not become cynical about romance and avoid the temptation of the accursed “loneliness influencers” peddling antisocial behavior as some sort of newfangled experiment that no one had thought of before. I stand here today saying,hey, I can’t be right all the time. Maybe it is better to be alone, since it costs a hell of a lot less.Apparently, young people across the country are forgoing dating because it’s too damn expensive. Or at least, I think they are, based on themultiplenewspaperarticlessaying so that came out in the last two weeks. As the New York Times put it, the “prospect of a tab of $150 or more for two entrées, two drinks, an appetizer and tip” is too pricey for many gen Z singles. I say, only $150? Where are you going, Chili’s? I went on a date with (shameful brag incoming) a very famous political figure from the late 90s and spent twice that amount, sending my bank account into cardiac arrest. I practically begged her to get dessert, even though it was clear our decade of age difference and general lack of chemistry meant I was better off going home and journaling about it. I paid for the whole thing, and in return, I got an amazing story to tell at parties.People once cited romcoms to describe the love they hoped for. Now the doomscroll has replaced the meet-cute | Lisa PortolanRead moreDating is akin to gambling, in that it costs a lot and there’s no guarantee you’ll get anything out of it. I’m not suggesting that the money one spends on a date should entitle that person to love. That’s absurd and antithetical to the entire modern conception of romance as a mutual experience shared by two people with equal agency. Rather, I’m saying that you’re better off enjoying the meal than worrying about the outcome. At least you’ll feel like you got your money’s worth.And anyway, in a huge city like mine, there’s no need to go for the $150 dinner. Numerous affordable date options exist: free museums, art galleries, parks, the beach. You can make anything a date, as long as it affords you the opportunity to assess compatibility. Sitting in traffic on the 10 freeway at rush hour could be a date if you wanted it to be. You could stand outside a restaurant for 30 minutes and never go in. You could ride an elevator in a large building up and down, then see if sparks fly. If so, just hit the emergency button and spend the time waiting for the fire department, doing as you please.The real problem isn’t if you’re both broke, though. In that scenario, both participants in the relationship can agree to be thrifty. The trouble comes when one person is doing significantly better financially. In my last relationship, I was the broke writer and she was, well … not. Self-employed creative types sometimes have down months (or in my case, years). What started as a pairing of equals quickly turned into me wincing every time the check came.Some think you absolutelyshouldn’t date if you’re unemployed, that you should lock yourself in a cage and wear a chastity belt if you have to leave the house. I suppose that would at least save people the embarrassment I went through, as my savings dwindled and my girlfriend tried to reassure me that it was actually fine that she was paying for everything. Better, then, to wait until your life is more settled and you can go back to blowing your money on extravagant evenings again.To the new couples ‘turbulence testing’ their relationships: just relax and enjoy good times instead | Emma BeddingtonRead moreI see the wisdom in that. Dating can be a huge distraction. A whole other human being requires not just your money, but your time and emotional support. With the economy as troubled as it is, more and more people are having to decide if they can actually afford to be in love, or if they’ll end up like me, a freeloader happy to take what he can get. Maybe I’m being a bit hard on myself here, but guilt is kind of my thing.But there’s never a good time to date. There’s no more convenient time to love and be loved. At no point do people become perfect and wonderful and without actual problems. If you wait for a signal that you’ve got it all figured out, life will pass you by. Love just happens, if you open yourself up to it. It might seem like gambling when you add up how much it costs to try, but it’s healthier to think about it as a part of the personal growth process. It’s possible to meet someone who likes you, despite your having more fingers on your hands than dollars in your bank account. Isn’t that the ideal we’re all searching for anyway? You aren’t a social pariah. This current moment is perilous for millions of people. It’d be a lot easier with someone else to go through it with.So, try not to despair. Ignore the trend pieces and influencers. Go on the cheap date, be honest about your situation, and leave the chastity belt at home.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsDatingOpinionRelationshipscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: The president was forced to hide in a catering truck amid the Iran war, in an encapsulation of the conflict’s failures
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: The president was forced to hide in a catering truck amid the Iran war, in an encapsulation of the conflict’s failures
Content: ‘It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse.’Photograph: Luis M Alvarez/APView image in fullscreen‘It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse.’Photograph: Luis M Alvarez/APOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actionsMohamad BazziThe president was forced to hide in a catering truck amid the Iran war, in an encapsulation of the conflict’s failuresMon 17 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.06 EDTShareFor decades,Donald Trumpcultivated a public image based on strength and dominance. He was a brash New York real estate mogul; a reality TV star who deployed his signature phrase: “You’re fired!” to eliminate contestants from The Apprentice; and eventually US president and undisputed leader of the Republican party.In recent months, Trump has taken his boastfulness to an extreme,reportedly tellingconfidants that he’s “the most powerful person to ever live” andcomparing himselfwith some of history’s most feared leaders, including Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin and Mao.But recent revelations have threatened to shatter Trump’s image as a strongman: the US president departed on asecret military flightout of Turkey after attending a Nato summit, while the White House told the public he was flying onboard Air Force One. The operation involved an elaborate ruse in which Trump boarded his jumbo jet in view of TV cameras, and then was hustled out by the Secret Service through an airportcatering truck. Trump was taken to an alternate military aircraft, which flew him to Britain – all unbeknown to journalists and several White House staff members who stayed on Air Force One and thought they were on the same plane as the president.The embarrassing necessity was a result of Trump’s unnecessary war against Iran. US officials used such levels of subterfuge because they were worried about an Iranian assassination attempt against Trump, according to reports in theWashington PostandNew York Times. On 11 August, Trump confirmed that he had secretly switched planes in Turkey, and attributed the decision to his protective detail and military advisers. “I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trumptold reporterswho asked why US officials had used such an intricate ploy and kept the public in the dark about it until the story was leaked. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane. Equal safety. But they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say.”Trump’s secret flight switch indicates severity of assassination threat by IranRead moreTrump tried to evadecriticismthat the decision left several cabinet members and senior White House officials – including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary; Stephen Miller, Trump’s top domestic adviser; and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director –on Air Force Oneto serve as decoys, along with other Trump staffers and journalists. To deflect more questions,Trump claimed, without providing evidence, that the secret military plane he flew on was actually at “greater risk” than the Air Force One jet that the world saw him board after the Nato summit. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he said.It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse after the danger had passed, as pastpresidents had donewhen they used subterfuge to visit war zones and other hazardous locations. The image of Trump hiding in anairport catering containerto avoid a potential Iranian assassination attempt is a stark contrast to the tough guy brand he spent years cultivating. It’s also an antithesis to the image Trump projected after he survived an assassination attempt at a presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In a series of photos captured by news photographers at the scene, Trump raised his fist in the air and mouthed the words: “Fight, fight, fight” to supporters as he was rushed off stage by Secret Service agents, bleeding from his ear.One imagein particular, showing a bloodied Trump pumping his fist with a US flag in the background, became iconic – and his campaign quicklytried to monetizeit by using the photo on the cover of a book andto sell$299 Trump-branded sneakers.Beyond the dueling imagery, the fact that Trump took refuge in a catering truck has deeper political implications. It encapsulates Trump’s failure in his war on Iran: a president who constantly boasts about US military prowess and tries to project personal strength instead appears weak in front of the world as he hides from the consequences of his own actions. Nearly six months ago, Trump launched his reckless war againstIranas an act of imperial hubris – and a culmination of a series of lawless acts since he returned to office in 2025.With little resistance from the Republican-controlled Congress or the US supreme court, Trump was able to gut government agencies, use federal law enforcement to target his political enemies, appoint his loyalists as top prosecutors, deploy national guard troops into US cities, and weaken decades-old anti-corruption laws designed to constrain presidential power after the Watergate scandal. He also steamrolled over Congress and its authority to declare war.In late February, when the US and Israel launched a series of devastating airstrikes against Iran, Trump had expansive goals: to destroy Tehran’s military capabilities and nuclear program, and to topple Iran’s theocratic regime by decimating its leadership and instigating a popular uprising. In the war’s early days, the US and Israel assassinated more than 30 senior Iranian military and political officials, including the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. But the Iranian system proved resilient and it quickly replaced those officials, partly by appointing Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader, to ensure continuity.Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreIran also turned its proximity to the strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which more than a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed each day, into an effective economic weapon. Tehran closed the passageway at the start of the war, increasing energy prices and disrupting the global economy. Since then, Trump has struggled to reach a deal with Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz and prevent the war from spiraling into a regional conflict that could cause severe economic damage.For months, Trump has tried to negotiate a face-saving agreement that would allow him to declare victory and shift US public attention away from the war before midterm elections in November that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. Iran’s leaders and Trump both say they don’t trust the other side to abide by any agreement – and a memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, which included reopening the strait of Hormuz and lifting a US naval blockade against Iranian ships in the region, has collapsed. Since then, tit-for-tat attacks by Iran and the US have rekindled fears of another all-out war.Not surprisingly, Iranian officials and state media are reveling in the extensive media attention over Trump secretly switching planes in Turkey – and especially the detail about him being ushered into an airport catering truck. A presenter on Iranian state TVcalled ita “scandal stemming from fear of Iran’s military power”, and described the incident as a source of “humiliation” for the US president.It will take time for Trump to undo the damage this ruse has done to his self-proclaimed image as a strong and dominant world leader. More importantly, his disastrous decision to launch a war against Iran will shape his legacy long after he leaves office.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS-Israel war on IranIranTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Sharks have always stoked panic in Australia. While scientific understanding grows, conservation efforts can be unseated by fear | Anna Clark | The Guardian
description: From Aboriginal rock art to colonial encounters, sharks have been a figure of fear and fascination throughout the long human history of this continent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Aboriginal rock art to colonial encounters, sharks have been a figure of fear and fascination throughout the long human history of this continent
Content: ‘Although many more Australians drown each year at the beach, it’s sharks that inhabit the jagged edges of our collective consciousness.’ Sculpture: A Tribute to the Mighty (Great White Shark) by Oceane Jacob.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Although many more Australians drown each year at the beach, it’s sharks that inhabit the jagged edges of our collective consciousness.’ Sculpture: A Tribute to the Mighty (Great White Shark) by Oceane Jacob.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianPast/PresentSharksSharks have always stoked panic in Australia. While scientific understanding grows, conservation efforts can be unseated by fearAnna ClarkFrom Aboriginal rock art to colonial encounters, sharks have been a figure of fear and fascination throughout the long human history of this continentMon 17 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTShareIs there a more primal fear among beach-goers than the shark? Although many moreAustralians drown each year at the beachthan are killed by these creatures, it’s sharks that inhabit the jagged edges of our collective consciousness.After aterrifying spate of bitesearlier this year,calls for shark cullsresurfaced.Ocean swimmingand surfing didn’t seem quite the same healthy pursuits they had just months earlier.TheAustralian Shark Incident Databaseregisters growing numbers of dangerous shark interactions in recent years. Anecdotal evidence also suggests an increase in unreported encounters. But no one knowsexactly why.Archives reveal sharks have been a figure of fear and fascination throughout the human history of this continent. Western Australia’sMurujuga rock art sitedates back tens of thousands of years and includes depictions of hammerhead and tiger sharks.On the other side of the continent, on the cliffs overlooking a First Nations fishing spot known asMurriverie, near Sydney’s Bondi beach, engravings also depict shark motifs. One, stretching eight metres across the sandstone outcrop, angles towards an ancestral or human-like figure and is thought to depict a shark attack.Early Europeans also noted the dangerous presence of sharks. William Dampier gave the nameSharksBay to that part of the west coast in 1699 after being struck by their “abundance”. When the First Fleet arrived in 1788, officer Watkin Tench noted “sharks of a monstrous size” in Sydney Harbour.In my years of spearfishing, I’ve never encountered more sharks than now. But I know where I stand in the underwater pecking order | Clarke GayfordRead moreEarly news reports catalogued the terror colonists felt. One article in theSydney Gazette in 1807reported an attack by a “voracious” shark on a swimmer in Cockle Bay which grabbed him by the arm before letting go.Anarticle from 1812described an enormous shark that was dissected to reveal an entire pelican inside.More famous was the tiger shark caught alive offCoogee beach in 1935, which, after a few days of captivity, regurgitated a tattooed human arm. Sydneysiders were aghast, but tests revealed the arm belonged to a murder victim and had been severed and dumped.At the turn of the 20th century, the growing popularity of surf-bathing also meant an increased risk of shark encounters. While the government recommended surf lifesaving clubs be supplied with first aid kits, swimmers were essentially responsible for managing their own safety.A spate of shark incidents in the 1920s changed all that. In Sydney in 1922, there were two fatal shark attacks in one month, and then another 13 at beaches in Sydney and Newcastle from 1924-34.This amounted to an average of just one shark attack a year, as the NSW Shark Menace Advisory Committee pointed out. But the public were panicking nonetheless.double quotation markThrough the middle decades of the 20th century … public sentiment largely held that a good shark was a dead sharkThe state government initially resisted large scale shark mitigation, offering rewards for shark captures and advising beach-goers to avoid “bathing at dangerous hours, in isolated places, and going too far out”.Some local councils adopted their own measures. In Coogee, enormous steel cables and nets were strung from the middle of the bay, cordoning off a large section of the beach. Swimming nets were also built at other protected beaches in Sydney, Port Phillip Bay and Perth.Other proposals suggested shark baiting and bombing, giant curtains of bubbles, concrete barriers, or electric fences, but each was rejected for being impractical or untested. By the mid-1930s, however, after further attacks in Sydney, the principal recommendation was for the “systematic meshing” of the city’s beaches.The nets wouldn’t be full enclosures but set parallel to the shore to catch and kill sharks. With no attacks in the following decades, meshing was extended to beaches in Newcastle, the Central Coast and Wollongong. In the 1960s, Queensland also adopted a strategy of beach nets and baited drum lines.There wasn’t huge opposition to these safety measures through the middle decades of the 20th century. Public sentiment largely held that a good shark was a dead shark, and big game fishers took up the challenge of catching monster sharks.Over time, however, the consequences of these strategies became clearer: shark mitigation and fishing were affecting entire ecosystems. Their efficacy was now thrown into question.Scientists pointed out theimportance of apex predatorssuch as sharks as keystone species, critical to the health of marine ecosystems, yet several are critically endangered. As more research was conducted, the language around our interactions also changed, from shark “attacks” to “incidents”.Meanwhile, public responses to recent shark encounters show how that shift towards conservation can be unsettled by fear. Politicians find themselves weighing up scientific evidence and public safety, but in the absence of robust data that tension will only continue.Anna Clark is a professor of history at the University of Technology Sydney. She is writing a history of the beach in Australia (Penguin, 2027). She is a member of the Australian Historical AssociationExplore more on these topicsSharksPast/PresentIndigenous AustraliansMarine lifecommentShareReuse this content

title: As Ebola kills thousands in DRC, a perfect storm is making the virus hard to stop | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: New species and regional instability are factors – but decisions made in the US and Britain are also costing lives, says Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: New species and regional instability are factors – but decisions made in the US and Britain are also costing lives, says Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
Content: Members of the Congolese Red Cross carry the coffin of a woman suspected of having died of Ebola, at a cemetery in Bunia in June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Congolese Red Cross carry the coffin of a woman suspected of having died of Ebola, at a cemetery in Bunia in June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionEbolaAs Ebola kills thousands in DRC, a perfect storm is making the virus hard to stopDevi SridharNew species and regional instability are factors – but decisions made in the US and Britain are also costing livesMon 17 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTShareDid you know that there is a major Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and it’s on trackto be the deadliest ever? It isalreadythe second-worst Ebola outbreak in history, with the fastest community transmission we have ever seen. It’s estimated that there have beenat least 4,900 cases and more than 2,300 deaths, giving a mortality rate close to 50%. The situation is bad. That’s the consensus among global health experts.Yet this Ebola outbreak isn’t attracting much media or public attention. If I compare it with working on the 2014 Ebola outbreak, the current silence is astounding. That year, Ebola wasone of the most Googled termsin the world, covered regularly on broadcast news in many countries outside the region, attracting newspaper headlines and magazine covers. Perhaps everyone is just tired of disease after the pandemic – Covid-19 fatigue, as it’s called. Trust me, no one wants to hear about infectious diseases.Unfortunately things are only getting worse in the region. A perfect storm of factors is making the spread hard to contain, even more difficult to slow down – and the health impact is devastating. One concerning factor is that most of the cases, and deaths, are happening in the community before patients even get to hospital: it’s estimated that local health workers are reaching only 30% of cases. Adding to the impact, children make up a quarter of confirmed cases, andalmost a third of all deaths. And those are just the direct deaths from the Ebola virus: routine health services such as childhood vaccination campaigns against measles and basic child survival interventions have been disrupted, meaning a higher number of indirect deaths from lack of healthcare.It’s not just children. Maternal deaths in Ituri (the worst-hit province) have doubled, from childbirth complications and a lack of trained health personnel but also because Ebola infection during pregnancy is linked tofoetal loss.Why is it proving so difficult to stop? First, there’s the virus itself. The outbreak was of a new species – Bundibugyo – and we don’t have an effective vaccine or antiviral against it. Previous outbreaks were the Zaire species. In addition,viral mutationhas been suggested as a factor behind why this outbreak is growing faster than efforts to stop it. Mutation could have made this species more transmissible, as community spread is large and faster than before.The location of the outbreak is also difficult: Ituri province is unstable, with roaming militias and ongoing conflict. Before it was confirmed asEbola, it looks as if the virus had been spreading for three months, being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. Effective government and safe living conditions are a prerequisite for health security, and both are missing right now.There are also larger global changes that make a coordinated response challenging. In the 2014 west Africa outbreak, the US, UK and French governments worked with the World Health Organization (WHO) to escalate a response, bringing military-like coordination, necessary resources, logistics and trained personnel. An Ebola commissionI co-chairedsoon after looked at some of the scientific lessons for the WHO health emergencies response, but we couldn’t predict what the next decade would bring politically.We’ve had two “America-First” Trump presidencies. The US isno longer partof the WHO or working multilaterally, favouring a “go-it-alone” response. This is in the context of the defunding of foreign aid, the censorship of scientists, the closure of USAID, the implosion of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and a“make America healthy again”movement focused on press-ups and visits to the sauna over core public health.Britain has also stepped back from its responsibilities, cutting foreign aid. It makes sense that the current prime minister, Andy Burnham, is focused on domestic issues: when health inequalities and rising poverty mean British children are some of theunhealthiest in western Europe, it’s tricky politically to divert resources overseas. But those political choices have consequences for countries left with fewer resources to fight the spread of disease.In a dire situation, a ray of hope is the vaccine and antiviral work under way. Using the same technology as the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine, Oxford Universityhas started human trialsof the Bundibugyo vaccine, while the WHO is sponsoringa clinical trial in the DRCon two existing antiviral therapies. It’s not just lab science. Social science and the humanities have been engaged to understand how to reach people in remote communities and how to build trust in public health campaigns: given the history of colonial health interventions and residents being used as“guinea pigs”, any health response must understand why people are fearful of external “help”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBudget cuts to higher education have also been consequential. Outbreaks such as this one demonstrate yet again why knowledge, education and research matter, and why political decisions taken in one part of the world have major ramifications for the lives of those in another.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsEbolaOpinionDemocratic Republic of the CongoInfectious diseasesAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Disabled creatives like me are behind many of your favourite shows – so why has our work support been withdrawn? | Annalisa Dinnella | The Guardian
description: Cuts to the Access to Work scheme will mean no more contributions to shows like Sex Education, Call the Midwife or The Hack. It will be devastating to lose such talent, says TV writer Annalisa Dinnella
Author: Annalisa Dinnella
Headline: Cuts to the Access to Work scheme will mean no more contributions to shows like Sex Education, Call the Midwife or The Hack. It will be devastating to lose such talent, says TV writer Annalisa Dinnella
Content: Chris McCausland and his dance partner, Dianne Buswell, lift the glitterball trophy after winning Strictly Come Dancing, 14 December 2024.Photograph: Guy Levy/PAView image in fullscreenChris McCausland and his dance partner, Dianne Buswell, lift the glitterball trophy after winning Strictly Come Dancing, 14 December 2024.Photograph: Guy Levy/PAOpinionDisabilityDisabled creatives like me are behind many of your favourite shows – so why has our work support been withdrawn?Annalisa DinnellaCuts to the Access to Work scheme will mean no more contributions to shows like Sex Education, Call the Midwife or The Hack. It will be devastating to lose such talentMon 17 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTShareWhen Chris McCausland won Strictly Come Dancing in 2024, he held his trophy aloft and said: “It’s for everyone out there that thought and got told they couldn’t do something. It just shows with opportunity and support and determination, anything can happen.” Later that month, he delivered Channel 4’sAlternative Christmas Message. In it, McCausland warned thatAccess to Work(AtW), a scheme run by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), was under threat due to a lack of funding.AtW provides grants to employers and self-employed workers to cover the cost of reasonable adjustments a disabled person may need in the workplace. Behind McCausland’s jovial reflection on the value of different mince pies was a heartfelt plea to protect this little-known yet vital cog in our national machine.Like Chris, I cannot do what I do without support. I am visually impaired (I have 5% vision) and I am a television writer. I’ve worked on shows such as Sex Education, Call the Midwife and The Hack. I am currently working on a drama for BBC One about the newspaper editor Harry Evans. My job is my passion, my obsession, my livelihood and a huge part of my identity. But thanks to recent cuts to my AtW support, it has become increasingly difficult, if not impossible, for me to perform.My grant from AtW is split into two pots: one for taxis (I cannot access public transport independently) and one for a support worker (sighted guide) when needed. In 2025, my grant was cut by 70%, and this year my travel pot was removed entirely. I need to travel. I can’t do my job without attending meetings, rehearsals, writers rooms, sets and post-production facilities. On top of that, I need to network in order to gain future contracts.AtW didn’t contest these needs – or, indeed, my sight loss – but argued that, as I’m self-employed, I can offset travel expenses against tax. This would reimburse only a fraction of my expenditure. Even more baffling, they also claimed I had failed to submit a contract for “work with ITV”. I had clearly stated that my current job is with the BBC, and had provided a contract and letter from my producer to back this up.I submitted a reconsideration request and my MP, Ellie Reeves, also contacted the DWP on my behalf. A few weeks later we both received a letter (by post and in small print, which they know I can’t read) informing us that my appeal had been rejected. They restated their earlier claims, including my failure to provide my mythical contract with ITV. So where do I go from here? Nowhere. There is no recourse to appeal against an appeal. I find myself at a legal dead end.Sadly I am not alone. In the past two years there have been many thousands of stories like mine. When challenged, AtW insists there has been no change in policy and points to a twofold increase in demand over the past five years. It’s true, the system is under strain. Increased demand without a corresponding increase in funding is going to cause a problem; I can’t argue with that. But I can ask: are these cuts by stealth really the best way to solve it?In 2011, theSayce reportfound that for every £1 the DWP put into AtW, it received £1.48 back; it’s obvious this scheme pays for itself. I can certainly prove that I am earning, and paying in tax, a sum far greater than the value of my grant. But must we reduce this argument to numbers on a spreadsheet? I could not make this claim at the beginning of my career. Was I less deserving then? Some claimants have more complex needs than others. Is anyone seriously arguing that their talents should go to waste?I’m also told this study didn’t take into account the money saved in health and social care. Being employed keeps us fit and well. It keeps the wolves of social isolation from the door. Sadly, it seems no further studies have been conducted. Somewhere along the line, AtW decided to stop collecting data.When sense-making grants were available, disabled newcomers had the freedom to take the same financial risks as their non-disabled counterparts. Comedians such as McCausland could dart around comedy festivals with their support workers, and many a star was born. Organisations such asGraeae Theatre(our national theatre for disabled people) became lighthouses for talented youngsters – Jack Thorne, the Emmy-winning writer of Adolescence, landed one of his first jobs writing for Graeae’s artistic director, Jenny Sealey (Jenny’s AtW grant was cut this year. After a fierce social media backlash and the support of her MP, it was restored). But in the past year, AtW has become so unworkable that it is already deterring potential talent. Call the switchboard and the recorded voice will tell you that the current waiting time for a new application is nine months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose of us campaigning to bring this scandal into public consciousness have spent much time wondering: is this cock-up or conspiracy? Is anyone at the DWP considering the impact on the McCauslands of the future? And what is the new prime minister going to do about it?If you back us, we will deliver. It’s what Chris was saying when he brandished his glitter ball trophy. A piece of public policy that made money and was a source of national pride has been twisted into something nonsensical, cruel and, quite frankly, shameful. It’s enough to make anyone stop dancing.Annalisa Dinnella is a television writerExplore more on these topicsDisabilityOpinionBlindness and visual impairmentChris McCauslandBenefitsWork & careersTV comedyComedycommentShareReuse this content

title: My generation had no voice on Brexit – but Burnham gives the young fresh hope | Ceira Sergeant | The Guardian
description: Brexit didn’t create all the problems young people now face, but renewing close ties with Europe will give us so many opportunities, says student and activist Ceira Sergeant
Author: Ceira Sergeant
Headline: Brexit didn’t create all the problems young people now face, but renewing close ties with Europe will give us so many opportunities, says student and activist Ceira Sergeant
Content: The National Rejoin March in London, 20 June 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe National Rejoin March in London, 20 June 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesOpinionBrexitMy generation had no voice on Brexit – but Burnham gives the young fresh hopeCeira SergeantBrexit didn’t create all the problems young people now face, but renewing close ties with Europe will give us so many opportunitiesMon 17 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTShareI was 14 when the UK voted to leave the EU. Too young to vote, but not too young to understand that a decision was being made that would affect the rest of my life.In many ways,Brexitwas my political awakening. It taught me that politics matters, because decisions made by people in power can change your future before you’ve even been given a say.Ten years later, my generation is living with that decision. We lost the automatic right to live, work and study freely across 27 other countries. Opportunities previous generations took for granted are now more complicated, more expensive or completely out of reach. But with a new prime minister who has a recorded history of stating thatwe should rejoin the EU, perhaps we can start to hope.If you have money, many of these barriers can be overcome. You are better able to cope with the extra costs, paperwork and bureaucracy involved in moving abroad. Someone from a wealthy family can afford more expensive routes to studying or living overseas. But what about everyone else?Freedom of movement wasn’t just a nice perk for people who could already afford to travel. For working-class young people like me, it meant opportunity. It was the possibility of studying in Paris, working in Berlin, or falling in love in Barcelona and building a life there. It was about experiencing different cultures, learning languages and feeling part of something bigger.Young people are already facing a difficult economic future. Housing is increasingly unaffordable, wages haven’t kept pace with costs and many of us wonder whether we’ll ever have the security our parents got to enjoy. The median income for those aged 25 and under hasnot increased for two decades. We are becoming the first generation in modern times to seriously contemplate having less than our parents.Brexit didn’t create all of these problems. But putting up economic barriers against our largest neighbouring market certainly hasn’t helped. We were told Brexit would create opportunities. For many working-class young people, it did the opposite. I think often of my friend: a British citizen who married a German, only to face endless challenges just so they could live together. And countless young people in creative industries have had theircareers stifledthrough lack of access to the continent.This is why Andy Burnham’s approach toEuropeis so important.The prime minister must start removing some of the walls Brexit put up. Make it easier for young people to study and work in Europe, restore opportunities for musicians, artists and young creatives, and make sure those opportunities aren’t reserved for people wealthy enough to pay their way around the obstacles.But closer ties aren’t enough. My generation wants theUK to rejoin the EU. So my message to Burnham is simple: be brave.Don’t become another prime minister whose time in office is cut short trying to find another way to make Brexit work. My generation didn’t get a vote last time. Give us one now and I believe we’ll vote for our future in Europe. And this time, give 16- and 17-year-olds a vote too. If they’re old enough to live with the consequences of a decision for the rest of their lives, they’re old enough to have a say in it.We young people have grown up connected to the rest of Europe and the world. We don’t see someone in France, Germany, Poland or Spain as being on the other side of some great divide. They’re our friends, colleagues and partners.Politicians worry about young people becoming disengaged from politics. Perhaps they should ask why.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionImagine being told at 14 you’re too young to have a say in one of the biggest political decisions in generations, then spending your 20s living with the consequences, while politicians tell you reversing it is impossible or can’t even be discussed. Is it any wonder many people have stopped believing politics can change anything?That is the test for Burnham’s government. Don’t just tell young people you understand and pat us on the head. Give us a voice and hear us.In June 2027, the National Rejoin March will return to London. Every host and rally speaker will belong to the generation that was too young to vote in 2016. We were the silenced generation. For 10 years, we’ve heard what those who voted in 2016 wanted. It’s time to hear from those who couldn’t vote then.We can’t change the fact that we didn’t have a voice in 2016. But we’re adults now. We can vote. We can march. And we can demand something better. We don’t intend to stay silent.Ceira Sergeant is a student and the founder of National Rejoin March YouthExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionYoung peopleEuropean UnionForeign policyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Nothing less than radical whole-system change is required to fix the NHS’s maternity services | Julia Sanders | The Guardian
description: It’s vital that Yvette Cooper’s taskforce acts on the Amos and Ockenden reports – and puts the needs of women and families at the heart of maternity services, says professor of midwifery Julia Sanders
Author: Julia Sanders
Headline: It’s vital that Yvette Cooper’s taskforce acts on the Amos and Ockenden reports – and puts the needs of women and families at the heart of maternity services, says professor of midwifery Julia Sanders
Content: ‘For women and families, cumulative systemic problems have resulted in failures of compassionate care.’Photograph: By Ian Miles-Flashpoint Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘For women and families, cumulative systemic problems have resulted in failures of compassionate care.’Photograph: By Ian Miles-Flashpoint Pictures/AlamyOpinionChildbirthNothing less than radical whole-system change is required to fix the NHS’s maternity servicesJulia SandersIt’s vital that Yvette Cooper’s taskforce acts on the Amos and Ockenden reports – and puts the needs of women and families at the heart of maternity servicesMon 17 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTShareIt is hard to find the words to describe the agony for those who have experienced preventable baby loss, injury or maternal death. Understandably, families who have been through this have campaigned relentlessly for local and national investigations. Every family deserves to know what caused their loss or trauma, but current and past reviews have failed to deliver on resolution and accountability.The vital debate about how to ensure safe maternity care has intensified since thepublication of two reports, led by Valerie Amos and Donna Ockenden, and the appointment of Yvette Cooper as secretary of state for health and social care, offering a golden opportunity for system-wide change. “I want to make it a personal crusade to put the cradle back at the heart of the NHS,” Coopertold the Guardian last week, adding that she was committed to introducing a new national maternity commissioner.For women and families, cumulative systemic problems have resulted in failures of compassionate care, with distressing examples described in both reports. Where behaviour is unkind or unprofessional, this is inexcusable, and the life-changing physical and psychological trauma caused by poor care must continue to be acknowledged.We also owe it to all staff groups, particularly midwives, who are often blamed in the media, to recognise that they provide high-quality care to many women every day, despite intense workplace pressures. TheAmos inquiryfound that just 22% of midwives reported having sufficient time to do their job well, while aGuardian reportlast month highlighted increasing numbers leaving the profession because of burnout.Undermining and villainising midwives helps no one. They are the only professional group working with women, babies and families throughout the entire maternity journey across hospital and community settings, providing the platform on which other services depend. For women and babies to be safe, all staff must work in supportive, well-managed and adequately resourced environments.By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive | Natalie MorrisRead moreThe public criticisms of maternity services over the past decade suggest poor care is common, but regular nationalsurveys by Oxford Universityreport high and relatively stable rates of overall satisfaction with care between 2006 and 2024.Poor outcomes do not necessarily equate to poor care. TheOckenden reviewincluded over 700 maternity cases with poor outcomes, including stillbirth, severe perineal trauma or major haemorrhage among more than 41,000 births between 2020 and May 2025. In over 80% of cases, care was judged to be in line with best practice, or it was considered that different management would not have altered the outcome.Work from theNeonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College Londonfound that the number of babies born at term with brain injury caused by oxygen deprivation declined between 2015 and 2021, and stillbirth rates have fallen. These are important gains,but reportsfrom the National Perinatal Epidemiology Unit at Oxford University show that in 2022-2024 the overall rate of maternal death in the UKwas20% higher than it was in 2009-2011and the Amos inquiry also found persistent inequalities, overt racism and continuingreports of physical and psychological trauma.Piecemeal initiatives have produced unintended consequences. Attempts to improve safety and maternal choice have been accompanied by rapidly rising obstetric intervention rates. NHS data shows thatlabour induction increasedfrom about 20% before 2010 to more than 34% by 2020, before slightly reducing.Caesarean section rates rosefrom 27% of births in 2016 to 45% in 2025, equating to about 100,000 additional caesarean births annuallycompared with a decade ago.Focusing on interventions as the solution to maternity safety risks displacing resources and overlooking a fundamental component of maternity care: women need more than technical interventions. Some need to be held safely through loss. All need skilled care, information and trusting relationships with their maternity team. Relationship-based midwifery continuity of care is proven to provide positive outcomes – but few women currently receive this.There is a risk that political, professional and media debate will deflect attention from the central priority: delivering safe and equitable care based on robust evidence and genuine partnership with women and families. The Amos inquiry concluded that nothing less than radical whole-system change is required.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis must be grounded in two key shifts. First, a fundamental reset of the relationship between services and women and families, to ensure that women, families and frontline staff have real influence over how services are designed, delivered and monitored. Second, decisions must be guided by evidence on effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, women’s experiences and sustainable implementation.Thenational maternity and neonatal taskforce, to be chaired by Cooper, has been challenged to deliver the recommendations of the Ockenden review and the Amos inquiry. It must be bold enough to redefine what NHS maternity services can and should provide and negotiate for the resources required. Strong commitment and accountability from politicians, NHS boards, regulators, professional leaders, educators and every member of the multidisciplinary team will be essential. The future health and wellbeing of our population requires nothing less.Julia Sanders is professor of clinical midwifery at Cardiff University and was an expert adviser to the national maternity and neonatal investigation led by Valerie AmosExplore more on these topicsChildbirthOpinionNHSPregnancyHealthWomenYvette CooperMaternal mortalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: Italy’s mythic ‘month off’ in August was hard won. It would be good for us all | Jamie Mackay | The Guardian
description: The villeggiatura, a month-long break, was popularised in the 1960s when trade unions were strong – and so was economic productivity, says writer and translator Jamie Mackay
Author: Jamie Mackay
Headline: The villeggiatura, a month-long break, was popularised in the 1960s when trade unions were strong – and so was economic productivity, says writer and translator Jamie Mackay
Content: The Old Bridge in Dolceacqua, Riviera di Ponente.Photograph: StevanZZ/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Old Bridge in Dolceacqua, Riviera di Ponente.Photograph: StevanZZ/AlamyOpinionItalyItaly’s mythic ‘month off’ in August was hard won. It would be good for us allJamie MackayThe villeggiatura, a month-long break, was popularised in the 1960s when trade unions were strong – and so was economic productivityMon 17 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTShareOn the Riviera di Ponente, sandwiched between the glitzy resort towns of the Ligurian coast, sits the Albenga plain. Dotted with campsites and bungalows, the area developed during Italy’s postwar boom as an affordable refuge for workers to escape the smog of nearby industrial cities like Turin and Milan. While much of the surrounding coast is now given over to boutique lidos, this corner of the riviera is still a place where families gather in the shade of eucalyptus trees to play cards, share picnics and nap through the afternoon heat to the chorus of cicadas.
