These are the stubborn devotees ofvilleggiatura: Italy’s mythic, month-long summer break.The origins ofvilleggiaturago back to the Renaissance, when nobles would leave their urban palazzos for gilded countryside villas in the hills, for weeks at a time. During the 20th century, however, middle- and working-class Italians made their own claim on it, transforming an aristocratic privilege into a mass ritual. By the 1960s, millions of Italians had come to consider a long summer break a fundamental right, spending holidays in ancestral villages, seaside campsites, or even company-sponsored holiday resorts. It was the era immortalised in Gino Paoli’s 1963 jukebox hit Sapore di Sale (The Taste of Salt), which celebrates “lazy days passing by” at the beach, dreaming “of a different world” beyond the factory and office.There is something undeniably nostalgic about this picture-postcard image, but the politics that made it possible are worth reflecting on, not least in contrast with our own overworked age. Italy’s enviable leisure culture did not emerge from nowhere. It was the once-powerful trade unions that fought for this right, securing Italian workerssome of the longest protected holidays in Europe. The forces of capital were forced to adapt. Firms like Fiat and Olivetti didn’t just shut down for most of August; they actively encouraged their employees to decamp for the summer, funding mountain retreats and seasidecoloniefor workers and their children. Even the state helped bankroll the long pause, offering low-cost train tickets and supporting budget holiday programmes to enable families of all classes to participate.There are analogues elsewhere in Europe, from the EnglishWakes Weeksto the Frenchvillages vacances. What was unique in Italy’s postwar period was the systemic collaboration between organised labour, business and the state, and it has provided Italy with a cherished ritual that remains rooted in the national culture to this day.Inevitably, some have bemoaned Italy’s August shutdown as the apotheosis of southern European laziness, asking how an entire country can simply pause for weeks on end. Yetvilleggiaturahas always possessed its own internal economic logic. During the 1960s, at the height of the phenomenon, Italian productivity grew at an average annual rate of 4-6%, higher than that of the US. Industrial output was robust, labour turnover was stable, and despite nascent protests against increased automation,urban unemployment reached historic lows. Decades on, international OECD data continues to show thatlonger working hours yield diminishing returns, thereby reinforcing a truth that many Italians once considered self-evident: that the right to rest sustains an economy, rather than depleting it.The true philosophy behindvilleggiatura, however, is less about economic metrics than human flourishing. In today’s Italy, where precarious employment has bred chronic insecurity, workers spend the year enduring long, erratic hours only to rush off on brief, overpriced breaks. The resulting cycle of burnout and manic consumption is, surely, unsustainable.Villeggiaturaoffers an alternative model. Instead of Airbnbs, it relies on long-term lets and family homes. Instead of sightseeing, it privileges sunbathing and sleep. Instead of tasting menus and overpriced cocktails, it prioritises simple rituals, like sharing focaccia and watermelon on the beach with family and friends.View image in fullscreenA beach at Torre dell’Orso, Italy, in August.Photograph: Diego Fiore/AlamyOn paper, this sounds like an ideal way to spend a summer. Unfortunately, though, fewer and fewer Italians are able to achieve it. Where workers were once able to decamp for weeks on end, the average holiday had dropped to 13 days by the 1990s as deregulation transformed the labour market, and the figure now stands at barely six. Last year, 35.7% of Italians reported beingunable to afford even a short break away. To make matters worse, the very concept ofvilleggiaturais being co-opted by luxury brands. The Belmond hotel group recently published a $120coffee table book titled Villeggiatura, explicitly appropriating the language of the long break to market hotels like Portofino’s Splendido, where a room can set you back several thousand euros a night.Despite these pressures, Italians have not yet surrendered their ritual. Places like Albenga remain popular destinations for long August breaks, as do the traditional lidos of the Riviera Romagnola on the Adriatic coast, where, despite the spread of exclusive beach clubs, pockets of affordability still endure. Heritage groups are working to revive the physical monuments of corporate vacation spots, from theEni village in Borca di Cadoreto Olivetti’s seaside retreat inMarina di Massa. Even remnants of state support persist, like government-funded grants that allow the children of lower-income public-sector workers to attend summer camps.For the most part, though,villeggiaturatoday requires far more compromise and financial strain than it once did. Many Italian workers opt for inland destinations away from the coast, where prices remain lower. Others juggle diminished workplace benefits, piecing together the limited time off their employers allow. Digital workers are perhaps the phenomenon’s most inventive contemporary adherents, with many choosing to forego pay to take time off, or surrendering some precious rest hours to answer emails from beneath a beach umbrella.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe fact that so many are fighting to keep this ritual alive against all odds tells us what is at stake here.Villeggiaturawas never just about taking a holiday, but reclaiming life from the totalising logic of the market. In an era when workers acrossEuropeare exhausted, isolated and struggling with the high cost of living, that simple idea remains quietly inspiring. Far from a relic of 60s nostalgia, or a gimmick for luxury brands, its true legacy is a defiant belief in the necessity of rest.Villeggiaturareminds us that a slower, healthier way of life should not just be an elite privilege, but a fundamental right – one that, with a dose of political will, could once again be accessible to the many.Jamie Mackay is a writer and translator based in FlorenceExplore more on these topicsItalyOpinionEuropeUnionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Scams have become a constant part of life. In a world full of distrust, how can we know what is real?  | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: There is something depressing about being scammed. Every unknown number, every marketplace purchase, every text with a link now arrives with suspicion
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: There is something depressing about being scammed. Every unknown number, every marketplace purchase, every text with a link now arrives with suspicion
Content: ‘I had been looking for gold trainers for months and finally found them on a second-hand retail site,’ writes Brigid Delaney. ‘But my pleasure faded as I tried to cross Old South Head Road.’Photograph: mirror-images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I had been looking for gold trainers for months and finally found them on a second-hand retail site,’ writes Brigid Delaney. ‘But my pleasure faded as I tried to cross Old South Head Road.’Photograph: mirror-images/Getty ImagesOpinionLife and styleScams have become a constant part of life. In a world full of distrust, how can we know what is real?Brigid DelaneyThere is something depressing about being scammed. Every unknown number, every marketplace purchase, every text with a link now arrives with suspicionSun 16 Aug 2026 21.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.57 EDTShareMy day started with exciting news. It was a long and gushing email frompopular Australian breakfast radio show host Sally Sara saying she was following up on a previous conversation (huh? wot?) and would love to interview me about my 2009 book, This Restless Life, on her program.“I remain genuinely enthusiastic about the opportunity to feature your work and to welcome you to an upcoming author conversation. I believe your insights and experience would make for a thoughtful and engaging discussion, and I would be delighted to work with you to create an enjoyable experience for both you and our audience,” she wrote.How bizarre, I thought. My book came out in 2009, I had not spoken to Sara about an interview, and I knew from years of listening to her program that it covered politics in depth but not out-of-print books published almost 20 years ago.Deepfake Anthony Albanese used in celebrity scams duping Australians out of $7.4m, Asic warnsRead moreAs the day went on, I wondered if I’d been scammed. If it was a genuine request, why did the email come from a gmail account and not one connected to the ABC?But scammed for what? What would a scammer want from an author? What would be their ask?I was thinking all this as I was lacing up a pair of gold trainers that I had bought second-hand from Depop. They were beautiful! As I got the train to Bondi Junction for an appointment with my shaman, a woman sitting opposite complimented me on my shoes. I told her with pride that I had been looking for gold trainers for months and finally found them on a second-hand retail site.But my pleasure faded as I tried to cross Old South Head Road.I was suddenly unsteady on my feet, as if suffering from vertigo or drunk. I stumbled, almost falling into oncoming traffic. The soles of my feet felt weird. Was I having a stroke?I looked down. My right gold trainer was splitting in two – the base of the shoe was in the process of separating from the bit that held my foot.After my appointment, the shaman gave me rubber bands to hold the shoe together but, on the way back to the station, the other shoe peeled away from the sole, also causing me to trip over my feet, as I tried to run across a road. I ended up walking barefoot four blocks to the station.Avoiding glass, feet freezing, people staring at me as if I was a freak, I thought of the description on Depop – “Barely worn!” – and wondered, not for the first time today, if I had been scammed and the seller had just glued some broken shoes together with a dab of Clag.The next day, the scams keep coming. An email from a US television company that wanted to interview me about my Stoicism book. I just had to send them money! And, in another email, a US book club that excitedly offered to include my book on their list that reached many thousands of readers. I just had to sign up and pay money to access their mailing list.I replied to the breakfast radio scam email out of curiosity and received pages and pages of forms, designed by the looks of it to harvest my personal data to some nefarious end.Only the week before someone tried to scam me pretending to be from the ATO and wanting my tax file number.And a friend told me about one of her friends, caught in a love scam. She was sending tens of thousands of dollars overseas to a man she met online.There is something depressing about being scammed, even if the scammer doesn’t succeed. It’s a sort of greasy, low-level unclean feeling, an ick.Sydney, you were a dream of warmth and ease. When I returned to wintry Melbourne, time collapsed – and the city was still romanticRead moreIn part this is because the scammers often work on our weaknesses – our soft, vulnerable underbellies, like the need for fame and recognition (a popular radio host wants to devote an hour of her program to your old book!), our appearance (cool gold sneakers!), and our need for love, money, a good reputation and security. When we realise we’ve been had, there is often a feeling of shame – not just for being tricked but for being seen as a human being with vanity, needs and desires, and then having those needs exploited and ultimately unmet.But something about the current generation of scams and scammers feels more diffuse, inserted into every crevice of modern life.We have internalised scams as just something that happens now – that every time our phones ring, it might be someone trying to trick us, steal from us, extract something that we don’t consent to. It’s a form of profound alienation where we no longer assume others are trustworthy.Being scammed is so common, it’s just the ambient condition of life in 2026. In this miasma of distrust, every unknown number, every Marketplace purchase, every text with a link in it, every stranger online, now arrives pre-filtered through suspicion.As I walked through Bondi Junction barefoot in the cold, I wondered what is real and honest in this life if I can’t even trust the shoes on my feet?Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the SageExplore more on these topicsLife and styleOpinionScamscommentShareReuse this content

title: Hayden Panettiere: an actor so magnetic that entire shows were rewritten for her | Television | The Guardian
description: She starred in her first soap opera at 4 – then the hit show Heroes was totally reworked to allow her character, Claire the regenerating cheerleader, to live on. We celebrate the star, who has died age 36
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: She starred in her first soap opera at 4 – then the hit show Heroes was totally reworked to allow her character, Claire the regenerating cheerleader, to live on. We celebrate the star, who has died age 36
Content: ‘She was more than an actress – she was a muse’ … Hayden Panettiere in Heroes.Photograph: Nbc/Universal Tv/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘She was more than an actress – she was a muse’ … Hayden Panettiere in Heroes.Photograph: Nbc/Universal Tv/Kobal/ShutterstockTelevisionHayden Panettiere: an actor so magnetic that entire shows were rewritten for herShe starred in her first soap opera at 4 – then the hit show Heroes was totally reworked to allow her character, Claire the regenerating cheerleader, to live on. We celebrate the star, whohas died age 36Hayden Panettiere – a life in picturesHayden Panettiere obituaryZoe WilliamsMon 17 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Hayden Panettiere arrived as Claire Bennet in Heroes, in 2006, she was 17 but not a newcomer. She’d starred in Tiger Cruise, a Disney Channel movie, two years before and was the pin-perfect image of that teen-star world – blond, cute, perky, resourceful and all-American. Bennet the superhero was all those things, amped up to the point of fascinating distortion. She was a cheerleader who could endlessly regenerate. It was a topic of hot debate on fan sites whether or not she could feel pain, a question that was resolved piecemeal through the series. She could, but could instantly overcome it with her superpower – that fact partly informed the view of one academic, professor Olvido Andújar Molina, that Bennet was standing in for the American dream, its core components being strength, resilience and a sweet-natured homeliness.In Tiger Cruise, Panettiere had filled a similar role, the cute-as-a-button daughter of a naval commander, producing this elemental, almost mournful Oz-like message: “Everything you long for is right here at home.” She was from a showbiz family, her mother, Lesley Vogel, was a soap actor, and her brother, Jansen, who also possessed those perfectly symmetrical features, co-starred in Tiger Cruise, and later, in 2011, in The Forger (better known as the last film Lauren Bacall ever made). Jansen also died horribly young, of complications from an engorged heart, in 2023 aged 28. Panettiere got her first soap opera gig, in One Life to Live, at the age of four, and went on to a recurring role into Guiding Light before she was 10. She was the voice of Dot in A Bug’s Life, and was nominated for a Grammy for her work on the film.View image in fullscreenPin-perfect image of the teen star … Hayden Panettiere with Bill Pullman in Tiger Cruise.Photograph: Disney/AllstarPerhaps because of how the cheerleader role landed on the collective imagination, and certainly because of Panettiere’s performance, which had a magnetic complexity that always seemed at odds with how appealing she was, Bennet came to define Heroes. The showrunners originally intended to refresh the superheroes each series, to create a giant stable of ridiculously capable archetypes. In the end, bowing to audience preference, they wrote Panettiere into all six seasons. At one fan convention, Panettiere addressed how she was funnelled towards certain roles by her inescapably wholesome good looks: “People look at me as either the popular cheerleader type or just the blond.”When Heroes ended in 2010, perhaps trying to branch out, she took the lead role in Amanda Knox: Murder on Trial in Italy, an ill-conceived and poorly received project. But in 2012, a role came along in Nashville, which was perfect for her. As Juliette Barnes, a young country singer in a hurry, Panettiere embodied that bubble gum country music trope, the Dolly-Parton-beautiful singer on to whom a nation projects all its fantasies – of sweetness and innocence, of pluck. That ran for six seasons, and viewers lapped it up, with its excesses of plot and heartache and intrigue, especially in the first two seasons.View image in fullscreen‘Dolly-Parton-beautiful’ … Hayden Panettiere as Juliette Barnes in Nashville.Photograph: ABC/AllstarDespite her on-screen success, Panettiere’s personal life was turbulent; after the birth of her daughter in 2014, she suffered postnatal depression. She separated from her fiance, the boxer Wladimir Klitschko, in 2018, relinquishing custody of their child to him the same year. Her relationship with her next boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was marred by domestic abuse allegations and Hickerson was arrested multiple times. In 2021, he was reportedly jailed after pleading no contest to domestic abuse charges. Unsurprisingly, she did very little work during this period. Bryan Fuller, a writer on Heroes, said in tribute that “she was more than an actress, she was a muse”. Such a patriarchally freighted remark, though clearly well meant, gestures at the challenges Panettiere faced, trying to create work while embodying so many people’s fantasies of girlhood; but they were challenges she met, and exceeded.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’ve got to see this girl!’ Tanita Tikaram on making Twist in My Sobriety | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘People tell me it helped them with their rehab. I have to explain: Sorry, it’s not about alcohol – I was just a kid singing about injustice’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: ‘People tell me it helped them with their rehab. I have to explain: Sorry, it’s not about alcohol – I was just a kid singing about injustice’
Content: ‘Once I had the groovy guitar riff, the song fell together’ … Tanita Tikaram on stage in 1989.Photograph: Gie Knaeps/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Once I had the groovy guitar riff, the song fell together’ … Tanita Tikaram on stage in 1989.Photograph: Gie Knaeps/Getty ImagesHow we madeMusic‘You’ve got to see this girl!’ Tanita Tikaram on making Twist in My Sobriety‘People tell me it helped them with their rehab. I have to explain: Sorry, it’s not about alcohol – I was just a kid singing about injustice’Interviews byDave SimpsonMon 17 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTanita Tikaram, singer-songwriterI wrote the lyrics on the floor of my bedroom in Basingstoke when I was 16 or 17, as a way of decompressing from studying for my A-levels. I had the idea for “Twist in my …” something, but didn’t know what else to put in there. I tried “Twist in my gravity” before ending up with “sobriety”, but it’s not a song about alcohol. It’s about feeling that things aren’t right in the world, and that adults can do terrible or immoral things – but none of it will change you. Fundamentally, it’s a song by an alienated teenager who feels there’s a lot of injustice. There’s something lovely about how intensely you feel things as a teenager.The opening line, “All God’s children need travelling shoes,” is the title of a book by Maya Angelou. Then “All good people read good books” is the language of a kid who reads a lot. It’s a little road song: you’re on a journey, kind of travelling, but really looking for something. Once I had the groovy little guitar riff, the song just fell together.double quotation markUnusually, I came up with a part for oboeI’d only previously sung in a school play, but some guys from a local band helped me record my songs in a nearby studio, so suddenly I had a tape. I sent it to the Mean Fiddler in Harlesden, London, and they gave me a spot at their open mic night. I played there to just three people, but one of them was the venue-owner,Vince Power, who told an agent: “You’ve got to see this girl!” Soon enough, I’d signed to a record label and they suggested Rod Argent and Peter Van Hooke as co-producers. Like me, Rod had been very young when he had his first hit inthe Zombies, so there was empathy there.Peter would pick me up at the train station and we’d drive to Rod’s home studio in St Albans, where we recorded Twist in My Sobriety. Rod wanted the right sound for the melody line and went through the whole woodwind section of samples. In those days, samples were all on floppy discs so you’d sit there for ages waiting for them to load, but then suddenly he tried a synthetic oboe and said: “My God, that works!”I never had an inkling that the song was going to be a hit, but it took off in continental Europe and everywhere else followed. I’m very proud of it. Recently, a young woman came up to me and said: “That song takes me to my happy place.” It’s a dark song to do that for someone. In the US, people tell me it helped them with their sobriety or rehab. I have to explain: “Sorry, it’s not about alcohol. I was just a kid.”Rod Argent, co-producerWhen Peter and I first met Tanita, she’d only ever played her own guitar. We thought she was really talented: we wanted to match the strength and direction of her composition with a really colourful, inventive backing. My studio was in a wonderful Georgian house called Red House, where we had two rooms: a control room and a recording room with a piano in it. Everything was done in there – and in those days we recorded on to tape.Pete came up with the brilliant idea of recording a master vocal with Tanita playing guitar to a guide rhythm track we’d then dispense with, because that was the way she was used to playing. That gave us a really confident vocal – Tanita sounded really in command. But it meant we could be really inventive around it, conjuring up a scenario with strings and such. We built up every track on her Ancient Heart album like that.View image in fullscreenThe 7in single sleeve for Twist in My Sobriety, 1988.Photograph: sjvinyl/AlamyFor Twist in My Sobriety, Pete created a definitive drum part and I had a ball coming up with the instrumental sections. The booming synth sounds at the beginning have a lot of attack, then I came up with a part for – unusually – oboe, which Pete was very unsure about at first as he wanted a more folky thing. But there was something classical about it that sounded really lovely. We did it using the oboe sound on the synth first, then a professional player called Malcolm Messiter came in and played an actual oboe.I thought the finished song had a fantastic feel: there was something very unusual about it. I played it this morning for the first time in a long time – and it sounded absolutely brilliant.Tanita Tikaram plays Beautiful Days,Escot Park, Devon, 20-23 August.Explore more on these topicsMusicHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: gang leader plotted killing to avenge beating of nephew, court hears | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors accuse Duane Davis of orchestrating 1996 shooting in retaliation for attack by rapper’s entourage
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Prosecutors accuse Duane Davis of orchestrating 1996 shooting in retaliation for attack by rapper’s entourage
Content: Rapper Tupac Shakur after his performance at the Regal Theater in Chicago, Illinois, in March 1994.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRapper Tupac Shakur after his performance at the Regal Theater in Chicago, Illinois, in March 1994.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesTupac ShakurTupac Shakur murder trial: gang leader plotted killing to avenge beating of nephew, court hearsProsecutors accuse Duane Davis of orchestrating 1996 shooting in retaliation for attack by rapper’s entourageDani AnguianoandSam LevinMon 17 Aug 2026 18.50 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trial of a former gang leader accused of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap starTupac Shakurbegan in aLas Vegascourtroom on Monday, featuring testimony from a witness to the shooting and a former police officer.Duane “Keffe D” Davis is on trial for murder for his alleged role in the shooting of Shakur, who died after a drive-by shooting. Prosecutors allege Davis was the “on-the-ground, on-site commander of the effort to kill Tupac” and that he planned the shooting in retaliation for Shakur’s entourage attacking Davis’s nephew.Davis has pleaded not guilty, though he acknowledged a role in the shooting in a 2019 memoir that authorities have said is key to the case against the 63-year-old. Davis is the only living witness from the car that fired shots at Shakur.Last week, a jury of six men and 10 women was selected in the trial, which is expected to last about a month.What we know about Tupac Shakur’s death and what to expect from murder trialRead moreDavis entered the courtroom in a blue suit and tie and scanned the audience to see who was there before sitting next to his lawyer, Michael Sanft, once the jury was sworn in and seated on Monday morning.Members of Shakur’s family, including his stepbrother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur, sat quietly in the front row of the courtroom behind prosecutors.Binu Palal, the chief deputy district attorney, showed jurors a picture of the Mike Tyson-Bruce Seldon fight with the date “September 7, 1996” and showed video of Shakur’s entourage beating Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’s nephew.“Let’s be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew,” Palal said. “Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself.”Palal showed multiple video clips and played audio of Davis describing his alleged role in the incident and anger toward Shakur for the attack on his nephew.Sanft, the defense lawyer, meanwhile, said that after 30 years, investigators still have very little evidence to prove their case.“At the end ​of the day you have to ask yourself: is what they are saying truth ‌or fiction?” Sanft told the jury.Sanft argued that while Davis spoke about the killing to different law enforcement agencies over the years, including the FBI, they did not follow up because, Sanft said, they did not believe what Davis said was credible.3:35Tupac Shakur murder trial: opening statements begin – videoThe trial is a major development in thecasethat for decades was unsolved.On 7 September 1996, the rap icon was attacked just off theLas Vegasstrip as he headed to an afterparty with the Death Row Records founder, Marion “Suge” Knight. While traveling in the vehicle, a Cadillac pulled up next to Shakur’s vehicle and fired eight shots. Shakur was hospitalized for his injuries and died days later.Shakur’s killing spawned countless conspiracy theories, and books and documentaries seeking to determine who was responsible for his death. But a fuller picture of what may have occurred that night has emerged in recent years as Davis, who was the last surviving passenger in the Cadillac, began speaking publicly.Earlier that evening Shakur had attended the Tyson fight at the MGM Grand hotel and afterward was involved in a physical confrontation with Davis’s nephew and several others.Davis sought retribution for Anderson and allegedly obtained a gun with the intent to “hunt down” Shakur and confront Knight. Theincidentunfolded quickly, Davis wrote.“No words were exchanged, the time for talking had passed, the shit was on! Tupac made an erratic move and began to reach down beneath his seat. It was the first and only time in my life that I could relate to the police command to, ‘Keep your hands where I can see them.’ Instead, Pac pulled out a strap, and that’s when the fireworks started. One of my guys from the back seat grabbed the Glock and started bustin’ back,” he wrote.Tupac Shakur: jury selected in trial of ex-gang boss accused of ordering killingRead moreProsecutors have said that Davis’s tell-all book and public statements ultimately revived the Las Vegas investigation.“Had he decided to never write the book, he would not, probably, have ever been prosecuted for the crime,” prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo recently said.His attorneys sought to exclude the book from trial by arguing that he and his co-author exaggerated in an effort to “falsely place himself at the center of it all for personal gain”. A judge denied the request.The first witness called by prosecutors was Garry Dale, a former Las Vegas officer who pulled over Shakur and Knight on the night of the shooting. Hesaidhe stopped the car because it lacked a license plate on the back, and that the interaction was “congenial”. The officer recounted later riding in the ambulance with Shakur after the shooting, saying he tried to convince the rapper to name his assailants, but that Shakurresponded: “No, we’ll take care of it.”Prosecutors’ second witness was Ingrid Stokes, a woman who was in a car with friends near Shakur’s car at the time of the shooting. Stokes’s car and Shakur’s car were both going to the same club, she said. “We heard the gunshots … all hell broke loose,” she said. Stokes added that she didn’t see who was in the car that fired on Skakur, and that she later spoke to police who were “rude” and “treated us like suspects”.Stokes said she didn’t think she had any valuable information to share with officers, and that she and her friends had fear at the time about talking to officers and being labeled as “snitches”.Brent Becker, a former homicide detective from Las Vegas, also took the stand and recounted interviewing Knight after the shooting, saying the record label boss was “very timid” and had three attorneys with him: “He just basically said he didn’t know anything. He didn’t recognize anybody.”Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s killing, can a murder trial offer justice?Read moreKnight, who is currently in prison over a different case, recently suggested he did not want to cooperate with police,telling ABC Newsin an interview last week: “This trial has nothing to do with me and if somebody brings me there, it’s gonna hurt whoever brings me there. I promise you that.”On the stand, Becker further recounted his collaboration with Los Angeles police who helped identify people connected to the beating of Anderson. While the southern California officers shared “interesting” information with Becker about how Shakur’s killing might be connected to other conflicts, Becker said they didn’t have reliable sources who would speak in court: “The problem was it was all from informants. We didn’t have any actual people that would come forward and testify.”The day ended with testimony from Fred Miller, a former Los Angeles police detective who had investigated Davis in connection with the 1997 murder of Christopher Wallace, the rapper known as Biggie Smalls or the Notorious BIG. Attorneys played a lengthy audio recording of Miller questioning Davis at the time.Davis was present at a party that Wallace had attended before he was shot, but Davis’s attorney emphasized he was not charged in Wallace’s murder, and the judge told jurors that law enforcement did not believe Davis was involved.The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurLas VegasRapUS crimeHip-hopnewsShareReuse this content

title: Buried With Michael Sheen review – this vital look at a toxic waste scandal is deeply enraging TV  | Television | The Guardian
description: The actor does a brilliant job of probing the alleged dumping of ‘forever chemicals’ in Wales. After grilling a stranger for two days, his investigation turns up horrible incidents – including potential links to cancer cases
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: The actor does a brilliant job of probing the alleged dumping of ‘forever chemicals’ in Wales. After grilling a stranger for two days, his investigation turns up horrible incidents – including potential links to cancer cases
Content: ‘Sober in his pursuit of truth’ … Michael Sheen in Buried.Photograph: BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsView image in fullscreen‘Sober in his pursuit of truth’ … Michael Sheen in Buried.Photograph: BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsTV reviewTelevisionReviewBuried With Michael Sheen review – this vital look at a toxic waste scandal is deeply enraging TVThe actor does a brilliant job of probing the alleged dumping of ‘forever chemicals’ in Wales. After grilling a stranger for two days, his investigation turns up horrible incidents – including potential links to cancer casesJack SealeMon 17 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou may scoff at celebrity-fronted documentaries, but there’s no need to moan about Buried With Michael Sheen, an investigation into how toxic“forever chemicals”were dumped in Welsh quarries in the middle of the 20th century. Much of our knowledge of the subject comes from a filmed interview given nearly 10 years ago by the environmental campaigner Douglas Gowan, who, after decades of trying to raise awareness, had only weeks to live and wanted to divulge all he had learned. The person behind the camera and asking the questions? Sheen.The actor and director is a little coy about how or why he came to spend two days – two days! – grilling a stranger to create the most valuable document we have about an underappreciated injustice. He says something about stumbling across Gowan online during a career lull and wanting to know more. But however it happened, the fact is that the best qualified person to present this two-parter is the award-winning Hollywood star, so here he is.And very good he is, too: passionate about the outrage, but sober in his pursuit of truth. It proves to be a story that keeps throwing up moments and characters for which a scriptwriter would congratulate themselves. Sheen fits right in.We’re talking about the now defunct American agrochemicals giant Monsanto, which after the second world war cornered the market in, shall we say, controversial chemical innovations. Agent Orange, DDT and Roundup were all made by Monsanto, as were polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) – indestructible compounds that were hailed as miracle chemicals until they were discovered to be toxic and carcinogenic. From the 1940s to the late 1970s, PCBs were made at the Monsanto plant in Newport, the city where Sheen spent some of his childhood.The question is what was done with the factory’s waste. Gowan deduced that it was buried in landfills across south Wales – in a way that he thought allowed PCBs to leech into the surrounding water and soil.Sheen travels first to the village of Ynysddu, where the two councillors who have spoken out most on this issue are both called Jan and are thus known as “the two Jans”. One of the Jans relays testimony from villagers who remember lorries arriving at night at the nearby quarry – now an eerie patch of unloved grass, ringed by trees – and leaving behind a jelly-like substance on the roads that children would play with the next morning. At a meeting inside Ynysddu Progressive Workingmans Club, residents describe the phenomenon that has convinced them that, decades later, something is still wrong: dogs that are walked in the woods keep dying of cancer.View image in fullscreenLucy Taylor and Dan Ashby with Michael Sheen in Buried.Photograph: BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsAs is customary with these scandals, the narrative repeatedly turns up horrible localised problems that those affected are sure they know the cause of, even if proof of direct causation is hard to find. Next, Sheen jets to Anniston, Alabama, formerly the site of Monsanto’s main PCB factory in the US. A paediatrician working there today says she has seen an unusual amount of birth defects, including children born without eyes or with their intestines on the outside of their bodies.Sheen meets the attorney Donald Stewart, who in 1993 sued Monsanto on behalf of the town, securing a $300m settlement. Stewart shares internal Monsanto memos from as long ago as 1949 that suggest the firm knew how dangerous PCBs were. How did Monsanto think it could get away with endangering the Anniston public, Sheen asks? This inquiry produces a breathtaking moment. “If you look at this area, they’re working people,” Stewart replies. Suddenly, this courtroom bruiser is choking back tears. “They wouldn’t be able to fight back.”Back at home, Sheen pores over parliament’s Hansard transcripts with Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor, the married investigative duo who present the BBC Radio 4 podcast series Buried. They reveal that, in 1973, shortly after the production of PCBs in Anniston was stopped, a government minister in Westminster was traducing Gowan from the dispatch box, insinuating that he had doctored his evidence. The parliamentary debate followed a Sunday Times expose by the journalist Peter Pringle, who used Gowan as a source.From there, Sheen dons wellies and embarks on a project to test the soil near the landfills, accompanied by an environmental scientist and – because although this tale is enragingly serious, it keeps turning up delightful quirks – a vicar. The Gowan of today is the Rev Paul Cawthorne, whose interest was sparked by a deathbed confession from a parishioner who used to drive trucks filled with barrels of seething crud.The PCBs affair has been rumbling on for years without many firm answers being obtained, but that may change in next week’s concluding episode: you wouldn’t bet against the actor, the vicar, the podcasting spouses and the two Jans cracking the case.Buried WithMichael Sheenaired on BBC Two and is available on BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMichael SheenDocumentaryFactual TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘His ache is real’: Bob Dylan and more on the wild genius of honky-tonk hellraiser Gary Stewart  | Country | The Guardian
description: Worshipped by everyone from Willie Nelson to Joe Strummer, the country star with the amazing voice imploded in a blaze of guns, knives, drugs and infidelities. What’s behind his astonishing posthumous rediscovery?
Author: Garth Cartwright
Headline: Worshipped by everyone from Willie Nelson to Joe Strummer, the country star with the amazing voice imploded in a blaze of guns, knives, drugs and infidelities. What’s behind his astonishing posthumous rediscovery?
Content: Spent his last 25 years in a blacked-out trailer … Stewart peeling fruit on the bumper of a vintage car.Photograph: Grandal StewartView image in fullscreenSpent his last 25 years in a blacked-out trailer … Stewart peeling fruit on the bumper of a vintage car.Photograph: Grandal StewartCountry‘His ache is real’: Bob Dylan and more on the wild genius of honky-tonk hellraiser Gary StewartWorshipped by everyone from Willie Nelson to Joe Strummer, the country star with the amazing voice imploded in a blaze of guns, knives, drugs and infidelities. What’s behind his astonishing posthumous rediscovery?Garth CartwrightMon 17 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘He sings like a man arguing with destiny. It sounds like the ache is real, that the ruin is real,”Bob Dylantells me. “There’s a cracked truth there. What’s unsettling about him is that he sounds like he’s already living in the aftermath.” Dylan is talking about the late US singer-songwriter Gary Stewart. I had approached him because he was one of the few people to speak highly of this country music maverick.Even while still alive, Stewart was a ghostlike figure. He had a period in the Nashville spotlight in the mid-1970s, but his death in December 2003 aged 59 barely registered. Stewart had been forgotten after he cast aside stardom in order to hunker down in a Florida trailer park where he and his wife Mary Lou consumed quaaludes, meth, marijuana and cocaine in industrial quantities.double quotation markHe was a natural disaster from an earlier time, one older folks still talk about outside of the bait shop“Growing up with parents who were drug addicts meant I just took this as normal,” says Shannon Ashburn, the couple’s daughter. “I loved them and they loved me and they never let any predators in, so I didn’t feel unsafe. But, looking back, I realise it was an insane situation.” A handful of aficionados – Dylan, Willie Nelson, John Waters, Tanya Tucker – maintained that Stewart was one of the 20th century’s most expressive vocalists, but it seemed unlikely he would generate the exalted posthumous cult status of Nick Drake or Karen Dalton.View image in fullscreen‘I didn’t feel unsafe’ … Mary Lou,  Gary, Shannon and Joey in the 1970s.Photograph: Grandal StewartBut now, after his chaotic life and overlooked death, Stewart is finally getting rediscovered thanks to Gary Stewart: I Am from the Honky Tonks, a formidable biography that was an unexpected critical and commercial hit in the US when it was published last November. Its author Jimmy McDonough, whose biographies of Neil Young, Al Green, Tammy Wynette and Russ Meyer have marked him as a brilliantly unconventional commentator on American lives, chuckles at his good fortune when I call him at home in Portland, Oregon. “Of all my books this one proved the most difficult to find a publisher for,” he says, “yet it’s getting the best response of any of them.”Meanwhile, reissue label Delmore Recording Society has just released One Track Mind, a mesmerising collection of Stewart’s early-1970s demos, and rising country and indie-rock stars such as Ella Langley, Zach Top, Wednesday frontwoman Karly Hartzman, Charley Crockett and Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band now sing Stewart’s praises – and songs.double quotation markHe scored a No 1 with She’s Actin’ Single (I’m Drinkin’ Doubles)“Gary Stewart is a superhero,” says Davis, the Kentucky-born singer-songwriter whose 2025 album New Threats from the Soul won wide acclaim. “He was, as his music still is and always will be, unfathomably real. And of near-ish my own geographic origins, making him simultaneously both realer and yet somehow even more fantastical.” Davis compares Stewart to “a natural disaster from an earlier time, one that the older folks still talk about outside of the bait shop”.Stewart was born in Kentucky in 1944, one of 12 children, his family shifting to Florida in 1956 after his coal miner father suffered a debilitating injury at work. From his early teens Stewart, a prodigy who absorbed rockabilly, country and R&B, was playing in bands and writing songs. He moved to Nashville, playing piano in Charley Pride’s band while seeking publishing and recording deals. Established singers sang Stewart’s songs but solo success was elusive until Nashville producer Roy Dea convinced RCA to sign Stewart in 1973.View image in fullscreenFierce intensity … Stewart blasting away in a honky-tonk in the 70s.Photograph: Shannon Ashburn collectionDea understood Stewart’s strengths – “I never knew anyone who blew me away like Gary,” Dea told an interviewer, “and I’ve seen Elvis, Hank Williams, all of ’em” – and in 1974 Stewart scored US hits with Drinkin’ Thing and Out of Hand. His 1975 debut album, also titled Out of Hand, won critical accolades and She’s Actin’ Single (I’m Drinkin’ Doubles) topped the country charts in the same year.Stewart’s albums over the next three years – Steppin’ Out, Your Place or Mine, Little Junior – feature some of the most exciting American music of the 1970s. As a vocalist Stewart was without artifice; he would sing ballads Quits and Ten Years of This with intense emotional eloquence, then crank out Little Junior and Your Place or Mine with the gusto of a man hungry for the wild side of life. While punk rock made zero initial impact on Nashville, Stewart, with his raucous swagger and distaste for Music City’s establishment, embodied punk’s spirit; Joe Strummer was a fan.Often likened to Jerry Lee Lewis – the fierce intensity of his rockabilly-flavoured country numbers marked them out as kindred spirits – and Hank Williams, Stewart shared with Williams a warm yet self-destructive character, addiction flattening his talent and leading to his exile from the music business. Stewart’s last quarter century was spent hiding from the world with Mary Lou in a Florida trailer home with blacked-out windows, taking drugs.Ashburn maintains that it didn’t seen abnormal at the time. “The only thing I resented was not being allowed to have sleepovers. I did have one of my girlfriends over once, and then dad OD’d. The ambulance was called and she started panicking and I was like: don’t worry, this happens all the time! But she called her mom to come and collect her …” Ashburn laughs in disbelief at what was her daily reality. “Once when dad was on tour my mom OD’d and I had to drive her to the hospital – I was only 12!”View image in fullscreenFamous fans … Tammy Wynette, Gary, Mary Lou and Willie Nelson in the mid-70s.Photograph: Shannon Ashburn collectionStewart and Mary Lou Taylor met when he was 16 and she 21. They shared an appetite for wild, destructive hedonism. As well as the drugs there were car wrecks, guns, knives, infidelities and mental illness. In his biography, McDonough sees the pair as exemplars of a white working class who swapped Kentucky’s hills for Florida’s coast – and moonshine for cocaine.Stewart’s addictions ended his run on the country charts. He had an opportunity to start afresh after McDonough sought out the reclusive singer in 1987 and wrote an 11,000-word profile for the Village Voice. It briefly resurrected Stewart’s career, and he signed to Californian indie label HighTone Records the following year and released three new albums. Yet these failed to match Stewart’s best RCA recordings. His voice sounded worn-down, his energy dissipated – and the interest around his return soon faded.‘I put a raging dent in Neil Young’s forehead!’ Tim Pope on his riotous videos for the Cure, Bowie, Queen, Soft Cell and moreRead moreWhy did a musician who once sounded so furiously alive choose to stupefy his senses? No one has an explanation, beyond the fact that Stewart just loved to get high. “People were rooting for Gary to make a successful comeback,” says McDonough, “but by then he didn’t really care.” Dea once wryly observed that “you get hooked on Stewart … he’s like a damn drug” – yet drugs snuffed out Stewart’s own spark.The darkness that enmeshed Gary and Mary Lou would end up overwhelming their family with the couple’s son Joey taking his own life in 1988, aged 25, depression and family dysfunction having been contributing factors. Ashburn says that it was when her parents started taking the opioid painkiller OxyContin that “things really spun out of control”. She says: “Gary was first prescribed it after he broke his leg in a car crash, and they didn’t know it was so addictive.” After being raised by addicts, and later enduring her own struggle with addiction, Ashburn is now helping others who are dependent on drugs.View image in fullscreenIn his Fort Pierce lair … Stewart in the 1970s.Photograph: Grandal StewartThe necessity of earning a living occasionally forced Stewart to venture outside the trailer to perform, and on a good night he could still leave audiences howling. “Dad loved playing honky-tonks and juke joints,” says Ashburn, “down-home places where people came to dance to his music. He’d tasted stardom, played arenas and didn’t like it – he liked the funky, backwoods places. And people loved him. In Texas he was a legend, could pull 2,000 to Billy Bob’s in Fort Worth.”Stewart also commanded a loyal following on Indian reservations; McDonough believes this is because “Native Americans live a hard life and, in Gary, they heard someone who sang of that life. There was nothing fake about him.”Mary Lou died on 26 November 2003. A despondent Stewart killed himself three weeks later. “They were Bonnie and Clyde, Romeo and Juliet,” says Ashburn. “One couldn’t live without the other.” Few noted Stewart’s death at the time but Ashburn never stopped believing her father’s music would again be recognised. “I’m determined to get Gary into theCountryMusic Hall of Fame,” she says. “With Jimmy’s book, the Delmore album of his demos and Sony finally putting some of his RCA albums up on streaming services, things are looking up. I have so many great recordings of him that I’d love to share with the world, because Gary Stewart was unique.”Gary Stewart: I Am from the Honky Tonks is published by Wolf & Salmon, £34.99In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgThis article was amended on 17 August 2026. An earlier version unintentionally included an embedded image of Gary Stewart that had been manipulated by being horizontally flipped; this has been replaced with the original.Explore more on these topicsCountryBob DylanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 25 Years in Afghanistan review – the extraordinary life of an optimist | Television | The Guardian
description: Mir Hussain has been followed by TV cameras since he was a child, and managed to deliver love and laughter alongside his struggle. Now his previous Bafta-winning documentary gets an update
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Mir Hussain has been followed by TV cameras since he was a child, and managed to deliver love and laughter alongside his struggle. Now his previous Bafta-winning documentary gets an update
Content: Mir Hussein, as a child, in the original documentary, My Childhood, My Country – 20 Years in Afghanistan.Photograph: ITVView image in fullscreenMir Hussein, as a child, in the original documentary, My Childhood, My Country – 20 Years in Afghanistan.Photograph: ITVTV reviewTelevisionReview25 Years in Afghanistan review – the extraordinary life of an optimistMir Hussain has been followed by TV cameras since he was a child, and managed to deliver love and laughter alongside his struggle. Now his previous Bafta-winning documentary gets an updatePhil HarrisonSun 16 Aug 2026 20.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMir Hussain remembers the first time he saw a video camera: “I looked at it and it looked straight back at me.” His relationship with this all-seeing eye has broadened and deepened in the years that followed. Since 2002, when Phil Grabsky and Shoaib Sharifi first started documenting his story, Mir has lived an extraordinary life: grinding poverty and impossibly hard work, eking out a living in the mountainous Bamiyan province and then in urbanAfghanistan, but combined with a remarkable level of exposure to the world, via modern media.Mir and his family first appeared on our screens in 2021, in the Bafta-winning film My Childhood, My Country – 20 Years in Afghanistan. This updated reversioning of that film contains plenty of the same footage but also, in a telling update, hits very differently in the light of what happened that year. In April 2021, US president Joe Biden announced the withdrawal of American soldiers from Afghanistan. Essentially, the US (and their allies, including Britain) abandoned the country to the Taliban extremists. The knowledge of this incipient horror looms unavoidably large; the whole film now feels like foreshadowing.“This is the story of my country,” says Mir. “A country that, despite everything, I love.” As even casual students of modern history will know, the word “everything” is doing a lot of work in that sentence – Afghanistan’s recent history has included invasions and occupations by Russia and America, and military engagements with other countries in the region, too. Afghanistan has gained a reputation for being unconquerable, but it’s tragic that every decade or so, someone still feels the need to test this.This documentary offers an insight into life at the sharp end. Mir is a bright kid, but he often misses school because he has to plough the fields, or drive his family’s donkeys or work down a coalmine. He’s remarkably ebullient as a child: “We lived in a cave. It was quite good fun.” All the time, American planes fly overhead and the family gaze at them, hoping they might represent salvation and progress. The grim, hardscrabble details of their lives are interspersed with the airy pledges of politicians including George W Bush, Tony Blair, David Cameron, Barack Obama and Donald Trump. In this new film, every public proclamation by a foreign leader feels like pitch-rolling for the betrayal we know is coming. Meanwhile, the poverty gets worse. “I never thought I’d end up eating grass,” says Mir’s mother, Murwarid. The footage is extraordinary – as intimate a depiction of a family in extremis as you can imagine.Eventually, Mir marries a woman called Shukria, starts a family and moves to Mazar-i-Sharif – and, when he can’t find work there, on to Kabul. Nothing doing there either. Then, in what should be the film’s central twist, he has a brainwave. “I grew up being filmed,” he says. “So I asked the film-makers if they could help me.” There’s a subtle, entirely understandable bending of the rules of documentary making here. Should the directors be altering the trajectory of the story they are telling? But if they have the ability to help, how could refusing be morally justified? And in any case, doesn’t their constant presence in Mir’s life mean they are influencing it anyway?Soon, Mir is a camera operator. The film-makers find him work in Kabul and the story gains a dimension. Now, Mir is its subject and, in another context, a professional observer himself. He turns out to be brave and resourceful, specialising in recording the aftermath of suicide bombings. He also diversifies into filming live sport. In a less turbulent country than Afghanistan, we’d be glancing tentatively in the direction of a happy ending.But no – in 2021, the western forces rolled out and the Taliban rolled back in. For women in particular, life became brutally circumscribed by religious dogma. Fittingly, therefore, in the parts of the documentary recorded in 2026, Shukria is given more space to speak for herself. The couple have had a fourth child, a girl. Shukria regrets this. Mir’s television work has dried up and he’s been forced to return to manual labour. Her husband “doesn’t think that deeply” about anything much, she says. “Mir has gone backwards. He has no plans.” As postscripts go, it’s incredibly sad. Even in their moments of greatest adversity, Mir and Shukria always kept a twinkle in their eyes. But now, the couple seem hesitant and lost. “We are all stuck in this backwardness,” says Shukria.Right from the start, when it was documenting a small, instinctively cheerful boy and his embattled family, this film managed to sidestep grinding misery. It was geopolitics writ cleverly small, but love and laughter were able to find their place alongside struggle. Throughout, there’s something undeniable about Mir: he has a remarkable capacity for optimism. For that reason, this 25th anniversary update casts a darker shadow altogether. From the moment Mir Hussain first looked at a video camera, he’s been central to a remarkable story. Let’s hope it’s not quite over yet – and that any future instalments might have a happier tale to tell.25 Years in Afghanistan aired on ITV1 and is available on ITVXExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVAfghanistanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Taiwan Season: The Wall review – close encounters in a city that never sleeps | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Seed Dance Company deliver a show that builds in intensity as it riffs on imprisonment and estrangement
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Seed Dance Company deliver a show that builds in intensity as it riffs on imprisonment and estrangement
Content: Silvery shades … Hsing-Yu Chen and Yu Chung in The Wall.Photograph: Chih Peng Lucas KaoView image in fullscreenSilvery shades … Hsing-Yu Chen and Yu Chung in The Wall.Photograph: Chih Peng Lucas KaoEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTaiwan Season: The Wall review – close encounters in a city that never sleepsSummerhall, EdinburghSeed Dance Company deliver a show that builds in intensity as it riffs on imprisonment and estrangementChris WiegandMon 17 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaiwan’sSeed Dance Companyvisited the fringe in 2024 with a rather literal yet haunting show about smartphone addiction,Lost Connection. This similarly coolly executed piece could share the same title as its predecessor but is more enigmatic. It makes use of two box-like, occasionally illuminated apparatus which are modified during the show to resemble apartments and various confines. The cast are repeatedly isolated from each other despite their close proximity on the thrust stage – one questing solo is delivered beneath another dancer on the roof, while one is in the room next door.There is a busy urban and sometimes uncanny anonymity to these restless vignettes, accentuated by an electronic accompaniment, with the dancers – including choreographer and artistic director Wen-Jen Huang – sharing silvery highlights in their hair and wearing similar shirts and trousers in subdued shades. In unison, they can bring the automated air of the commute, making a counterpoint to one aching duet choreographed with a behind-closed-doors tenderness.View image in fullscreenBehind closed doors … Kapitjuan Kadrangian and Wen-Jen Huang in The Wall.Photograph: Chih Peng Lucas KaoClambering over the bars of the set brings an inevitable acrobatic air but even that movement is carefully restrained rather than flamboyant. The performers also form walls with their bodies, whether alone or accompanied, facing off against each other.I Made You a Mixtape review – frothy fringe fun as dorm mates party like it’s 1999Read moreThese 45 minutes build in intensity, the set seeming at first cumbersome – and sometimes distracting from the dance when the structures are being reconfigured. The apparatus can be used to liberating effect, offering an assortment of micro-stages, but often suggests imprisonment. Dancers don’t bounce off the walls but rather melt into them.The show ends with a forlorn and otherworldly solo, performed inside two clingfilm-wrapped frames forming a tunnel. As Hsing-Yu Chen presses against her surroundings, the impression is of how little divides us but how hard it can be to break through.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026DanceTheatreSummerhallEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Brandon Flowers: Thrasher review – Killers frontman’s country pivot is a rootin’ tootin’ cowboy-bootin’ hoot! | Brandon Flowers | The Guardian
description: Even a couple of bafflingly misguided social commentary songs can’t detract from the joys of Flowers’ classically full-throated commitment to the Nashville bit
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Even a couple of bafflingly misguided social commentary songs can’t detract from the joys of Flowers’ classically full-throated commitment to the Nashville bit
Content: Never does anything by halves … Brandon Flowers.View image in fullscreenNever does anything by halves … Brandon Flowers.Brandon FlowersReviewBrandon Flowers: Thrasher review – Killers frontman’s country pivot is a rootin’ tootin’ cowboy-bootin’ hoot!(Island)Even a couple of bafflingly misguided social commentary songs can’t detract from the joys of Flowers’ classically full-throated commitment to the Nashville bitShaad D'SouzaMon 17 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere are three immutable facts about Brandon Richard Flowers: he was born just outside Las Vegas, Nevada. He is 45 years old. And he never does anything by halves. When he and his band the Killers debuted in the early 2000s, as disaffected New York cool was on the rise, he was writing scream-along choruses sung in his upper register. When the Killers were searching for a sound even bigger and grander than the euphoric Springsteen pastiche of 2006’s Sam’s Town, they didn’t think twice before recruiting Stuart Price to produce the spangly 2008 disco-rock record Day & Age.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Thrasher.That’s how you get a record like Thrasher. Flowers’ third solo album finds Vegas’s chosen son decamping to Nashville for a full-throated exploration of country music – not subtle, trendy Americana, but rip-snorting, honky-tonking, Nudie suit-wearing country. In many ways, Thrasher is a stylistic follow-up to the Killers’ maudlin 2021 Pressure Machine, which saw Flowers explore windswept balladry and tasteful story-songs. But that record was as forgettable as Thrasher is a hoot; Flowers wilts when he doesn’t fully commit, as was the case on Pressure Machine, and he doesn’t make that mistake here. Thrasher features many of Nashville’s most revered country musicians, including pedal steel legend Bruce Bouton, 85-year-old harmonica player Charlie McCoy, Gillian Welch’s musical partner Dave Rawlings and lauded Americana musician Margo Price.This deep bench doesn’t obscure Flowers’ oddball tendencies. On rollicking opener Does It Ever Cross Your Mind?, he writes like a man who’s done his 10,000 hours absorbing pop music cliches and now feels equipped to write his own. “I could’ve been born in Bangladesh / But I wasn’t, I was born here / With just enough jellybeans in my basket / To ask you to go a’wishing on a star,” he sings, injecting his nonsense with such gravitas and moxie that it’s easy to believe that’s something people say.Brandon Flowers: Paradise (Live From Historic RCA Studio A) – videoThose weird turns of phrase invigorate Thrasher’s many character studies. Tiger’s Blood would be good-but-ordinary Springsteen pastiche, with its repeated refrain of “like a runaway train”, but Flowers makes this story of a “cheerleader working the till [who] wants to get outta this podunk place” his own with weird, specific images – of “peach-fuzz boys getting hard in the corner on Mortal Kombat” and a “swamp cooler leaking down the bricks outside”. Especially great is all the idiosyncratic detail on closer An American Dream, its universal-sounding title concealing seemingly the most surreal song on Thrasher. As it builds, Flowers stacks evocative image upon evocative image: “A Guinness World Record holder / For the longest fall living”; “Elvis in a Tesla Model X”; “lights that flicker on hubcap chrome.”As on Pressure Machine, Flowers takes a couple of big swings, both of them misses. On Miss America, he writes from the perspective of a young woman in an abusive relationship. Although this is something of a pet topic for Flowers, he is not a particularly elegant writer; amid all the salacious euphemisms for abuse, he sings things like: “Truth be told / Grown men have noticed me since I was 12 years old / It always made me feel like some kind of prize / I guess I saw my worth through their porno eyes.” But even that feels graceful in comparison to Angel. There’s no way to sugarcoat it: Angel is a song about a talented Black baseball player who starts dating a white girl. Angel and the girl have a daughter, and Angel is deployed to be in the navy, after which he abandons his wife and kid to become a drug smuggler. The song ends with Angel being pulled over by the cops and attempting to evade them on foot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia TaitRead moreIt’s impossible to comprehend how Flowers thought this song was a good idea. When Angel and his girlfriend have their baby, he sings the lines “Chocolate and vanilla swirls / There’s gonna be a little girl”. Flowers supposedly wrote more than 30 songs for the record, meaning there were at least 20 alternatives. The place Flowers lands – “It don’t matter how far you’ve come / Or how well you ran the race / You’re gonna have to come face to face / With that thing you’ve always known to be true / That you buried inside of you” – could be a critique of American racial hegemony, or it could be flat-out racist, implying that our fates are hardwired. I strongly suspect that it’s an attempt at the former, but that it could feasibly be taken either way is an indictment in itself.Flowers has always had occasional bouts of foot-in-mouth – this simply feels like a particularly bad one. A big part of Angel’s failure is that it is one of the few genuinely dull songs on the album – plodding and dirgey, with an attempt at a pathos-drenched chorus that has little of the spark or fleet-footedness of the rest of the album. Although it lacks the attention-grabbing singles of 2015’s The Desired Effect, Flowers’ last solo record, Thrasher is front-to-back a far stronger, more enjoyable album that could even win over fans who haven’t tapped in since Mr Brightside. The westernwear suits him.Explore more on these topicsBrandon FlowersThe KillersPop and rockCountryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour review – fringe gem leaves you ecstatic | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Connor Dariol, AKA Australian clown Conk, does exactly what he claims – and with such skill and relentless pep we are helpless to resist
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Connor Dariol, AKA Australian clown Conk, does exactly what he claims – and with such skill and relentless pep we are helpless to resist
Content: We are all involved by the end … Australian clown Conk in Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour.Photograph: Madeline RoyceView image in fullscreenWe are all involved by the end … Australian clown Conk in Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour.Photograph: Madeline RoyceEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMan Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour review – fringe gem leaves you ecstaticSummerhall, EdinburghConnor Dariol, AKA Australian clown Conk, does exactly what he claims – and with such skill and relentless pep we are helpless to resistBrian LoganMon 17 Aug 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 12.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I saw the title to the Australian clown Conk’s show Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour, I thought I knew what the trick would be. Yes, the terms of the show’s billing would be fulfilled, but (I imagined) by twisting whatever that song was into a diverting variety of new shapes – rather as the comedy trio Sheeps did when performing the same sketch repeatedly for an hourway back in 2014.More fool me, for doubting that Conk – AKA Connor Dariol – would keep things as ruthlessly simple as his Ronseal title suggests. He really does sing the same song over and again, with the same backing track and surprisingly little embellishment, for 60 minutes – with a bloody great clock marking the limits of your endurance on an upstage screen. And wait until you hear what song it is! Its opening chords are greeted by an aghast laugh from the audience. Reader, this experience felt like an endurance test before that song had reached the end of its first cycle.Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughRead moreOne recalls with unease that the US military tortured people during the “war on terror” by playing bad songs at them over and again. So how does Conk fashion this experiment in patience-testing into one of the most joyful hours in town? It’s a subtle process. His near-relentless pep is part of it. Then, he starts throwing the odd anxious glance at the clock:how longis there still to go?! It’s not till the fourth or fifth performance that he modulates the delivery of the lyrics, putting a suddenly funny spin on the singer’s relationship to the story the song tells.We’re deep into the second half before he really cuts loose, and even then his wilder antics usually remain tethered to the truth of this deeply ridiculous song, now performed in a sinister whisper or while posed scantily-clad on a chair. Without the show ever having coerced us – call it Stockholm syndrome – we’re all involved by the end, Conk’s exercise in absurdist perseverance devolving into the most ecstatic communal experience I’ve shared at this year’s fringe.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreSummerhallComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lara Ricote: Inkling review – this fizzy standup’s smart new set is her best yet | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A show about maturing and learning to listen to life’s signals doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and has some great gags
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A show about maturing and learning to listen to life’s signals doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and has some great gags
Content: Great command … Lara Ricote performing at Monkey Barrel Comedy.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenGreat command … Lara Ricote performing at Monkey Barrel Comedy.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLara Ricote: Inkling review – this fizzy standup’s smart new set is her best yetMonkey Barrel Comedy, EdinburghA show about maturing and learning to listen to life’s signals doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and has some great gagsBrian LoganMon 17 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 11.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat a rich and enjoyable show this is fromLara Ricote, a leap forwards from her already-excellentfirst two shows. It finds the Mexican-American comic in as endearing fettle as ever, her urge to communicate bubbling over in a show about divining the messages life puts your way, however indecipherable they (like this show) can sometimes appear.It begins at the oracle at Delphi, with a hymn to belief over rationalism. “This is a show about mystery and messages,” says Ricote, and if we only understand 65% of it, that need be no bar to our appreciation. And there’s truth in that – I often felt I was chasing along in the show’s slipstream. It flits and fizzes between narrative strands, Ricote abstracting her voice into burbling, and blurting water over herself, for (at least at first) minimal apparent reason.View image in fullscreenFinding herself … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThere is reason, but it’s up to us make the connections, while Ricote recounts the end of a long-term relationship, and the beginning of a friendship with another comic who, like her, is hard of hearing. How does that condition relate to her sense of two-thirds understanding as the golden mean? And why is she so down on sign language? A further encounter, in which a man tries to discuss a painting with her in a museum, dramatises her interest in the signals life sends us, and her (and our) difficulty in always perceiving them.Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughRead moreRicote weaves these sections with great command (“blackout!”), but also a goofy amusement at her presumption in doing so. This show about maturing doesn’t stint on tomfoolery and great jokes – see Ricote deploying her whole body to imitate “split-tongue guy”, or the very funny establishing shot she performs to evoke New York City. But Inkling also lets us watch her grow up as if in real time, as her confidence grows in interpreting the world for herself, and as she inches towards a fuller embrace of her hard-of-hearing identity. The sense, and it’s an exciting one, is both of a person finding themselves, and an artist too.AtMonkey Barrel Comedy, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laugh | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: There are shades of Vic and Bob as well as Frank Sidebottom when this embittered git with bloodshot eyes holds court
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: There are shades of Vic and Bob as well as Frank Sidebottom when this embittered git with bloodshot eyes holds court
Content: Fantastic joke-writing … Sam Eley as Basil Crumbwick.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFantastic joke-writing … Sam Eley as Basil Crumbwick.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughMonkey Barrel, EdinburghThere are shades of Vic and Bob as well as Frank Sidebottom when this embittered git with bloodshot eyes holds courtBrian LoganMon 17 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery room in Edinburgh has its ghosts, and its particular character. This one is all about the late-night cult hits, from Rob Kemp’sEvil Dead-meets-Elvis mashupnine years ago toJoe Kent-Walters’ debut as Frankie Monroe– a character whom this year’s cult-in-waiting, Sam Eley as Basil Crumbwick, slightly resembles.Crumbwick is Eley with a giant papier-mache head on, an unreconstructed git with bulging bloodshot eyes and strips of carpet for what is left of his hair. He’s an unlikely candidate to be addressing us all in a cellar at an arts festival. But, having been banned from all his favourite Peterborough pubs, what’s a big-headed old bigot to do?You might have misgivings about trapping yourself in a dungeon with this unlovely an outlook, and with a character who, like Frankie Monroe, screams at you if you step out of line. Nor can I claim new trails are being blazed by an act who brings to mind Vic and Bob or (obviously)Frank Sidebottombefore them. The show is conventionally assembled, as Basil rants about his “rat” of a neighbour, Beverly, ruminates on the relative merits of having sex with or eating a pig, and reads extracts from a self-help guide he’s written – which offers reveries about visiting the Playboy mansion as a solution to all your mental health ills.View image in fullscreenHow about a visit to the Playboy mansion? … Sam Eley as Basil Crumbwick.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianNo denying the illicit thrill of his off-colour pontificating – even if one wonders whether we’re mocking the character’s bigotry here, or indulging it. Of course, Eley clarifies that Basil’s opinions are those of a lonely and embittered old cove, trying and failing to befriend his bin man. And there’s more to the character than a dyspeptic worldview. It’s all richer and stranger than that: see the Treason for Beginners class he teaches at his local church.Joseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70 review – a dork’s last day at school is one to rememberRead moreBut really, the character, and our experience, is redeemed by Eley’s fantastic joke-writing, which guarantees laugh after unexpected laugh as Basil comes to miss his departing nemesis Beverly, and Eley sweats to near-death under his prosthetic head. An arresting new comedy alter ego is born, another late-night cult hit assured.AtMonkey Barrel, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I Made You a Mixtape review – frothy fringe fun as dorm mates party like it’s 1999 | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Nine college students fall out and make up as they dance to punk-pop and alt-rock in this lively show
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Nine college students fall out and make up as they dance to punk-pop and alt-rock in this lively show
Content: Infectious … I Made You a MixtapeView image in fullscreenInfectious … I Made You a MixtapeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewI Made You a Mixtape review – frothy fringe fun as dorm mates party like it’s 1999TheSpace Triplex, EdinburghNine college students fall out and make up as they dance to punk-pop and alt-rock in this lively showLyndsey WinshipMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 02.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is such a festival show: uncategorisable, buzzing, slightly chaotic and unlike anything else. As director Christie Lee Manning of ResponseTheatreCompany tells us at the outset, I Made You a Mixtape is not a play, not a musical, not (really) a dance show, even though it is pretty much only dance all the way through, plus some hand-written captions. But it’s the kind of dance that real people do – or how you’d like to think you could dance, especially if you were nine girls at a college dorm party somewhere in North America in the 1990s, which is the setting here.The show fully embraces nostalgia from the off: camcorder, cassette tapes, the Friends board game, Sporty Spice’s wardrobe, and a pop-punk, alt-rock soundtrack (Blink-182, No Doubt, Red Hot Chili Peppers – not the Britpop/trip-hop 1990s of the UK), with live drums and guitar to make it all the more visceral.View image in fullscreenThe kind of dance that real people do … I Made You a Mixtape.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockWhether it’s the music of your youth or not, what’s universal, and infectious, is the palpable sense of possibility among these young women about to set out in the world, on the brink of all the good things to come. It’s the beautiful time where it feels like life is yours for the taking (maybe the 90s felt more like that than today). You can go wild because you feel safe, and the giddy energy is frothing like that bottle of Dr Pepper they’ve got on the snack table. The girls feed on music and friendship, they hug and cry and fall out and make up, and sway to songs, mouthing words with faraway eyes or punch out lyrics; all that pure joy and hope lived out through moving your body to music.They each have their own physical signature: Latin dance, waacking, hip-hop, straight off MTV, but together they add up to more than that – that’s female friendship all over. We’re introduced to the women and told that after tonight each will have a different path. Some of this plays out within the songs, but there’s a real missed opportunity to make the emotional life of the piece sing and so much more could be made of the characters and inner drama.
