With a bit more intention it could be a CoverGirl mascara-down-the-face tearjerker as well as just a good party.AttheSpace Triplex, Edinburgh, until 29 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalDanceTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She never forgot where she came from’: Bonnie Tyler mourners turn out for Swansea service | Bonnie Tyler | The Guardian
description: Many in the crowd watching on screen outside minster have stories of meeting or knowing singer, who died in July
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Many in the crowd watching on screen outside minster have stories of meeting or knowing singer, who died in July
Content: A floral arrangement spells out the singer’s name outside Swansea Minster.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA floral arrangement spells out the singer’s name outside Swansea Minster.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianBonnie Tyler‘She never forgot where she came from’: Bonnie Tyler mourners turn out for Swansea serviceMany in the crowd watching on screen outside minster have stories of meeting or knowing singer, who died in JulyBethan McKernanWales correspondentMon 17 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBonnie Tyler’s songs have echoed through her home town of Swansea in recent days in memory of the late singer, but on Monday the church bells stopped and wellwishers lining the streets fell silent as her coffin arrived for a service celebrating her life.As the white coffin, covered in bouquets of white roses, was carried into the minster, shouts of “God bless you Bonnie” and “bye Bonnie” punctured the quiet. Those gathered to pay their respects burst into applause. Tyler’s If I Sing You a Love Song and It’s a Heartache played before the private service began, which mourners outside watched on a screen in nearby St David’s Square.View image in fullscreenThe service was broadcast in St David’s Square.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianTheTotal Eclipse of the Heartsinger, whose real name was Gaynor Hopkins, split her time between Mumbles, in a house overlooking Swansea Bay, and the Algarve. She died aged 75 in July in hospital in Portugal after a period of ill health and is survived by her husband of 53 years, Robert Sullivan.The couple were well known in the area, and many people the Guardian spoke to on Monday had met Tyler or knew her personally. Mourners began arriving from 7.30am for the noon service, bringing camping chairs and supplies, with some having travelled from as far away as Germany and Austria.“We went to a few parties at the Mumbles house, they were wonderful. There was karaoke, performances,” said Allyson Thomas, 58, whose partner played in a band with Tyler’s brother. “As we got in the taxi home, Bonnie handed us some champagne for the journey home. She was really special, she was so down to earth and a star at the same time.”View image in fullscreenAllyson Thomas (left) with friends.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianTyler grew up as one of six children in a musical family in a council house in Skewen, a village north-east ofSwansea. A “painfully shy” teenager, she started gaining confidence at 17 after singing and coming second in a local rugby club talent competition. “After that, she never looked back,” Roger Bell, the talent scout who discovered the singer, said in his tribute during Monday’s service.Sandra Bartlett, 63, from nearby Port Talbot, said she knew Sullivan during his days as a Swansea nightclub manager, and her ex-husband had been friendly with the couple. “We went out to the first house she had in Portugal and they were great hosts,” she said.“Gaynor was lovely, always ready for a chat or a gossip. She went from strength to strength as she got older, she was still performing a lot. I think it says a lot about her that she came home to Skewen. It’s not like she was from a big place like London or something. Now Bobby’s brought her home for the last time.”View image in fullscreenThe Cash family: Bill, Billy and Jane.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianThe Cash family said they had met Tyler a few times in Swansea’s shopping centre and Debenhams, when the singer was out with her mother. “She never forgot where she came from and she was proud of where she’s from,” said Bill, 50, who had come to pay his respects with his wife, Jane, 49, and son Billy, 11.Among several events in and around Swansea to mark Tyler’s passing, fans were invited to watch the procession as the singer’s coffin, wrapped in a Welsh flag, travelled to her home in Mumbles on Saturday, and again after the service at Swansea Minster as the hearse made its final journey to Tyler’s home village of Skewen.One onlooker in Skewen said: “I wouldn’t come out for the king. Half the people here wouldn’t.”View image in fullscreenThe coffin at Swansea Minster.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianThe singer achieved international fame in 1983 when Total Eclipse of the Heart shot to the top of the charts in the UK and the US. Recognisable for her husky voice, Tyler’s other hits include Holding Out for a Hero, It’s a Heartache and If You Were a Woman (and I Was a Man).She represented the UK in the 2013 Eurovision song contest and was still touring internationally, releasing records and active in charity work before she died.View image in fullscreenBonnie Tyler in 2013.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian“I class myself as a working-class girl, and I’ve never stopped working,” Tylertold the Guardian in 2013. “I do an awful lot [of performances] because I feel other people would love to be offered what I’m offered.”Ki Wodehouse, 26, from Clydach, said: “Bonnie was an amazing ambassador forWales. Wales gets forgotten about even in the rest of the UK, so for someone from here to get that level of recognition is a rare thing.”Explore more on these topicsBonnie TylerSwanseaWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Next year’s Eurovision host is Burgas, not Sofia. Some Bulgarians are baffled | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Next year’s competition won’t take place in the country’s capital, an announcement that even surprised Bulgarian winner, Dara
Author: Eden Maclachlan
Headline: Next year’s competition won’t take place in the country’s capital, an announcement that even surprised Bulgarian winner, Dara
Content: All systems go … Burgas flies the flag for Bulgaria’s Eurovision Song Contest.Photograph: Valentina Petrova/APView image in fullscreenAll systems go … Burgas flies the flag for Bulgaria’s Eurovision Song Contest.Photograph: Valentina Petrova/APEurovisionNext year’s Eurovision host is Burgas, not Sofia. Some Bulgarians are baffledNext year’s competition won’t take place in the country’s capital, an announcement that even surprised Bulgarian winner, DaraEden Maclachlanin SofiaMon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver since Bulgarian singer Dara was crownedwinner of the Eurovision song contest this May, it has been clear that the Balkan nation would for the first time in its history have the opportunity to host Europe’s biggest party.So when Bulgarian officialsannounced last weekthat the world’s largest live music event in 2027 will be held not in the capital Sofia but in Burgas, a Black Sea port city home to 200,000 people, it came as a surprise – even to last year’s winner.“I am really surprised,” singer Dara told the Guardian. “I think that BNT [Bulgarian National Television] will do a great job at producing the whole show. I trust them completely. If they decided Burgas, then probably Burgas is better.”This spring in Vienna, Dara became the first Bulgarian to win Eurovision with her high energy party anthemBangaranga, in an edition boycotted byIreland, Spain, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Icelandover Israel’s participation.Following her victory, Bulgaria’s four largest cities, Sofia, Plovdiv, Dara’s home town of Varna and Burgas sent an application with only Sofia and Burgas left as possible candidates in recent weeks. As the country’s capital and international hub, Sofia always seemed the obvious choice.View image in fullscreen‘If they decided Burgas, then Burgas is probably better’ … Eurovision winner Dara.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe preference for Burgas, Bulgaria’s fourth largest city, has been heavily discussed across the Balkan country of 6.5 million people, with many taken aback.“We were surprised, because Sofia has the biggest arena,” said Pavel Stefanov, 29, an air traffic controller at Sofia airport.Milena Ouzounova, 54, a designer from Sofia said she was surprised and disappointed that the capital wasn’t chosen as host city and was sceptical over Burgas’ capacity to pull off such an event.“I’m disappointed,” she said. “I think Sofia is a better place, it is bigger, we have a big arena. Burgas is a nice place but I am not sure it could be prepared enough after one year. I think the space is much smaller in Burgas.”View image in fullscreenDiffering views … Katrin Ninova, left, is relieved Sofia will avoid Eurovision mayhem, while Milena Ouzounova, right, thinks it would be better in Sofia, as the city is bigger.Composite: Eden MaclachlanLocated on the southern Black Sea coast, approximately 400km east of Sofia, Burgas is closer in distance to Istanbul than the Bulgarian capital.Nestled among three lakes and the Black Sea, it has an established tourism industry and is a popular seaside destination among Bulgarian and international tourists. Meanwhile, it is home to Bulgaria’s second largest port and the largest oil refinery in southernEurope, accounting for a considerable chunk of the city’s industrial production.Earlier this year, it hosted the arrival of the first stage of the 2026 Giro d’Italia, the Italian equivalent to the Tour de France, and hosting Eurovision will most likely boost Burgas candidacy forEuropean Capital of Culture in 2032.Preparations to host the Eurovision grand final have already started aroundArena Burgas, the 15,000 concert capacity hall completed in 2023 which will have the herculean task of throwing Europe’s favourite party, while the city’s airport said it is ready to welcome the increased passenger flow for Eurovision 2027.The accompanyingEurovisionevents will be in the centre of Burgas and the Sea Garden, the city’s biggest public park directly facing the Black Sea, where locals usually gather to hang out or have a drink.View image in fullscreenReady to welcome big audiences … port view, Burgas.Photograph: Valentina Petrova/APHowever, it isn’t the smallest city to ever arrange Eurovision, still considerably bigger than Harrogate, which hosted it in 1982 following Bucks Fizz’s victory.The Eurovision final will take place on 15 May, with the semi-finals on 11 and 13 May and will have Canada participating for the first time. Meanwhile new rules will be implemented such as increasing the minimum participation age from 16 to 18 and potentially barring countries involved in armed conflicts from hosting.Many in Bulgaria believe this to be the perfect opportunity to showcase the beauty of the Bulgarian coast and boost tourism, while others are thankful it won’t be organised in Sofia.Dimitar Nikolov, mayor of Burgas, said he was honoured that Burgas was chosen and thanked BNT and the EBU [European Broadcasting Union] “for the unique chance to present the beauties of Bulgaria and, through Burgas, to all the guests and fans who will follow the live broadcast to feel Bulgaria.”Prime ministerRumen Radevtold local reporters that he believed Burgas will succeed in representing Bulgaria with dignity.“I think that every Bulgarian city has something to offer both in terms of culture and history, especially in terms of people and modern services. So let’s present ourselves with dignity. I think that Burgas is a really good choice,” he said.Katrin Ninova, 20, a data science student at the Sofia University said she was relieved that Sofia will avoid Eurovision mayhem. “It’s crowded enough here. We don’t need to organise Eurovision,” she said.Evtim Vodenicharov, 32, a data manager from Burgas said he was thrilled that his home town would be organising the event and believed that it will boost the region’s economy and tourism. Meanwhile, he hopes to attend next year’s Eurovision in the arena.“Of course I’m excited,” said Vodenicharov. “I hope I will be able to get a ticket and go watch it live instead of being at home and watching it on TV. It’s in my home town.”Meanwhile Dara urged visitors who will attend Eurovision to take the opportunity to visit Bulgaria, the Black Sea coast and discover the unique culture of the Balkan country.“We should look at all of the positive sides. I think people should go to the seaside and all around Burgas, there are really good places,” she said.Explore more on these topicsEurovisionEurovision 2026BulgariaEuropeAwards and prizesPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beatles film recreates iconic Abbey Road album cover | Movies | The Guardian
description: Social media footage this weekend revealed the cast of Sam Mendes’ four-film band biopic on the zebra crossing near the studio, posing for the famous image
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Social media footage this weekend revealed the cast of Sam Mendes’ four-film band biopic on the zebra crossing near the studio, posing for the famous image
Content: All you need is hair … Harris Dickinson, Barry Keoghan, Paul Mescal and Joseph Quinn filming in Abbey Road, LondonPhotograph: MCPIX/JBURNSView image in fullscreenAll you need is hair … Harris Dickinson, Barry Keoghan, Paul Mescal and Joseph Quinn filming in Abbey Road, LondonPhotograph: MCPIX/JBURNSMoviesBeatles film recreates iconic Abbey Road album coverSocial media footage this weekend revealed the cast of Sam Mendes’ four-film band biopic on the zebra crossing near the studio, posing for the famous imageAndrew PulverMon 17 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 17.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe production team behind the forthcoming four-film Beatles biopic, directed bySam Mendes, has been spotted filming outside Abbey Road studios in London; this included a recreation of the celebrated Abbey Road album cover, for which the band was photographed on the nearby pedestrian crossing – now a popular tourist landmark.Footage posted on social mediaon Sunday shows the actors playing the Beatles lining up on the kerb and walking across the road. Harris Dickinson, as John Lennon, is leading the walk, with Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr, Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney and Joseph Quinn as George Harrison following in sequence.View image in fullscreenThe fab four … Harris Dickinson (John Lennon), Paul Mescal (Paul McCartney), Barry Keoghan (Ringo Starr), and Joseph Quinn (George Harrison).Photograph: John Russo/Rex/ShutterstockThe Beatles recorded Abbey Road mostly in the summer of 1969, and thecover photo was taken on 8 Augustafter an initial idea to travel to Nepal for a photograph was abandoned. (The album’s working title was Everest, after a cigarette brand smoked by engineer Geoff Emerick.) Freelance photographer Iain Macmillan was commissioned to take the image, and took six stills from a stepladder positioned in the middle of the road – of which one was chosen.Mendes announced the project in February 2024– four films that each focus on an individual Beatle – with backing from Hollywood studio Sony Pictures and the permission of both McCartney and Starr, as well as from the estates of Lennon and Harrison. In addition to the actors playing the central roles, a host of major names have joined the cast, including Saoirse Ronan as Linda McCartney, James Norton as Brian Epstein and Lucy Boynton as Jane Asher.The films are due for release in April 2028.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe Beatles filmsSam MendesThe BeatlesLondonPaul MescalBarry KeoghannewsShareReuse this content

title: Johnny Depp in talks to return to Pirates of the Caribbean franchise  | Johnny Depp | The Guardian
description: The actor, who previously said he would not play Captain Jack Sparrow again for ‘$300m and a million alpacas’, is being lined up for sixth film in the series according to producer Jerry Bruckheimer
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: The actor, who previously said he would not play Captain Jack Sparrow again for ‘$300m and a million alpacas’, is being lined up for sixth film in the series according to producer Jerry Bruckheimer
Content: Johnny Depp as Jack Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (2011).Photograph: Peter Mountain/APView image in fullscreenJohnny Depp as Jack Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (2011).Photograph: Peter Mountain/APJohnny DeppJohnny Depp in talks to return to Pirates of the Caribbean franchiseThe actor, who previously said he would not play Captain Jack Sparrow again for ‘$300m and a million alpacas’, is being lined up for sixth film in the series according to producer Jerry BruckheimerLaurence PhelanMon 17 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohnny Depp is in talks to return as Captain Jack Sparrow in a sixth Pirates of the Caribbean film, according to the producer of the series, Jerry Bruckheimer. Bruckheimertold Deadline: “We’re talking with Johnny, we’re working on a screenplay, and hopefully we can get this done.” This is despite the actor having said under oath in 2022, during the notorious televised trial of the defamation case he brought against his ex-wife, Amber Heard, that Disney had dropped him from the series and he would not play Sparrow again even if he were offered “$300m and a million alpacas”.Depp first appeared as the charismatic, roguish, rum-swilling Captain Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl in 2003, and it has become his most recognisable – and profitable – role. Taking its name and golden age of piracy setting from a ride at the Disney World theme park, the swashbuckling adventure also featured Keira Knightley, Orlando Bloom and Geoffrey Rush, and grossed more than $650m (£480m) at the worldwide box office.Four sequels followed between 2006 and 2017, and it was the first franchise to produce two films that each made more than $1bn. The series has made more than $4.5bn in total. The most recent entry, Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, was released in 2017. Although reviews were not especially positive, it grossed almost $800m.However, Depp has had well-publicised legal issues since then, which have affected his career. The defamation trial against Heard in the US was preceded in 2020 by a libel lawsuit he brought in the UK after the Sun newspaper characterised him as a “wife-beater”;the court foundthe characterisation was “substantially true”. After this verdict, Depp wasasked by Warner Bros to resignfrom the Fantastic Beasts franchise, when shooting on a third film had already begun.The jury in the 2022 trialruled in Depp’s favour, finding that Heard had defamed her ex-husband in a Washington Post editorial in which she said she “became a public figure representing domestic abuse”.Depp subsequently played Louis XV in the 2023 French-language historical dramaJeanne du Barry, and voiced a puffin in the feature-length animation Johnny Puff: Secret Mission in 2024. But whether audiences will welcome him making a comeback as a major film star may be determined when he plays Scrooge inEbenezer, directed by Ti West, due to be released in the UK and US in November.Explore more on these topicsJohnny DeppPirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales (aka Salazar's Revenge)Action and adventure filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thom Yorke, Romy and Brian Eno among 200 musicians urging PM to reject new North Sea drilling | Oil | The Guardian
description: Robert Smith, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma also among signatories to letter saying exploitation of Rosebank and Jackdaw fields defies climate reality
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Robert Smith, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma also among signatories to letter saying exploitation of Rosebank and Jackdaw fields defies climate reality
Content: From left, Thom Yorke, Romy  from the XX and Brian Eno were among more than 200 musicians arguing against further North Sea drillingComposite: Getty Images and Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFrom left, Thom Yorke, Romy  from the XX and Brian Eno were among more than 200 musicians arguing against further North Sea drillingComposite: Getty Images and Jill Mead/The GuardianOilThom Yorke, Romy and Brian Eno among 200 musicians urging PM to reject new North Sea drillingRobert Smith, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma also among signatories to letter saying exploitation of Rosebank and Jackdaw fields defies climate realityBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaMon 17 Aug 2026 07.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 200 musicians including Massive Attack and Brian Eno have written toAndy Burnhamurging him to reject plans for more oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.The letter, signed by 211 artists such as Bobby Gillespie, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma, called on the prime minister to reject theRosebank oilfield, warning that the project would fail to lower energy bills or provide energy security as most of the oil was likely to be exported.Other performers who put their name to the missive include Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, Ed O’Brien and Philip Selway; the Cure’s Robert Smith; Bobby Gillespie of Primal Scream; Alexis Taylor of Hot Chip; Anoushka Shankar, Kevin Rowland, Anna Calvi, Jacob Collier, David Gray, the electronic duo Bicep and the xx singer Romy.The government’s consultation on the project, which lies about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands, closed on Monday. Ministers will now decide on its future as well as that of the Jackdaw gasfield off Aberdeen, whose consultation concluded a week ago.Adura, the company behind both projects, has said the projects would result in £10.8bn in investment and support 3,500 jobs at the peak of construction, with 880 employees over its production lifetime.View image in fullscreenRomy Madley Croft of the xx performs during this year’s Lollapalooza festival in Chicago, US.Photograph: Josh Brasted/FilmMagicHowever, environmental activists argue that extracting fossil fuels from the UK’s largest remaining untapped oilfield willaccelerate climate chaos. Estimates suggest Rosebank could produce more than 250m tonnes of CO2over its lifetime, equivalent to 70% of the UK’s annual emissions.The artists wrote in their letter: “The climate crisis is no longer something we fear for future generations; it is shaping our lives today. Heatwaves are disrupting schools, workplaces, hospitals, transport networks, festivals and live events.”Eno, who is a co-founder of the campaign group EarthPercent, said Burnham had previously stood with artists and campaigners calling for an end to fossil fuel expansion.“So he has a choice to make,” Eno said. “He can stand with the fossil fuel industry and approve Rosebank, or he can stand with the people who will live with the consequences of that decision.“We are already seeing what a hotter world looks like, with record heat and devastating wildfires across Britain and Europe. At this point, continuing to expand fossil fuel production isn’t pragmatism, it’s a failure to face reality.”View image in fullscreenClimate activists from Greenpeace and Uplift protest against new drilling in the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAThe Met Office has said this summer in the UK ison course to be the hottest since records began, with 2026 likely to be the first year in which the country has recorded four separate days with temperatures of 36C or above.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExtreme heat has driven a surge in attendance at hospital emergency departments over the summer, with more than 2.4 million patients attending each month in May, June and July – the three highest monthly totals ever recorded.Production at Rosebank and Jackdaw was initially approved by the previous Conservative government. However, those decisions were quashed after a legal challenge from the campaign group Greenpeace, pending more detailed climate assessments. These were put out for consultation last month, leavingLabourministers to decide whether drilling should go ahead.Suzi Shingler, of the campaign group Stop Rosebank, said there had been “radio silence” from Burnham on climate change despite heatwaves and wildfires across the UK and Europe.“The devastating wildfires that are tearing across the UK are not because of disposable barbecues. They are caused by climate change and are only set to get worse,” she said.A Department forEnergySecurity and Net Zero spokesperson said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”Explore more on these topicsOilEnvironmental activismFossil fuelsEnergyGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisEnvironment policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hayden Panettiere, actor in Heroes and Nashville, dies aged 36 | Television | The Guardian
description: Panettiere’s death was announced by her father, who called her ‘an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy’
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Panettiere’s death was announced by her father, who called her ‘an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy’
Content: 1:10Hayden Panettiere's most memorable on-screen roles – videoTelevisionHayden Panettiere, actor in Heroes and Nashville, dies aged 36Panettiere’s death was announced by her father, who called her ‘an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy’Hayden Panettiere – a life in picturesHayden Panettiere: an actor so magnetic that entire shows were rewritten for herHayden Panettiere obituarySian CainMon 17 Aug 2026 00.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHayden Panettiere, the actor known for her roles in television shows such asHeroesandNashville, has died at the age of 36.Panettiere’s death was confirmed in a statement from her representative to the Guardian on Sunday night, after it wasfirst reported on US network ABC News. No cause of death was given.Hayden Panettiere – a life in picturesRead more“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen,” her father, Skip Panettiere, said in a statement.He asked for privacy “as our family takes time to process this unimaginable loss”.A police spokesperson toldVarietythat “an acquaintance” of the actor placed an emergency call and that the “preliminary investigation has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances”. A statement from the Greenville County coroner’s office said that responders found a woman in cardiac arrest and an autopsy found no signs of trauma.Born in 1989, Panettiere was a child star who began acting at just 11 months old, appearing in a toy commercial. She made her big screen debut as the voice of Dot in A Bug’s Life, aged nine.In 2000, she appeared in Remember the Titans. In 2004, she landed her first starring role as the daughter of Bill Pullman’s character in Tiger Cruise on the Disney Channel.View image in fullscreenHayden Panettiere at the premiere of Pixar’s A Bug’s Life in Hollywood in 1998.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyPanettiere rose to global fame at the age of 17 as the invulnerable cheerleader Claire Bennet in Heroes, a series with the well-known, mysterious mantra: “Save the cheerleader, save the world.” The show was a hit and ran for four seasons between 2006 and 2010.Panettiere also earned two Golden Globe nominations for her performance as the troubled country music star Juliette Barnes on Nashville. Eleven songs that Panettiere recorded for Nashville appeared on Billboard’s Hot Country Songs charts during the show’s run, including two featuring her co-star Connie Britton.She also appeared as Kirby Reed in 2011’s Scream 4 and 2023’s Scream VI. Her co-stars have paid tribute online. David Arquette commented on a post, writing: “💔 I love you Hayden” while Melissa Barrera shared a story with the words “Rest in peace sweet Hayden”.In 2014 she gave birth to her daughter, Kaya Klitschko, whom she had with her ex-fiance, the Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko. Panettiere gave full custody to Klitschko in 2018 in order to focus on recovering from what she called a “horrible cycle for years of battling depression and anxiety and alcoholism and substance abuse”.View image in fullscreenHayden Panettiere as Claire Bennet in Heroes.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty Images“I didn’t know where the alcoholism was ending and the postpartum was beginning,” Panettiere said in a 2022 interview. “And I ran myself pretty ragged.”She entered rehab in 2015 while filming Nashville, which ended up informing some of the show’s storylines.“This hasn’t been easy and there were a lot of ups and downs,” Panettieretold People magazine in 2022. “But I don’t regret even the ugliest things that have happened to me. I feel incredibly accomplished. And I feel like I have a second chance.”Earlier this year she published a memoir titled This is Me: A Reckoning, which touched on her struggles with fame, postpartum depression, addiction and recovery. In the book Panettiere wrote about the troubling link she made between acting and love: “Directors, fans, and Mom praised me endlessly for my over-the-top dramatic responses. Subconsciously, I began to associate catastrophe with adoration; people loved me because make-believe bad things happened to me.”Hayden Panettiere obituaryRead moreIn May, shegave an emotional interview to podcaster Jay Shettyabout her daughter. “I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she said. “I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment … I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.”Oscar-winner Viola Davis, who starred with Panettiere in drama Custody, shared atributeon Instagram. “What an amazing talent you were … so gifted”, she wrote. Davis added: “I wish the world had more time with you because I had a burning curiosity about who you were becoming. I saw this beautiful Phoenix rising from the ashes. Your tests became your testimony, and your testimony became your legacy. You will be remembered.”Panettiere’s Heroes co-star Masi Oka alsowrotethat she was “way wiser beyond her years” when they worked together. “Absolutely heartbroken to hear about Hayden,” he posted online. “I had the privilege of working closely with her, and I’ll always remember her for her beautiful spirit, immense talent, and the joyful energy she brought to everything she did and the people around her.”Panettiere is survived by her father, Skip Panettiere, and her mother, Lesley Vogel, who is also her former manager. Panettiere’s brother Jansen died suddenly in 2023 at the age of 28 from cardiomegaly – an enlarged heart – coupled with aortic valve complications.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionLos AngelesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swedish Chamber Orchestra/Fröst review – dance, dynamism and a wild rumpus as maverick clarinettist-conductor takes charge | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: The ferociously dynamic Swedish Chamber Orchestra help Fröst drill down to the rhythmic essence of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony as well as works by contemporary composers
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The ferociously dynamic Swedish Chamber Orchestra help Fröst drill down to the rhythmic essence of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony as well as works by contemporary composers
Content: Charismatic … Martin Fröst and the Swedish Chamber Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenCharismatic … Martin Fröst and the Swedish Chamber Orchestra.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewSwedish Chamber Orchestra/Fröst review – dance, dynamism and a wild rumpus as maverick clarinettist-conductor takes chargeRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe ferociously dynamic SCO help Fröst drill down to the rhythmic essence of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony as well as works by contemporary composersAlexandra CoghlanMon 17 Aug 2026 05.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a Sunday morning, and as the Royal Albert Hall darkens and the stage is suddenly back-lit, spotlighting a charismatic figure speaking sibilantly at its centre, you’d almost swear you’d wandered into an American megachurch. But the gospel preached by maverick clarinettist-conductor Martin Fröst is altogether more ancient and more primal: dance. What could be more fundamental, not just to music but life itself, he argues. And with the ferociously dynamic Swedish Chamber Orchestra helping him make his case, it’s hard to disagree.Wagner famously declared Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony “the apotheosis of the dance”, and the SCO’s DNA project (“Dance Now Always”) transforms his description into a concert that drills down to the rhythmic essence of the symphony, seizing those cells and pulses that are its heartbeat and amplifying them into an ear-bending, time-warping sequence that suspends the work at the centre of its own musical genealogy – past and future.So while the symphony stands alone after the interval, we approach it via a continuous first-half drawing together works by Bach and Rameau, contemporary composers Jacob Mühlrad, Shai Wosner and both Fröst and his brother Göran, into a constantly evolving commentary and dialogue.View image in fullscreenPrincipal cellist and dancer Anna Garde  with Martin Fröst and the Swedish Chamber OrchestraPhotograph: Chris ChristodoulouThe fluid arabesques of Fröst’s solo Cradle Song (nobody makes the instrument sing in so many different voices) stretched imperceptibly into Mühlrad’s Helix – a specially commissioned introduction that demands principal cello Anna Garde set aside her instrument and turn dancer, mirroring and melting into Fröst as jazz, klezmer and the concert-hall dissolve into a haunting miniature. Drift for even a second and you’ll have missed the arrival of a Gigue from Rameau’s Dardanus – arrangements by Hans Ek smudging the edges of the baroque works into the new until we lose stylistic landmarks and it’s all just pulse and energy and sensation.But the real test of the programme was the symphony itself. Suspense built irresistibly through the opening before the Vivace released a performance that was pure impulsion. The silvery spareness of the SCO sound sketched a swift, architectural account, the gorgeous woodwind solos the only embellishment. Fröst stripped performing conventions away to reveal the work’s sharp corners and discontinuities – the motoric finale not just a dance but the original wild rumpus.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 16 September. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Michael Sheen’s furious investigation into a pollution scandal | Television | The Guardian

Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The actor’s anger grows as he seeks answers about toxic ‘forever’ chemicals in Wales. Plus: speed dating with the Gypsy Wives. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Toxic truths …  Buried with Michael Sheen.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsView image in fullscreenToxic truths …  Buried with Michael Sheen.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Michael Sheen’s furious investigation into a pollution scandalThe actor’s anger grows as he seeks answers about toxic ‘forever’ chemicals in Wales. Plus: speed dating with the Gypsy Wives. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hannah J Davies,Graeme Virtue,Hannah VerdierandSimon WardellMon 17 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBuried With Michael Sheen9pm, BBC TwoIncreasingly as much an activist as he is an actor, Michael Sheen draws attention to a grim pollution scandal several decades in the making in this enraging two-part TV take on the award-winning podcast he co-hosted. Are parts of Wales contaminated with the toxic “forever chemical” PCB? As Sheen speaks to reporters, visits the towns and villages affected and journeys to Anniston, Alabama, in the US to hear of a connected outrage, his anger grows.Phil HarrisonMy Life Is Murder8pm, U&AlibiFishy puns are guaranteed in the latest episode of this quirky, funny crime drama. This time, Alexa (Lucy Lawless) is searching for the murder of an aquarium owner who has beef with a marine biologist – and has been killed by a sting from a rare jellyfish.PHLong Lost Family: Born Without Trace – What Happened Next9pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenNicky Campbell and Davina McCall in Long Lost Family: Born Without Trace.Photograph: Harry Page/ITVIn a 2024 episode of the moving documentary series, Susanne – who was left in a phone box as a baby – met her older brother. This follow-up sees another life-changing update, this time about her birth mother. Meanwhile, Tom – found at a train station – meets a cousin with a shockingly similar backstory.Hannah J DaviesCelebrity Hunted9pm, Channel 4As the chase-’em-up in aid of Stand Up to Cancer reaches its halfway stage, Ray Howard’s supposedly elite team of manhunters still have five fugitive duos at large across the UK. After a flurry of near misses, the net does seem to be finally closing in – particularly as celebrities love doing live TV. Continues Tuesday.Graeme VirtueSecret Lives of Gypsy Wives10pm, Channel 4The reality TV show you didn’t know you needed is packed with warmth, humour and glamour. This week, Trewley Presh drops her first rap track, but is the world ready? Meanwhile, Mummy offers a poignant insight into married life before the girls all head out to a speed dating event.Hannah VerdierWalter Presents: Everybody Lies12.05am, Channel 4This French crime drama introduces Vince Verner, a cop turned maverick outlier who has been fired for getting too close to bringing down a rich, corrupt and well-connected man. He’s now part of a new unit charged with investigating organisations whose power and influence makes them too big to fail.PHFilm choiceThe Wedding Singer (Frank Coraci, 1998),6.20pm, Sky Cinema GreatsView image in fullscreenGoing for a song … Adam Sandler in The Wedding Singer.Photograph: Kimberly Wright/New Line Cinema/AllstarThe first inkling that there was more to Adam Sandler than puerile physical comedy came with this 1998 romantic comedy set in 1985. A streak of melancholic sweetness runs through his portrayal of the titular musician, Robbie, who loses his way after being dumped at the altar. Will helping the ineffably lovely Julia (Drew Barrymore) plan her own nuptials cure him of his gloom? As weird as it may seem to make a film nostalgic for the previous decade, the wall-to-wall 80s bangers make it a pretty joyful experience.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Agrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient Rome  | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for power
Author: Sam Leith
Headline: This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for power
Content: A Roman statue of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa.Photograph: Andrea Izzotti/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Roman statue of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa.Photograph: Andrea Izzotti/AlamyBook of the dayFictionReviewAgrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient RomeThis fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for powerSam LeithMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week,Robert Harrishas you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assassination of Julius Caesar, with all the bickering and bloodshed that follows, on to the decisive battle of Actium and Octavius’s apotheosis as Caesar Augustus. We meet Cicero, Fulvia, Lepidus, two Caesars and a burly Antony (“Imagine, if you will, a statue of Hercules with a club in one hand, a wineskin in the other”).Here’s the clever bit: he narrates it all from the point of view of Octavius’s right-hand man, Agrippa, a much less well-remembered figure. Harris tells us he “left behind no speeches, few letters and only a couple of sentences of direct quotation”. Yet Agrippa was “effective co-ruler of the Roman world for many years” and “the greatest general of the period”. Octavius couldn’t have risen without him, but he seems to have done his best to write him out of the story afterwards, according him only two passing mentions in the Res Gestae Divi Augusti.Harris’s Octavius is vain, clever, sickly, ambitious, manipulative and prickly. His childhood friend Agrippa, the only person he sort-of trusts, is established early on as a bit of a meathead. Their first encounter is when Agrippa duffs up a couple of bullies he catches picking on a weaker boy; mostly for the pleasure of duffing a couple of people up. He doesn’t know at the time that the beneficiary of this duffing is Caesar’s nephew. They become friends: “He helped me with my classwork. I showed him how to fight.” They share a teacher: “He instilled in Octavius especially a lifelong love of poetry, although my literary tastes, to his despair, have always tended towards works on engineering and military history.” Even as they rise to power, our man’s eye is on the duffing. Octavius returns to Rome amid great danger to give a rousing speech, and Agrippa reports only: “His voice carried well. I did not pay much attention to what he said. I was too preoccupied scanning his audience for potential assassins.”double quotation markIt is a sign of Harris’s discipline as a novelist that he has Agrippa tell his tale in almost comically unambitious proseHarris’s framing conceit is that the text we are reading is Agrippa’s memoir, written in some haste and high feeling. Agrippa, now an old man of 50, has come home early from an expedition to duff up the barbarians in Illyricum. He has a gammy leg, which is about to kill him. He limps in to find his wife in bed with his son-in-law. Since the son-in-law is also the emperor’s adopted son, he hesitates to get busy with his sword and instead retreats to his chamber. He’s feeling a bit sorry for himself and, uncharacteristically, he turns to words.It is a sign of Harris’s discipline as a novelist that he has Agrippa tell his tale in almost comically unambitious prose. There’s a lot of pipe-laying in the military history department, of the “then the legions would wheel around the far side of the Black Sea by way of Hyrcania, the Captain Sea and the Caucasus, and march west” type. And he’s a bastard for an aqueduct, is Agrippa. Loves them; maybe even more than having a scrap. He’s never happier than when building infrastructure and explaining the engineering principles and logistics to the reader.When Agrippa is stirred to reflection, he tends to reach for a well-worn phrase. “The sickly, pungent stink of death lurked round every corner.” “Mercy was now the order of the day.” “War, which I had once so relished, was gouged into the countryside like an open wound.” “Power makes monsters of us all.” “In the words of the old saying – if you strike at the king, you must be sure not to miss.” (That particular old saying, I think, comes from The Wire, but never mind.)But from all this elegantly drab stuff emerges a more subtle portrait of the man and the age than you might expect. You get a persuasive portrait of a Rome exhausted by civil strife, and of the serpentine manoeuvrings of its rulers. Everyone is betraying everyone else, raising armies, marrying each other’s children, forming and breaking alliances. It’s hectic. And, gosh, all these people redrawing the map of the world and changing the course of history areyoung. The plot twist – a feature of scholarly speculation since 1937, Harris’s afterword tells us – concerns the real parentage of the apparently low-born Agrippa.But that, like much else, it suited him to keep quiet about. His most enduring real-world monument is seven terse words in stone above the entrance to the Pantheon: M F AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIUM FECIT. “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, in his third consulship, did it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatments | Books | The Guardian
description: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted him
Author: Oliver Bullough
Headline: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted him
Content: A Sonoran desert toad.Photograph: Tierfotoagentur/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Sonoran desert toad.Photograph: Tierfotoagentur/AlamyBooksReviewThe Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatmentsA journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted himOliver BulloughMon 17 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhich, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you don’t have to choose between them. He’s all five wrapped into one objectionable package, and so much more besides.The tale begins with the Sonoran desert toad, an improbable amphibian that spends most of its life hiding underground in the baking badlands along the Mexico-Arizona border, and has done so blamelessly for millions of years. Whenever it rains, the toads emerge from their hiding places to mate, laying strings of eggs wherever water has pooled.There have long been fanciful tales of hippies getting high by licking toads, but these ones are the real deal: the world’s only known psychoactive animal. In the early 1980s, humans discovered that the toad’s poison glands secrete a venom that contains, among other chemicals, 5-MeO-DMT, a potent hallucinogen also known as the “God molecule”. The first known user squirted the glands of a toad that his dog caught on to the windscreen of his Chevy Sport, where the substance dried and he smoked it.He wrote a manual describing “an overload of thoughts and perception, brief collapse of the ego, and loss of the space-time continuum”. It was, in short, a lot. The prospect enticed other users, and those included, two decades later, Rettig.A troubled young man from Mexico, Rettig started smoking dried toad venom in the first decade of this century, and claims it helped him kick his crack cocaine habit. That was a time when popular interest in psychedelics was re-emerging after the long post-1960s winter, and many medical practitioners were wondering if these mind-altering chemicals couldn’t help patients who weren’t responding to their traditional treatments. Much of the focus had been on LSD, psilocybin and ketamine, but 5-MeO-DMT provided a whole new level of experience. The shatteringly powerful effect of the chemical was said to replicate the effect of years of therapy in just half an hour, which is clearly an attractive prospect for a psychedelic entrepreneur keen to maximise patient throughput.double quotation markHe engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakesRettig was no pioneer in his enthusiasm for smoking toad. Instead, his contribution was to create a tradition for this new hallucinogen, thus giving it the kind of mystical authenticity that peyote, morning glory and ayahuasca gain among devotees thanks to their association with ancient Native American rituals.The Seri people, who live between the Sonoran Desert and the Gulf of California, have suffered terribly both under the Spanish colony of Mexico, and the independent republic. By the time Rettig visited in 2011, there were just a few hundred of them left, living in squalid and trash-strewn villages, predated upon by drug cartels and plagued by addiction. Rettig adopted their chants, claimed their ancient toad-based tradition had been suppressed and was only now being rediscovered, and started presenting himself globally as a practitioner of indigenous medicine.There may well be a medical case for treatment with 5-MeO-DMT, but it’s hard to see any argument for treating people with it the way that Rettig did. He offered huge doses with minimal screening, sometimes inflicting treatment forcibly. (In response to footage of him being aggressive to clients, he told De Greef: “I am open to acknowledge that some of my actions might be disturbing for most audiences, but this is a very deep therapeutic work.”) He engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakes. Rettig claims: “My work has been misunderstood, misinterpreted, and misused.” But it is an incredibly dark tale.A different writer might have been tempted to go gonzo, to smoke toad himself, and to come back with stories of ego death, the space-time continuum and the rest of it, but Kimon de Greef mercifully avoids that temptation. A South African, he came to the story of Rettig not from the world of psychedelics but from researching wildlife smuggling, which gives him an unusually clear-eyed view of how grim these kinds of practices are.A lot of the reporting for this book began life in the New Yorker, and it is as methodical, exacting, well-written and exceptionally reported as you’d expect. Fortunately, De Greef avoids the fate that can befall books based on American magazine articles that fail to break free of them, and really enjoys the extra space. He launches into entertaining digressions into how exactly the toads’ psychedelic powers were first discovered, into how pharmaceutical companies are harnessing 5-MeO-DMT for their own ends, introducing fascinating cameos, before he returns to the main story.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe is not a man for grand conclusions, but I challenge any reader not to see this highly enjoyable book as a parable for so much that’s wrong with the current economy. Everything from the undeserved authority of charlatans, to the rampant exploitation of the natural world, to the hiding of hyper-capitalism behind a shield of cod-mystical woo-woo: it’s all in there.Rettig’s ultimate fate has been to be largely forgotten by the movement he helped to popularise, which has mutated and expanded at the speed of social media, with new influencers appearing and new markets opening. The toads, meanwhile, have become just another commodity to be exploited.The Ego Trip: Psychedelic Toads, a Trail of Deaths, and the Guru Who Peddled Transcendence by Kimon de Greef is published by White Rabbit (£23).
