title: Mark Rydell obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Actor and director whose movies notched up more than 20 Oscar nominations between them
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: Actor and director whose movies notched up more than 20 Oscar nominations between them
Content: Mark Rydell said that he was ‘attracted to material that is substantial enough to deal with life and death issues. I don’t like to waste my time with trivia.’Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenMark Rydell said that he was ‘attracted to material that is substantial enough to deal with life and death issues. I don’t like to waste my time with trivia.’Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyMoviesObituaryMark Rydell obituaryActor and director whose movies notched up more than 20 Oscar nominations between themRyan GilbeyMon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStars flocked to work with the director Mark Rydell, who has died aged 97, and no wonder: he had trained as a performer alongsideJames DeanandSteve McQueen, later becoming west coast artistic co-director of the prestigious Actors Studio, while his movies notched up more than 20 Academy Award nominations between them.Henry FondaandKatharine Hepburnwon best actor and actress Oscars respectively for his reflective, sentimental drama On Golden Pond (1981), which put Fonda, then a frail 75-year-old, on screen withhis daughter Janefor the first and only time. Rydell received a best director nomination for the picture, which ruminated on the themes of family and mortality. “I’m attracted to material that is substantial enough to deal with life and death issues,” he said in 2001. “I don’t like to waste my time with trivia.”View image in fullscreenRydell, centre, with John Cassavetes, left, and Sal Mineo in Crime in the Streets, 1956.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyOthers who benefited from his expert direction includedBette Midler, who got her only best actress Oscar nominations after working with him on the musical dramas The Rose (1979) and For the Boys (1991), and James Franco, who won a Golden Globe for playing the title role in the TV movie James Dean (2001), in which the director himself had a small role as the studio boss Jack Warner.Rydell believed all film-makers should try their hand at acting: “I think directors need to stay in touch with the agony of narcissism.” He was as good as his word, continuing to act even once his directing career was in full swing. He played the gangster Meyer Lansky in his friendSydney Pollack’s drama Havana (1990) and a permanently smiling agent in Woody Allen’s comedy Hollywood Ending (2002). Towering above these was his indelible performance in Robert Altman’s The Long Goodbye (1973) as a charming hoodlum who casually smashes a Coca-Cola bottle in his girlfriend’s face. “I grew up in the Bronx,” he said in 1981. “I know those street thugs.”Born in New York, he was raised in that corner of the city by his parents, Sidney, a stockbroker, and Evelyn, whose passion and talent for the piano rubbed off on him: Mortimer – a name that he traded for Mark early in his career – trained at the Juilliard School of Music under the great jazz pianist Teddy Wilson, then worked on the New York and Chicago club circuits for five years before abandoning that career to avoid the temptations of heroin. “Knowing that I have an addict’s personality … I knew I was in danger,” he said. He served in the army and later won a scholarship for Sanford Meisner’s Neighborhood Playhouse, where he studied alongside McQueen and was instructed in dance byMartha Graham. From there, he joined the Actors Studio and appeared with his classmate Dean in 1953 in a TV version of William Inge’s play Glory in the Flower.View image in fullscreenHenry Fonda and Katharine Hepburn in On Golden Pond, 1981.Photograph: Universal/AllstarIn Don Siegel’s Crime in the Streets (1956), a drama about juvenile delinquency, Rydell acted alongside John Cassavetes and Sal Mineo. In the same year, he made his debut on the soap opera As the World Turns, where he had a recurring role for the next six years. The end of that job overlapped with his beginnings as a director. Pollack had already employed him as his assistant on the TV medical drama Ben Casey, and soon Rydell was calling the shots on episodes of that show, as well as other series such as Gunsmoke and I Spy.He graduated to film with two literary adaptations: The Fox (1967), based on the DH Lawrence novella, and a version of William Faulkner’s The Reivers (1969) starring McQueen. While shooting The Cowboys (1972) he reprimanded his star, John Wayne, in front of the entire cast and crew for calling “Action”. Rather than being sacked as Rydell expected, he was instead congratulated by the actor for having had the guts to stand up to him. “He took to calling me ‘Sir’ for the rest of the picture.” The film was notable for featuring the rare spectacle of Wayne being killed on-screen, his death occurring a full 40 minutes before the end.Rydell made two consecutive pictures withJames Caan– Cinderella Liberty (1973), with Caan as a sailor who falls for a sex worker played by Marsha Mason, and the period romp Harry and Walter Go to New York (1976) – before lobbying hard for Midler to be given the lead role in The Rose, despite her lack of acting experience.View image in fullscreenMel Gibson, left, with Shane Bailey and Sissy Spacek in The River, 1984.Photograph: Universal/AllstarWhen Jane Fonda picked him to direct On Golden Pond, Rydell had the privilege of introducing her father to Hepburn. “Kate just said, in that trilling voice of hers, ‘It’s about time,’” he recalled a year later. “Then she gave Henry a precious present – Spencer Tracy’s favourite hat. He wears it in one of the opening scenes.” Though respectful, Rydell was not too awed by his stars to correct some of their indulgences. “Kate, who is luminous, has too much and you have to control it. She’s all over the place if you don’t watch her very carefully. Henry is a miniaturist … The detail is superb but he has to be watched too to make sure he’s on target with what he’s doing.”Later films included The River (1984), a rural drama which gave Mel Gibson his first US role, and Intersection (1994), starring Richard Gere and Sharon Stone. For television, he directed Stephen Rea and Isabella Rossellini in Crime of the Century (1996), about the 1932 Lindbergh baby kidnapping case. His final movie was Even Money (2006) starring Kim Basinger and Forest Whitaker as gambling addicts. “Directing is a very paternal occupation,” he said. “You have to lead [actors] in a way that they don’t resent or rebel against.”But he confessed in 2001 that the film-making process had been “all uphill” for him since the mid-1970s. “I can tell you without hesitation, not one of my movies could be made in today’s market. This is a time for special effects that substitute for human drama.”He is survived by Amy and Christopher, his children from his first marriage, to the actor Joanne Linville, which ended in divorce in 1973, and by his son Alexander from his second marriage, to the producer Esther Rydell, which ended in 2007, also in divorce.Mark (Mortimer) Rydell, born 23 March 1929; died 13 August 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmOscarsTelevisionActingobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon review – a brave glimpse inside the mind of the Scottish artist | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Finlay Pretsell captures Gordon setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint and throwing shapes with a bullwhip
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Director Finlay Pretsell captures Gordon setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint and throwing shapes with a bullwhip
Content: Blowing bubbles … Douglas Gordon in Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon.Photograph: Courtesy Edinburgh Film FestivalView image in fullscreenBlowing bubbles … Douglas Gordon in Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon.Photograph: Courtesy Edinburgh Film FestivalMoviesReviewDouglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon review – a brave glimpse inside the mind of the Scottish artistDirector Finlay Pretsell captures Gordon setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint and throwing shapes with a bullwhipAndrew PulverMon 17 Aug 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a brave and not entirely orthodox artist documentary; not so much a dates-and-shows-and-talking-heads profile, but resembling something of an act of art in itself. The subject is Douglas Gordon, the Scottish film and video-maker, possibly best known for 24 Hour Psycho, his radically slowed-down presentation of Alfred Hitchcock’s masterwork, andZidane: A 21st Century Portrait, the feature-length film about the legendary French footballer he co-directed with Philippe Pareno – which apart from anything else popularised the single-player camera that is now a fixture of mainstream TV coverage.The film’s intention is essentially to put you inside Gordon’s day-to-day wrestling with the act of creativity, and therefore inside his mind; the vast majority of which is spent inside his Berlin warehouse studio, where Gordon cuts a basically solitary figure. Apart from the camera crew of course; Gordon spends a good deal of the film’s running time berating director Finlay Pretsell, in between setting things alight with a miniature blowtorch, smearing himself with silver paint, throwing shapes with a bullwhip and blowing bubbles from a family-sizebubble tube.Gordon appears to be acutely aware that the way he conducts himself – like a kid, as he openly admits – may appear self-indulgent and even ridiculous; and he’s not wrong; someone with this apparently radioactive level of self-involvement is hardly the most engaging of characters. But, as Gordon labours to explain, his art is all about taking a risk, generating interesting moments, and attempting to preserve them even decades down the line. The struggle to articulate this is what keeps Gordon – leathery, grizzled, inked all over, just about to turn 60 – committed to the film: he even suggests a title, Portrait of a Perilous Character, that would actually work pretty well.Pretsell, you would think, has to have the patience of a saint to put up with this, but allows Gordon the time and space to get his point across. (The film’s actual title, with that “by Douglas Gordon”, suggests that the subject is pretty keen to assert his authorship of the final result.) Be that as it may, Pretsell drops in blip-sized clips of Gordon’s previous work, which is just about all the context we are allowed – other than a short bit of archive footage showing an amazingly fresh-faced Gordon collecting the Turner prize in 1996. The way that time makes fools of us all is a sub-theme here, especially when we see Gordon sobbing over his absent kids while encased in a pair of leopard-print leggings.For all his flamboyance, Gordon remains a somewhat elusive figure; by the end we’re not much closer to identifying what really spurs him on. You get the sense he doesn’t really know either, and perhaps that’s the point.Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon screened at the Edinburgh film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsDouglas GordonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fated to become a cult classic’: why Barcelona is my feelgood movie | Romance films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most pleasurable comfort films is a trip to 1980s Spain courtesy of Whit Stillman
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most pleasurable comfort films is a trip to 1980s Spain courtesy of Whit Stillman
Content: A still from Whit Stillman’s Barcelona.Photograph: RONALD GRANTView image in fullscreenA still from Whit Stillman’s Barcelona.Photograph: RONALD GRANTMy feelgood movieRomance films‘Fated to become a cult classic’: why Barcelona is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers detailing their most pleasurable comfort films is a trip to 1980s Spain courtesy of Whit StillmanRyan ChapmanMon 17 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn hour into Whit Stillman’s 1994 film, Barcelona, the protagonist, Ted Boynton (Taylor Nichols), considers using “maneuver x” in his stalled romantic life. He’s an American working in the Spanish branch of an auto conglomerate, looking for love in the titular city’s post-Franco, sexually liberated nightlife. As Ted explains to his cousin Fred (Chris Eigeman) – visiting as an underqualified scout for a naval diplomatic mission – the sales tactic of “maneuver x” involves removing all pressure and allowing the customer to cross the threshold themselves. No tricks, no cloying, no badgering. Fred thinks the move is just another way of “playing it cool”, and it’s a handy metonym for the film. Barcelona plays it very, very cool.‘I am left grinning’: why The Dish is my feelgood movieRead moreWhich isn’t to say Stillman’s second film, after his Oscar-nominated Metropolitan, is itself cool. Ted likes Glen Miller. He opens conversations with “You know how at parties, everybody talks about marketing?” If you want cool, look to Stillman’s The Last Days of Disco, where Chloë Sevigny frequents an unnamed Studio 54.Barcelona, on the other hand, is my feelgood movie because it’s several movies in one. An Austenesque romantic comedy, with wit dry as an albariño. A slow-boil cold war intrigue, where characters discuss the consequences of American foreign policy. A nostalgic, autobiographical portrait of young Americans abroad. And, however improbably, a defense of business-section self-help books. Where Stillman’s contemporaries riffed on Death of a Salesman, he offers us Willy Loman’s Homage to Catalonia.The scope is both modest and international. It’s the early 80s. Two American cousins pursue love while endlessly debating and taxonomizing it. Stillman, who loves verbose characters like Scorsese loves needle-dropping the Rolling Stones,callshis films “moralistic identity comedies for young people”, and here he throws in US-Spanish relations and the locals’ hyperawareness of anything signifying fascism. The joke is that Fred’s Reagan-era patriotism strikes them as “facha”; in 2026, it’s no longer funny. The incompetent diplomat, always primed for offense, would rise quickly in Trump’s administration. In the penultimate scene Fred orders a Cuba libre, so perhaps there’s hope?As for the plot: characters fall in and out of love; they step on rakes. In a twist out of a Graham Greene novel, someone is violently attacked as a result of a misinformation campaign. The ugly Americans never understand how ugly they are, even if the film does. On a rewatch, note the extras’ silent reactions to Fred’s complaints. Though even he isn’t completely oblivious. After a disastrous picnic with an influential journalist, Fred tells his cousin: “I did not confirm their worst assumptions. I am their worst assumptions.”Barcelona was fated to become a cult classic. It hit theatres during American independent cinema’s annus mirabilis and was pushed down critics’ lists by Pulp Fiction, Hoop Dreams and debuts from Kevin Smith, James Gray and Kelly Reichardt. Other films set in the Catalan capital make Stillman’s look drab by comparison. Take Almodóvar’s technicolor melodrama All About My Mother, from 1999, or Cédric Klapisch’s EU-philic sex comedy L’Auberge espagnole, from 2002. It also doesn’t help that most of the Spanish roles are played by Americans, Australians and Brits – though Mira Sorvino and Tushka Bergen are wonderful.Perhaps feelgood movies, like cult classics, require the gift of time. If Barcelona is several films in one, it’s also several films over time. Pete Townshend once referred to Dylan’s Like a Rolling Stone as “quantum”: its lyrics mean something wholly different to you at each decade of life.When I was in college, Ted’s transcontinental lifestyle felt aspirational. To live abroad, besotted by locals while positing undercooked theories about love! I took its advice to heart, too. Sometimes it really is too early for dancing.By my early 30s, having traveled a fair bit, I better understood Stillman’s caustic take on global politics. I could appreciate, too, his prescience. Wherever Americans discover romance and an asymmetric exchange rate, set the countdown to over-tourism. (I can confirm the gilda pintxo in La Boqueria is better than a dozen cheeseburgers.) And the American adventurism and Spanish anti-Nato isolationism remains sadly topical. Reagan’s “shining city on a hill” became gold flake stapled to the wall of the Oval Office.Now, in my 40s, I empathize with the sentimental attachment to the film’s pre-globalized milieu. A time of all-night dancing, a rejection of the old order and dating without smartphones. The costume design has come back around, too. Ted’s preppy, oversize fits can be seen at Ralph Lauren, Noah and Jonathan Anderson’s Dior.Barcelona still feels good because it’s uniquely of its time and of our time. Stillman created a film that’s knotty, ambiguous – but never ambivalent – and unafraid of confronting politics alongside its characters’ quotidian concerns. Perhaps indie cinema will make more like it. (Although I know Fred would say, “God, your naiveté is astounding!”) The directorput it best: “[Y]ou can look at films with a critical eye, a skeptical eye, or just a sort of sit-back-and-enjoy-it eye.” The beauty of Barcelona is you can do all three at once, and over time. That’s quantum.Barcelona is available on YouTube in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsRomance filmsMy feelgood movieComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Skintown review – Northern Irish scamps rave their Troubles away | Edinburgh film festival | The Guardian
description: Catholics and Protestants find E-fuelled common ground at a hallowed Portrush club in Ciarán McMenamin’s adaptation of his own 2018 novel
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Catholics and Protestants find E-fuelled common ground at a hallowed Portrush club in Ciarán McMenamin’s adaptation of his own 2018 novel
Content: Defiant apoliticism … Skintown.Photograph: Brendan DuffyView image in fullscreenDefiant apoliticism … Skintown.Photograph: Brendan DuffyEdinburgh film festivalReviewSkintown review – Northern Irish scamps rave their Troubles awayCatholics and Protestants find E-fuelled common ground at a hallowed Portrush club in Ciarán McMenamin’s adaptation of his own 2018 novelLaurence PhelanMon 17 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 03.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerry Girls meets Human Traffic in this spirited, larky and at times poignant period piece about raving and drug dealing scamps inNorthern Irelandin the 1990s. It doesn’t go quite so far as to suggest that the social revolution that MDMA engendered in youth culture and spread to the rest of the UK in that decade played acausalrole in the Northern Irish peace process – the way some people suggest ecstasy put a stop to football hooliganism, for example. But it does note the coincidence of the timing.The centrepiece of the film is a club night and beachside afterparty at which Carl Cox DJs and “Catholics and Protestants come together and dance, all juiced up on vitamin E” – on the same day in August 1994 that the IRA announces an end to hostilities. At the afterparty, our heroes from the Catholic side of Enniskillen – “Skintown” to the locals – get loved-up and giggly with a British squaddie, and all their troubles, ietheTroubles, seem to melt away. “I love Brits,” one says with a spliff in his mouth. “I love the IRA. I love the RUC … If you love them, you defuse them, they have no reason to fight you.”The film, and the historical record, both note that there was a comedown after the highs of that night, and that the 1994 ceasefire was provisional. But Skintown is able to maintain a mood of defiant apoliticism, and forcefully states the rights of young people to ignore their forefathers’ enmities and to write fresh pages in the stories of their lives.It is for reasons of wanting a fresh start that our somewhat depressed and traumatised, indie-loving protagonist Vinny (Jack Rowan) has an escape fund in a biscuit tin under his bed. It’s also why he and Jonty (The Young Offenders’ Chris Walley), his ravey best mate and co-worker of an evening at Tony Pepperoni’s Pizzeria, agree to take a bag of 400 pills that were stolen from the Ulster Volunteer Force and daringly, or foolhardily, flog them in a club under the noses of the very same paramilitary thugs.Adapting his own 2018 novel about these escapades, Ciarán McMenamin has ported too many chunks into the voiceover, giving the film a bit of a telling-not-showing problem. But there are also lots of vivid specifics, such as the cheekily sacrilegious way Jonty says “body of Christ” as he places an ecstasy tablet into each of a row of outstretched hands. And in one of those details a writer probably wouldn’t think up if they hadn’t grown up with sectarian violence in the background, there is a topless raver really going for it in a wheelchair. He was paralysed from the waist down by an IRA bullet – but he’s there dancing in the club every week, so the dealers stash their pills in his chair and call it “deals on wheels”.The club in question, Kellys in Portrush, County Antrim, really was a utopian haven for wide-eyed dancers at the time and Cox really did play there in 1994 (albeit probably not on the night of the ceasefire, which was a Wednesday). The soundtrack is spot on, featuring aural madeleines by the Prodigy, Josh Wink, Jaydee and, in one glorious peak moment, some choral Debussy. So while viewers who were there and really lived it in the 90s might cavil about minor lapses in authenticity here and there, it’s more likely viewers are going to savour the rush of youthful hedonism the film has to offer – and willingly succumb to its free-spirited impulses.Skintownscreened at the Edinburgh film festival.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh film festivalDrama filmsComedy filmsClubbingDance musicNorthern IrelandComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Rimbaud review – legendary poet’s unlikely transformation into entrepreneur is as odd as ever | Movies | The Guardian
description: Australian actor Blake Draper delivers a committed one-man performance tracking the writer as he morphs from enfant terrible to merchant
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Australian actor Blake Draper delivers a committed one-man performance tracking the writer as he morphs from enfant terrible to merchant
Content: Could be more illuminating … Blake Draper as Arthur in A Rimbaud.Photograph: Rimbaud Movie LLCView image in fullscreenCould be more illuminating … Blake Draper as Arthur in A Rimbaud.Photograph: Rimbaud Movie LLCMoviesReviewA Rimbaud review – legendary poet’s unlikely transformation into entrepreneur is as odd as everAustralian actor Blake Draper delivers a committed one-man performance tracking the writer as he morphs from enfant terrible to merchantPeter BradshawMon 17 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 04.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS experimentalist Patrick Wang here curates an intriguing if very austere experience, a theatrical-style one-man show about the eventful life of the poetArthur Rimbaud, presented as a microbudget epic of nearly three hours, an episodic piece taking place entirely within a “black box” stage space, ventilated occasionally by back-projection videos of the great outdoors.Australian actor Blake Draper plays Rimbaud, with an English accent tinged occasionally with scouse, speaking to a range of invisible characters including his mother, his sister and his lover and artistic comrade Paul Verlaine, whose voices are represented by musical instruments. But fundamentally this is an extended, bravura monologue.As a young aesthete, Draper’s Rimbaud sports floppy long hair (very different from the spiky short cut from the famous portrait photo) and he declaims his poetic yearnings while lounging and preening and pouting. It is at the stage that he is escaping from the stultifying home town of Charleville forParis, near-penniless and experiencing nights in jail; it is in the city that he meets and has an ecstatically transgressive relationship with Verlaine. But the second act of Rimbaud’s life, for which he cuts his hair and grows a moustache, sees him put poetry and amours behind him, embarking instead on a new and equally demanding career: as an export merchant in Cyprus and Africa.It’s a diverting spectacle, yet for all the vehemence and the commitment of the performance, it’s not easy to gauge precisely what makes Rimbaud change his mind and art as radically as he does from poetry to commercialism. This new career is pursued with a vigorous mature competence and severity of which his previous life had given no hint. And even that first half of his life, the era of literature, is a little opaque here, given that Rimbaud was, after all, a published poet; his relationship with his public is not clearly represented. A distinctive, demanding experience of mysteries unsolved.A Rimbaud is at theICA, London, from 22 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPoetryParisFrancePeriod and historical filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Jolly Fisherman review – last orders for an east London boozer in tense tale | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A real-life pub closure inspires a sensitive and subtle drama about friendship and community by John Dinneen
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: A real-life pub closure inspires a sensitive and subtle drama about friendship and community by John Dinneen
Content: Avoids stereotypes … Jonny Khan and Alex Hill in The Jolly Fisherman.Photograph: ChewBoy ProductionsView image in fullscreenAvoids stereotypes … Jonny Khan and Alex Hill in The Jolly Fisherman.Photograph: ChewBoy ProductionsEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Jolly Fisherman review – last orders for an east London boozer in tense taleUnderbelly, George Square, EdinburghA real-life pub closure inspires a sensitive and subtle drama about friendship and community by John DinneenMark FisherMon 17 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo years ago, it was reported that a pub in Barking calledThe Jolly Fisherman had found a buyerafter five years of dereliction. The prospective owner was a Muslim charity, which planned to turn a former business based on alcohol into a place of abstinence.In one respect, a building that had been the focus of community life in this part of east London for 150 years would continue to be the focus of community life. In another respect, the community had changed.To examine what that change might feel like, playwright John Dinneen imagines two school friends, Alan (Alex Hill) and Amir (Jonny Khan). Alan’s father is a fixture in The Jolly Fisherman – the kind of regular who has his own seat and a nickname for every drinker. Amir’s parents, by contrast, are British-Pakistani immigrants who would never step over the threshold.Come Back Home review – loss and love in Palestinian artist’s intriguing fringe hourRead moreThe playwright avoids stereotypes. Yes, there are Brexity opinions among some of the drinkers, but they nonetheless broadly welcome Amir into their fold (he tells his parents he is at a homework club). For his part, Alan takes enough of an interest in Amir’s religion to join him for prayers. The tension comes when economic pressures expose the racism andIslamophobialurking just below the surface – even for the seemingly open and accepting Alan.In Layla Madanat’s lively production, they bounce across a decade and more, from the boom days of beer-garden parties to the isolation of the pandemic and thefar-right march and counter protestsof July 2024. Hill and Khan have the boyish exuberance of natural friends and we pity their falling out, but the play is subtle enough to understand the social importance of gathering places and the threat to community cohesion when they are lost.AtUnderbelly, George Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreRaceIslamophobiaPubsReligionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high water | Games | The Guardian
description: Frogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edges
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Frogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edges
Content: ‘Distant howls of rabid fish men’ … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresView image in fullscreen‘Distant howls of rabid fish men’ … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresGamesReviewThe Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high waterPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; FrogwaresFrogwares’ Lovecraftian action-horror is full of grim tenacity and pulp paperback charm, despite a few frayed edgesNic RuebenMon 17 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m standing in the prosthetics lab of a campy horror hospital, hunting for a preacher’s flayed face to wear so I can trick the world’s grisliest smart doorbell. Pinned to a board in the corner of the room are a dozen X-rays: shattered bones and metal splints in sepia negative, each with a note attached. It’s a stark, clinical intrusion on the theatrical gore elsewhere. It takes a beat to realise that I’m reading the stories of injuries sustained by soldiers fighting for Frogwares’ native Ukraine. Fingers amputated after severe burns. Limbs lost in mine explosions. Toes torn off by shell fire.Like so many of my favourite PS3-era seven-out-of-tens, The Sinking City 2 is a pulpy action horror. It’s fuelled by scrappy ambition, Lovecraft fan fiction and wonderfully unhinged scenario design. A puzzle that has you determine which talking jarred brain is telling porkies. A scavenger hunt to fix a crane to move a rotting whale carcass. A gunfight amid the grisly results of a siren pop star’s fan meet-up turned battle royale.Frogwares’ latest is also fuelled by the trauma and grit of developers who refused to let an invasion stop them making it. “As of writing, 85,183 air raid sirens registered across our cities,” reads an intro screen. “Work continued, and so did life.” As Weird Tales magazine-cover gumshoe Calvin Rafferty steps out from his apartment, sirens and the public address system blare out over the flooded town of Arkham, heralding the final calls for evacuees.View image in fullscreenTime to evacuate … The Sinking City 2.Illustration: FrogwaresThrough an open window, a couple resign themselves to abandoning their dead daughter’s toys. Rafferty’s decided to stick around, despite the floods and the strange infestation of worms that came with them. His girlfriend’s in a coma, and it’s “cursed pacts with interdimensional gods” serious. Hoping for a cure, he hops in the boat you’ll use to explore the first act’s semi-open city map, and makes for the Miskatonic library.Out is the first Sinking City’s clumsy but earnest exploration of Lovecraft’s provincial racism; in is shooting unknowable cosmic horrors in whatever passes for the face with a tommy gun. To be fair, it’s a great tommy gun. The influence of 2019’sResident Evil 2remake is immediately apparent from the identical UI of an achievements menu. Inventory space is tight, as are the corridors that diverge and fold back into themselves like puzzle boxes. Supplies are scarce but ambushes frequent. The distant howls of rabid fish men and worm-riddled zombies dare you to preserve bullets, while the score and every instinct scream at you to let loose like a startled skunk.Frogwares cut its teeth on Sherlock Holmes games, a lineage evident here in some clever puzzles that offer a reason to veer off the main path. Things get rougher when the studio ventures into new territory. Enemies are so relentless that most combat is unavoidable, undermining the intricate map design by offering no reason to take advantage of shortcuts. Elsewhere, the plot’s central romance flops like a soggy fish finger due to some stiff acting and overwrought dialogue.Generous doses of squishy gallows humour, elaborate secrets and expert tension pick up the slack. As does writing that skirts the grim glorification of overt war allegory to tell a story about refusing to leave what you love in the rubble, so long as the faintest signs of life remain. If you’re going to create, wrote Bukowski, you’ll do it “while the whole city trembles in earthquake, bombardment, flood and fire”. And there’s me thinking he was being dramatic.The Sinking City 2 is out 18 AugustExplore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5PCXbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ithaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent moment | Games | The Guardian
description: The latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with it
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with it
Content: Tantalising … Ithaca.Illustration: the Pixel HuntView image in fullscreenTantalising … Ithaca.Illustration: the Pixel HuntSummer games previewsGamesIthaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent momentThe latest game from ‘reality-inspired’ studio the Pixel Hunt sees you transporting precious human cargo – and deciding what to do with itLewis GordonMon 17 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIthaca has one hell of an opening: Penelope, a disillusioned environmental lawyer, stops her car at a petrol station. But upon returning, she discovers something shocking: the unconscious body of an oil company CEO in her boot, his hands hog-tied together, dangling limply towards the vehicle’s number plate.This tantalising eco-thriller setup is a long way off the typical knights-and-castles fantasy fare of most role-playing games, moreHow To Blow Up a PipelinethanDragon Quest. But road-trip RPG Ithaca arrives via refreshingly original developer the Pixel Hunt, a French outfit that specialises in what it calls “reality-inspired” games. The studio has made a number of arresting works in recent years.One was about a Syrian refugee couplemaking a perilous migrant journey across Europe;another tackledthe life-shattering effects of child sexual abuse. The climate crisis was always in the back of Pixel Hunt founder and Ithaca writer Florent Maurin’s mind. After all, he says, it is the uber problem of our day, the problem that touches all others. It was just a case of when, and, more importantly: “What do we say about it?”Then, one summer afternoon a few years ago, while out for lunch in the French medieval town of Cluny, Maurin was posed a question by his wife: “How, considering all we know scientifically about the climate crisis, do we explain to our daughters that we didn’t spend every weekend marching, protesting and demanding the powers that be to take meaningful action?” Maurin was silenced. “I had no fucking clue,” he says. “I had no answer to that question.”View image in fullscreenRaising prickly, ethical questions … Ithaca.Illustration: The Pixel HuntMaurin’s eventual response was to tackle the subject the way he knew best – by making a video game. In Ithaca, you drive along a procedurally generated road, soaking up vistas of huge windfarms, mountains passes and gorges filled with clean blue water. You talk to family and friends, with the decisions you make affecting the direction you take on the asphalt highway and the branching storyline. Slowly, you uncover what the radical climate group Penelope is now part of, the Earth Protection Association, is really planning to do with the oil exec in her car’s trunk, this nefarious avatar of petro-capitalism. Does he walk free or pay for his Earth-heating sins? Or does something else happen entirely?The prickly, ethical questions that Ithaca raises are influenced by the real world’s growing upheaval. Maurin has been struck by what he sees as a sea change in attitudes towards political violence. He cites the reactions to Luigi Mangione’s alleged killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and the assassination of rightwing activist Charlie Kirk. “You might have expected people to say this is not something that they, or anybody, should do, but actually, a sizable part of the population in the US cheered and was like: ‘This is right. It’s deserved.’”The road Penelope ventures down is something of a metaphor for “where we are all heading”, says Maurin. As the mythic home of Odysseus, Ithaca, Penelope’s ultimate destination, was chosen for its allegorical meaning: Maurin says it offers an opportunity to think through ideas of home in a broader, almost planetary sense. He sees the current moment as one in which “we’re trying to discover where we want to go collectively as a species”.Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanRead moreIt is an urgent question, dovetailing with Ithaca’s high-octane story and what Maurin sees around him on a daily basis in Burgundy, central France. When he arrived, 10 years ago, it was verdant, an almost staggeringly green place. “You felt as if water was everywhere in the landscape,” he says. Now, drought arrives every summer, killing any trees ill-suited to such high temperatures and a lack of water. Hillsides are littered with their grey and yellow arboreal remains. “Every time, I look out of the window and I think, ‘We have to talk about this very fast,’” says Maurin. “Because things are changing way too quickly for nature to be able to adapt.”Ithaca is in development now for PC and consoles for release in 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: An Agatha Christie classic with an impressive cast: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Toni Collette heads a list of familiar voices playing out the village murder-mystery. Plus, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe go off on some rather wild tangents
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Toni Collette heads a list of familiar voices playing out the village murder-mystery. Plus, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe go off on some rather wild tangents
Content: Toni Collette stars as Miss Marple in The Murder at the Vicarage.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenToni Collette stars as Miss Marple in The Murder at the Vicarage.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioAn Agatha Christie classic with an impressive cast: best podcasts of the weekToni Collette heads a list of familiar voices playing out the village murder-mystery. Plus, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe go off on some rather wild tangentsHannah J DaviesMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe Murder at the VicarageToni Collette is an eagle-eyed amateur sleuth in this big adaptation of Agatha Christie’s first Miss Marple novel. When Colonel Protheroe is found dead in sleepy St Mary Mead, suspects include his spouse, Anne, and daughter, Lettice. But as false confessions and red herrings stack up, can Marple crack the case? Kit Harington, Lolly Adefope and Vicki Pepperdine – who wrote the adaptation – are among the cast.Widely available, episodes weeklyGuz and Kiell Will Not SurviveView image in fullscreenKiell Smith-Bynoe teams up with Guz Khan in Guz and Kiell Will Not Survive.Photograph: Fred Hayes/Getty Images for SAGindieIn something of a contrast to Off Menu-style podcasts where celebrities put themselves in nice, imaginary situations, Guz Khan and Kiell Smith-Bynoe (pictured right) find themselves imagining life in tick-laden swamps and icy peril for this new series. It’s silly stuff, but survival expert Megan Hine helps to keep it on the right side of self indulgent.Audible, all episodes out nowGangster: The Story of the MilkmanInfamous cocaine trafficker Brian Brendan Wright was nicknamed the Milkman because “he always delivers”. So says a law enforcement source in this new series. Livvy Haydock investigates a story that brings together Irish gangs with 90s Cool Britannia, as well as sensitively exploring the human cost of the drugs trade.BBC Sounds, all episodes out nowOur TownWidely available, episodes weeklyThis investigation from Bloomberg and iHeart centres on a small Appalachian town in Tennessee which, say the pod-makers, is “at the centre of a fight over American identity”. Certainly, there is something very much of the moment about its tense tale of Christian nationalists – among them two controversial podcasters – who descended on Gainesboro.Widely available, episodes weeklyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUncover: The Mile Zero MurdersOver the past few years, there has been a surge in the number of people who have gone missing or been murdered in Dawson Creek, British Columbia (population: 13,000). title: Away with the ferries: exploring Switzerland’s forgotten lake district by boat | Switzerland holidays | The Guardian
description: The Jura and Three Lakes region is often overlooked by visitors, but on a lake-hopping adventure I discovered its gentle beauty as well as great food and wine
Author: Mike MacEacheran
Headline: The Jura and Three Lakes region is often overlooked by visitors, but on a lake-hopping adventure I discovered its gentle beauty as well as great food and wine
Content: Day breaks over vineyards beside the small town of Ligerz on Lake Biel.Photograph: Roman Burri/Switzerland TourismView image in fullscreenDay breaks over vineyards beside the small town of Ligerz on Lake Biel.Photograph: Roman Burri/Switzerland TourismSwitzerland holidaysAway with the ferries: exploring Switzerland’s forgotten lake district by boatThe Jura and Three Lakes region is often overlooked by visitors, but on a lake-hopping adventure I discovered its gentle beauty as well as great food and wineMike MacEacheranMon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ferry cuts across the waters of Lake Biel, creating soft ripples, as if someone has taken a brushstroke to a blue canvas. To starboard, as we approach St Peter’s Island, are gentle mountains; to port side, lie golden fields. Straight ahead, the isle looks empty and Crusoe-esque.On the jetty, Max Frey, a boatman, historian and guide, is waiting for me. He’s a man of dates and paperwork and pulls a handful from his satchel as he greets me, thrilled at the prospect of leading a tour; Switzerland’sJura and Three Lakes region, this idyllic nook on the French border, is often overlooked by visitors.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Graphics“Welcome to paradise,” he says, raising his voice above the ferry engine thrum. “That’s how Jean-Jacques Rousseau felt about the island when he came in 1765. He was always running away from places, but spent the happiest days of his life here.”Beach-fringed St Peter’s Island is now actually a peninsula (in the mid-19th century the level of the surrounding lake was lowered, creating a land bridge to the mainland) but it is still best reached by boat, and is car-free. With golden light falling on the sand and silver zander ghosting through the clear water, it undoubtedly feels heavenly. Rousseau – the philosopher, writer, composer, rebel who spent six weeks on the island in exile – wasn’t the only one to fall under its spell. “Alexandre Dumas and Goethe stayed, too,” says Max, proudly. “So did Joséphine Bonaparte, the first wife of Napoleon. When she arrived, it is said that more than 1,000 boats sailed on to the lake to see her.”double quotation markIt’s a wholly different side of the Switzerland I’m used to – low on pomp, lower on price, but high on noveltyHome to the country’s gentlest summits, the Jura Mountains, and the glacial-blue lakes Biel, Neuchâtel and Murten – linked by the beautiful Zihl and Broye canals – the region is connected by regular ferries (perhaps it could offer an alternative to Greek or Croatian island hopping, only with better cheese). It’s also wine country, the lakesides fringed by tidy vineyards, and small towns such as Ligerz, La Neuveville, Le Landeron and Erlach contain dozens of understated family cellars.I’m here on a three-day, DIY ferry-hopping trip, travelling from Biel to Murten, hiking, swimming, birding and wine tasting along the way. It’s a wholly different side to the Switzerland I’m used to – low on pomp, lower on price, but high on novelty.View image in fullscreenThe medieval square in Biel.Photograph: Stefan WeberTheferry journeyto St Peter’s takes just 15 minutes from the mainland towns of La Neuveville or Ligerz (or 55 minutes from Biel, where I’d arrived from), and Max and I are as good as alone as we explore. Paths slalom through chestnut trees to empty coves. Butterflies flit by. A farmer cycles past to tend to an Angus herd grazing beside swans and reed-bed warblers on the shore. An information panel gives notice that St Peter’s was once home to Romans, then Benedictine monks who, it is said, with free rein on the island lured in the most beautiful girls from around the lake.We explore the western side on foot, and vineyards take over from forests and sandy coves as we cross to the east. I arrive at my accommodation for the night,Hotel St Petersinsel, housed in a beautiful monastery dating back to 1127, complete with a restaurant courtyard, sarcophagi, Roman-era columns and a museum-piece bedroom where Rousseau slept. As dusk approaches, I dine alone on zander with lemon risotto and summer tomatoes with burrata from nearby Fribourg, paired with local wine.The next morning, I start the day with a swim by the jetty as a heron flaps overhead. The Three Lakes are full of easily accessible swimming spots and beaches, but I’m alone apart from a family of ducks watching me from the sand. Afterwards, I hop on a ferry to Ligerz, a wine village halfway along Lake Biel’s northern banks on the Franco-German linguistic border.double quotation markIn a country of beautiful summits, the view from Chasseral’s gentle crest is still one of the most dazzlingLigerz’s name is said to come from an ancient Roman settler, Ligerius, and it turns out to be a village bursting with grapes and bacchanal bliss. Every house seems to have its own vineyard plot leaning towards the shore, which is ideal if it’s lunchtime and a hike around pretty-as-pie St Michael’s Chapel has helped you work up a thirst.Wine drinking in Switzerland has its challenges. The Swiss keep nearly all they produce and it’s pricey compared with German or Italian wine. But I arrive atAndrey Schafis, a fifth-generation family cellar overlooking the water, where drinkers on the restaurant terrace enjoy chilled lemony chasselas for 15 Swiss francs (£13.50) a bottle, accompanied by charcuterie and cheese. The feeling is less Alpine, more Amalfi.View image in fullscreenThe steamboat Neuchâtel sails between the lakes.Photograph: Mark Bachmann“Almost everything we make is drunk here,” says Arielle Andrey, uncorking a bottle. We chat over a glass before she dashes off into the wood-beamed cellar to bring out more fresh-baked bread, cheese and wine.With a spring in my step, I take the village’sVinifuni– a short, steep funicular through the vineyards – all the way through a cleft in the limestone to the Tessenberg plateau and the petite village of Prêles in the shadow of Chasseral, Jura’s flat-topped mountain. This is a country of preposterously beautiful summits, and although this crest is a gentle one, the view from it is still one of the most dazzling; the fields below look like a gigantic eiderdown of gold and green stitched around three enormous patches of blue.I follow the lonely path to the highest point through a forest of pine, then stand awhile on its observation deck beneath a 120-metre telecommunications tower that has all the exposed platforms, gantries and satellites of a rocket launch pad.From here, I zigzag downhill to the village of Nods, as sleepy as it sounds, and then take a bus back to Prêles and the family-runHôtel de l’Ours Prêles, sitting high above the lake. It isn’t the most celebrated address in the Alps, but it quickly becomes one of my favourites, because of its delightful hosts, Mélanie and Marcello Pigozzo. Marcello cheerfully brings me a cold BLZ beer from nearby Orvin and Mélanie serves an entrecôte steak and profiteroles on the terrace. My meal is soundtracked by bell-rattling cattle in the next-door field.View image in fullscreenThe writer found boats to be an ideal way of exploring Switzerland.Photograph: Mike MacEacheranOn my final morning, I take one last boat ride, a three-hour journey from Lake Biel via the Zihr canal to Lake Neuchâtel, and on via the Broye canal to Lake Murten and its lakeside fortress town. The ferry putters past radiant sunflower fields and fruit crops. While the verges are scattered with campsites, cycle paths and bird reserves, includingLa Grande Cariçaie, the country’s largest marshland, the medieval town of Murten is a time capsule.Church spires soar, swifts nest in the towers and the battlements can be patrolled, offering a Mary Poppins view of old rooftops and stone chimneys. Beyond the ramparts, beneath a vivid blue sky, vineyards gather on the hazy hills and I watch the ferry depart on its sailing back to Biel. The horn blows. A heron takes flight. A dozing fisher stirs on the jetty. A different Switzerland is out there. You simply need to take the slow boat to find it.The trip was provided byJura & Trois Lacs,supportedbySwitzerland Tourism.St Petersinselhas doubles from£128 B&BandHôtel de l’Ours Prêleshas doubles from£175 B&B.ASwiss Travel Passfor three days covering all public transport, including lake ferries, costs£238Explore more on these topicsSwitzerland holidaysEurope holidaysBoating holidaysJura holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Cucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to life
Content: Alexina Anatole’s cucumber and avocado gazpacho.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s cucumber and avocado gazpacho.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.Quick and easyFoodNo oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipesCucumber and avocado gazpacho and addictive carrots: when it’s too hot to cook, contrast, texture and seasoning bring dishes to lifeAlexina AnatoleMon 17 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeat brings caramelisation, char, the slow collapse of ingredients into something rich and deep, but when it’s too hot to cook, flavour has to be built differently – through contrast, texture and a more deliberate hand with seasoning. Salt, in particular, becomes transformative: drawing out moisture, softening structure, shifting raw into something more yielding. That principle underpins this carrot salad, inspired by the Japaneseyamitsuki(‘addictive’) method most commonly used on cabbage, while a chilled cucumber gazpacho offers clean, cooling clarity.Cucumber and avocado gazpacho (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep20 minChill1 hr+Serves4For the gazpacho4 cucumbers(about 1.2kg),peeled and deseeded100ml extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to garnishZest and juice of 1 lime2garlic cloves,peeled and finely grated1 tsp flaky salt1 tsp white miso pasteFlesh of 1 avocadoTo garnishBlack olives,slicedWhite grapes,sliced,Soft herbs(mint, dill, basil, say)Black pepperPut all the gazpacho ingredients except the avocado in a food processor, add 100ml cold water and blend thoroughly. Add the avocado, blend again until well combined, then taste and adjust the seasoning to your liking.Pass the soup through a fine sieve, pressing it down with the back of a spoon. For a silky-smooth soup, blend again with a stick blender for one to two minutes, then cover and refrigerate for at least an hour, until well chilled.Serve the gazpacho in bowls, and garnish with sliced black olives and grapes, herbs, freshly cracked black pepper and a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Addictive carrotsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s addictive carrots.This is an extremely simple but delicious salad that can be bolstered with the likes of chickpeas, avocado and feta, should you want to make it more substantial.Prep15 minRest25 min+Serves4 as a side3 large carrots(about 500g), topped and tailed1 tsp flaky sea salt1 garlic clove, peeled and finely grated½ tsp dashi powder, or to taste (optional)1 tbsp toasted sesame oil, plus extra to garnish1 tbsp sesame seeds, lightly toastedPeel the carrots, then run them through the slicing attachment on a food processor (alternatively, slice very finely on a mandoline). Transfer to a large bowl, scatter over the salt and gently massage for a minute. Leave to soften for 10 minutes.Drain off any liquid from the carrots, taste and adjust the salt as preferred (if they’re too salty, rinse the carrots and pat dry, but this shouldn’t be necessary!).Whisk the garlic and dashi powder into the sesame oil, then pour over the carrots along and scatter over two-thirds of the sesame seeds. Toss thoroughly to combine, then transfer to the fridge for 15 minutes to an hour to give the flavours time to meld (the carrot mix will keep for three to five days in the fridge).Serve cold, garnished with the remaining sesame seeds.Alexina Anatole is the author of theSmall Wins Substackand Sweet: the Secret to the Best Desserts, published by Square Peg (£27). To order a copy for £24.30, go toguardianbookshop.com.Explore more on these topicsFoodQuick and easySummer food and drinkVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkAvocadosSaladSouprecipesShareReuse this content

title: Sabrina Ghayour’s recipes for mango and chilli chicken, sticky spring onions and latke | Food | The Guardian
description: A sweet, tangy and spicy chicken dish that matches well with crisp fried potatoes and apricot-glazed spring onions
Author: Sabrina Ghayour
Headline: A sweet, tangy and spicy chicken dish that matches well with crisp fried potatoes and apricot-glazed spring onions
Content: Sabrina Ghayour’s mango, lime and chilli chicken.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenSabrina Ghayour’s mango, lime and chilli chicken.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodSabrina Ghayour’s recipes for mango and chilli chicken, sticky spring onions and latkeA sweet, tangy and spicy chicken dish that matches well with crisp fried potatoes and apricot-glazed spring onionsSabrina GhayourMon 17 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 04.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIuse this exact cooking method to make every kind of traybaked chicken, and this one is a blend of store-cupboard staples with the addition of fresh lime to push the flavour. Then, I love hash browns, röstis and latkes – give me crispy fried potatoes of any description, and I’m a happy girl – but I won’t lie and tell you that I love frying, because, if I can avoid it, I do: it’s messy, greasy, smelly and uses a fair bit of oil, which is pretty costly. But how to produce a perfectly crispy latke by baking? Well, I’ve managed to do it, and I’m really happy with the results.Mango, lime and chilli chicken (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIf you don’t have mango chutney, use any sweet chutney instead.Prep5 minCook45 minServes3-4600gboneless, skinless chicken thighsFor the marinade3 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed3tbsp sweet mango chutney2tbsp Greek-style yoghurt1 heapedtsp sriracha, or any chilli sauce1tsp ground turmeric1tsp paprika1tsp olive oilFinely grated zest and juice of 1 unwaxed limeFlaky sea saltandblack pepperHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7, and line an oven tray with baking paper. Arrange the chicken thighs in a single layer on the lined tray.Mix all the marinade ingredients in a small bowl, adding a generous amount of salt and pepper, until well combined. Pour this all over the chicken thighs and then, using your hands, toss to coat both sides really well.Bake the chicken thighs for 40 minutes, until they’re burnished, cooked through and juicy, then serve with the latkeand spring onions below.Ludicrously good traybaked latkeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenSabrina Ghayour’s ludicrously good traybaked latkes.Prep10 minCook1 hr 10 minServes3-41–1½kgfloury potatoes(maris piper or russets), peeled or unpeeled, scrubbed and coarsely grated1 very large onion, peeled and grated, or blitzed in a small bullet blender or mini food processorFlaky sea salt andblack pepper1 heapedtsp dried sage1 heapedtsp dried oregano1 heapedtsp garlic granules2tbsp cornflourOlive oil spray or olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6, and line a large oven tray with baking paper.Put the grated potatoes and onion in a large bowl, add a generous amount of salt and, using your hands, mix well. Leave to sit for 10 minutes.Put the potato mixture in a clean cotton tea towel, gather up the corners and spend a good five minutes squeezing out as much liquid as you can – the drier the mix, the crispier the latke. Transfer the mixture to a dry bowl, season, then add the dried herbs, garlic granules and cornflour, and mix really well until evenly combined.Spray or brush the baking paper with a generous amount of olive oil and loosely scatter the potato mixture evenly on top – I like to make one big rectangular latke, but you can form it into any shape you like, or even make individual ones. Pat the latke flat without pressing too hard, tidy the edges, if need be, then spray or brush the top generously all over with more olive oil.Bake for 40–45 minutes until deeply crisp and golden with burnished edges (if making smaller ones, you will need to check them after 35 or so minutes). Remove from the oven, cut into squares and serve.Sticky-glazed spring onions with sesameWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenSabrina Ghayour’s sticky glazed spring onions with sesame.If the Spaniards can obsess about eating calçots (a cross between a leek and a spring onion), then I can happily allow myself to eat spring onions as a vegetable in their own right. If you know my books, you’ll know I’ve shared a few spring onion recipes before, and here is another one of my favourites. They’re great with grilled meat or fish or in wraps with kebabs.Prep5 minCook20 minServes3-42 bunchesfat spring onions(14–16), thoroughly washed and patted dryOlive oil spray, or olive oil1tbsp sesame seeds(I use a mix of black and white)For the glaze2tbsp apricot jamFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemon½tspblack pepper1 pinchflakysea saltHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/ gas 9 and line a large oven tray with baking paper.Mix the glaze ingredients in a small bowl until evenly combined.Put the spring onions on the lined tray, spray or drizzle them with olive oil, rubbing in to ensure each one is well coated, then roast for seven minutes.Remove from the oven and pour the glaze over the spring onions until well coated. Sprinkle over the sesame seeds (do not stir), then roast for another six or so minutes, until the seeds are toasted – check after three minutes to ensure the spring onions are not drying out. Serve immediately.These recipes are edited extracts from Persiana One, by Sabrina Ghayour, published by Mitchell Beazley at £28.
